They were intent on hearing the Dharma and desired to illuminate the accomplishment of the purpose of mantra practice.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having gazed upon that entire circle of the assembly and with a pure intention, having understood the realm of sentient beings—which is of the nature of non-existence, of the nature of space, and which transcends the three periods of time—addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Pay attention, Mañjuśrī!"

Cultivate the bodhisattva samādhi named *Mārabalābhivardhana*—which brings about the conduct for the benefit of sentient beings, rejoices according to their inclinations, fulfills their desired fruits of action through faith, accomplishes the purpose of mantra practice, consists of the words of the Dharma and the words of action, is the state of peace and the state of liberation, removes conceptual construction, attains non-conceptual equality, and possesses the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the universal power, and the supreme power.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta entered the meditative absorption that had just been described by the Blessed One.

As soon as Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had entered it, he caused this trichiliocosm—the great trichiliocosm world-system, which is equal in number to the atoms of hundreds of thousands of many world-systems—to tremble violently; having illuminated it with a great radiance, he displayed his own power of purity and spoke these words of his own mantra.
Homage to all Buddhas,
who have emerged from the nature of non-existence. Homage to the Pratyekabuddhas and the noble Śrāvakas.
Homage to the Bodhisattvas, the lords established on the ten stages, the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas! It is as follows:
Oṃ khakha khāhi khāhi, O subduer of wicked beings! O you who hold a sword, a mace, an axe, and a noose in your hands!
O four-armed one! O four-faced one! O six-legged one!
Go, go, O destroyer of great obstacles! O you of deformed countenance! O you who cause fear to all beings!
O you who roar with a loud laugh, clad in a tiger skin! O Śrīmūlakalpa-sana! Perform, perform all rites!
Sever, sever all mantras!
Shatter, shatter the supreme mudrā!
Attract, attract all mudrās!
Grind, grind all the wicked!
"Enter, enter into the center of the mandala!
O Destroyer of Vaivasvata! Accomplish, accomplish my purpose!"
Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Do not delay, do not delay! Recollect the pledge! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ!
Shatter, shatter, O fulfiller of all hopes!
Ho ho, Blessed One!
Why do you delay? Accomplish all my purposes, svāhā!
This great wrathful king of the Blessed Mañjuśrī, named Yamāntaka, slays even King Yama; he brings [him] under control— how much more so other sentient beings?

As soon as the Great Wrathful King had been spoken, all sentient beings approached the presence of the Blessed One— afflicted, terrified, trembling, agitated in mind, and broken-hearted; they had no other refuge,
no other protection.
There is no other refuge,
except for the Buddha, the Blessed One, and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

Now, whatever beings there may be—whether moving on earth, moving in water, or moving through the air; whether stationary or mobile; born from a womb, born from an egg, born from moisture, or born spontaneously—even they, dwelling in infinite and boundless world-systems above, below, across, in the cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions, were at that very moment and in that very instant driven away by the Great Wrathful King himself and led forth.
Furthermore, this Wrathful King must not be recited in front of one who has not yet abandoned passion (*avītarāga*), for such a person would either die or wither away.
Having taken up the vow (*samaya*), it should be recited before an image of the Buddha, or before Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta;
it must not be recited for the sake of other rites, nor here or there at random.
The reason is that such a practice would result in a great calamity and lead to one's own ruin.

For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, are supremely compassionate; they act solely for the sake of establishing the knowledge of omniscience, for the purpose of leading the entire realm of sentient beings to nirvāṇa, and for the instruction of those who have not yet been instructed. They possess the three measures, the three fetters, and the illumination of the mantra practice that ensures the three lineages are never interrupted. With a mind that is the natural outflow of the power of great compassion, they overcome the forces of Māra, destroy great obstacles, ward off wicked kings, subdue their own strength, and suppress, stun, strike down, terrify, instruct, wither, and satisfy the strength of others. By revealing their own mantra practices and increasing longevity, health, and sovereignty, they accomplish their tasks swiftly. Possessed of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great equanimity, and great joy, they spoke with a mind free from all discursive thought and reasoning, having that as its cause and motive.
The First Chapter.

17. Then there were those *nāgas* and great *nāgas*, *yakṣas* and great *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas* and great *rākṣasas*, *piśācas* and great *piśācas*, *pūtanās* and great *pūtanās*, *kaṭapūtanās* and great *kaṭapūtanās*, *mārutas* and great *mārutas*, *kūṣmāṇḍas* and great *kūṣmāṇḍas*, *vyāḍas* and great *vyāḍas*, *vetāḍas* and great *vetāḍas*, *kambojas* and great *kambojas*, sisters (*bhaginīs*) and great sisters, *ḍākinīs* and great *ḍākinīs*, *cūpakas* and great *cūpakas*, *utsārakas* and great *utsārakas*, *ḍimphikas* and great *ḍimphikas*, *kimpakas* and great *kimpakas*, diseases (*rogas*) and great diseases, epilepsy (*apasmāras*) and great epilepsy, planetary spirits (*grahas*) and great planetary spirits, sky-mothers (*ākāśamātṛs*) and great sky-mothers, *rūpiṇīs* and great *rūpiṇīs*, *krandanās* and great *krandanās*, shadows (*chāyās*) and great shadows, *preṣakas* and great *preṣakas*, servants (*kiṅkaras*) and great servants, *yakṣiṇīs* and great *yakṣiṇīs*, *piśācīs* and great *piśācīs*, fevers (*jvaras*) and great fevers, quartan fevers (*cāturthakas*) and great quartan fevers, constant fevers, irregular fevers, continuous fevers, momentary fevers, those caused by wind (*vātika*), bile (*paittika*), phlegm (*śleṣmika*), and the combination of all three (*sānnipātika*). There were spells (*vidyās*) and great spells, perfected ones (*siddhas*) and great perfected ones, practitioners of yoga (*yogins*) and great practitioners of yoga, seers (*ṛṣis*) and great seers, servants (*kiṅkaras*) and great servants, great serpents (*mahoragas*) and great great serpents, *gandharvas* and great *gandharvas*, gods (*devas*) and great gods, humans (*manuṣyas*) and great humans, provinces (*janapadas*) and great provinces, oceans (*sāgaras*) and great oceans, rivers (*nadyas*) and great rivers, mountains (*parvatas*) and great mountains, treasures (*nidhis*) and great treasures, the earth (*pṛthivī*) and the great earth, trees (*vṛkṣas*) and great trees, female birds (*pakṣiṇīs*) and great female birds, kings (*rājñas*) and great kings, Śakras and great Indras, Vāsavas, sacrifices (*kratayas*), beings (*bhūtas*), Īśāna, Yama, Brahmā and Great Brahmā, Vaivasvata, Dhanada, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūpākṣa, Kubera, Pūrṇabhadra, Pañcika, Jambhala, Sambhala, Kūṣmala, Hārīti, Harikeśa, Hari-hārīti, Piṅgalā, Priyaṅkara, Arthaṅkara, Jālendra, Lokendra, Upendra, Guhyaka and Mahāguhyaka, Cala, Capala, Jalacara, Sātata, Giri, Hemagiri, Mahāgiri, Kūṭākṣa, and Triyaśiras.

Together with these and other great yakṣa generals, surrounded by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of yakṣas, they assembled right there in that great circle of the assembly in the Śuddhāvāsa palace; through the empowerment of the Bodhisattva and the application of supernatural power, they gathered and sat down to listen to the Dharma.
Also those great rākṣasa kings, accompanied by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rākṣasas, were brought there by the Great Wrathful King.

They were as follows: Rāvaṇa, Praviṇa, Nidrāṣaṇa, Śaṅkukarṇa, Kumbha, Kumbhakarṇa, Samantakarṇa, Yama, Vibhīṣaṇa, Ghora, Sughora, Yakṣa, Yamaghaṇṭa, Indrajit, Lokajit, Yodhana, Suyodhana, Śūla, Triśūla, Triśiras, and Anantaśiras—these and others, including Dharmapāpa, Pāpama, and Piśācas, assembled together with retinues of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions.
They were as follows: Pīlu, Upapīlu, Supīlu, Anantapīlu, Manoratha, Amanoratha, Sutāya, Grasana, Sudhāma, Ghora, and Ghorarūpī; these were assembled there for the purpose of hearing the Dharma.

Those great nāga kings as well, who were brought by the King of Wrath together with a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nāgas, through the empowerment of the supernatural power of the Bodhisattva—
namely:

Thānanda, Upananda, Kambala, Upakambala, Vāsuki, Ananta, Takṣaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, Saṅkhapāla, Saṅgha, Saṅkhapāla, Karkoṭaka, Kulika, Akulika, Māṇa, Kalaśoda, Kuliśika, Cāṃpeya, Maṇināga, Mānabhañja, Dukura, Upadukura, Lakuṭa, Mahālakuṭa, Śveta, Śvetabhadra, Nīla, Nīlāmbuda, Kṣīroda, Apalāla, Sāgara, and Upasāgara.

Together with these and other great Naga kings, surrounded by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of great Nagas, they assembled and sat down in that great circle of the assembly to hear the Dharma; as did those seers and great seers.

Namely: Ātreya, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Bhagīratha, Jahnu, Aṅgiras, Agasti, Pulasti, Vyāsa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa-Gautama, Agni, Aṅgirasa, Jāmadagnya, Āstīka, the Sage Munivara-Aśvara, Vaiśampāyana, Parāśara, Paraśu, Yogeśvara, Pippala, Pippalāda, Vālmīki, and Mārkaṇḍeya—these and other great ṛṣis, accompanied by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of great ṛṣis, approached that assembly circle.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni, they sat down together with the Bodhisattva-piṭaka for the purpose of understanding and rejoicing in the practice of mantras.
Those who were the kings of the mahoragas also entered that circle of the assembly and sat down;
namely: Bheruṇḍa, Bhūruṇḍa, Maruṇḍa, Mārīca, Dīpa, and Pradīpa.
Those who were the kings of the *garuḍas* also assembled in that circle of the assembly, with retinues of many hundreds of thousands,
such as: Suparṇa, Śvetaparṇa, Pannaga, Parṇaga, Suprathama, Jātapakṣa, Ajātapakṣa, Manojava, Pannaganāśana, Vainateya, Vainateya, Bharadvāja, Śakuna, Mahāśakuna, and the kings of birds (*pakṣirāja*).
They too would assemble in that circle of the assembly;
and those who were kings of the *kinnaras*, accompanied by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of *kinnaras*, they too would assemble in that circle of the assembly, namely:
Druma, Upadruma, Sudruma, Anantadruma, Lokadruma, Leḍuma, Ghanoraska, Mahoraska, Mahojaska, Mahoja, Maharddhika, Viruta, Susvara, Manojña, Cittonmādakara, Unnata, Upekṣaka, Karuṇa, and Aruṇa.
These and other great kinnara kings, accompanied by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of kinnaras, assembled there to hear the Dharma.

Likewise, Brahmā Sahāmpati, Mahābrahmā, Ābhāsvara, Prabhāsvara, Śuddhābha, Puṇyābha, Aṭṭaha, Atapā, Akaniṣṭha, Sukaniṣṭha, Lokaniṣṭha, Ākiñcanya, Naivakiñcanya, Ākāśānantya, Naivākāśānantya, Sudṛśā, Sudarśanā, Sunirmitā, Paranirmitā, the Śuddhāvāsas, Tuṣita, Yāma, Trāyastriṃśa, Cāturmahārājika, Sadāmatta, Mālādhāra, Karoṭapāṇi, Vīṇātṛtīyaka, Parvativāsins, Kūṭavāsins, Śikharavāsins, Alakavāsins, Puravāsins, Vimānavāsins, those who move through the atmosphere, those who dwell on the earth, those who dwell in trees, and those who dwell in houses.

Likewise, the lords of the Dānavas— Prahlāda, Bali, Rāhu, Vemacitti, Sucitti, Kṣemacitti, Devacitti, Rāhubāhu, and others, headed by these— accompanied by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of millions of Dānavas, possessing threefold diverse movements and various purposes, those Asuras who fight with the gods— they too gathered around that circle to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the miraculous transformation of the Bodhisattva through the empowerment of the Buddha.
Also those planets and great planets, which act for the welfare of the world and move through the intermediate space;

Namely: Āditya, Soma, Aṅgāraka, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, Kumpu, Ketu, Aśani, Nirghāta, Tāra, Dhvaja, Ghora, Dhūmra, Dhūma, Vaja, Ṛkṣa, Vṛṣṭi, Upadṛṣṭi, Naṣṭārka, Nirnaṣṭa, Haśānta, Māṣṭi, Ṛṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Lokānta, Kṣaya, Vinipāta, Āpāta, Tarka, Mastaka, Yugānta, Śmaśāna, Piśita, Raudra, Śveta, Abhija, Abhijata, Maitra, Śaṅku, Triśaṅku, Lūtha, Raudraka, Ṛtunāśana, Balavān, Ghora, Aruṇa, Vihasita, Māṣṭi, Skanda, Sanat, Upasanat, Kumārakrīḍana, Hasana, Prahasana, Nartapaka, Nartaka, Khaja, and Virūpaścevi.

Thus these great grahas, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands [of followers], through the empowerment of the Buddha, assembled and sat down in that palace of the Pure Abodes within the assembly circle described in the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*.

The constellation *Ṛiṇa*, accompanied by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of stars: Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Āśleṣā, Maghā, both Phalgunīs, Hastā, Citrā, Svāti, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, both Āṣāḍhas, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, both Bhadrapadas, Revatī, Devatī, Prabhijā, Punarṇavā, Jyotis, Aṅgirasā, Nakṣatrikā, both Phalgu and Phalguvatī, Lokapravarā, Pravarāṇikā, Śreyasī, Lokamātā, Īrā, Ūhā, Vahā, Arthavatī, and Asārthā.

Thus these lords of the constellations, surrounded by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of constellations, gathered and sat down in that assembly of the great circle of the congregation in that Śuddhāvāsa palace through the empowerment of the Buddha.

There are thirty-six zodiac signs (*rāśis*), namely: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces; monkey, sub-pitcher, tortoise, rhinoceros, elephant, buffalo, deity, human, bird, gandharva, world-being-conqueror, fierce-splendor, moonlight, shadow, earth, darkness, passion, secondary-passion, suffering, happiness, liberation, awakening, solitary-buddha, disciple, water-dweller, knowledge-holder, great-splendor, great-power, animal, hungry ghost, asura, flesh-eater, *piśāca*, *yakṣa*, *rākṣasa*; all-ground-born, elemental, downward-moving, upward-moving, sideways-moving, blossomed, meditative, established-in-yoga, superior, middling, and inferior.

Thus these great hosts, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of various hosts, approached the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa deities and the great assembly circle of the Great Lotus; having arrived, they prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down in their respective places.
Those great yakṣiṇīs also, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of yakṣiṇīs, [did likewise].

They were as follows: Sulocanā, Subhrū, Sukeśā, Susvarā, Sumatī, Vasumatī, Citrākṣī, Pūrāṃśā, Guhyakā, Suguh yakā, Mekhalā, Sumekhalā, Padmoccā, Abhayā, Jayā, Vijayā, Revatikā, Keśinī, Keśāntā, Anilā, Manoharā, Manovatī, Kusumāvatī, Kusumapuravāsinī, Piṅgalā, Hārītī, Vīramatī, Vīrā, Suvīrā, Sughorā, Ghoravatī, Surasandarī, Surasā, Guhyottamārī, Vaṭavāsinī, Aśokā, Andhārasundarī, Ālokasundarī, Prabhāvatī, Atiśayavatī, Rūpavatī, and Surūpā. This concludes the first chapter.
Asitā, Saumyā, Kāṇā, Menā, Nandinī, Upanandinī, and Lokāntarā— these great yakṣiṇīs,

accompanied by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of yakṣiṇīs, stood at a distance from that great assembly circle, paying homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni. Those great piśācīs also, surrounded by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of piśācīs, gathered there, paying homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni.

They were as follows: Maṇḍitikā, Pāṃsupiśācī, Ulkāpiśācī, Jvālāpiśācī, Bhasmodbhirā, Piśitāśinī, Durdharā, Bhrāmarī, Mohanī, Tarjanī, Rohiṇikā, Govāhiṇikā, Lokāntikā, Bhasmāntikā, Pīluvatī, Bahulavatī, Bahulā, Durdāntā, Dhaṇā, Cihnitikā, Dhūmāntikā, Dhūmā, and Sudhūmā.
These great piśācīs, surrounded by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of piśācīs, also entered that circle of the great assembly gathering.
And those Mothers and Great Mothers who roam the world, who afflict sentient beings and receive offerings of oblations and garlands—namely:

Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Vaiṣṇavī, Kaumārī, Cāmuṇḍā, Vārāhī, Aindrī, Yāmyā, Āgneyā, Vaivasvatī, Lokāntakarī, Vāruṇī, Aiśānī, Vāyavyā, Paraprāṇaharā, Sukhamaṇḍitikā, Śakunī, Mahāśakunī, Pūtanā, Kaṭapūtanā, and Skanda.
Thus these Great Mothers, with retinues of many hundreds of thousands of mothers, also remained in that great circle of the assembly, uttering the words, "Homage to the Buddha! Likewise,
from many hundreds of thousands of humans and human beings—
down as far as the Avīci Great Hell and up as far as the summit of existence— the entire expanse of the sky became filled.
Within that assembly of beings, there was no hostility toward any living creature;
and through the Buddha’s empowerment and the adornment of the Bodhisattva Saṅgha, every single being beheld the Blessed One, the Buddha Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, standing before them at their very heads.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed the entire world-system with his Buddha-eye, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Speak, speak, O Pure Being! [Speak] the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, which is the detailed exposition of the chapter on the meditative absorption for the definitive determination of the meaning of mantra practice; do so now, as you deem it the right time."

In the *Somūlakalpa*, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having been authorized by the Blessed One Śākyamuni, entered the samādhi called "The Array and Ornament of the Nature of Space" and "The Array and Ornament of the Hardened Continuum of the Vajra-Smash. Immediately upon his entering it, he empowered that abode of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsabhavana*), which extended for many hundreds of thousands of yojanas, to become composed of vajra.

There, many yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, maruts, and piśācas—in short, the entire realm of sentient beings—by means of the bodhisattva’s empowerment, became established and seated within that palace which resembled a diamond-jewel, remaining without harming one another.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having perceived that great assembly, addressed Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath:
"O, O Great King of Wrath!"

The destroyer of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, thus [protect, protect] this great assembly-circle of the gathering of the multitude and of all sentient beings; bring them under control, subdue the wicked, awaken the gentle,
and cause those who are not serene to become serene.
Until I have spoken this Bodhisattva-piṭaka concerning the practice of my own mantra-conduct, the Vaipulya, and the ritual procedures for the maṇḍala of mantra-practice, go outside and protect it.

Thus addressed, the Great Wrathful King, assuming a most terrifying form, awaited the command and went forth for the protection and instruction of all sentient beings. Surrounded by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of wrathful deities, the wrathful king Yamāntaka stood encircling the entire assembly circle on all sides—in the four directions, above, below, and across—uttering a formidable roar.
Then they all became gentle and well-disposed; they did not transgress his command and listened to this word:
"Whoever should overstep this agreement..."
"His head is clearly visible like the flower-cluster of an *ajaka* plant"— this was due to the empowerment of the Bodhisattva.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta spoke these verses on the meaning of the Dharma concerning the practice of his own mantra:
"The mantras of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is endowed with a single quality shall attain accomplishment.
What is that one quality? It is the contemplation of all phenomena as being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*)."
For a bodhisattva established in two qualities, mantras may attain accomplishment.
Which two? Not abandoning the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Through these three qualities, one attains the fulfillment of the purpose of the instructions on the practice of one's own mantra.

By these two, or by three, or by four dharmas— namely, not abandoning any sentient being through the protection of the bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline, and not abandoning one's own mantra— the mantras of a bodhisattva who has generated the thought of awakening and is endowed with these qualities shall attain accomplishment. This is the first chapter.

And by which four? By these four qualities—non-abandonment of one’s own mantra, non-interruption of the mantras of others, the application of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, and a mind cultivated with great compassion—the mantras of a bodhisattva who has first generated the thought of awakening shall attain accomplishment.
Furthermore, those qualities that lead to the convergence of the bodhisattva’s scriptural collection and the emergence of mantra practice shall proceed to the fulfillment of awakening.
Which five? Dwelling in secluded places, not harboring malice toward other beings, not looking toward worldly mantras, and establishing oneself in ethical discipline, learning, and proper conduct—
these five qualities lead to the fulfillment of the purpose of mantra practice.
Six qualities lead to the fulfillment of the purpose of mantra practice.

What are these six? They are: the non-interruption of faith in the Three Jewels; the non-interruption of faith in the Bodhisattvas; the non-censure of mundane and supramundane mantras; the honoring of the non-conceptual realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu); the non-rejection of the Mahāyāna sūtras containing profound meanings; a mind free from weariness; and the pursuit of mantra practice without falling away from the side of virtue.
These six factors lead to the convergence of the practice of knowledge (*vidyā*) and the accomplishment of mantras (*mantrasiddhi*).
There are seven factors that lead to the entry into the mantra practice conducive to the time of accomplishing knowledge.
What are the seven?

The profound method consists of the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom through reciting, teaching, studying, writing, and the liberation of the bodhisattva conduct; the non-delayed [practice] of time, place, discipline, mantra-recitation, fire-offerings, silence, and austerity, resulting in movement, intelligence, mindfulness, wisdom, and fortitude; the entry into the bodhisattva accumulations and the Mahāyāna dharma-method; skill in the activities of one’s own mantras, such as summoning, protection, and accomplishment; the cultivation of the perfections of great compassion, great loving-kindness, great equanimity, and great sympathetic joy; the convergence upon the realm of sentient beings, the realm of phenomena, and suchness which are free from conceptual proliferation; the thorough seeking of the omniscient gnosis in its two aspects; the non-abandonment of all sentient beings; and the lack of longing for the Hīnayāna.
These seven factors lead to the complete fulfillment of the accomplishment of knowledge, ignorance, and mantras.

What are they? They are: faith in the unseen, faith in the seen, faith in the fruit of what is unseen, curiosity, the desire to know, and the absence of doubt; these eight factors lead to the convergence upon the accomplishment of the purpose of the practice of knowledge and mantras.

Through the miraculous manifestation of the purity resulting from devotion to the Bodhisattva; through the unerring reception of mantras and reverence for the Guru; through the non-deceptive reception of the instructions of the Ācārya regarding the mantras and tantras of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and the renunciation of all one's possessions; through the skillful revelation of dreams concerning auspicious and inauspicious places of accomplishment (*siddhakṣetra*); through being free from the stain of envy, abandoning all sloth and torpor, and the application of vigor by offering oneself to the seven Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; in brief, being firmly armored with great equanimity toward previously planted roots of merit and desiring to strike down all obstacles; and through a selfhood characterized by the aspiration for great wealth at the treading upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and the status of a person of great renown; and through not being separated from the company of persons of great renown and from the presence of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, who is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
These eight factors lead to the attainment of the goal and the fulfillment of the practice of mantra.

In brief, O friends, for one who is never separated from the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), who is not forsaken by the Three Jewels, and who—though even of extremely poor conduct—is tireless in mind and constantly devoted, the array of my mantra chapters, which arises from a mind overflowing with the infinite and marvelous conduct of the bodhisattvas, shall be accomplished;
it must not be understood otherwise.
Having become free from conceptual construction in mind, one should practice this even for the sake of inquiry.

Then that entire assembly—sustained by the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the noble Śrāvakas—uttered these words: "Excellent, excellent, O Son of the Victor! It is well-taught this exposition of the Dharma which follows the entry into the methods of the Dharma and the purposeful activity of the various mantra practices. Oh, Mañjuśrī, the Youthful!"

O Great King, whoever shall recite, uphold, or keep in mind this chapter on the Assembly— which conforms to the teaching of the diverse Dharmas and is conducive to the practice of mantras, being well-spoken— we shall bring his adversaries and enemies under his control and cause the destruction of the enemy forces. Furthermore, if one places it at the forefront of battle upon an elephant, or honors it with various flowers, incense, perfumes, and ointments, we shall likewise act as described.

"Or, having had it written in a book, if one shall place it in one's own home—whether it be a son of good family or a daughter of good family, a great king or a great queen, a monk or a nun, a layman or a laywoman—I shall provide for them great protection, great wealth, long life, health and well-being, and the constant increase of their prosperity."
Thus addressed, that entire assembly became silent.

The first chapter, on the assembly, from the *Mūlakalpa*, which is an extensive section on the miraculous manifestations of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, extracted from the great ritual manual (*mahākalpa*) that teaches the practice of mantras of the Mahāyāna.
Then follows the second chapter.
Now, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having surveyed the entire circle of the assembly, entered the samādhi called "The Surveying that Enters the Essence of All Beings.
As soon as Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had entered this samādhi, a ray of light issued forth from the region of his navel.

Surrounded by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays, it illuminated the entire realm of sentient beings on all sides, and having again illuminated that abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, it remained there.
Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Speak, speak, O Son of the Jina!
[The samaya] of all sentient beings..."
"Entry" means that having entered, they attain your collection of mantras and the accomplishment of all worldly and supramundane mantras.

When the Lord of the Guhyakas, the King of Yakṣas, had spoken thus, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta spoke the *Paramaguhyamaṇḍalatantra* called "The Incitement of All Vidyās," which makes known the miraculous transformations of the [mantra] host.
Raising his right hand, he beckoned toward the circle of the assembly with the tip of a finger;
from that fingertip, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of vidyārājas issued forth,
and having issued forth, they illuminated the entire Śuddhāvāsa heaven with a great radiance and remained there.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta [expounded] the heart-mantra of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, which accomplishes all rites, is the sole hero, and bestows the powers of summoning and dismissal, pacification and enrichment, malevolent sorcery, invisibility, traveling through the sky, entering the subterranean realm (pātāla), walking upon trees, attracting, causing enmity, and subjugation; as well as the swift attainment of perfumes, garlands, unguents, lamps, and the application of one’s own mantras within the tantras—in short, however it is practiced, when being accomplished, it is the syllable known as the Great Hero, the accomplisher of all aims, the Great King of Wrath.
And what is that?
Oṃ Āḥ.
HŪṂ.
This is the heart-mantra of the Great Wrathful One, which attracts all; it has been taught by the Great Being Mañjughoṣa for all mandalas and for all mantra-practices, and it destroys all obstacles.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta raised his right hand and placed it upon the head of the Wrathful One, and spoke thus: "Homage to you, who are attended by all the Buddhas! O Blessed Buddhas, look upon me with compassion! (as described in the *Gumūlakalpa*).
"Whosoever Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power, infinite and boundless, are established throughout the world-systems of the ten directions, may they empower this moment!
Having spoken thus, he whirled that King of Wrath and hurled him.

As soon as the Great King of Wrath was hurled, within a single moment, he subdued and brought under control all those beings of evil intent and great supernatural power throughout the entire world-system.
He caused that great assembly circle to enter the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods;
having established them in their proper positions, he became surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides and stood upon the heads of the wicked beings.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, looking again at that assembly circle, said: "Listen, all you beings! Should anyone transgress this my samaya, this King of Wrath shall bring about his subjugation."

Because the paths of the words, meanings, and secret mantras of the timing of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as well as those of the Bodhisattvas of great power, are not to be transgressed, I shall explain them by way of a concise summary;
listen to that, and attend to it well and thoroughly, for I shall speak.
Homage to all the Buddhas!

Oṃ ra ra smara apratihataśāsanakumārarūpadhāriṇa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! This, O practitioner of the samaya, is my root mantra. The mudrā known as the five-crested great mudrā (pañcaśikhā mahāmudrā) belongs to the noble Mañjuśrī; one should employ it with this root mantra, for it performs all activities. This is the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
The Buddha is the bringer of all prosperity and auspiciousness;
"Oṃ Dhānyada Namaḥ.
The mudrā used here is renowned as the Triśikhā, which increases all enjoyments.
And here there is a subsidiary heart-mantra: *hūṃ*. And here the mudrā is known as the "Three-Peaked" (*triśikhā*), which attracts all sentient beings.
And here is the supreme heart-mantra;
and here is the mudrā known as Mayūrāsana, which brings all sentient beings under control.

This is the heart-mantra of all Buddhas, known as the "Great Hero," consisting of eight syllables. It is the supreme excellence, a great purifier, the severer of the path of the three realms of existence, the warder-off of all miserable destinies, the pacifier of all calamities, the performer of all rites, the secure means for attaining Nirvana, and stands before one like a Buddha manifest in person.

This Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī himself has appeared in the form of this mantra as the supreme heart-essence for the benefit of all sentient beings; it fulfills all hopes, and by its mere recollection, it completely purifies even the five sins of immediate retribution.
What more need be said? Which one would arise?
Oṃ Āḥ Dhīra Hūṃ Khacara!
O worthy ones, this is that very [mantra], the eight-syllabled, the great waterless [ocean], the most secret heart, established as a condition like Buddhahood itself;
it is the second chapter,
which in brief brings about the attainment of the Great Secret.
And here the mudrā is that known as Mahāvīrā, which fulfills all hopes. And here the summoning mantra is:
Oṃ he he, you whose own form has the appearance of a youth, who awakens all that is spoken by the Bālas; come, Blessed One, come!
O you who hold the play-lotus of Kumāra, stay, stay in the center of the mandala; remember your pledge! O you whose command is unimpeded, hūṃ!
Do not delay!
Ru ru phaṭ svāhā!
O Blessed One, this is the invocation mantra of Mañjuśrī.

Having consecrated sandalwood water seven times with it, one should sprinkle it in the four directions—above, below, across, and everywhere—for all sentient beings, all bodhisattvas, all pratyekabuddhas, noble śrāvakas, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, piśācas, rākṣasas, and all spirits.

All the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, Mañjuśrī himself with his retinue, all mundane and supramundane mantras, all hosts of spirits, and all sentient beings shall come. Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! Oṃ dhura dhura dhura dhūpavāsini dhūpārciṣi hūṃ tiṣṭha samayamanusmara svāhā!
The incense mantra:
having combined sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, one should then offer incense;
thus, the minds of the Tathāgatas and all Bodhisattvas who have arrived are nourished by the incense, and they become attracted.
And there is a mudrā in this regard, renowned as the *mālā*, which is auspicious and attracts all sentient beings.
This very same mudrā, the auspicious *padmamālā*, is for the mantra of invocation;
and for all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have arrived, as well as for all sentient beings who have arrived, an offering of respect (*arghya*) should be given.

Having stirred water with camphor, sandalwood, and saffron, and having mixed it with one or another of these flowers—jāti, navamālikā, vārṣika, punnāga, nāgavaktra, bakula, piṇḍitagara—or with whatever fragrant flower is available, an *arghya* offering should be presented with this mantra:
"Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! Tadyathā: He he, O Great Compassionate One!"

O you who assume all forms! Accept the water offering, cause it to be accepted; remember the pledge; stay, stay; enter into the center of the mandala, enter! O you who have compassion for all beings, take, take! HŪṂ! To you who move through the sky, svāhā!
And here the mudrā is renowned as Pūrṇā, which follows all Buddhas and is constant;
and here the mantra for incense is as follows.
Homage to all Buddhas! Homage to the Tathāgata Samantagandhāvabhāsaśrī!

It is as follows: *Gandhe gandhe gandhāḍhye gandhamanorame pratīccha pratīccha imaṃ gandhaṃ samatānusāriṇe svāhā!* Furthermore, in this *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, there is a mudrā called Pallavā, which fulfills all aspirations.
And here is the flower mantra:
*Namaḥ sarvabuddhānām apratihataśāsanānām,
namaḥ sakusumitarājasya tathāgatasya*.
Namely: *kusume kusume kusumāḍhye kusumapuravāsini kusumāvati svāhā*.
Having paid homage to all the Buddhas of inconceivable and wondrous form, one should fumigate with the aforementioned incense using that very same incense-mantra.
I shall now proclaim the bali-mantra spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One:
*Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānām apratihataśāsanānām*. Tadyathā: *He he bhagavan mahāsattva!*
O Buddha-Avalokita, do not delay!
Accept this *bali* offering! *Gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇa hūṃ hūṃ sarvaviśva ra ra ṭa ṭa phaṭ svāhā!*
One should cause the food offering (nivedya) and the oblation for all spirits (sarvabhautika bali) to be presented with this [mantra].
And in this regard, there is a mudrā called Śakti, which wards off all evil beings.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded and who have destroyed all the darkness of ignorance; homage to the Tathāgata Samantajyotirgandhāvabhāsaśrī.
It is as follows: *He he*, O Blessed One, whose body is adorned with hundreds of thousands of rays of light!
"Transform! Transform! O you whose form is illuminated by the universal flames of the Great Bodhisattva! Leap! Leap! Behold! Behold all sentient beings! Svāhā! This is the lamp-mantra;
with this, one should cause a lamp to be offered.
The mudrā called Vikāsinī, the beholder of all sentient beings:
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
It is as follows: *jvala jvala jvālaya jvālaya*.
Huṃ,
O awakener, O Hari-Kṛṣṇapiṅgala, svāhā!
This is the mantra for the fire-kindler.
And there is a mudrā here, renowned in the world by the name *Sampuṭa*, which illuminates all sentient beings; it was spoken in the past by the excellent sages for the wise Bodhisattva.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi:
O Lord of the Guhyakas, these mantra-words are accompanied by secret instructions and are supremely esoteric. Your son, renowned in your lineage, who is formidable and ever-terrible,
is known as Mūrdhaṭaka among all the mantras being accomplished by the wise, and he is likewise so for the two families.
To effect its destruction, the second chapter shall now be proclaimed.
Homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose teachings are unimpeded!
Uṃ! Act! Act! Perform! Perform! Accomplish my purpose! Shatter! Shatter all obstacles! Burn! Burn all Vajra-Vināyakas!

O you who bring an end to life with a blow to the crown of the head, you of great and hideous form! Cook, cook all the wicked ones! O bringer of an end to the life of Mahāgaṇapati! Bind, bind all the seizing spirits!
O Six-faced One! O Six-armed One! O Six-legged One! Bring Rudra here!
Bring Viṣṇu;
bring the gods, beginning with Brahmā;
do not delay, do not delay!
Jhal jhal, enter into the center of the mandala! Remember the pledge! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phara phaṭ svāhā!

O Lord of the Guhyakas, this is that most secret one, the Great Hero Mañjuśrī, the great wrathful king named Ṣaṇmukha, the destroyer of all obstacles. Merely by reciting this, even bodhisattvas established on the ten stages flee; how much more so, then, wicked obstructors?
By the mere recitation of this, great protection is established.
And here there is a mudrā known as the "Great Spear," which destroys all obstacles; it is the heart-mantra of this very King of Wrath.
Oṃ hauṃḥ jñīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ!
Destroy all enemies, paralyze them, phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
By means of this mantra, one causes all enemies to be seized by a great piercing disease (mahāśūlaroga) or by quartan fever.

Or by reciting [the mantra] continuously for as long as one pleases, until one attains a state of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); otherwise, if one does not attain a state of loving-kindness, one will obtain a mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) at the conclusion of the recitation, but there shall be no liberation.

Regarding those who harm the Three Jewels, it is said that they must die; however, for those with gentle minds, the *mudrā* of the Great Spear (*mahāśūla*) alone should be employed, and the *upahṛdaya* mantra used here is:
OṂ HRĪṂḤ KĀLARŪPA HŪṂ KHAṂ SVĀHĀ.
The mudrā of the Great Trident alone should be employed;
it causes whatever one desires among all malevolent beings to be accomplished through the supreme heart-mantra.
Blessed by all the Buddhas, this single-syllable mantra named *HŪṂ* performs all activities.
The Mahāśūla mudrā alone should be employed; it wards off all misfortunes and brings all beings under one's control— in brief.
This King of Wrath is to be employed in all rites; recitation in the center of the mandala is especially distinguished at the time of accomplishment.
The mantras for dismissal are:
*Namaḥ sarvabuddhānām apratihataśāsanānām*.

Namely: Victory! Victory! O Victorious One, Great Compassionate One, you who possess all forms! Go, go to your own abode; dismiss all the Buddhas along with their retinues, cause them to enter their own abodes, and remember the pledge (*samaya*).
"May all my purposes be accomplished; fulfill my heart's desire, svāhā!
This is the dismissal mantra (*visarjanamantra*), which should be employed in all rites.
She is renowned as Sudrā Bhadrapīṭhā.

One should cause him to offer a seat with this [mantra] recited seven times in the mind; the dismissal is for all mundane and supramundane maṇḍalas and mantras. Furthermore, the accomplishment of mantra should be employed during the observances of the pledges, recitation, and time-regulations.

In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having again gazed upon that palace of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana), spoke to that great assembly circle and his own extensive section on the vidyā-gaṇas and mantras:
"Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
Oṃ riṭi svāhā!"

This is the follower of Mañjuśrī, the vidyā named Keśinī, which performs all rites; it is to be employed with the great five-crested mudrā in all malevolent activities. Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
Oṃ Niṭi!
This vidyā named Upakeśanī accomplishes all rites; one should employ it with the Vikāsinī mudrā in all activities concerning the grahas.
Homage to all Buddhas of unimpeded movement!
Oṃ niḥ!
This is the powerful Vidyā named Savarkamakarā, which is auspicious.
When joined with the *bhadrapīṭhī* mudrā, she brings the *yakṣiṇī* under control for certain.
Homage to all Buddhas of inconceivable and wondrous form!
When joined with the *śakti* mudrā, she is the slayer of all *ḍākinīs*.
Oṃ jñaiḥ svāhā!
This vidyā named Kāpatalinī was spoken by Mañjughoṣa and praised by all the Buddhas everywhere; she possesses a divine form.
Homage to all Buddhas who move with unimpeded gait.
It is as follows: Oṃ varade svāhā.
One should employ this with the three-crested mudrā.
Homage to the Goddess who consists of the supreme good, who assumes many forms, and who swiftly brings about the accomplishment of enjoyments;
homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous.
Accompanied by the mudrā joined with a trident, it destroys all fevers:
Oṃ bhūri svāhā,
Oṃ nure svāhā.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous!
There is a vidyā named Tārāvatī, praised for all ritual actions;
when joined with a small spear-staff, she is the destroyer of obstacles.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous.
The second chapter.
It is as follows: Oṃ vilokini svāhā.
The Vidyā named Lokavatī, who brings all treasuries under control; when joined with the Vajra-mudrā, she bestows all happiness.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous!
Namely: Oṃ viśve viśvasambhave viśvarūpiṇi kaha kaha āviśāviśa samayamanusmara ruru tiṣṭha svāhā.
This knowledge-mantra (vidyā) of great power has been revealed by the Leaders of the World; accompanied by the Daṃśa mudrā, it is auspicious, entering into all beings,
bestowing boons upon all spirits, and is proclaimed as "Viśvā" (the All-pervading).
Homage to all Buddhas, who possess inconceivable and marvelous forms.
It is as follows: Oṃ śvetaśrī vapuḥ svāhā.
When applied with the peacock-throne mudrā, this is effective for all rites.
Renowned as Mahāśvetā, possessing inconceivable and wondrous forms,
she who brings about good fortune in the world and subdues men and women;
homage to all the Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and wondrous!
Namely: Oṃ! Khikhirikhiri bhaṅguri! Paralyze all enemies! Stupefy them! Delude them! Bring them under control! Svāhā!
This mantra is proclaimed as the Great Vidyā, the Yoginī; when employed with the *vakramudrā*, it pacifies malevolent beings.
Homage to all Buddhas who move with unimpeded gait!
It is as follows: Oṃ Śrīḥ!
This vidyā, Mahālakṣmī, was taught by the Lords of the World.
When joined with the *sampuṭa* mudrā, it bestows great sovereignty. Homage to all Buddhas, who grant fearlessness to all sentient beings!
It is as follows: Oṃ! O Invincible One! O You who possess the form of a youth! Come, come hither; accomplish my purpose! Svāhā!

In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, the maiden renowned as Ajitā, born from nectar, joined with the Pūrṇā mudrā, is the warder-off of all enemies. Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous!
Namely: Oṃ jaye svāhā, vijaye svāhā, ajite svāhā.
"O Aparājitā, Svāhā,
and the one renowned as Caturbhaginy— these attendants of the Bodhisattva wander throughout the entire earth, acting for the benefit of sentient beings."
Their brother, known as Stumburu, was their attendant; they were inhabitants of Andurdhetu, traveling upon a boat.
When applied with the fist-mudrā, it fulfills all hopes. Homage to all Buddhas, the sovereign lords of the world!
Namely: Oṃ!
Kumāra! Mahākumāra!
Play, play, O Six-faced One, authorized by the Bodhisattvas!
You whose hand is raised while firmly seated upon a peacock throne; you of red limbs, who are fond of red perfumes and ointments!
Kha kha khāhi khāhi khāhi!
Huṃ nṛtya nṛtya!
O you whose form is radiant with red flowers, remember the pledge!
Wander, wander! Cause to wander, cause to wander, cause to wander!
Quickly, quickly! Do not delay! Accomplish all my tasks, accomplish them! O you who assume manifold forms, stay, stay! Hūṃ hūṃ! O you authorized by all the Buddhas, svāhā!
This was spoken by the Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa, the leader.
The entire earth, together with its six constituent parts, trembled on all sides.
For the benefit of all beings and to ward off wicked beings,
the terrible son of Maheśvara has come here for the sake of those to be trained.
Skanda and Aṅgāraka were clearly marked by the signs of the planets; then Mañjubhāṣiṇī spoke with a heart filled with compassion.
This great-souled Bodhisattva is a benefactor of the ignorant; since he is said to practice the conduct of a sentient being, he wanders everywhere throughout the world.
Endowed with the staff of the power of mudrā, that great-souled one causes even those beginning with Brahmā to revolve; how much more so, then, the fruit of human [attainment]?
The Second Chapter. In brief, this entire ritual for the protection of youth was proclaimed by Mañjuśrī as a mantra dedicated to Kārttikeya.
A Bodhisattva has come here out of a desire to favor sentient beings;
the heart-essence of this mantra is declared to consist of three syllables.
Intent on attracting enjoyments for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings,
when applied with the Śakti staff mudrā, it accomplishes all activities.
HŪṂ JAḤ.
This mantra, in brief, shall produce human results:
"Homage to all Buddhas whose forms are universally radiant."
Oṃ vikṛtagraha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
And its subsidiary heart-mantra (upahṛdaya), when joined with the power of the mudrā,
causes all beings— including the grahas and the mātṛs— to turn [toward him].
When applied to all the sealed mudrās, it becomes fruitful;
it terrifies the spirits and liberates those possessed by evil influences.

This youth named Kārttikeya-Mañjuśrī is a follower of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta; he performs all rites merely by being recited. He terrifies all spirits, draws them in, brings them under control, withers them, and slays them; or rather, he accomplishes everything according to the desire of the vidyādhara. Homage to all the Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! It is as follows: Oṃ brahma subrahma brahmavarcase śāntiṃ kuru svāhā!
This mantra was spoken by the Bodhisattva Mahābrahmā;
at that very moment, all beings attained peace and became cooled.
The mudrā joined with five crests (pañcaśikhā) will swiftly bring about well-being;
it is likewise recited in all rites of malevolent magic (ābhicāruka).
This ritual procedure has been briefly explained in summary.
Homage to all the Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
Namely: Oṃ, Garuḍavāhana!
Cakrapāṇi!
Four-armed one!
Hūṃ hūṃ! Remember the pledge! The Bodhisattva commands: svāhā!
Commanded by Mañjughoṣa in the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, he swiftly accomplishes auspicious purposes;
in the form of Viṣṇu, he causes the spirits of embodied beings to flee.
When joined with the three-crested mudrā, it is stable and swiftly accomplishes one's purpose;
indeed, those extensive ritual manuals (kalpa) which have been taught in the Vaiṣṇava tantra [are here applied].
Spoken by Mañjughoṣa for the sake of beings to be disciplined through skillful means: Homage to all Buddhas, whose teachings are unimpeded!
Namely: Oṃ, Great Maheśvara!
Lord of Beings, Bull-bannered One!
Wearer of the crown of long matted locks, whose form is grey with white ashes! Hūṃ Phaṭ Phaṭ!
The Bodhisattva makes known: svāhā!
This mantra has been proclaimed by me out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings;
when joined with the trident mudrā, it is the destroyer of all malevolent spirits.
"Beings dwelling upon the earth will say, 'This is exactly what was previously told by me in this ancient kalpa.'"
The various extensive qualities have been proclaimed by me in the Śaiva Tantra. Homage to all the Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
It is as follows: Oṃ śakuna mahāśakuna, you whose wings are spread like a lotus, destroyer of all serpents, va kha, devour, devour! Remember your pledge! Hūṃ!
Stay!
The Bodhisattva commands: svāhā!
This mantra is of great power, renowned as Vainateya;
it is the supreme subduer of the difficult-to-tame and the destroyer of the poison of serpents.
Joined with the Mahāmudrā, it destroys even the most terrible misfortune;
it undoubtedly neutralizes all poisons, both stationary and mobile.
To discipline beings through skillful means, that king of birds of great splendor wandered about in the form of a garuḍa at the command of the Bodhisattva.
Whatever extensive ritual manuals have been taught in the Gāruḍa Tantra,
all of them have been proclaimed by me alone for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Garuḍa, having come here for the sake of Vainateya,
wandered about in the form of a bird to destroy the poison of the serpents.
The Second Chapter: As many worldly mantras as there are, they have been proclaimed in this ritual manual;
for the sake of training sentient beings, I move about in such and such ways.
As for those mantras of the Tathāgata family, as well as those of the Vajra and Jewel families,
they have already been taught previously in this extensive ritual manual.
Just as a nurse diligently caresses children in many ways,
so do I move among those of childish intellect in the form of mantras.
What was taught by the Ten-Powered Ones in the past has now been spoken by me;
the entire meaning of mantra and tantra was also declared by the Greatly Radiant Youth.
Those [teachings] which were sung by the supreme Jinas and sung by the sons of the Ten-Powered One, they were sung by Mañjusvara, who possesses inconceivable and wondrous forms.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having surveyed the entire Śuddhāvāsa abode and that great circle of the assembly, entered the meditative absorption named "The Exhortation of All Samayas."

In that state, while Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta remained absorbed in samādhi with a mind intent on the conduct of bringing all sentient beings to perfection, all sentient beings became established therein. Immediately upon his entering this meditative absorption, the entire realm of the Śuddhāvāsa deities became a mandala adorned with various arrays of precious jewels and inconceivable manifestations of light from the Bodhisattvas. Even by Bodhisattvas who have entered the conduct of all Pratyekabuddhas and noble Śrāvakas, or even by those lords established on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), it would be impossible to draw such a mandala; how much less so for beings who are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*)? Upon seeing Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta abiding in the state of the determination of the sacred commitment (*samaya*) of that divine noble mandala, all the Blessed Buddhas, all the Pratyekabuddhas, all the noble Śrāvakas, all the Bodhisattvas established on the ten stages, the noble ones who have attained the consecration of the crown prince (*yauvarājyābhiṣeka*), and all beings—both those with outflows (*sāśrava*) and those without outflows (*anāśrava*)—perceived themselves through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta as having entered a mandala born of the mind’s excellence of samādhi, which is the inconceivable natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
It cannot be grasped even mentally by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), let alone written down or caused to be written;
then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having entered that great assembly-circle (*maṇḍala*) of the *samaya*, addressed the beings:

"Listen, O noble ones! This is not to be transgressed; it is the covenant of those Bodhisattvas who have gone [to the higher realms], let alone that of other beings, whether noble or non-noble. Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of the Guhyakas:

"O sons of the Victorious One, that which transcends the human realm—the temporal manifestation arising from the mind—has been taught. Now I shall speak of the human [realm] and of those Tathāgatas who have entered final nirvāṇa, wherein sentient beings, having fully entered, may attain all great mundane and supramundane accomplishments.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Speak, speak, O son of the Victorious One!"
Now, when you deem it the right time,
after the Protector of the World, the Lion of the Śākyas, has entered final nirvāṇa,
your mandala shall appear upon the earth for sentient beings, just like the state of Buddhahood itself.
For in this world, mantras attain success as soon as they are seen;
however, if one is ignorant, lacks the proper ritual procedure, or is lying down or in a state of agitation,
the mantras will not achieve success even for the great-souled Brahmā himself.

Mantras taught in this tantra do not attain accomplishment through effort, even many times, for those who are uninitiated in this tantra and have not seen the revealed samaya; for one devoid of the application of samaya, they fail even with the exertion of Śakra himself.

Mantras do not attain accomplishment even on earth among humans; how much less so when one knows the reality of the commitments (samaya) and the scriptures, and engages in the activities of conduct and the means of achievement?
For both mundane and noble mantras are accomplished merely by being recited.
Having entered the maṇḍala of Mañjughoṣa, which performs all rites,
one attains mantra-siddhi on this very earth within the teaching of that Youthful Lord (Kumāra).
Then, indeed, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, spoke to that Great Being in their midst.
"In brief, O Great Bodhisattva,
please explain the ritual procedure for the mandala for the benefit of sentient beings.
Thus addressed by the Lord of the Guhyakas, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta explained the ritual procedure for the mandala for the benefit of all sentient beings.

First of all, during the fortnight of the messenger, in the months of Caitra or Vaiśākha, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day inspected by pure planets and conjoined with a favorable lunar mansion—either on the first day of the waxing moon or the full moon, or at another time excluding the rainy months—one should occupy the ground in the forenoon, having approached a great city or wherever one may personally reside. This is the second chapter.

The Maṇḍala Master, having taken recourse either to a river flowing toward the ocean or to the vicinity of the seashore, should dwell for seven days or for a fortnight in a secluded hut constructed by the Maṇḍala Master in a spot that is neither too far nor too near from the northeastern quarter of a great city, for the sake of sentient beings.

In that place, one should take a very clean area of ground, square on all sides, measuring sixteen cubits or twelve cubits, cleared of stones, gravel, ash, charcoal, husks, potsherds, and bones; having made that area of ground very clean and well-prepared, one should sprinkle it with water mixed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), or with water scented with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, which has been empowered by reciting the mantra of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, eight thousand times while forming the great mudrā of the five crests (*pañcaśikha-mahāmudrā*). One should thus sprinkle that area of ground in the four cardinal directions, as well as above, below, across, and in all intermediate directions.

Then, one should draw that mandala on a square plot of ground measuring sixteen cubits, twelve cubits, or eight cubits on all sides. Among these, the sixteen-cubit is declared by the All-Seeing Ones to be the superior (jyeṣṭha), the twelve-cubit the middling (madhya), and the eight-cubit the inferior (kanyasa); thus the mandala is said to be of three kinds. For one desiring sovereignty, the superior is used; the middling increases enjoyments; and the inferior, which is merely for the sake of the pledge (samaya), performs all rites and is auspicious. Thereafter, one should draw whichever mandala is desired by the mind.
There, one should dig that spot of earth to the depth of two cubits;
if stones, charcoal, ashes, bones, hair, or various kinds of living creatures are seen there, one should dig another spot of earth that is free from defects and free from obstacles.

If he has not previously inspected a great mass of mountain peaks, river sandbanks, ocean shores, or the sands of great rivers, and having made that spot of earth very clean and free of living beings with great effort, he should write there; then, having filled it with water free of living beings mixed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), or with pure clay from a riverbank, or with anthill-clay where no living beings exist,
and having leveled it so that it is well-scratched and even on all sides, he should have a threefold mandala constructed as desired.

In the four directions, one should drive in four stakes of *khadira* wood, having consecrated them seven times with the King of Wrath (*krodharāja*). Then, using a five-colored thread consecrated seven times with the Heart-mantra of the Wrathful One, one should encircle that entire mandala in a square shape.
Thus, one should fashion a square shape in the central area as well as within the interior.

The Maṇḍala Master, stationed in the center, should recite the root mantras of the Vidyās eight thousand times. Having bound the five-crested Great Mudrā (mahāmudrā), he should perform protection for his good companions and protection for himself by means of the root mantra. While reciting, having emerged from the entire maṇḍala and circumambulated it, he should sit facing east upon a bundle of kuśa grass, keeping all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in mind, and surround that maṇḍala on all sides with a square-shaped enclosure.
Having kept her outside for one night, he should expel her from there.

There, the mandala master—having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), being skilled in the independent mantras, devoted to the Mahāyāna for the sake of sentient beings through skillful means, having stayed for one night, and accompanied by good companions—should, according to the ritual procedures seen in the scriptures, place that powder in the center of the mandala. This powder should consist of five colors, finely ground and radiant, well-prepared, and consecrated with the six-syllable mantra and the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). He should then place that powder in the middle of the mandala.

Outside, one should prepare a section of ground adorned with raised banners, flags, and archways at the crossroads, decorated with hanging clusters of fruit-bearing plantain trees, and made to resound with the noise of beaten *bherī*, *mṛdaṅga*, conchs, and lutes.
One should have the Mahāyāna sūtras recited from books in the four directions—sūtras that are conducive to the fourfold assembly hearing the Dharma through auspicious sounds;
for example, one should have the *Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā* recited in the southern direction.
The Noble Candrapradīpa Samādhi is in the western direction;
the Noble Gaṇḍavyūha is in the northern direction;
and the Noble Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra is in the eastern direction.

In this way, one should seek out a person who has studied the four Sūtras and is a preacher of the Dharma, in the absence of a physical book, for the purpose of hearing the Dharma. Then, the Maṇḍala Master, having risen, should scatter white fragrant flowers mixed with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron over that entire maṇḍala while reciting the root mantra;
and having scattered them, he should go outside.

After seven days, having subsisted on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) and observed the fast, two or three highly skilled painters who have generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), who are observant of the *upoṣadha* vows, and who are accustomed to fasting, should be brought in. Having bound their heads with the root mantra itself, they should then receive fine powders of gold, silver, various jewels, and five-colored, brilliant, beautiful, and subtle pigments. This [image], which leads to awakening and is certain to lead to awakening, should be caused to be painted by beings of great wealth and by righteous great kings.
If even by the mere sight of the maṇḍala [such results are obtained], how much more so when accomplishing the mantras?
For beings of little merit, now that the Bull of the Śākyas has passed into nirvāṇa, from where could such enjoyments come? This is merely a ritual procedure that is being conceptualized.
Seeing the poor people, Mañjughoṣa of great splendor shall proclaim this concise ritual manual for the mandala in brief,
using fine powders of polished rice, radiant with five colors.
The second chapter:

The preceptor of the maṇḍala, having personally taken the powder previously prepared, should color it with white, yellow, red, black, and green pigments; then, having bound the five-crested great mudrā and reciting the root mantra, he should seal that powder with the mudrā.
Furthermore, another master practitioner should have a fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) constructed outside the mandala in the southeast direction according to the prescribed ritual:

two cubits in measure and one cubit deep, shaped like a lotus bud on all sides, with an exterior shaped like a lotus bud. Having kindled a fire with fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood, he should summon [the deity] by forming the fist-mudrā while reciting either the root mantra or the six-syllable heart-mantra, using moist fuel-sticks of *śrīphala* wood, one span in length, smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
Having summoned [the deities], one should again offer one hundred and eight oblations with the previously mentioned single-syllable root-heart mantra.
Then, the mandala master, having bound his turban and prepared his equipment, should personally supervise the painters and have them work with great skill.
Thereafter, the mandala master, keeping the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in mind and burning incense with the incense mantra as previously described, [should proceed].

Having joined his palms in reverence and bowed to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and having paid homage to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, he should take powdered pigments and cause the form to be fashioned;

by this procedure, first of all, one should have the Blessed Buddha Śākyamuni depicted, endowed with the excellence of all marks, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne in the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, teaching the Dharma.

Likewise, having written [the names] and performed the rite of self-protection (*ātmarakṣā*) by means of the root mantra, the mandala master, together with the assistant, should offer a bali-oblation for all spirits (*sarvabhūtika*) and cast it outside the mandala in the four directions, above, and below.

Then, having bathed and gone near the fire-pit, being pure and clothed in clean garments, and having performed the protective rites, one should offer eight thousand oblations of ghee mixed with saffron while reciting the root mantra. Thereafter, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass and performing the recitation (*japa*), one must remain right there.
Having consecrated white mustard seeds eight times and empowered them with the wrathful king Yamāntaka, one should place them in a pair of shallow bowls joined together.
If one sees any obstacle having arisen—such as various forms of deformity, terrifying sounds, wind, rain, or gloomy weather—one should offer seven oblations of mustard seeds with the *huta* mantra;
by this, the obstacles will perish.
Alternatively, five oblations should be offered with human hair.
Men become paralyzed and rendered powerless, or they die, or they are seized by non-human beings at that very moment; of this there is no doubt whatsoever. Even Śakra would swiftly perish.
How much more so, then, will humans with evil minds or other obstacles flee here and there, utterly destroyed by the fear of the wrathful Yamāntaka?
Then, the practitioner, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass at that very spot, should remain performing the recitation of the wrathful king Yamāntaka.

Thereafter, the master of the mandala should depict two Pratyekabuddhas seated upon lotus thrones in the full-lotus posture on the right side of the image of the Blessed One Śākyamuni; beneath them, two Great Śrāvakas should be depicted listening to the Dharma.

To their right is the Blessed One, the Noble Avalokiteśvara, adorned with all ornaments, white as an autumn reed, seated upon a lotus throne; holding a lotus in his left hand, he grants boons with his right hand. To his right is the Blessed Lady Pāṇḍaravāsinī, holding a lotus in her hand, saluting the Blessed Śākyamuni with her right hand, seated upon a lotus throne, wearing a crown of matted hair, dressed in white silk garments, with a silken upper robe, and marked with three lines of black ash.
In this manner, Tārā and Jhukuṭī should be depicted well-established in their respective seats and postures;
above them are the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā, Tathāgatalocanā, and Uṣṇīṣarāja, each in their proper forms.
In this way, the sixteen Bodhisattvas are to be depicted.

They are as follows: Samantabhadra, Kṣitigarbha, Gaganagañja, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Maitreya who abandons the lower realms, [the Bodhisattva] with a yak-tail whisk in hand, gazing at the Buddha, the Blessed One; Vimalagati, Vimalaketu, Sudhana, Candraprabha, Vimalakīrti, Sarvavyādhicikitsaka, Sarvadharmīśvararāja, Lokagati, Mahāmati, and Patidhara—these sixteen great Bodhisattvas, with serene forms and adorned with all ornaments, are to be depicted.

The Sovereign King of Knowledge (vidyārāja), the Queen of Knowledge (vidyārājñī), and the image-seal (rūpakamudrā) of Anñjakūla should be drawn in their respective places according to tradition and scripture; furthermore,
at the end, one should establish a square-shaped area adorned with lotus flowers.
"May the deities of the vidyā whom we have remembered remain in this place."
Thus, on the right side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, two Pratyekabuddhas, Gandhamādana and Upāriṣṭa, [should be placed].
In this manner, the maṇḍala should be made facing east with an entrance door on all sides;
on the other side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, two further Pratyekabuddhas, Candana and Siddha, should be depicted.

Below them, two great śrāvakas, Mahākāśyapa and Mahākātyāyana, are to be depicted. To their left is the noble Vajrapāṇi, dark blue like a water lily, with a serene form, adorned with all ornaments; his right hand holds a chowrie, while his left hand, in a wrathful form, forms a vajra-fist. [Also to be depicted there are] Vajrāṅkuśī, Vajraśṛṅkhalā, Subāhu, and Vajrasena—the second chapter—along with all the vidyārājas and vidyārājñīs together with their retinues, each according to their respective attire, emblems, positions, and seats, and to be drawn according to tradition in their forms, mudrās, and so forth.

To their left as well, one should draw a square-shaped double-vajra mudrā and say: "Those hosts of vidyās who have not been remembered in this place, those hosts of vidyās are now remembered by this place; may they abide here in this place."
Above them, the Blessed Goddesses Prajñāpāramitā and Māmakī are to be depicted, adorned with all ornaments and possessing serene forms.
Above them as well, the eight Uṣṇīṣarājas, surrounded by garlands of all-pervading flames, should be depicted;
their respective seals and the forms of great universal monarchs (cakravartin) should be painted,
golden-hued, with serene faculties, and adorned with every ornament.
The Tathāgata slightly resembles those born with the pratimadṛṣṭi [mark], namely: Cakravartin, Uṣṇīṣa, Abhyudgatoṣṇīṣa, Sitātapatra, Jayoṣṇīṣa, Kamaloṣṇīṣa, Tejorāśi, and Unnatoṣṇīṣa.

Therefore, these Uṣṇīṣa Kings should be painted to the left of the Pratyekabuddhas. At the entrance, to the right of the Buddha and the Bodhisattva who has entered his task, one should paint the deity named Lokātikrāntagāmin, wearing a crown of matted hair, with a serene form; holding a rosary in his right hand and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) in his left, facing the door, with a face slightly furrowed by a frown. To the left, at the entrance, the Mahābodhisattva named Ajitañjaya should be painted.

He should be depicted with a serene form, wearing a crown of matted hair, with a staff and water-pot resting in his left hands; holding a rosary in his right hand, he grants boons, his face slightly frowning, and facing toward the door.

Beneath the lion throne is the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), surrounded on all sides by a garland of blazing flames. Beneath that is a jeweled celestial palace (*ratnavimāna*). Seated therein is the Blessed One, the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, in the form of a youth, with a complexion as fair as saffron, a serene form, and a beautiful appearance. His face is slightly smiling; his left hand holds a blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), and his right hand, holding a *śrīphala* fruit, is in the gesture of granting boons (*varada*). He is adorned with all the ornaments of a child and beautified by five locks of hair (*pañcacīraka*). He wears a necklace of pearls as a sacred thread (*upavīta*), a silken upper garment (*uttarīya*), and is clothed in fine silk raiment. Radiant on all sides and surrounded by a garland of blazing flames, he is seated upon a lotus throne. His gaze is fixed upon the wrathful king Yamāntaka, and he faces the entrance for entry into the mandala. He is to be depicted everywhere as one of exquisite beauty.

In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, on its right side, beneath the lotus, the wrathful king Yamāntaka is to be depicted; he has a greatly distorted form, is surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, awaits his command, and is to be painted everywhere with his gaze directed toward the Great Bodhisattva. On the left side, beneath the lotus, five bodhisattvas in the form of sons of gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm are to be depicted, namely: Sunirmala, Sudānta, Suśānta, Saṃśuddha, Tamodghātana, and Samantāvaloka.

And all of them should be depicted seated within the abodes of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, having the appearance of stone surfaces blazing with many jewels, strewn everywhere with various flowers emitting flames, and possessing a beautiful form.

Outside, on all sides, an inner maṇḍala should be constructed in the shape of a square with four archways in the four directions, blazing with various five-colored hues and bound by well-proportioned lines.

In the eastern direction, above the Blessed One Śākyamuni, there should be made in the center a small-sized image of the Tathāgata named Kusumitarājendra, seated upon a lotus throne, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, with his hand in the gesture of granting boons (varada-mudrā), and sitting in the cross-legged posture (paryaṅka).
To her right, the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin mudrā should be drawn;
to her left, the Tejorāśi mudrā should be drawn;
and above Tathāgatalocanā, the Prajñāpāramitā mudrā should be drawn.

Above the Blessed One Āryāvalokiteśvara and to the right of the Prajñāpāramitā mudrā, the Blessed Tathāgata Amitābha should be depicted, with his hand in the gesture of granting boons (varapradāna), seated upon a lotus throne, and surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides.
To the right of that as well, the mudrās of the bowl and the robe should be made; likewise, in successive order at the entrance, lotus mudrās should be made.
Or, according to the opinion of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarāja, the uṣṇīṣa-tejorāśi mudrā should be drawn, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides.

To his left, the Tathāgata Ratnaketu should be depicted, seated upon a mountain of jewels, teaching the Dharma, with various blazing rays of light— blue beryl, emerald, and ruby— issuing forth from him, surrounded on all sides by a universal radiance.

To his left as well, the Jayoṣṇīṣa mudrā, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, should be depicted. To his left as well, the Dharmacakra mudrā, possessing flames on all sides, should be depicted.
To his left as well, the khakharaka, the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), the rosary (akṣasūtra), and the Bhadrapīṭha mudrā should be depicted.

In due order, at the location of the door, a vajra-needle with flames blazing on both sides and all around should be drawn; this is the second chapter. Below the Blessed One Mañjuśrī, the great mudrā named Pañcaśikhā, or the utpala mudrā, should be depicted.
These two, blazing on all sides, should be painted joined together in the form of a complete circle.
From the entrance, one should enter facing west and be made to face east.

In all cases, there is an outer mandala, brilliant with five-colored pigments, variegated and beautiful to behold, divided into four corners, having the form of four archways (toraṇas) in the four directions, and to be painted outside the inner mandala at a distance of two cubits.

In the eastern direction is Mahābrahmā, four-faced, wearing white garments, with a white upper robe and a white sacred thread; he is golden-hued, wears a crown of matted hair, and holds a staff and water-pot in his left hand.

To his right, the son of the gods Ābhāsvara is to be depicted, golden-colored, his form absorbed in the intermediate dhyāna; he is clothed in silk garments with a silken upper robe, his face is very serene, he wears a crown of matted hair and a white sacred thread, and he sits in the paryanka posture, granting boons with his right hand.
To his right, the god Akaniṣṭha should be depicted, adorned with all ornaments, of serene form, with a mind absorbed in meditation, dressed in silk garments, and wearing a silken upper robe.
To his right, seated cross-legged, he has his right hand in the boon-granting gesture and wears a white sacred thread.
In this manner, the sons of the gods—Santuṣita, Sunirmita, Paranirmita, Suyāma, Śakra, and so forth—should be depicted in successive order, adorned according to their respective attire.
Below Śakra, the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods—namely the Sadāmattas, Mālādharins, Karoṭapāṇis, and Vīṇādvitīyakas—are to be depicted.
Furthermore, the terrestrial sons of the gods (bhauma-devaputras) are to be painted in their proper order and according to their respective attire.

In the same way, in the southern direction, the sons of the gods such as Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, Parīttābha, and Puṇyaprasava should be depicted according to their respective attire and positions.
In this manner, they should be depicted in two rows situated below them in the western and northern directions.
Outside the second maṇḍala is the third maṇḍala;
there, the four Great Kings should be depicted in sequence in the four cardinal directions.
As he enters from the northern direction, there is the southern Dhanada, who is adorned with all ornaments, wears a slightly broken crown, and has the form of a yakṣa, standing near a treasure.
To his right, the two yakṣa generals Maṇibhadra and Pūrṇabhadra are to be depicted.
In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, Hārītī, the great yakṣiṇī, should be depicted in this sequential manner. The youth Priyaṅkara, seated upon her lap and gazing at the maṇḍala, should be depicted;
as well as Pañcika, Piṅgala, and Bhīṣaṇa.
And near them, the mudrās of the yakṣas should be drawn.
In this same sequence, Varuṇa, holding a noose in his hand, should be drawn in the western direction;
and the two nāgas, Nanda and Upananda, as well as the eight great nāga kings, Takṣaka, Vāsuki, and so forth, should be drawn.

In this manner, those residing in the two rows should be depicted in successive order: yakṣas, rākṣasas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and ṛṣis; siddhas, pretas, piśācas, garuḍas, kinnaras, humans, and non-humans; as well as medicinal herbs, various kinds of precious gems, mountains, rivers, and islands—all the principal features in their proper sequence.
In the southern direction, Yama is to be painted together with his retinue.
In the southeastern direction are the seven Mothers.

Agni is surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides; his hands are occupied with a staff, a water-pot, and a rosary; he wears a crown of matted hair, is clothed in white garments, has an upper robe of fine silk, a white sacred thread, is golden-hued, and is marked with the triple sectarian line of ashes.
In this manner, they should be depicted in two rows, distinguished by their various implements, attire, postures, complexions, and essential natures.

Entering from all sides into the outer mandala are Umāpati, mounted upon a bull and holding a trident in his hand; and the goddess Umā, golden-hued and adorned with every ornament; and Kārttikeya, seated upon a peacock, with a spear raised in his hand, possessing the form of a youth, six-faced, with a body of reddish luster, and clothed in yellow garments.

Wearing a yellow upper garment, holding a bell in his left hand and a red banner, and progressively becoming increasingly emaciated in form, [he is depicted]. Mahāgaṇapati, Nandikeśvara, Mahākāla, and the Seven Mothers should be painted according to their respective ornaments, weapons, attire, and postures.
Also, the eight Vasus and the seven Ṛṣis; and Viṣṇu, who holds a discus, has four arms, carries a mace, a conch, and a sword in his hands, is seated upon Garuḍa, and is adorned with all ornaments.

The eight planets, the twenty-seven lunar mansions, and the eight subordinate deities (upagrahas) who move within the terrestrial mandala should be depicted in successive order. Likewise, the fifteen lunar days—both bright and dark—the twelve zodiac signs, the six seasons, the twelve months, and the year [should be included]. Furthermore, the four sisters mounted upon ships, with their brother as the fifth, who dwell in the waters, should be established in brief within the mudrās. Indeed, these deities should be arranged in sequence and depicted as resting upon the two-legged [human form] in summary within the three mandalas, based upon the mandala of the ancestors (pitṛmaṇḍala).
It should be drawn as a square;
this same arrangement applies even to the three circles.
In brief, the Blessed Buddha is the second chapter.
The foremost of all beings must certainly be depicted.
In the Lotus family, the noble Avalokiteśvara must certainly be depicted on the right;
on the left, in the Vajra family, Vajrapāṇi must certainly be depicted.

The noble Samantabhadra, foremost among the Bodhisattvas, must certainly be depicted; Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta must certainly be depicted. These are to be depicted according to their established positions within the mudrās.

Within this inner circle, in the middle mandala as well, Brahmā Sahāmpati must certainly be depicted in the eastern direction.
