Likewise, Ābhāsvara in the southern direction; and the Akaniṣṭha and formless (arūpin) gods, who are circular in shape and indistinct—the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—as well as Śakra, the king of the gods, along with Suyāma, Santuṣita, Sunirmita, Paranirmita, Parīttābha, and the other sons of the gods, each one of these kings of the gods must certainly be depicted in the northern direction.
These are to be established among the mudrās.
Likewise, in the third mandala, Īśāna, the lord of spirits, must certainly be depicted in the northern direction together with Umā.

Near the second gate, Kārttikeya Mañjuśrī—seated upon a peacock, holding a spear in his hand, his form radiant with red light, dressed in yellow lower garments and upper robes, with a bell and a banner attached to his right hand, possessing the appearance of a youth, and gazing at the mandala—must be depicted. In the eastern direction, Vainateya in the form of a bird and the sage Mārkaṇḍeya must certainly be depicted.
This very [mudrā] is to be established among the mudrās.
To the southeast, four maidens accompanied by their princely brothers, situated upon a boat, should be depicted wandering about the great ocean;
and Agni, the king of the gods, must certainly be painted there.

Likewise, in the southern direction, the city of Laṅkā and Vibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, must be depicted; and situated there, resting beneath a Picumanda tree, the Bodhisattva in the form of a Yakṣa named Jambhalajalendra must certainly be painted.
In this manner, proceeding in due order, King Yama, the great lord of the pretas, must certainly be depicted;
likewise, the Piśāca king named Vikarāla must certainly be depicted.
This is how they are to be arranged among the mudrās.
In this manner, in the south-western direction, the two chief nāgas, Nanda and Upananda, must certainly be depicted.

In the western direction, the chief of planets, Āditya, and the excellent sage named Kapila-muni—the bull among the Nirgrantha Tīrthaṅkaras—must be shown in the form of a Nirgrantha, arranged in successive order.
These are to be established within the mudrās.
And in the northwestern directions, the Yakṣa king Dhanada, the Gandharva king Pañcaśikha, and the Kinnara king Druma—these must certainly be depicted.
They should be drawn according to their respective positions, arranged in succession along with the mudrās.

The fourth maṇḍala is outside, consisting of five lines, adorned with garlands of mudrās, square in shape, having the form of four archways, and decorated by the four Great Kings situated in their proper order. As for the mudrās: in the front region, a blue lotus (*nīlotpala*) should be drawn; to the right and to the left, a lotus, a vajra, an axe, a sword, a trident, a spear, a mace, a wheel, a svastika, a jar, a fish, and a conch.

One should fashion various weapon-mudrās (praharaṇamudrā) with these: the discus, banner, flag, noose, bell, double-headed drum, bow, arrow, and mallet; this should be surrounded on all sides by a square garland. Beyond that, in the four directions, the four great oceans are to be established.

Having made a square-shaped mandala in the northern direction, one should place there a triangular-shaped mandala that has two faces, the form of three threads, and is surrounded by flames on all sides.
In the southern direction, having made a bow-shaped mandala, one should place a bowl blazing all around.

In the western direction, having made a mandala with a circular radiance, one should place a blue lotus, complete with its stalk and petals, blazing all around. And in the intermediate directions, there are four mudrās.

In the northwestern direction, having fashioned a circular mandala for the noose with flames on all sides; in the southwestern direction, having fashioned an elongated mandala for the staff with flames on all sides; in the southwestern direction, having fashioned a triangular mandala for the axe with flames on all sides; and in the northeastern direction, one should place the sword with flames on all sides.

Having drawn [the mandala] on all sides—above, below, and across—three seals (mudrās) are to be drawn outside the maṇḍala at the time of the gate, using colored powders alone; namely, a vajra, a fan, and sandals, all of which are to be depicted as being surrounded by flames.
This procedure for the maṇḍala has been taught here in brief by the wise Mañjughoṣa, out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings.

Then, the mandala master should first of all accept as disciples those who have unimpaired faculties, whose limbs are beautiful in every part, who belong to the castes of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, who have generated the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), who follow the Mahāyāna, whose nature is not to desire other vehicles, who are great beings (mahāsattva), endowed with faith and virtuous qualities, who long for great sovereignty, who loathe meager enjoyments, and who take delight in great enjoyments. This is the second chapter.

There were as many auspicious, disciplined, and virtuous monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, established in their vows and observing the fast-day restraints (*upoṣadha-saṃvara*), who were free from malice toward the Mahābodhisattvas, born of noble *yakṣa* lineages, naturally practicing the Dharma, having fasted for a day and night, clad in clean garments, with fragrant hair, bathing three times a day, and remaining silent.

On that day, those who possess the fragrance of camphor, saffron, and cloves in their mouths, who have constantly performed ritual ablutions (*upaspṛśita*), who sit upon bundles of *kuśa* grass, who have performed the rites of protection (*rakṣāvidhāna*), who are celibate (*brahmacārin*) and truthful, should be stationed not too close to the mandala.
They must be pure and very clean; from eight down to one, and no others.
And they should be Kṣatriyas, consecrated kings (*mūrdhābhiṣikta*), and great monarchs, who do not touch one another.

And their sons—both boys and girls—who are ignorant of the ways of the world, have as their cause the Blessed One, Mañjuśrī, the Great Bodhisattva in the form of a youth; he is the awakener of childish beings and is devoted to the play of a youth.
Therefore, the youth should be entered first.

For one who desires the increase of great kingship, long life, health, and sovereignty, there is specifically the increase of enjoyments, and the accomplishment of mantras for children is certainly established.

Having established these [deities] as previously positioned, and being well-armed and vigilant, the Maṇḍala Master, burning camphor incense, should then go out from behind the maṇḍala. Having gone out, he should bathe and sip water consecrated eight hundred times with the root mantra and water marked with the great five-crested mudrā, using water appropriate for the season. Then, pure and clothed in clean garments, he should go to the fire-pit and, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing northeast, offer eight thousand oblations mixed with camphor, saffron, and sandalwood.

Having summoned [the deities] and dismissed them again according to the previously mentioned rite, one should re-enter the maṇḍala. Having entered, one should present eight full vases— adorned with clean cloths and decorated with mango sprouts, their interiors filled with gold, silver, gems, grain, and rice— one to the Blessed One Śākyamuni, and the second to all the Buddhas.
The third is for the entire Saṅgha of Pratyekabuddhas and noble Śrāvakas;
the fourth is for all the Mahābodhisattvas;
the fifth is for the Mahābodhisattva, the noble Mañjuśrī.
The sixth [deity] is for all the gods.
The seventh and eighth are to be placed in the door-chamber of the second maṇḍala;
they are to be provided with clean garments.
One is for all beings;
the second, dedicated to previous sentient beings, should be established as a common possession.

Then, burning incense according to the very same procedure previously described, and having formed the great mudrā with five crests (*pañcacīraka*) as taught in the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, one should again perform the invocation.

One should invoke all the Buddhas, all the Pratyekabuddhas, the noble Śrāvakas and Mahābodhisattvas, all spirits (*bhūtas*), and all sentient beings, as well as Mañjuśrī in his youthful form (*kumārabhūta*), according to the previously stated ritual.
In this manner, one should present flowers, incense, perfumes, lamps, and food offerings by means of the very same ritual procedure previously specified.
One should perform this for all [deities] in every respect, following the proper sequence.
By the mention of "lamps," one should specifically offer a lamp of ghee.

Having offered to all—both noble and non-noble—by means of receiving the consecrated food (nivedya), one should present to all the Tathāgatas rice cooked with milk (śālyodana) mixed with curds, along with honeyed milk-porridge (madhupāyasa), various specially prepared cakes fried in ghee, aśokavarti, sugar-candies, and other such delicacies.

One should also present to all the Pratyekabuddhas, Noble Śrāvakas, Great Bodhisattvas, and Noble Deities offerings of clarified butter (havis), śrīveṣṭa, honey-syrup (madhuśiras), and various foods cooked in milk.

In this manner, one should offer the aforementioned specific types of *āraka* contained within the sweetmeats (*laḍḍuka*), along with the ingredients for the cakes, to all the hosts of gods and spirits and to all sentient beings, accompanied by mantras according to the ritual procedure.

Likewise, one should offer fragrant flowers—such as jasmine (*jāti*), tagara, nāgapuṣpa, punnāga, and so forth—as previously specified, to all the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, noble Śrāvakas, and Great Bodhisattvas, both noble and non-noble.

Specifically, the *jātī* flower is for the Tathāgata family, the lotus (*padma*) for the Padma family, and the blue water-lily (*kuvalaya*) for the Vajrapāṇi [Vajra] family; for other mantras, one should use something else, such as camphor incense for the Tathāgata family and sandalwood for the Padma family. For the Lord of the Guhyakas, the Vajrī himself, *guggulu* resin is recommended. One should offer incense for all other mantras, and one should cause clarified butter lamps to be given for all noble [mantras], while for non-noble mantras, one should cause fragrant oil to be given.
Thus it is said.
By means of the gradual rite according to the previously observed cause,
that which was spoken regarding the fragrance is likewise always [to be applied] to all mantras.
That which was proclaimed by Avalokita and that which was proclaimed by Vajrapāṇi in their respective tantras for the purpose of accomplishing the practice of mantra.
They too are to be seen and always followed here in this *kalpa*.

Then, the mandala master, having performed the rites of invocation, worship, incense-offering, and the presentation of food offerings according to the previously observed procedure, the skillful assistant, acting with haste, should perform a second circumambulation in all four directions and intermediate points. This circumambulation should be accompanied by the sounds of drums, conchs, and the proclamation of the *nandī* drum, and adorned with incense, flowers, lamps, and garlands, while offering a child dedicated to all spirits (*sārvabhautika*) that is free from meat.

Thus, having circumambulated clockwise three times the outer mandala above, below, and across in every direction, one should offer eight thousand oblations of rice grains smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.

For one who performs the fire offering with the heart of the six-syllable root mantra, those great beings previously stationed [in the mandala]—who have performed the rites of protection, who have been accepted as disciples by the mandala master, who have generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), who observe the fast (*upoṣadha*), who have offered their bodies to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who share in the enjoyments of sentient beings for the sake of accomplishment, who are skilled in ascending to the seat of unsurpassed awakening, and who desire to obtain the omniscient knowledge of a Buddha—are liberated from all sins merely by the sight of the mandala.
"Even those people who have committed the immediate transgressions (ānantarya) are liberated at that very moment."

Then, the Maṇḍalācārya, having wrapped the faces of those wishing to enter the maṇḍala with a cloth that is unwashed, drawn from the tantra, free of hair, consecrated seven times with the root mantra, and smeared with fragrant sandalwood and saffron, should first cause a prince who has been consecrated (*mūrdhābhiṣikta*), or a son of a Kṣatriya, or another person desiring great energy or a great kingdom—whether he be aged sixteen or as young as three years, adorned with five locks of hair (*pañcacīra*), or adorned with a single lock (*ekacīra*), or adorned with a topknot (*śikhā*), or even headless—to enter.

Having wrapped the face of one standing in the second mandala and having formed the utpala mudrā, one should recite the root mantra of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta once; then, having caused [the disciple] to offer fragrant flowers, he should be made to cast the flowers with both hands that have been cleansed and mixed with sandalwood and saffron. Wherever his flower lands, there one should give him the mantra; this is proclaimed as "one's own mantra."

That very [root of goodness] follows him through his successive births; that very [root of goodness] acts as his spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for the sake of attaining the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), ascending it, and fulfilling the great wisdom of a Bodhisattva; and that very [root of goodness] brings about for him the attainment of great wealth, great sovereignty, and association with persons of great renown, all of which are to be accomplished by him.
In this very life, without deliberation, that which is to be accomplished is achieved in all rites;
thus, in due order, one should proceed toward each [rite] until the eight are mastered, and not others—so say those who desire accomplishment.

For others, for the sake of exhausting their sins as desired, it may be merely a formal observance (*samaya*). Thus, when bestowing the consecration, the mandala master should first, in a region of ground to the northeast of the mandala, neither too far nor too near, having empowered and purified it with mantras by means of the root mantra; then, regarding himself as one being consecrated to kingship, [he should accept] one who has supreme faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, who is devout, highly enthusiastic, not separated from the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), a follower of the Mahāyāna, a benefactor of the Three Jewels according to the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, whose faculties are unimpaired, who is not blameworthy, and who desires to accomplish the mantras in this very life.

Those who possess a noble disposition, whose minds are engaged in the practice of mantras, and who are of a curious nature—even if it is merely for the sake of inquiry—whose minds are focused on the meaning of the mantra and its application without conceptualization; from one person onwards as many as there may be, they are to be consecrated, served, and honored.
Thus say the wise, for those of unerring conduct are to be consecrated in their entirety.
Nor for others;
therefore, having gathered the requisites like those for a universal royal consecration, one should act so that the preceptor is satisfied.

Then, with a canopy spread above and banners and flags raised high, a white parasol held over his head and white yak-tail whisks fanning him, he was honored with great ceremony amidst the resounding noise of drums, conchs, kettledrums, and clay drums, along with shouts of "Victory! and songs of praise, auspicious verses, and hymns of benediction spoken by the Jinas. Having circumambulated that mandala and bowed down to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and having bowed his head to the Ācārya, he should speak as follows: "O Ācārya, I wish to enter the profound practice of the mantras of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; I wish to enter the secret mandala of liberation that transcends all worldly things; I wish to attain Buddhahood through entry into the sovereignty of all dharmas. In brief, I say: 'May I become a Buddha!'"
Then, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass and facing east, one should have the five-crested topknot (*pañcaśikhā*) tied.
Next, whichever mantra is pleasing to oneself should be written with yellow pigment (*gorocanā*) on birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*).
Having written it and washed both hands with sandalwood and saffron, one should then place that birch bark, contained within a pair of earthen bowls (*śarāva*), inside the vessel.

Then, having sat down there at the feet of the Bodhisattva, one should recite the root-mantra of the vidyā one hundred and eight times. After that, the person seated upon the bundle of kuśa grass should be consecrated within the outer maṇḍala; the preceptor, taking the full vase—which was previously placed near the entrance and contains water common to all sentient beings—should sprinkle it upon the head while reciting the root-mantra.
The remaining [mantras] are [to be recited] with water as desired;
then that pair of earthen bowls (śarāva-sampuṭa) should be given to him, and he should be made to recite it by means of a lamp.
If that very mantra succeeds through diligent effort over time,
yet another [mantra] succeeds merely from its recitation,
or if it is deficient or excessive in syllables, this is the second case.
She becomes given; she is accomplished even in the very first practice, thus without conceptualization.
This very [consort] previously described by the Master is accomplished effortlessly by performing the three practices.
Thus, one should first bestow the initiation of the Vidyā.

Regarding the second maṇḍala consecration: with the full vase that was offered to all the deities in the second maṇḍala, one should sprinkle it upon the head according to the same procedure as before; by this, one is liberated from all sins and becomes authorized by all the Buddhas. One also becomes unimpeded in the accomplishment of all worldly and transcendent samaya-maṇḍalas and in the application of all mantras and mudrās.
"By all the Bodhisattvas"—thus one should bestow the Master’s Empowerment (*ācāryābhiṣeka*).

In the third maṇḍala, the full flask that was offered to all the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas should be used; with that very same rite, one should sprinkle [the candidate] on the crown of the head. It should be said: "You are authorized by all the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power to yourself practice or to teach the writing, recitation, maṇḍala-instructions, mantra-tantras, mudrās, and conduct of all mundane and supramundane mantras."
"In this very life and in successive births until the very last one, Buddhahood is to be attained with certainty.

Thus, during the *jayavijaya-abhiṣeka*, he was likewise consecrated by the Blessed One with the full vase offered by the Buddhas and the full vase offered by the Bodhisattvas, according to the previously described ritual. And it should be said: "You have been authorized by all the Blessed Buddhas, by the Great Bodhisattvas, and by the Śrāvakas; you are invincible to all spirits and unconquerable by all embodied beings."
"You are the victory of all mantras; accomplish [your goals] according to your desire.
Then, by the mandala master, the five empowerments should be bestowed upon each individual according to their desire; indeed, the same five are to be given to all.
Then, having led her into the mandala in due order and offered her to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should circumambulate the mandala three times to the right and dismiss her.
On the following day, she should be instructed in due order and appointed to the mantra practices.

At that very moment, taking the full jar which was previously offered to the Blessed One, the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, one should have those who have entered the mandala drink three handfuls of water while facing the east.

And they should be told: "O, do not transgress this secret pledge of the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta! Do not produce much demerit! Furthermore, no mantras whatsoever should be rejected, and no Buddhas or Bodhisattvas should be deceived.
The guru must be propitiated;
otherwise, there would be a transgression of the samaya,
and the mantras would not attain accomplishment.
Thinking, "There shall be great merit," they should be dismissed in this manner;
then the Maṇḍala Master should again offer oblations of *śāli* rice grains smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, using the eight-syllable heart mantra.

Then, having risen and entered the center of the maṇḍala, one should offer the *arghya* to all [the deities] with the flowers previously specified and according to the previously mentioned ritual. One should mentally contemplate them with the very same incense as described before, and having perfumed all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, noble Śrāvakas, and all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, siddhas, and ṛṣis, as well as all sentient beings, and having scattered flowers over them, one should sprinkle them with water mixed with sandalwood and saffron, and then dismiss them according to the previously mentioned ritual.

"Liberation from all [sufferings] is through the mind"— thus it is said for the sake of all beings. Therefore, the mandala master should cause the offering, the bali, and the powder to be washed away in a river,
or they should be given to suffering living beings.
Having made the area of ground well-swept, well-scrubbed, and well-adorned, it should be smeared with cow dung or sprinkled with water; or else,
having anointed it with very clean clay or sand, one may go wherever one desires for this very purpose.
Those who have entered the maṇḍala must subsist on a diet of milk-rice or sacrificial food (haviṣya).

Thus ends the second chapter, the Instruction on the Ritual of the Maṇḍala, from the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvatamsaka*, the Great Sovereign of Ritual Manuals (*Mahākalparājendra*), specifically from the section on the Manifestations of the Youthful Mañjuśrī, within the Extensive Array of Bodhisattva Practices.
Now begins the third chapter.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having again surveyed that abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and having bowed to that great assembly gathered in the maṇḍala—including all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—spoke the single-syllable mantra, which is supremely secret, destroys all poisons, accomplishes all rites, serves as the means for the practice of his own maṇḍala, and is to be employed in all minor rites.
And what is that?
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām*.
It is as follows: *Jaḥ*.
This is the second mandala procedure for this very single-syllable mantra, which includes the assembly of all classes of beings;
it should be applied in brief by first purifying a patch of ground measuring either eight or four cubits, and then drawing it oneself using powders of five colors.
Whether by others or oneself, in whatever place it may be, there is no fault;
one should first draw the great mudrā of five crests, which is symmetrical, well-proportioned, and adorned with three circles.
The lotus mudrā, the fang mudrā, the curved mudrā, and the staff mudrā of the Blessed Mañjuśrī—
these mudrās should be drawn in the eastern sector of the inner maṇḍala.
Then, at the base of the outer gate, one should draw the lotus, vajra, lily-flower banner, flag, parasol, archway, chariot, elephant, horse, ox, buffalo, svastika, peacock, goat, ram, man, and youth;
these should be painted arranged in successive rows, resting upon the three circles (maṇḍalas), and so they should be made.
Then, with the single-syllable mantra itself, the fire ritual (agnikārya) should be performed in the southeastern direction.
One hundred and eight oblations of Apāmārga wood, smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, should be offered;
then a flower should be offered with the single-syllable mantra (Oṃ). The offering of bali, food, and lamps should be given according to one's desire.
One should offer incense, perform the rites of invocation and dismissal,
and then cause one who desires a kingdom to enter and draw [the mandala] in the center of the city.

One who desires wealth should be [treated] near a *vaṭa* tree; one who desires a son, near a *putrañjīvaka* tree; one who is childless and desires elephants or horses, in an elephant stable or a horse stable; one who has been bitten [by a snake], in a great lake or a temple of the *nāgas*; one afflicted by quartan fever, constant fever, or any other fever, at a single-liṅga shrine or in the southern direction of the village; one seized by a *rākṣasa*, in a cremation ground or an empty house; one seized by a *piśāca*, near a *vibhītaka* tree or an *eraṇḍa* tree; and for those seized by the *mātṛs*, at crossroads or near a house where there is a death or birth impurity; one seized by a *brahmarākṣasa*, at a *tāla* tree or a *śleṣmātaka* tree. One who has been poisoned should have water consecrated seven times with the single-syllable mantra itself and be made to drink it right there in the center of the mandala; thus he is liberated.
In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, it is stated: "Likewise, for a woman or a man seeking fame, [the image] should be drawn at a crossroads or on a sacred site (*brahmasthala*).

For a woman whose children have died, it should be drawn on a fruit-bearing tree or a milk-exuding tree. For a woman who is childless, it should be drawn in the middle of a field where rice crops are being cultivated. For women afflicted by various diseases caused by evil spirits, or those stricken by great illnesses, it should be drawn on rafts and the like. To ward off demons (*rakṣas*), it should be inscribed on a riverbank, on a shore, or on a mountain peak."

In all diseases, even those caused by *ḍākinīs* from every quarter, one should draw [the deity] at midnight or at noon— at all times— in a place such as a temple of Brahmā, an empty house, a secluded spot, or a low-lying region; this applies to all rites.
Having offered the *arghya* with flowers using that very same single-syllable mantra and having performed the dismissal (*visarjana*), the mandala should be flooded with water;
thus a great protection is established for all the sick,
they are liberated from all diseases, and their desired aims are accomplished.
A sonless man obtains a son, the unfortunate becomes fortunate,
and the poor man obtains wealth merely by seeing this mandala;
it is effective for both women and men, and even for one performing a śrāddha rite.
"May one always attain prosperity in various forms as desired.
Thus ends the third chapter on the ritual for the mandala, from the *Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta-mūla-kalpa*, which is an extensive section of the *Bodhisattva-paṭala-visara*.
This is the fourth detailed exposition of the section.
Homage to the Buddha, and to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!

Then Mañjuśrī, having surveyed the entire abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, and again having looked upon that great assembly gathered in the maṇḍala, prostrated at the feet of Śākyamuni, and with a smiling face, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

Therefore, O Blessed One, out of compassion for us and for all sentient beings, please speak on that which is the excellent rain from the cloud of Dharma—the outflow of the accomplishment and application of the ritual procedures for the practice of mantras—which brings about the fulfillment of desired fruits; which is the production of supreme merit; which brings forth the seed of perfect enlightenment; which brings forth the complete knowledge of the Omniscient One; which, in brief, fulfills all hopes; which is correctly joined with the fruits of all mantras; which makes them fruitful; which renders the practitioner’s efforts not in vain; which fulfills the conduct of all Bodhisattvas; which is the donning of the armor of the Great Bodhisattva; and which overcomes and turns back the forces of all Māras.
When Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had spoken thus, the Blessed One Śākyamuni said this to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! You have set out for the benefit of many people and out of compassion for the world, you who consider it necessary to ask the Tathāgata about this matter. Listen well and attend closely; I shall speak to you. I will explain to you, in due order, the entry into the accomplishment of the conduct of all sentient beings through the extensive ritual procedures of your cloth-painting (paṭavidhāna), as previously taught by all the Tathāgatas."
Now I shall also speak:
first of all, on a clean spot of ground free from dust, cotton should be taken and purified by beings who have entered the pledge (*samaya*).
Having purified it, the mandala master should consecrate that cotton with this mantra one hundred and eight times.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who move with unimpeded intelligence and course;
homage to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha, the King of Kings who purifies and pacifies suffering.
It is as follows: Oṃ, purify, purify! O destroyer of all obstacles! O Great Compassionate One! O you who assume the form of a youth!
Manifest, manifest! Recollect the pledge!
Stay, stay!
hum hum phaṭ phadaṃ svāhā.

Then, [one should select] a maiden who has not previously engaged in sexual intercourse, born of a brahmin family, a kṣatriya family, or a vaiśya family—not from a family of excessively dark complexion nor from one of inferior birth—whose limbs are unimpaired and beautiful in every part, approved by her mother and father, who observes the *upoṣadha* vows, has generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), is compassionate, fair-complexioned, and free from other complexions; in brief, one endowed with the most excellent marks of female characteristics. On an auspicious day during the bright fortnight, when observed by white and favorable planets, in a clean place where smoke, dust, clouds, and wind have subsided, one should bathe the aforementioned maiden. Having dressed her well in pure garments, one should perform protection for her using this very mantra together with the *mahāmudrā*. Then, having stirred white sandalwood and saffron with water free of living organisms, one should sprinkle that girl—who is drinking it—with that same purifying mantra.

And one should scatter white sandalwood and saffron water in the four directions; likewise, having combined white sandalwood, saffron, and camphor, one should cause them to be offered above, below, and in the intermediate directions, either by oneself or by the master practitioner (sādhakācārya).
Thus, one should speak these words three times: "May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the great Bodhisattvas established on the ten stages, preside over this cloth-thread.
Then those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the great Bodhisattvas will attend to it.

At that time, while burning the effigy of the king, various auspicious birds— peacocks, curlews, swans, cranes, ruddy geese, and other such auspicious omens— whether moving on water, on land, or through the air, should pass by or utter auspicious cries;
this must be understood by the practitioner.
Fruitful is this action of mine; it has been empowered by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the great Bodhisattvas.
This cloth and its thread have been well-lived for me in this birth; my accomplishment of the mantra is not in vain.
There shall be the sounds of drums, kettledrums, clay drums, conchs, lutes, flutes, small drums, and large drums.

Furthermore, at that time, they might speak thus: "O Jayasiddhi, Siddha, Datta, Dinna, Gṛhṇa, Śreyasa, Saphalaka, Śakrabhūta," or other such auspicious words may be uttered, or there may be the sound of bells or the sound of drums;
then it should be known by the Vidyādhara.
This is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the great Bodhisattvas; it is not otherwise, for its accomplishment is never in vain.

Then, at that time, as they utter cruel cries, words such as "Seize!", "Eat!", "Make them eat!", "Perished!", "Ruined!", "Wretched!", "Far off!", "Sudra!", and "It does not exist! issue forth. Furthermore, the sounds of monkeys, buffaloes, jackals, donkeys, cats, and other contemptible animals—whether two-legged or four-legged—shall issue forth.
Then the practitioner should know: "I have no success.
In this life, the fourth section of the chapter must be concluded; or else, having performed the preliminary service once more, one should begin again.
In this manner, up to seven times,
even for one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution, success is achieved on the seventh application of the rite;
therefore, the practitioner, having performed the protection ritual for that maiden, should have her sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass.
Having seated her facing either the east or the north, and having himself partaken of sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), he should feed that girl sacrificial food as well;
then, by the same procedure, he should have her spin the cotton from the tuft of *kuśa* grass previously prepared.

Having gathered that well-spun white thread from a girl previously instructed, one who knows the mantras should perform this highly praised counting for all rites—starting from eight, five, three, or one, up to sixteen *mātrās* or *palas* or *karṣas*. For middling rites, there should be eight recitations; for others, five or one; and for minor rites to be accomplished, one should act according to one's ability. From that point on, whatever sinful karma was previously committed perishes at that very moment through the power of the thread, even if it was not consciously intended.
Having rolled up this sūtra, one should place it in a clean container; indeed, having placed it within the threads, one should fumigate it with camphor incense,
or with substances derived from the limbs of living beings, such as saffron, sandalwood, and so forth.
Having placed it in a clean location, honored with fragrant flowers such as *mallikā* and *campaka*, and having performed the protective rites and sealing,
the knower of mantras— who understands all rituals, has completed his recitation, and is well-composed— should proceed.
Then, having gone to a weaver and paid him whatever price was desired,
[he should obtain] one who is free from physical defects, not emaciated, always devoted to pure dharma,
not afflicted by disease, not aged, and free from cough and asthma.
Free from cough and asthma, not impotent, born of a pure womb, blameless, not humpbacked, and devoid of lameness or crippled limbs;
endowed with all auspicious marks, praiseworthy, and beautiful to behold.

One who desires success should request such a person— whose conduct is virtuous and who follows worldly custom— to weave a superior cloth; he should be wise, well-trained, and skilled in weaving cloths of excellent color.

With the most excellent, supreme, and finest cloths for weaving, [one should perform] the *bhāganjī*; thus it is said in the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*: "In the supreme [rite], one should perform the supreme; in the middling, the middling accomplishment."
Other minor works are indeed inferior in every respect;
having paid their price according to value, the knower of mantras should act as the artisan directs at the first utterance of the artisan's word.
One should then quickly give the merchandise; thus it is called "Vīrakraya" (Heroic Purchase).
Indeed, by the mere request for this [image], through the power of merit, this supreme and unsurpassed cloth-painting brings swift accomplishment to the reciter.
Performing all rites, worthy of worship, bestowing divine and human happiness, and the source of welfare for all beings— this was spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Then, having given the *poṣadha* vows to the weaver, the *vidyādhara*—at an auspicious lunar mansion during the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), on a bright day under the gaze of favorable planets, or at another time during the waxing moon—at that most excellent season of spring when the mango trees are in full bloom with clusters of blossoms and the finest flowers abound; at that very moment, when the sun has risen in the forenoon—he should cause the previously designated weaver to eat sacrificial food (*haviṣyāhāra*), clothe him in clean garments, bind a turban around his head, bathe him well, and anoint his limbs with either white sandalwood or saffron paste, scenting his face with camphor. Having ensured he is joyful in mind and free from hunger and thirst, he should wash all the vessels and tools such as ropes with cow dung and earth, and repeatedly cleanse them with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) until they are brand new.
Then, having washed [the image] with water free of living organisms, one should sprinkle it with white sandalwood and saffron.
On a pure spot of ground, free from clamor, devoid of people, in a secluded seat that is serene, protected, and adorned with flowers, the practitioner—

having consecrated white mustard seeds eight hundred times with the purification mantra itself— should scatter them in the four cardinal directions, as well as above, below, and in the intermediate directions.
Then, having struck the weaver with mustard seeds and bound the five-crested Great Seal (mahāmudrā), one should perform the binding of the topknot;
thus a great protection is established.
If it is the supreme cloth, one should have the weaver prepare it to these dimensions: four cubits wide and eight cubits long.
The medium [size] is two cubits in width and five cubits in length;
the smallest is measured by the Sugata’s span and four *anuṣṭha* cubits in length. This is the fourth chapter from the collection [of rituals].
In that regard, the span of the Blessed Buddha is equal to the measure of a man from the Middle Country; this is proclaimed as "one span of the Sugata.
By means of this measurement, the standard of authority is declared.
Furthermore, it has been stated by the preeminent ones in the world that "the highest success arises when one stands up."

For those desiring sovereignty, success is declared in the middle [son]; for men seeking great enjoyments, it is in the disappearance of the other son; and for those possessing the enjoyments of the three classes of gods and asuras, it is in the youngest. In the middle [case], middling success is attained.

Minor rites are always accomplished on a small cloth when performed according to the ritual procedure, even for one who has passed away; this path has been fully proclaimed by the Victors and the sons of the Supreme Victors.
For the welfare of all sentient beings who are poor, protectorless, and suffering,
the path to enlightenment has been shown in its entirety by those who perceive reality;
this path, which is the cause of enlightenment, has been revealed through the way of mantra.
The mantras of all worldly maṇḍalas are accomplished without effort,
and even the supramundane maṇḍalas that have been described are accomplished; for those whose minds are set on the cause of awakening, success shall always be theirs.
Success is not proclaimed for others who are always harmful to the world; rather,
success is always declared for those beings set forth toward enlightenment,
and especially here for the great-souled youth Mañjuśrī.
In order to accomplish his purpose quickly, the artisan should here obtain all necessary materials and then diligently weave the cloth for fifteen,
eight, sixteen, twelve, or four days.

In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, it is said that the completion of the cloth-weaving indeed occurs quickly within a single day and night; for those desiring the supreme accomplishment, it is better to complete it in a day and night,
provided the artisan is endowed with purity and proper conduct and remains constantly attentive.
Having gone from afar to that place, he should leave behind the prospect of a hut; then, having bathed with his clothes on, and having put on other garments,
wearing white robes and adorned with a garland, he should sip water again and again.
With his limbs smeared with white sandalwood paste, the artisan should raise his hands and always diligently polish them until they are smooth and well-cleaned;
by means of such practices or others spoken by the Jina.

One who is reflective should strive with effort until the entire weaving of the cloth is finished; when the cloth has been described as completed according to the previous instructions, being of the correct dimensions and lacking nothing, one should perform [the rite] on an auspicious day at the proper time.
Then, during the beautiful bright fortnight, one should bring down [the deity] from the tantra;
having made the cloth-painting clearly manifest and having attached auspicious fringes,
one should take the cloth-painting bound upon a bamboo pole and proceed.
Having ensured the well-being of the artisan with extensive distributions of gifts,
the minister— being of excellent conduct and firm in his vows— should go wherever he desires,
worship [the image] with fragrant flowers, and place it in a pure location.

Having previously purified that *picuka* in many ways, one who has performed protection and established the foundation by means of this very mantra should perform the protection of both oneself and the cloth (*paṭa*) with that same [mantra].
The great hero Mañjuśrī has been spoken of in the form of mantras by many past [Buddhas], and by me as well, now and again.
He alone wanders among all mantras in the form of mantra;
he is of great heroism and great splendor, the accomplisher of the purpose of all mantras.
Sentient beings dwelling in Jambudvīpa, whose conduct and intentions are deluded, perform three kinds of diverse acts that serve as causes for protection.
The fourth chapter: However, those who lack faith, are perverse, engage in wrong conduct, and are full of greed, do not accomplish the mantras nor any ritual substances whatsoever.
For this very reason, those wander in the dark prison of saṃsāra who lack a pure mind, whereas one who is always faithful and ever intent on auspicious rites is liberated.
Eager for the constant grasping and retention of all mantras, those great-souled ones, possessing great energy and great splendor, desire spiritual accomplishment.
For them, the mantras spoken by the Jinas succeed without effort;
however, for beings who lack faith, the white dharma does not take root.
Just as a seed sown in barren soil produces no sprout,
so too has faith been declared by those who perceive all truths to be the root of the Dharma at all times.
The accomplishment of mantras is always proclaimed for those who are devoted to the practice of dharma and artha.

Then, for the sake of the accomplishment, an artisan, or a well-trained painter, or one who is himself skilled in drawing, should be employed. Taking pigments that are non-adhesive, brilliant in every way, and endowed with color, the painter—endowed with the characteristics previously mentioned and following the very same procedure as the weaver—should perform the work in detail; the same procedure as for the weaver was described before. By that [method], it should be painted by another, or painted by oneself;
the image should be perfumed with camphor, saffron, sandalwood, and so forth.

Having incensed [the painting] with that very mantra recited one hundred and eight times, and having scattered over that cloth flowers such as *nāgakeśara*, *punnāga*, *vakula*, *campaka*, *vāpīka*, *dhānuṣkārika*, and *mālatī*, he—facing east, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, with a composed mind, his thoughts directed toward all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, holding a fine brush in his hand, and with a mind free from effort—should paint that cloth.
First, he should paint the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.

One should draw the two Naga kings, Nanda and Upananda, who possess all excellent features, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), their bodies adorned with the eighty secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), seated upon a jeweled lotus stalk, blazing on all sides and beautified by a halo extending a fathom in every direction, teaching the Dharma with a serene form. They stand in the center, holding that lotus stalk from below; they are white, adorned with all ornaments, having human forms with the lower halves of serpents, and gazing at the Tathāgata while paying homage with their right hands. They should be depicted as being of great essence. They should be drawn as being situated in the middle, possessing all excellent features, and appearing like physicians. Below them, the two Naga kings, Nanda and Upananda, should be drawn holding that lotus stalk, looking toward the Tathāgata, and paying homage with their right hands; they are white, adorned with all ornaments, and have human forms with the lower halves of serpents. They should be drawn thus.

And all around that lotus-shaft, it should be depicted as filled with lotus leaves, flowers, and blossoming aquatic creatures such as birds and fish, arranged in their entirety in a most beautiful and enduring form.

From the very stalk and branches of the Blessed One’s primary lotus, many other lotus flowers emerge, gradually increasing in height; on the left side, there are eight lotus flowers, and upon those lotuses, the forms of the eight Great Bodhisattvas should be depicted seated.

First of all, one should depict the noble Mañjuśrī, slightly pale like the filaments of a lotus or the color of saffron and gold, having the appearance of a youth, in the form of a young boy, with five locks of hair on his head, adorned with the ornaments of a prince, holding a blue lotus in his left hand, bowing to the Tathāgata with his right hand, possessing a beautiful form, with his gaze directed toward the Tathāgata, gentle in appearance, with a face slightly smiling, surrounded by a halo of all-pervading flames;
and on another lotus, the noble Candraprabha, likewise depicted as a youth in the same manner.
In the third [assembly] is Sudhana; in the fourth, Sarvanīvaraṇa; in the fifth, Gaganagañja; in the sixth, Kṣitigarbha; in the seventh, Anagha; and in the eighth, Sulocana.
All these should be depicted in the form of young boys.

On the right side of the Blessed One are eight great bodhisattvas, adorned with princely ornaments and decorated with all manner of finery, with the exception of Maitreya. Near the Blessed One is the noble Maitreya, wearing the garb of a celibate student (*brahmacārin*); his head is bound with a crown of matted hair, he is golden-colored, wears saffron-dyed robes, and has a red silk upper garment. He bears the mark of three sectarian lines (*tripuṇḍra*) on his body; his physical form holds a staff and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his left hand, while his right hand, holding a rosary, rests upon his right shoulder with a black antelope skin draped over his left shoulder. Paying homage to the Tathāgata, his gaze is fixed upon him, and his mental activity is absorbed in the object of meditative concentration.

In the second panel, Samantabhadra should be depicted in this manner: dark green in color like the priyaṅgu flower, his body adorned with all ornaments; his left hand resting upon a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇiratna), and his right hand holding a śrīphala fruit while granting the boon of charity; he should be drawn with a beautiful form.

In the third [panel] is the noble Avalokiteśvara, white as a stalk of reed, adorned with all ornaments, wearing matted hair and a crown, and clad in a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). He bears the image of the Omniscient One upon his head and sits nestled within the matted locks of the noble Amitābha, the Possessor of the Ten Powers. His form is beautiful; he holds a lotus in his hand from which a fly-whisk emerges, and his right hand is in the gesture of granting boons (*varada*). His mind is intent upon the object of meditation, and his body is illuminated on all sides.

In the fourth [panel], there is the noble Vajrapāṇi, golden-colored, adorned with all ornaments, holding a vajra in his left hand, and with his right hand raised in the boon-granting gesture while grasping a fruit; he is of beautiful form and gentle aspect. This concludes the fourth chapter.

One should likewise visualize Āryāvalokiteśvara and Samantabhadra; [Āryāvalokiteśvara] has his body draped with necklaces and half-necklaces, a pearl necklace as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), a crown shimmering and radiant with jewels, and is clothed in a lower garment of fine silk with a white silk upper robe. Samantabhadra likewise has a lower garment and upper robe of the *tīrtha* style, and in their physical form, they are exactly as previously described.
Likewise, in the fifth stage is Ārya Mahāmati; in the sixth, Śāntamati; in the seventh, Vairocanagarbha; and in the eighth, Apāyajaha.

Thus these Bodhisattvas are to be depicted with fruits and books placed in their hands, beautified by all ornaments, wearing silk upper garments, adorned with every kind of ornament, and clothed in lower robes of fine calico.
And above them, eight Pratyekabuddhas are to be depicted,

wearing the robes of monks, their bodies endowed with the marks of a Great Man, clad in saffron-colored garments, seated in the cross-legged posture upon jeweled stones, possessing peaceful demeanors, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, and strewn with fragrant flowers.

That is to say—one should paint a celestial palace (*vimāna-maṇḍala*) constructed from many jewels, long in shape, adorned with the king of mountains, and resembling a mountain covered with precious stones; this should be depicted being strewn on all sides with flowers such as the *mālatī*, *vārṣikā*, *dhānuṣkārikā*, *puṇṇāga*, and *nāgakesara*, located to the left of the Blessed One Śākyamuni and above the noble Mañjuśrī.
One should draw eight Blessed Buddhas situated therein.

One should paint the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin, who is surrounded by a radiance extending for a fathom (*vyāma*) and shimmering with the light of jewels such as *ratnāśakhī* and *vaiḍūrya*; who is illuminated on all sides by excellent great maṇi-jewels such as *padmarāga*, *indranīla*, *marakata*, *vaiḍūrya*, and *aśmagarbha*; whose body has the color of the sun at its slight rising; who is clad in an upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) of yellow saffron cloth and sits cross-legged teaching the Dharma; who is dressed in yellow lower garments; whose body is armored with the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*); whose form is adorned with the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*); who is serene in appearance and endowed with the excellence of all aspects.

One should paint the second [deity], the Tathāgata Kusumitarājendra, golden in color, beautifully strewn with flowers such as nāgakeśara, vakula, and others; he should be depicted gazing intently at the Noble One (Mañjuśrī), possessing universal radiance, and shining with a splendor interspersed with jewel-lights.
Third, one should depict the Tathāgata Śālendrarāja,
with the luster of the filaments of a lotus, teaching the Dharma.
In the fourth [position], one should likewise paint the Tathāgata Sunetra; and in the sixth, this Jina Vairocana, Duḥprasaha.
One should depict the seventh, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyavaidūryarāja, and the eighth, the Tathāgata Sarvaduḥkhapraśamana-rājendra.
All the forms of the Tathāgatas should be depicted as having a golden complexion and granting the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayapradāna*).

Above the Tathāgatas, situated within the clouds at both corners of the cloth, two divine sons (*devaputra*) belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm should be painted, standing in the intermediate space and raining down flowers. They should be depicted paying homage to all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas.
To the north of the divine [deities] and the Pratyekabuddhas, the eight great Śrāvakas are to be depicted, seated in subordinate positions beneath the heads of the Bodhisattvas;
namely: the Elder Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, Rāhula, Nanda, Bhadrika, and Kaphiṇa.
The Pratyekabuddhas were as follows: Gandhamādana, Candana, Upariṣṭa, Śveta, Sitaketu, Nemi, and Sunemi—all of them exceedingly beautiful, with peaceful appearances and forms of great self-restraint;
and the Mahāśrāvakas also, with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the Buddha, the Blessed One Śākyamuni.

And above, close to the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, two other sons of gods should be depicted wearing celestial garments, holding beautiful long banners with cloth streamers on all sides, bearing them above all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas.

Above the head of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, one should depict a cluster of jeweled threads woven with pearl necklaces, rubies, emeralds, sapphires, and other gems; this should be well-arranged beneath a silk canopy and adorned on all sides by hanging pearl necklaces.

And below the lotus seat of the Blessed Buddha, near the feet of Yamāntaka Mañjuśrī and beside the Nāga king Upananda, one should paint a great jewel mountain rising from a lotus lake, encircled by jeweled sprouts, caves, ravines, and coral creepers, and frequented by great ṛṣis and siddhas. On the summit of that mountain, one should depict the wrathful king Yamāntaka, of most terrible form, holding a noose in his right hand and a staff in his left, with a frowning face, awaiting orders. His gaze is fixed upon Noble Mañjuśrī; he has a leonine belly, hair standing erect, and resembles a black cloud of crushed collyrium. He has a long, formidable beard of tawny color, long nails, and blood-red eyes. His neck is adorned with snakes, he is clothed in a tiger skin, and he is the destroyer of all obstacles. One should paint this supreme, most fierce Great Wrathful King Yamāntaka, blazing on all sides.
The fourth chapter:

Beneath that mountain, one should depict the practitioner seated upon a stone slab on the ground with his knees bent, his hands occupied with an incense burner, wearing his appropriate attire and bearing the characteristic marks, his conduct consistent [with the rite], and his gaze fixed upon the noble Mañjuśrī.

Near the king of the Nanda nāgas, beneath the Blessed One Śākyamuni, one should likewise depict the great jewel-mountain king, the Lord of Mountains, which has emerged from a lotus lake, as previously described. One should depict it facing the Tathāgata.
One should depict it as being devoid of the wrathful king Yamāntaka and strewn with divine flowers;
one should depict that mountain as belonging to the noble Avalokiteśvara,
and one should depict that lofty, towering mountain as consisting of ruby stones and having a single peak made of beryl.

Therein, one should depict the Noble Goddess Tārā, who is the compassion of the Noble Avalokiteśvara, adorned with all ornaments; wearing a jeweled silk scarf as an upper garment and a multicolored silk lower robe; decorated on all her limbs with the three types of ornaments; holding a blue lotus in her left hand; golden-hued, with a slender waist, neither too thin, nor too young, nor too old; her mind absorbed in meditation, awaiting a command; her body slightly bent forward, her right hand in the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*); seated in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). The Noble Avalokiteśvara should be depicted looking slightly away from her. She is surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides. Right there, upon that peak of lapis lazuli, she should be painted covering the Punnāga tree which encircles it; a tree whose branches are everywhere laden with blossoms and fully bloomed flowers, and which, through those very branches, is beautifully adorned, entwined with sprouts and coral, radiant with various forms and colors, while she gazes toward the face of the Goddess Tārā.
One should draw the auspicious, boon-granting goddess— the destroyer of all obstacles, the supreme dispeller of fear— for the protection of the practitioner.
One should depict the Goddess who assumes the form of a woman, the daughter of the Compassionate One endowed with the ten powers, the bestower of boons for the welfare of all beings.
Here, the mother of the youth Mañjughoṣa of great splendor, the goddess,
[is present] on all sides for the sake of destroying all obstacles for the practitioner.
For the protection of lords of men and for their ultimate welfare, one should install that King of Wrathful Lords who is stationed upon the mountain peak upon a cloth-painting.
For the destruction of all obstacles, it has been taught by the sons of the Supreme Victors:
it is most terrible, a great bond, exceedingly fierce, and of great splendor.
In the Mūlakalpa, it is ordained for the very purpose of subduing those beings who are hostile toward the teaching,
and for the protection of the practitioner, it is the destroyer of all obstacles.
Fierce and wrathful by nature, he is the invoked deity of mantras;
most terrible and of horrific form, he is the restrainer of all who are merciless.
He brings under his control those who are otherwise unsubdued, even those who act with sin and ferocity—
whether they move through the sky, upon the earth, or throughout the netherworld.
One should paint a square cloth with four corners on all sides, which destroys all those who are wicked and hostile toward the teaching of the Sage.
And at the bottom edge of the cloth, one should depict the abode of the vast ocean, marked everywhere by the coils of individual nāgas.
Born from bodies in human form, with white and auspicious limbs, they always remain with their heads turned toward the north, hands joined in reverent salutation.
The Tathāgata named Ananta, renowned for his great majesty and possessing sevenfold clarity and great heroism, was adorned with precious jewels as he gazed upon the Tathāgata.
One should draw the renowned great lord of nāgas, who is exceedingly beautiful, of lovely form, adorned with jewel ornaments, and garlanded with flames.
One who is engaged in the teaching of the Sage, intent on the welfare of the entire world,
should write this nectar of the river for the destruction of all obstacles.
This supreme procedure for the cloth-painting, spoken by the Jina and described both in brief and in detail, was previously taught by the Tathāgatas.
Indeed, for that wise person who has it painted, the merit is infinite;
[it destroys] whatever extremely terrible sinful karma was committed over ten million eons.
Upon seeing that cloth upon the ground, even one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution, one who is immoral, or one who is loathsome, is destroyed at that very moment.
For those engaged in all manner of evil, wandering in the darkness of saṃsāra, and born into the lowest of destinies and wombs— one should not withhold this cloth from them.
The fourth detailed chapter:
The vision of this cloth-painting spoken by the Lord of Sages is fruitful;
merely upon seeing it, they are instantly liberated from that evil.

How much more so, then, would human beings attain accomplishment, being of pure conduct, possessing perfectly purified conduct, embodied, and ever-exerting themselves in the attainment of mantra-perfection?
Whatever merit all sentient beings might obtain by making offerings for ten million eons, that same merit a mantra-practitioner attains on this earth through the painting of a cloth mandala.
As many as are the grains of sand in the Ganges that have been proclaimed, so many would be the Buddhas and the noble sons of the Pratyekabuddhas.
O Queen, practitioners who possess the sword, having conquered many times in this world, shall obtain that fruit through the vision of the painted cloth and the excavation of the treasure-chamber.

Merely by reciting it, or by making offerings to the body [of the deity], or even by rejoicing [in its merit], the accomplishment of the mantra becomes certain for him; all ritual actions are thereby accomplished.
As many worldly mantras as have been spoken by the preeminent Jinas,
by their disciples, by the sword-wielders, by the divine ones, and by the great-souled Bodhisattvas;
Indeed, all mantras are accomplished by those who stand at the very forefront of others.

The fourth [chapter], the first detailed exposition on the ritual for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*), from the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, is completed.
The Fifth Chapter.
Then the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, having surveyed the entire circle of the assembly, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Mañjuśrī, there is yet another medium-sized cloth-painting procedure belonging to you."
I shall speak of that; listen, and attend to it well and properly.

First of all, by means of the very same thread previously specified and according to the very same procedure previously described, one should have the central cloth-painting made by artisans previously selected, using cloth of the previous dimensions that is very beautiful, white, well-woven, with fringes, and free from stains such as hair or refuse; exactly as it was done for the first [painting], so should one do for this, except for the size and form, after which it should subsequently be caused to be painted.

First, one should depict the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, beautiful in every aspect, appearing as if made of radiant jewels, and adorned with white pearl necklaces. In its center, the Blessed One Śākyamuni is to be painted, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, teaching the Dharma, endowed with all the supreme marks. On his right side is the noble Mañjuśrī, with the luster of lotus filaments or the color of saffron and the sun; on the region of his left shoulder he holds a blue lotus, his hands joined in the gesture of reverence (*añjali*), gazing at the Blessed One Śākyamuni with a slightly smiling face. He has the form of a youth, his head adorned with five locks of hair, decorated with the ornaments of a young child, and his head is bowed toward the circle of his right knee. And on the left side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the noble Avalokiteśvara, fair as an autumn reed, is to be depicted exactly as described before.

However, as the Blessed One’s fly-whisk is being raised, [the following should be depicted] at his side: Ārya Maitreya, Samantabhadra, Vajrapāṇi, Mahāmati, Śāntamati, Gaganagañja, and Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin.
These should be painted in successive order;
just as with the first, they are all to be depicted adorned with every ornament.

And above them, eight Buddha-Bhagavats are to be depicted standing, with their right hands granting protection from fear (*abhaya-pradāna*), their bodies draped in yellow upper robes (*uttarāsaṅga*), their left hands holding the corners of their robes, wearing well-dyed saffron lower garments that emit a slight reddish glow, possessing a universal radiance, and endowed with all the excellent marks. They are as follows: the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, Ratnaśikhin, Śikhin, Viśvabhuk, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Sunetra.
These Buddha-Bhagavats are to be thus depicted.
The fifth chapter:
On the right side, near the Blessed One Āryamañjuśrī, the great assembly maṇḍala should be depicted.
The eight great śrāvakas and the eight pratyekabuddhas should be depicted exactly as they were previously described.
However, the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Śāriputra should be depicted standing with fly-whisks being waved over the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
In this same manner, the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm should be depicted.

Śakra, the Indra of the gods, as well as Suyāma, Santuṣita, Sunirmita, Śuddha, Vimala, Sudṛśa, Atapa, Ābhāsvara, Brahmā Sahāmpati, Akaniṣṭha, and other such sons of the gods belonging to the realms of form (rūpāvacara) and desire (kāmāvacara), should be depicted in successive order, standing near the noble Mañjuśrī, arranged within the surrounding assembly circle, and painted in their own characteristic forms and attire.

Beneath the lion throne of the Blessed One, a great mountain rising from the great ocean should be painted all around, extending to the edge of the cloth. In one corner of the cloth, the practitioner should be depicted according to his dress, posture, and form, with his knees, elbows, and head bowed down, and his hands occupied with an incense burner.
And on that jewel mountain, beneath the noble Mañjuśrī, the wrathful king Yamāntaka should be drawn as previously described.
On the left side, beneath the lion throne of the Blessed One and near the feet of Noble Avalokiteśvara, the goddess Tārā should be depicted as seated upon that mountain of jewels;
she should be painted exactly as previously described.

Furthermore, the entire cloth [painting] should be strewn all around with loose flowers—campaka, blue lotus, saugandhika, mālatī, varṣikā, dhānuṣkārīka, punnāga, kesarā, and so forth—and the cloth should be covered on all sides with such blossoms.

And at the upper edge, in both corners of the cloth, two sons of gods (devaputra) should be depicted, white in color, wearing various forms, standing in the intermediate space, emerging from within clouds of water, leaping upward, and scattering a great mass of flowers.
This is declared to be the Madhyamaka, the manifestation of the cloth for the sake of supreme welfare;
the middling accomplishment of human beings on this earth depends upon it.
Whatever evil has been committed previously while wandering through saṃsāra,
it perishes at that very moment upon seeing the cloth-painting here.
Deluded beings do not know you, wandering through the five destinies;
however, those who behold the painting of Mañjughoṣa in the center [of it] [do].

Even one who commits sins, even one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution, and even one of immoral conduct—such persons shall succeed in the mantras spoken in various ways in the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa.
Furthermore, one who has performed the recitation shall attain accomplishment even more swiftly; the sick person is freed from disease, and the poor person obtains wealth.
A sonless man obtains a son upon seeing the middle panel;
by merely seeing it, he shall then attain vast and great merit.
That person will certainly partake in the happiness of gods and humans, and at the end of that birth, Buddhahood will certainly be his.
By writing, by reading, by worshipping, by drawing [it],
and likewise by seeing or touching it, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus, through prayer, supplication, and rejoicing, one quickly attains a fruitful birth from this most radiant painting.
It is not possible to describe by speech, even in tens of millions of aeons, the merit that a living being would obtain from the fruitful sight of this cloth-painting.
From the *Ārya-mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, this is the fifth detailed chapter.
The second section on the ritual procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhānavisara*) is completed.
The sixth detailed chapter. Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni again addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Mañjuśrī, there is yet another secret procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*), the third one, called the 'Minor' (*kanyasa*). By means of this, all sentient beings shall attain accomplishment without even effort."

In accordance with the very same procedure previously specified, the cloth should be painted by skilled artisans as before, square and equal in measure, with the dimensions of one Sugata-span across, using the previously mentioned constituent parts.

First of all, the noble Mañjuśrī should be depicted seated upon a lion throne in the form of a young boy, as before, teaching the Dharma, with beautiful forms and rays of light radiating in all directions.

On the left side, the noble Samantabhadra should be depicted as before: standing upon a jewel-stone, with a yak-tail whisk in his right hand, his left hand resting upon a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), and dark green in color like the priyaṅgu plant.
On the right side of Noble Mañjuśrī, Noble Avalokiteśvara is to be depicted as before, standing upon a jewel-stone,
with a fly-whisk in his hand and his left hand resting upon a lotus, his form radiant on all sides.
Below the lion throne, the golden-colored mountain should be depicted as far as the edge of the cloth.

At the corner of the cloth’s edge, beneath the lion throne of the noble Mañjuśrī, on the right side, Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, should be depicted as before, holding an incense burner in his hand; the practitioner should be depicted exactly as before.
Above the noble Mañjuśrī, that Tathāgata Kusumitarājendra should be depicted, measuring sixteen finger-breadths, nestled within a cave in a mountain of jewels.
Ten mountain peaks resembling gabled pavilions (*kūṭāgāra*) are to be depicted.
One should draw that cloth painting (*paṭa*) surrounded on all sides by the forms of mountains.

Above, situated at the corners of the cloth and joined to the mountain slopes, two sons of gods (*devaputra*) from the Śuddhāvāsa realm named Śuddha and Viśuddha are to be depicted as before, emitting showers of flowers from celestial palaces (*vimāna*) as they fly upward.
And that cloth-painting should be caused to be painted strewn with various flowers.
Thus has been described the threefold characteristic of the cloth;
indeed, this one called "the inferior" is the most excellent cloth for minor rites.
Whatever extremely terrible sinful karma has been committed or caused to be committed,
one is liberated from it through the vision of the painting for thousands of millions of eons.
In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, it is said that by merely seeing the cloth painting, one is liberated at that very moment; indeed,
the wise person who honors thousands of millions of Buddhas does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of one who has seen the "Youngest" cloth painting.
Whatever merit is gained by performing worship to all the Buddhas, the compassionate ones—
that same merit the wise person shall obtain by beholding the cloth painting (paṭa) in its lowest form;
and for the sake of enjoyments, one should perform auspicious rites here.
Whatever mantras have been spoken by Brahmā, Indra, and the ṛṣis; those uttered by Vainateya; and those of Varuṇa, Āditya, and Kubera;
as well as those of all the Rākṣasas led by Dhanada, the lords of the Dānavas, and the great serpents—[all these are mastered].
All mantras spoken by Soma, Vāyu, Yama, and others, as well as by Hari, Hara, and the rest, when brought here, are perfected in front of this cloth-painting;
one should always perform rites for pacification (śāntika) and likewise rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika) here.
And one should avoid those things that are cruel and censured here by the best of Jinas.

Thus ends the sixth detailed chapter from the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka; specifically, the third [section], the ritual for the small cloth-painting (*kanyasa-paṭavidhāna*).
The seventh detailed chapter.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One Śākyamuni three times, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One thus: “Excellent, excellent! This Dharma-discourse, well-spoken by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, is for the sake, benefit, and happiness of those who practice the vows of all vidyās, and out of compassion for the world. It demonstrates the skillful means of the Bodhisattvas and leads toward Nirvāṇa. It is a distinguished armor, a lineage that leads inevitably to awakening, and it shall serve to accomplish the purpose and practice of all mantras. It will be a revealer of the secret of this mantra to all people in the future age, when the Teacher of the World has passed away, when the sun of the Tathāgata has set, when the lineage [of Buddhas] has been extinguished in all Buddha-fields, and when the world-vessel has become shrouded in darkness due to the absence of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas; when the Noble Path has been severed, and the realm of sentient beings has become lightless, devoid of all vidyās, mantras, herbs, jewels, and gems, and abandoned by virtuous people. At that time, sentient beings will become indolent, lacking aspiration, faithless, fragmented, taken hold of by evil friends, deceitful, fraudulent, and of rogue conduct.”

Having heard this Dharma-discourse, those who delight in indolence and laziness will fall into terror; those who seek after sensual pleasures will have no faith, and those who delight in wrong views will not believe.
Rejecting the true Dharma, they will produce much demerit, destined for the Avīci hell, having gone from the terrible to even more terrible states.

"For the sake of those who are suffering, for bringing under control those who are uncontrollable, and for instilling fear in those who are already subdued, may the Blessed One, through the gathering of skillful means, speak the ritual procedure for the mantra-painting at whatever time he deems appropriate. Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni gave his approval to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you consider it necessary to question the Tathāgata regarding this matter.
There is, Mañjuśrī.

This most secret and supreme exposition of the ritual procedures for the chapters on the practice of the vidyā-vows and accomplishments, which contains the ultimate meaning of the supreme heart-mantras and serves as a treasury of great significance for all mantras—these six six-syllable supreme heart-mantras attain accomplishment without conceptualization at that time. For the sake of subduing those beings, for their entry into the mantras of the equipment of skillful means, and for their certain attainment of perfect enlightenment, they were previously spoken by seventy-six crores of Buddhas; I too shall now speak of them this very day.
Out of regard for future generations, listen to it well and attend to it thoroughly;
I shall speak it to you— what is that?
In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, the Blessed One Śākyamuni then spoke this mantra:
“Oṃ vākyārthe jaya oṃ vākyaśeṣe sva.”
Oṃ, obeisance to the one who leads by speech; Oṃ, obeisance to the one who is established in speech;
Oṃ, obeisance to the one who is the essence of speech.

"Oṃ vākyedanamaḥ"—these six-syllable mantras of yours, Mañjuśrī, are of great power, equal in strength, supreme heart-mantras, and supremely effective. Arisen like a Buddha for the benefit of all sentient beings, they have been proclaimed by all the Buddhas. Bound by the pledge (samaya), thoroughly activated, and efficacious for all rites, they teach the path to enlightenment. As the preeminent mantras in the Tathāgata family, they are applied in three ways—superior, middling, and inferior—and being most auspicious, they bestow the ripening of karmic fruits; they shall achieve accomplishment at the time when the teaching is on the verge of disappearance.

Those who will accomplish these for the sake of protecting the eye of the True Dharma during the final assembly, they shall accomplish them by means of the mere application of their value for the sake of great kingdoms, vast enjoyments, and sovereign power;

at that time, in that very moment, they will attain accomplishment even more swiftly. Indeed, these supreme heart-mantras should be accomplished even for the sake of mere investigation. In brief, in whatever manner they are applied, in that very manner they will attain accomplishment; this is the summary.

At that time, at that moment, during the Great Terrifying Age of the Five Corruptions, sentient beings will have little merit, little renown, short lifespans, and few enjoyments; they will be weak and unable to undertake the extensive rituals such as the preparation of the cloth-painting (paṭavidhāna).
For their sake, I shall speak of it in a much more concise form.

First of all, having purchased thread by sale—either a full *pala* or half a *pala*—one should have a weaver weave a cloth dwelling (*sadana*) one cubit in length and half a cubit in width; or else, taking another new piece of cloth that is fresh, free from hair, and very white, measuring two cubits, four cubits, six, five, ten, or eight [cubits] according to one's desire, one should have it painted by a painter as desired.

Having combined the cloth with sandalwood, camphor, saffron, and white [pigments], and having mixed them together with water that is free of living organisms and free of impurities, one should soak the cloth in a new vessel. Having kept it well-covered for three days on a clean spot along the road while performing protective rites, and having become pure oneself, one should—during the bright fortnight on the full moon day—sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing east in front of the vessel containing the cloth, and recite these mantra-words one hundred and eight times, as follows:
*Oṃ he he bhagavan*.

O wearer of many forms, O one with divine vision, look upon me, look upon me! Remember your pledge! O Mahābodhisattva who holds the form of a youth, why do you delay? This is the seventh chapter from the extensive [tantra].
Having performed recitation with this mantra— *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*— one should sleep right there;
it will reveal in a dream whether there is success or failure.
Then, having risen and seen a dream that is a sign of unimpeded accomplishment, one should have that cloth painted; provided that dreams indicating non-accomplishment are not seen.
Having removed that cloth from that container, one should dry it in the sun;
and having dried it, one should place it again into another new container.
One should then place it in a well-guarded and protected location;
thereafter, having taken up one of those supreme heart-mantras (*paramahṛdaya*), one should recite [it] for more than a hundred thousand syllables of the six-syllable mantra as desired.
Then that cloth-painting (*paṭa*) will quickly be accomplished.

First of all, having taken that cloth-painting on a day of miracles, or on another bright day joined with an auspicious lunar mansion (nakṣatra), on an auspicious lunar date (tithi), or on a day of the waxing fortnight, when the omens are very favorable, at the time of midnight during an auspicious night, one should have the painter paint that cloth-painting while observing the fast (upoṣadha) in a clean place, burning camphor incense.

First of all, one should paint Noble Mañjuśrī in the form of a young boy, with hair tied in five tufts and adorned with the ornaments of a child; he is golden-colored, clothed in a lower garment of blue silk and an upper robe of blue silk, teaching the Dharma; seated on a lion throne in the half-lotus posture with his right foot resting upon a jeweled footstool; endowed with all ornaments, beautiful to behold, with a slightly smiling face, and his gaze directed toward the practitioner.

On the right side, one should depict the noble Samantabhadra, with a white yak-tail whisk being waved over him, dark green like the priyaṅgu flower, holding a cintāmaṇi jewel in his left hand, beautiful in all his limbs, adorned with every ornament, dressed in a lower garment of blue silk, wearing a pearl necklace as a sacred thread, and seated upon a white lotus throne.
