To the left side of Noble Mañjuśrī is Noble Avalokiteśvara, dressed in a lower garment of blue silk, beautiful in all his limbs, and adorned with all ornaments; he has a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) of pearl necklaces, holds a red lotus in his left hand, and in his right hand holds a white fly-whisk (*camara*) being waved, fixed upon a golden handle; he is of gentle appearance and his gaze is directed toward Noble Mañjuśrī. Likewise, Noble Samantabhadra is seated upon a white lotus throne; both of these should be depicted in this manner.
In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, there are three lotuses arising from a single lotus-stalk.
On the pericarp of the central root-lotus is the lion-throne and jeweled seat of the noble Mañjuśrī. On the other lotus is the noble Samantabhadra, and on the third lotus is the noble Avalokiteśvara.

And that lotus-stalk is beautiful, shaped like an emerald lotus, with many lotus buds and leaves, and with flowers both fully blossomed and half-opened, rising from a great lake as hot as the Anavatapta; its base is supported by two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda. Those two nāga kings are white in color, adorned with seven hoods, their bodies beautified by all ornaments, having human-like upper bodies and forms marked by serpent coils; they should be depicted gazing at the noble Mañjuśrī, submerged within the water, with their heads adorned with precious jewels.

And all around the great lake, at the bottom, on the right side in the corner at the edge of the cloth, the practitioner should be depicted according to his dress and complexion, looking toward the face-mandala of Noble Mañjuśrī, with a censer held in his hand, his head bowed, and his body positioned with hands above his knees.

Above the noble Mañjuśrī, at both corners of the edge of the cloth, two sons of gods wearing garlands and holding flower garlands should be depicted, flying upward from within the clouds, emitting a great shower of flowers, and appearing most beautiful.

One should depict that site strewn all around with flowers such as *nāgakeśara* and others; or one may depict it as presided over by the three forms according to one's preference. Noble Mañjuśrī, teaching the Dharma, and Noble Samantabhadra and Noble Avalokiteśvara, with chowries held in their hands, should be caused to be painted.
Alternatively, the practitioner must have three images painted according to his own preference;
they may be of whatever form he desires, arranged in whatever configuration he prefers, and should be painted exactly as it pleases the practitioner.
In the center is Noble Mañjuśrī; at both ends are Noble Avalokiteśvara and Samantabhadra, or whichever others are desired, must certainly be caused to be painted.

On whatever cloth fragment is available—whether measuring a span or a cubit—it should be caused to be painted either by oneself or by another artist, whether that artist observes the *poṣadha* vows or does not, whether they have faith or lack faith, whether they are pure or impure, and whether they possess moral discipline or are of bad character.
The seventh chapter:
The practitioner himself must necessarily have completed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), be endowed with faith, and have generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). This is mandatory.
In this way, mantras are indeed accomplished, but not for others who are evildoers;
having become faithful, one should thus practice the mantra-deities.
The king of mantras is accomplished for one who possesses faith, and not otherwise;
for faith is the supreme vehicle by which the Vināyakas proceed.
In a person devoid of faith, the pure dharma does not grow,
just as a green sprout does not emerge from seeds scorched by fire.
For a mortal established in faith, the deities are indeed accomplished through his ritual action;
for one devoid of faith, they are not accomplished.
All mantras without exception, as well as those deities who are mundane and likewise those who are supramundane.
For one who possesses faith and is free from defilement, everything indeed succeeds;
for those whose minds are devoted to that, enlightenment and its accomplishment come swiftly.
Success is not declared for others; they are excluded from this teaching.
The cloth [painting] is proclaimed as being either small, special, or middling.
Now, however, I shall explain the means of accomplishment for all ritual actions.

Thus concludes the fourth chapter on the ritual procedure for the cloth painting, from the seventh section of the cloth painting, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra belonging to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
The Eighth Chapter.
Then the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"O Mañjuśrī, those who..."
This procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*), along with its detailed exposition, has been taught by you for the benefit of those beings whom you have designated;
they shall accomplish [their goals] by means of very little effort.
For their sake, I shall fully explain the division of the ritual actions (*karmavibhāga*) according to the distinctions and classifications of the qualities suitable for accomplishment.
Listen to that well and thoroughly; take it to heart, and I shall speak for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Blessed One:
"Excellent, excellent, Blessed One! Well-spoken by you are these words, which illuminate our own realization and bring about the manifestation of the qualities of mantra practice."
May the Blessed One speak on that matter, as he deems it now the right time,
out of compassion for us.
Then the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, having surveyed the entire circle of the assembly, smiled.
Then, from the mouth of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, rays of light—blue, yellow, crystal-colored, and so forth—issued forth.

As soon as those rays had issued forth, they illuminated the entire circle of the assembly and, having eclipsed all the abodes of Māra within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, they also eclipsed the light of all the stars, the luminaries, the hosts of mountains, and even the moon and sun—those two which possess such great purpose and majesty—so that they no longer shone and became devoid of luster.

They did not shine and appeared eclipsed; having rendered the radiance of all jewels, mantras, medicinal herbs, and gems lusterless, they then vanished once more into the opening of the Blessed One Śākyamuni’s mouth.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇivara was present, having assembled in that very circle of the assembly.
Having sat down, he rose from his seat with a hurried manner, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"The Buddha-Blessed Ones do not manifest a smile without cause or without condition. What, Blessed One, is the cause; what is the condition for manifesting this smile?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi:
"It is so, Vajrapāṇi! It is so!"
It is just as you say.
There is no smiling on the part of the Tathāgatas that is without cause or condition.
There is a cause; there is a condition.

Whoever shall undertake this eighth chapter, the sovereign king of sūtras from the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, which relies upon the Dharma-cloud of the means for accomplishing the rites of the practice of vidyās and the methods of attainment, and who shall enter into and follow it—whether by memorizing it, retaining it, reciting it, or having faith in it after it has been written in a book—and who shall worship it with sandalwood powder, ointments, incense, and garlands, with parasols, banners, and flags, or with various kinds of musical instruments, diverse types of music, and various percussion instruments; [for them, there shall be success].

Even those who shall obtain a mental continuum accompanied by rejoicing, or who shall experience horripilation and the arising of joy upon hearing the power and efficacy of the *vidyā*, or who shall rejoice and approve of it, or who shall undertake its practice—they have all been prophesied by me for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; they shall all become Buddhas, Blessed Ones. For this very reason, the Victors manifest a smile, and not otherwise.

First, one who has seen the ritual commitments (*samaya*), performed the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), and received initiation, having taken hold of either the root-heart mantra, the secondary heart mantra (*upahṛdaya*), or another mantra from this King of Rituals (*kalparāja*), or a single-syllable mantra, or any other according to his desire, should go to a great forest and recite it three million times while subsisting on water from fruit or eating only roots and leaves; thus he becomes one who has completed the preparatory rites.

Then, having ascended a mountain and installed the senior cloth painting facing westward, one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing eastward oneself. One should offer one hundred thousand white lotuses smeared with white saffron beneath the painting to the Blessed Śākyamuni, as well as to all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Noble Śrāvakas.
One should also burn camphor incense according to one’s means and perform worship for the sons of gods and the *nāgas*.
With whatever flowers have been obtained.

Then, at the time of midnight on the full moon of the bright fortnight during a *prātihāraka* [auspicious] period, one should prepare a fire-pit in front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*) in the shape of a lotus. Having kindled a fire with white sandalwood logs and having combined saffron and camphor, one should offer eight thousand oblations according to one's means, while maintaining the protective rite (*rakṣā*).

Then, rays of light issue forth from the Blessed One Śākyamuni, and the cloth becomes a single mass of flame on all sides. Thereupon, the practitioner, moving with great haste, should circumambulate the cloth three times, prostrate before all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Noble Śrāvakas, and take hold of the cloth at the edge where the practitioner was previously drawn. As soon as it is grasped, he flies up.
In the mere snap of a finger, he transcends the Brahma-world and arrives at the world-system Kusumāvatī,

where that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, resides, dwells, remains, and teaches the Dharma. There he beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face, hears the Dharma, and sees many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, whom he serves for a thousand great kalpas, remaining free from old age and death.

The cloth painting remains right there; it becomes empowered by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and one perceives their empowerment. One traverses hundreds of thousands of fields or manifests hundreds of thousands of bodies; one becomes endowed with the arising of manifold miraculous powers, and Noble Mañjuśrī becomes one’s spiritual friend. One becomes destined for enlightenment. Thus ends the first [chapter] from the *Aṣṭama Uttamasādhanopāyika-karmapaṭalavisara*, a section of the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvatamsaka*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Then the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, addressed the hosts of gods seated within the entire circle of the assembly:

"Listen, O noble sirs, to this most secret heart-mantra, the supreme king of great vidyās spoken by all the Tathāgatas, which serves as the means for accomplishing the practice and the mandala-mantra of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, and which is for the protection of the practitioner."
By the recitation of which all mantras become recited; this King of Vidyās, O assembly of gods, is not to be transgressed.
Even Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta was summoned by this King of Vidyās, brought under control, and rendered submissive;

how much more so, then, other Bodhisattvas? This one of great heroism destroys all mundane and supramundane mantras as well as all obstacles. Possessing singular power, he alone is declared the foremost of all mantras.
There is but one, which among syllables is declared to be the single syllable (*ekākṣara*).

And what is that single syllable? It accomplishes all aims, performs all tasks, cuts through all mantras [of adversaries], destroys the evil deeds of those who act wickedly, annihilates all sins, fulfills all mantras, brings about auspiciousness, and stands above and beyond all worldly and transcendent mantras. It is the unimpeded heart of all Tathāgatas, the fulfiller of all hopes. And what is that?
It is as follows: *Kllhīṃ*.
O friends, this is the King of Vidyās named Ekākṣara (the Single Syllable), which is the most supreme secret, efficacious for all rites, and impossible for any sentient being to transgress.

It is unassailable by any spirits (*bhūta*), an auspiciousness for all Buddhas, the accomplisher of all mantras, the lord of all worlds, the sovereign of all masters of wealth, friendly toward all who are hostile, compassionate toward all living beings, and the destroyer of all obstacles. In brief, however it is employed, it performs exactly that; it accomplishes its tasks even when not formally consecrated.
By reciting the mantra, whoever he touches becomes submissive; by consecrating garments with the mantra and wearing them, one becomes fortunate;
by consecrating a tooth-stick and chewing it, one removes toothache;
by consecrating a white *karavīra* tooth-stick and chewing it, food is obtained without having to ask for it.

For eye pain, one should grind rock salt (*saindhava*), empower it seven times with mantras, and fill the eye; this removes the eye pain. For ear pain, one should cook a small ball (*chattrikā*) made from elephant dung, produced from an elephant's body, wrapped in *kedhuka* leaves, over a gentle fire until it is well-cooked. Having made it comfortably warm and purified with rock salt powder, one should fill the ears with it after empowering it seven times.

At the moment [of application], it pacifies [the pain] for a woman at the time of childbirth, or for one with a malpresented fetus, or for one overcome by labor pains; having boiled the root of *āṭarūṣaka* in water free of living organisms, one should smear it on the region of the navel, and she will give birth easily. Or, in the case of a man with an embedded splinter, if one causes him to drink old ghee over which the mantra has been recited eight hundred times, or smears that region with it, he becomes free of the splinter at that very instant.

In cases of indigestion, cholera, or diarrhea, one should take either black salt (*sauvarcala*), rock salt (*saindhava*), or another type of salt, recite the mantra over it seven times, and consume it; one is liberated from that disease and becomes healthy on that very day.
In cases of both types of diarrhea or acute diarrhea, one should grind the fruit of the *mātuluṅga* and drink it with water free of living organisms; one is thus liberated from that affliction.

If one desires the birth of a child for a woman who is barren or incapable of bearing offspring, one should cook the root of *aśvagandhā* with cow’s ghee, grind it with cow’s milk, and then boil it again with cow’s milk. Having consecrated it twenty-five times, one should have her drink it at the time of her menses after she has bathed. Then, the householder—avoiding the wives of others and abstaining from sexual misconduct—should approach his own wife.

Whether she gives birth to her own husband, or to a son after an excess of fifteen years from the time of conception, or if there has been a suppression of many years, or if it is caused by the supreme mantras, tantras, and herbs of another, or by the binding seal of a wicked person, or if the fetus is held back, or if it arises from disease, or any other ailment—whether produced by the binding of another, or by artificial and natural poisons of both stationary and moving things, or caused by the application of all roots, mantras, and herbs by friends or enemies—one should grind together twenty-seven times aged ghee and the eye of a peacock feather.

Then, having ground it well and mixed it with sugar, one should eat a dose the size of a *harītakī* for seven days; furthermore, one should have [the patient] drink boiled milk mixed with sugar after consecrating it repeatedly. In the case of a headache, one should rub [the head] with a crow’s wing-feather over which the mantra has been recited seven times; [the patient] becomes healthy.

In diseases such as menorrhagia and others, one should cause [the patient] to drink the root of *ālambuṣā* boiled with milk and combined with the root of *nīlikā*, having consecrated it eight hundred times and stirred it with milk.

Likewise, in cases of quartan, quotidian, tertian, quaternian, continuous, and chronic irregular fevers, one should have them eat milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with ghee, having consecrated it eight hundred times;
thus they will become healthy.
Likewise, for those seized by *ḍākinī* spirits, one should empower one’s own face with the mantra one hundred and eight times and gaze upon them;
they will become restored to health.

Similarly, for those seized by all non-human, wicked, and terrible entities such as the *mātṛs*, *bālapūtanās*, *vetālas*, and *kumāragrahas*, one should empower one’s own hand one hundred and eight times and touch the head of the possessed person.

One becomes healthy by reciting it once; self-protection is achieved by reciting it twice; protection for one's companions by reciting it three times; protection for the house by reciting it four times; protection for the village by reciting it five times; and protection for those who have gone out into the range of the watch (the countryside) by reciting it six times. Thus ends the ninth chapter.
When recited one thousand times, protection for an army camp or a circle of followers is accomplished;
moreover, he performs all these and other minor rites even without having mastered the mantra.
Now, if he wishes to accomplish the minor rites that are to be performed:

Having gone to a solitary place in a secluded region—either at the source of a river flowing toward the ocean on the seashore, or on the bank of the Ganges River, or else resorting to the bank of a great river—one should construct a hut in a clean spot. Bathing three times a day, changing one’s clothes three times, observing silence, and subsisting on alms-food, barley gruel, milk, or fruit, one should recite [the mantra] thirty lakhs for the sake of attaining accomplishment (*siddhi*). Then, having seen the signs of success, one should begin the ritual practice (*sādhana*).

In that very region and at that place, having performed a great worship of the supreme cloth-painting (*paṭa*), one should offer one hundred thousand lamps for the painting, using lamps made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, filled with either *turuṣka* oil or cow’s ghee, with wicks fashioned from pieces of fresh cloth. By means of these rows of lamps ignited simultaneously on all sides, rays of light will issue forth from the painting.
Immediately upon the rays having issued forth, the cloth becomes enveloped on all sides by a garland of flames,
and from above in the sky, drums resound and the cry of "Excellent! is heard.

Then, by the Vidyādhara, appearing in a form of great haste, having given half of the previously painted cloth that had emerged from the corner of the practitioner’s cloth, and having circumambulated it and bowed to all the Buddhas, it should be taken up.
As soon as it is taken up, one flies up together with all those beings holding lamps, or they go toward a single extraordinary celestial mansion (*vimāna*).

Surrounded on all sides by *vidyādharīs* accompanied by divine musical instruments and endowed with sweet-sounding songs, instrumental music, and dance, they consecrate that practitioner in the sovereignty of the *vidyādhara* universal monarchs;
together with those who hold lamps, he becomes one who sports in the state of being free from old age and death.
He remains for a great eon (mahākalpa),
resembling the risen sun, adorned with the splendor of divine limbs and decorated with variegated garments;
they themselves become his servants (kiṅkara).
He wanders together with them;
all the kings of the Vidyādharas attend upon him as his servants,
and he becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) of the Vidyādharas.
He becomes long-lived and invincible;
he becomes supremely fortunate among all the Siddhas and gains mastery over the maidens of the Vidyādharas.
One worships all substances as well as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
consequently, in a mere instant, one goes even to the Brahma-world and does not reckon even Śakra.
How much more so for other vidyādharas?
In the end, he attains Buddhahood,
and this becomes his means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) for the noble Mañjuśrī.

Having gone to a more secluded spot at night, having entered a great forest that is solitary, devoid of people, free from attachment and social ties, and situated in a place endowed with lotus ponds and rivers, one should ascend a mountain peak or rely upon a single mountain. There, taking up either the King of Vidyās consisting of a single syllable spoken in the *Mañjuśrī-kalpa*, or one spoken by other Tathāgatas or Bodhisattvas, or any other mantra according to one’s desire, one should subsist on lotus roots and fruits or on milk products and recite the vidyā thirty-six thousand times.

At the conclusion of the recitation, having installed the supreme cloth-painting according to that very same previously described procedure, one should kindle a fire with *khadira* wood and offer thirty-six thousand lotus flowers smeared with white sandalwood and saffron—lotuses previously prepared—for the fire sacrifice (*homa*). Then, at the conclusion of the *homa*, rays of light will issue forth from the painting of the Blessed One Śākyamuni; they will illuminate the practitioner and then dissolve into the crown of his head.
Immediately upon being touched, the practitioner becomes possessed of the five superknowledges, attains the stage of a bodhisattva, possesses a divine form, wanders about as he pleases,
and lives for thirty-six kalpas.
He traverses thirty-six fields of battle and becomes embraced by the noble Mañjuśrī as his spiritual friend until the culmination of awakening and the finality of nirvāṇa.

Thus ends the second section on the ritual procedures for the supreme accomplishment (*uttamasādhanopayika-karmapaṭalavisara*), from the ninth chapter of the *Ārya-Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke once again of the supreme accomplishment of ritual actions.

In this King of Rituals (*kalparāja*), having taken up any one of the mantras, one should descend into the great river Gaṅgā and, staying upon a boat in the middle of the Gaṅgā, subsisting on a diet of milk-rice, recite [the mantra] three million times over as many days as desired. Then, at the conclusion of the recitation, one beholds all the *nāgas*.
Thereafter, one should begin the practice (*sādhana*) right there in the middle of the boat; one should have a fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*) constructed in the shape of a lotus.

Then, having performed a great worship of the cloth with *nāgakeśara* flowers, one should install the superior cloth facing westward and sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing eastward. One should offer one by one *nāgakeśara* flowers, each consecrated seven times, into a fire kindled with fuel of *khadira* wood, until thirty thousand have been offered. [The offering should consist of] *nāgakeśara* flowers purified with white sandalwood and saffron, and not others. One must not look at other *nāgas*, for they will attempt to entice one with perfected substances (*siddhadravya*), which must not be accepted.
Then, at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, he flies up together with the boat and becomes a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas;
and all the kings of the Nāgas become his attendants.
They stand by him like servants;
he lives for thirty intermediate kalpas and moves according to his own will.
With unimpeded movement, one beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face;
he touches [the practitioner] on the crown of the head, and as soon as he is touched, one becomes possessed of the five superknowledges and will certainly attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, there is another supreme ritual procedure for the accomplishment of the task:

having descended to the great river Gaṅgā, one should construct a boat from a single piece of wood made of the *bilva* tree, ensuring it is well-examined and well-crafted. Having boarded it, one should propel that vessel made of *bilva* wood by means of that very boat-pole, using a steersman who is clear-sighted, skillful, and highly expert; one should navigate it throughout the great river Gaṅgā, moving in every direction—whether crosswise or lengthwise—without leaving the river.

Therefore, having taken one or another mantra—whether it be the root mantra, the six-syllabled, the eight-syllabled, or the single-syllabled; or having taken the mantra of a wrathful messenger (krodhadūtī), a male messenger (dūta), or any other—one should install the supreme cloth-painting (paṭa) right there facing west, while oneself faces east. First, one should remain thus, and afterwards, one may act as desired. Subsisting on milk, barley-gruel, or fruit; or subsisting on water, tubers, roots, and fruit; observing silence; bathing three times a day; changing one's clothes three times; practicing pure deeds; and possessing a perfectly pure intellect.

First, in front of the cloth painting, one should recite the mantra six million times according to the previously taught and observed procedure; then, at the conclusion of the recitation, a boat bound for the great ocean appears. Thereupon, the practitioner, having gathered the necessary implements, should place them upon that very boat as previously arranged.
Therefore, one going to the great ocean should not fear,
nor should they be restrained;
for they cannot be turned back, except by the power of the practitioner.

Then, in just a moment, he enters the great ocean even if it is situated at a distance of a thousand *yojanas*, let alone a short distance; having entered that abode of rivers, he should begin the ritual of accomplishment (*sādhana-karma*) by kindling a fire with *khadira* wood in a previously prepared fire-pit or in an earthen vessel made by a potter, and offer sixty million oblations of *nāgakeśara* filaments mixed with white sandalwood and camphor, in either very small or very large quantities.

And as they were making offerings, the Rākṣasas dwelling in the city of Laṅkā, assuming many forms and crying out "Alas! Alas!", rose up; and the Nāga kings dwelling in Bhogavatī, the city of the Nāgas, also rose up, assuming various forms—some more cruel and some more gentle.
Those Nāgas and Rākṣasas spoke thus: "Arise, Blessed One! Arise, Blessed One! Be our lord!"
In this way, asuras, yakṣas, gods, mahoragas, siddhas, and all humans will attempt to entice him;
neither should he rise up nor should he be afraid.
Instead, the vidyādhara, while reciting the mantra, should threaten them with the index finger of his left hand.
Then they flee in all directions, running away by the tens of thousands and perishing;
thereafter, at the conclusion of the *homa*, that boat takes the practitioner and in an instant goes to the Akaniṣṭha realm.

It also travels to and returns from other world-systems; he becomes a knower of the minds of Bodhisattvas, possesses the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), and becomes one of great supernatural power and great majesty.
He constantly beholds the noble Mañjuśrī,

and all nāgas, all rākṣasas, all devas, all asuras, and all sentient beings become subject to him and carry out his commands— except for all the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and noble śrāvakas, as well as those who have attained mantra-siddhi in this world.
And they become well-disposed toward him with a mind of loving-kindness, granting their approval until he becomes unassailable by all beings;
furthermore, there is another supreme ritual procedure for practical application: one should have a large boat constructed from *vilva* wood.
Or one may construct a large structure using a collection of logs from a single tree;

on an island situated in the middle of the Ganges, one should place a boat there. In that boat, one hundred and twenty persons—clad in white garments, having performed protective rites, holding lamps in their hands, and embarking upon the vessel—should be stationed before the image established according to the previously described procedure for the Great Cloth (jyeṣṭhapaṭa). This is the tenth chapter of the extensive [tantra].

Then, having performed a great worship of the cloth painting, one should offer thirty-six thousand oblations of *nāgakeśara* powder mixed with saffron, white sandalwood, and camphor into a fire of *khadira* wood. At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, that boat will go to the world of Brahmā in a mere instant.
He comes at will, wanders about as he pleases,
and beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face.

As soon as he sees it, he attains the [spiritual] grounds, becomes possessed of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), and lives for a long time, remaining for a great eon (*mahākalpa*). He becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the great holders of vidyā-mantras (*mahāvidyādhara*). Furthermore, those perfected vidyādharas who hold lamps become his companions;
together with them, he wanders at will and moves according to his own pleasure.
One becomes delighted in making offerings to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
and ultimately one's attainment of Buddhahood becomes certain;
furthermore, this is the supreme means for accomplishing the application of karma.
One should accomplish this supreme rite on a riverbank or by the shore of the ocean, as well as on the Himalaya mountain, on the Vindhya king, on Mount Saha,
Malaya, Arbuda, or Gandhamādana.

One should accomplish the supreme rite on Trikūṭa, the king of mountains, as well as upon the great ocean, or on a mountain rich in trees and abounding in flowers. In these places, indeed, the mantras spoken by the Jina are perfected.
[They are also perfected] in a secluded, pure, and remote place, free from the ways of the village.
All the kings of mantras are accomplished likewise in mountain caves, and similarly in delightful, remote lodgings and seats praised by the Jinas.
In a land free from wicked beings, where the king is righteous and the people are devoted to purity and proper conduct, all the sovereign mantras attain accomplishment.
In that place where there is devotion to mother and father and which is free from the twice-born castes, the deities attain success; it is not otherwise.
On the delightful bank of the Bhāgīrathī, on the most beautiful Yamunā, on the banks of the Sindhu, the Narmadā, and the pure Candrabhāgā;
In the Kalpa, the Kāverī, the Sarasvatī, and the Sitā, the great river of the gods—these are declared by the sons of the Daśabala to be fields of spiritual accomplishment (siddhikṣetra).
In Kashmir, in the land of China, in Nepal, and likewise in Kāviśa.
In Mahācīna, indeed, all the fields of accomplishment (siddhikṣetra) without exception are found;
as are the mountains and rivers situated in the northern direction.
In those lands declared to be meritorious, where the inhabitants eat barley and wheat, and where beings are compassionate, success will certainly be achieved.
On the great mountain Śrīparvata, known as Dakṣiṇāpatha, at the shrine of Śrīdhānyakaṭaka on this earth which contains the relics of the Jina.
Indeed, mantras are swiftly accomplished there in all matters of purpose—at the Vajrāsana, at the great Caitya, and at the beautiful Dharmacakra.
The supreme sage has attained peace; there too, perfection is seen at the great shrine of Devāvatāra and at Saṅkāśya, the site of the great miracle.
In the excellent city of Kapilavastu, in the preeminent grove of Lumbinī, the kings of mantras are accomplished there, as praised by the most eminent of Jinas.
Likewise on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, always in the Sītavana grove on earth, in the city of Kusumapura, and likewise always in the delightful city of Kāśī;
In Madhura, Kanyakubja, and the city of Ujjayinī on earth; likewise in Vaiśālī, at the Caitya, and always in Mithilā on earth.
Whether they be the foremost cities, capitals, or other inhabited places, accomplishment is ordained in those that are praised as meritorious regions.
These and other regions—villages, districts, market towns, cities, and excellent, preeminent, and holy cities situated along rivers.
There, following the practice of begging for alms, one should be devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, always remaining in an open space, in the open air, or in an empty dwelling.
The tenth chapter:
One should perform the preliminary service for mantras in all rites; the practitioner of mantra should always recite the mantra everywhere in the Middle Country.

Constantly engaged in recitation and ever-disciplined, the knower of mantras is devoted to the practice of renunciation, is perfectly truthful in conduct and behavior, and delights in the welfare of all living beings.
A faithful practitioner, observing the vow, should first perform the recitation of mantras in a pure place, an excellent field, free from barbarians and thieves.
It is prescribed that [the offering] be free from all creeping creatures and the like; it should be placed in a place endowed with fruits and flowers, which is auspicious and possesses pure water.
The knower of mantras should recite all mantras; they are not proclaimed in other places, but rather in a temple, a cremation ground, or a place characterized by a single tree.
Likewise, at a solitary linga in a remote place, the knower of mantras, having performed self-protection and the protection of his companions, indeed undertakes the *puraścaraṇa*.
The practitioner of mantra, always joined with mantra, should practice the supreme mantra in a great forest, amidst a large tree rich with flowers and abounding in fruit.
Furthermore, on a mountain, by a river, in a pure and clean place near water, or on the excellent bank of a great river—
The knower of mantras should practice the mantra in these places here: in the eastern region, at Lauhitya, and at the auspicious Mahānadī river.
Likewise, in the region of Kāmarūpa, in the most excellent city of Vardhamāna, where that most meritorious and foremost of rivers flows along.
In that place, one who is pure and always engaged in recitation should worship the excellent cow; therefore, one should indeed perform the preliminary service for all ritual acts.
Likewise, at Gaṅgādvāra, always at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, and at Prayāga, one who is pure and observant of vows should indeed recite the mantra.
These are the great cremation grounds; there the reciter should always perform his recitation, as well as by rivers with pure water that are free from worms.
Therefore, the reciter, being composed, should recite the mantra there; indeed, no merit whatsoever is seen in the worldly activities occurring there.

However, under the pretext of receiving mantra-instructions, he should indeed reside there for a short time; or else, at the proper occasion, such as during a lunar eclipse, he should depart from that place.
Having reached the [proper] time, he should dwell there for some time, and not otherwise; or else, the knower of mantras who is capable should depart from there quickly.
One should always dwell upon the ground at caityas where the Sugatas have resided, as well as at all the worldly shrines that have fallen into wrong views.
A knower of mantras should always avoid other sites of pilgrimage; a master of mantras should not dwell there, for such places give rise to the path of false doctrines.

The surface of the earth is traversed by the supreme Victors, by the Pratyekabuddhas who are like rhinoceroses, by the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, and by the Śrāvakas, the sons of the supreme Victors.
The knower of mantras, reciting the mantra, should always frequent all those places with such effort as previously described; he should always practice in that location.

One who knows the mantras should recite the mantra again and again according to the prescribed rite; for by means of recitation and burnt offerings, he destroys the sins of embodied beings without exception.
Therefore, with every effort, one should recite the mantra while being well-composed in meditation.

These places have been described for all rites and for the practice of the supreme rites. In the absence of these, one who is free from doubt should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvassevā*) in any pure location whatsoever, and carry out the supreme rite suitable for accomplishment.

First, having installed the superior cloth-painting facing west, and having positioned oneself facing east, one should take earth from the top of an anthill or earth from the bank of the Ganges river, mix it with uśīra, white sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and so forth, and fashion the form of a peacock.

Having placed that [image] before the cloth painting, one should fashion a circle out of *kuśa* grass with uncut tips grown in a pure location; then, holding it with the right hand while grasping a peacock with the left hand before the cloth painting, one should perform a great worship of the painting on a night during the white fortnight of the full moon, burning camphor incense, and recite the mantra until dawn.

The tenth chapter: Then, at the time of sunrise, that clay peacock becomes the Great Peacock King. His wheel is ablaze; he himself possesses a divine body, adorned with celestial garlands, garments, and ornaments, resembling the rising sun, able to assume any form at will. Having prostrated to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and circumambulated the cloth painting, he takes hold of the painting and sits upon that peacock throne. In a mere moment, he transcends the Brahma-world.
Surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *vidyādharas*, he becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the *vidyādharas*.
He lives for sixty intermediate eons (*manvantarakalpa*),
and his movement proceeds according to his own will.
He becomes one whose movement is unimpeded and who is endowed with divine prosperity;
he beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face, he beholds him face to face; he himself is his [protection].
He becomes a spiritual friend and, in the end, attains Buddhahood.

In this manner, one should take staffs, water-pots, sacred threads, *manāśalā*, *ārocanas*, swords, iron arrows, *bhiṇḍipālas*, axes, and various other types of weapons; as well as clay figures of bipeds, quadrupeds, and specific mounts such as lions, tigers, and peacocks; or objects made from anthill earth or river mud, saturated with fragrant scents; or various types of seats, vehicles, beds, canopies, umbrellas, crowns, and ornaments; all kinds of precious gems; and all the various requisites of renunciants, such as rosaries, sandals, wooden shoes, alms bowls, robes, small bells, needles, and tools—whatever else there may be, including all implements and vessels made of flower-metal (*puṣpaloha*), or those made of anthill earth or river mud. Having washed or sprinkled all these with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and consecrated them one hundred and eight times with the purification mantra, or the single-syllable mantra, or any other mantra taught in this King of Rituals (*Kalparāja*), excluding those used for the subsidiary practice (*anusādhana*); and having performed protection for oneself and provided defense for one’s companions, being well-versed in the secret mantras and tantras; one should place them facing west in the previously specified locations. Then, having performed a great worship of the cloth painting (*paṭa*) as before, burning camphor incense for the eldest [deity], one should select one of those aforementioned artificial weapons, implements, or various items on the night of the full moon of the bright fortnight. During that night, one should recite the mantra until the time of sunrise.
In the meantime, a cloth [painting] encircled by great radiance is seen;

if a particular vehicle has been taken up by the practitioner, he should mount it and goes wherever he desires. If it is a particular ornament or a particular weapon, having taken that, he becomes a bound lord of the Vidyādharas (Vidyādharacakravartin) according to the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa.

Possessing a divine form, he travels at will, resembling the rising sun, garlanded with great radiance, his body illuminated like lightning; he becomes the lord of all *vidyādharas*, long-lived, remaining for a great eon (*mahākalpa*), surrounded by hundreds of thousands of millions of *vidyādharas*, moving through the sky with divine great jewels and *maṇi*-gems, and whatever vehicle was previously envisioned by him when he attained accomplishment, that very thing becomes his source of great power.

That very [being] becomes his vehicle, and he alone becomes his companion. Having warded off the accomplishment of others' mantras, he applies the accomplishment of his own mantra; being one whose nature is loving-kindness, desiring welfare, and constantly following him, those very specific weapons, ornaments, jewels, seats, beds, vehicles, living beings, and so forth, become eternally attached to him for the sake of great protection, defense, and concealment.
He becomes possessed of great majesty, great heroism, and a great body, and he beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face.
He gives his approval,

and with his head touched [by the other's hand], he attains the state of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) until he reaches the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍala), whereby he will certainly attain the state of the ten powers (daśabala).

He becomes worthy of worship by all sentient beings, unconquerable, and unassailable by all spirits; he is one who does not sever the lineage of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), has attained the stages (*bhūmi*), and follows the certainty of the Bodhisattvas regarding the ten powers. In brief, one who delights in supreme worship before the supreme cloth painting situated in a supreme place should perform only supreme deeds.

For the sake of attaining the state of a Vidyādhara, the power of traveling through the sky, entry into the stage of a Bodhisattva, the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), the attainment of the [Bodhisattva] stages, the ability to traverse world-systems with this very body, the fulfillment of the lineage of the Ten Powers, the direct vision of Noble Mañjuśrī, the hearing of the Dharma teaching from him whose vision is never fruitless, the non-interruption of the lineage of the Buddhas, the sequential attainment of the knowledge of the Omniscient One, the entry into the outpouring of the clouds of Dharma, the pacification of the afflictions (*kleśa*) by bearing the rain of nectar that does not dry up, the performance of activities for the benefit of the world, the protection of the eye of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, making the words of the Tathāgata fruitful, the manifestation of the methods for the accomplishment of mantra practice, and the revelation of the majestic Dharma of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Noble Śrāvakas—one should accomplish this extensive King of Ritual Manuals (*kalparāja*). This King of Cloth-paintings (*paṭarāja*) is to be accomplished according to the procedural path in all mundane and supramundane mantra rituals and all tantras, including those spoken in other ritual manuals, even when accompanied by the recitation of mantras and the foremost cloth-painting.
"What I have stated—that the accomplishment of those mantras is swift—will certainly be realized.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, the detailed section on the ritual for the supreme cloth-painting, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again surveyed the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Mañjuśrī, there exists your middle-sized cloth-painting ritual, the procedure for the means of accomplishment involving middling rites; I shall explain it in brief."
Listen to that; attend to it well and thoroughly,
and I shall speak.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One, the Teacher who has compassion for the world and delights in the welfare of all beings, speak now,
if he deems it the right time, out of compassion for us and having regard for future generations."
When Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Listen, Mañjuśrī!

First of all, [learn] the rule for ethical discipline, vows, purity, conduct, observances, recitation, fire-offerings, and meditation, established in which all ritual activities for the accomplishment of mantra-practices become fruitful and productive."
And quickly all the rites for the practice and accomplishment of mantra-conduct become fruitful and not in vain;
and quickly all applications of mantra attain success.
And what is that?
"I shall speak; listen, O Youth!
First of all, one should undertake the undertaking of the conduct of the vows and observances of knowledge (*vidyā-vrata-śīla-caryā-samādāna*).
At the very outset, one should first enter the time of instruction from the Maṇḍala Master."

Having found one who is clear-minded and intelligent, as prescribed in your *Kalparāja*, who has received the initiation of an Ācārya, is skilled in the teachings, proficient, manifestly righteous, truthful, highly energetic, grateful, firm in friendship, neither too old nor too young, free from desire for all gain and honor, a celibate practitioner (*brahmacārin*), compassionate, and who does not speak falsely out of mere greed, for the sake of enjoyment, or for the sake of conciliation—let alone for the slightest forms of greed or delusion—one who is firm in his vows, impartial toward all beings, merciful, generous by nature, having completed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), a reciter of your secret mantras, one who has mastered the sciences through prior service, who has entered your maṇḍala in the proper sequence, knows the world, knows the ritual procedures, is benevolent, desirous of action, discerning, intent on the highest good, fearless, undaunted, free from anxiety, firm in vigor, free from disease (for by whatever disease one becomes incapable of action), and born of a very high lineage.

One endowed with these qualities becomes a mandala master (*maṇḍalācārya*) or an adept (*sādhaka*) equal to him, or perhaps slightly deficient in some minor limbs [of the requirements]. Having requested such a mandala master, one should pray:
"I desire, O Master, to enter the pledge (*samaya*) of the Noble Mañjuśrī, the Great Bodhisattva Kumārabhūta, according to the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*."
"Therefore, let the Ācārya, being compassionate, benevolent, and merciful, speak for our sake out of compassion.
Then, that Maṇḍala-Ācārya, having examined the disciples according to the previously prescribed rite as before, should cause them to enter;
and having bestowed the initiation as before, he should give the mantra.

One should demonstrate the commitments (*samaya*), the secret tantras, the mudrās, and the ritual actions in their proper order and gradually; having examined [the disciple] for a long time and knowing their disposition, one should reveal the rituals of all tantras, mantras, and so forth, but not to others— this is the proclaimed rule.
Then, the disciple should offer himself and his possessions to the mandala master according to his ability, or whatever else might please the master; thereafter,
that mandala master should regard him as a son and treat him like a son.
And the enjoyments of the mother should be provided;

then that practitioner, having taken up a certain mantra and gone to a secluded place, should—in the previously specified location—perform, in detail according to the ritual prescribed for the mandala, the *peyāla* (the intermediate rites), including the invocation, dismissal, lamps, perfumes, incense, offerings, and food-oblations (*bali*) with those very mantras. Having invoked [the deity] and offered the water of respect (*argha*) and a seat, he should perform the recitation (*jāpa*) three times at each junction of the day (*trisandhyā*), bathing three times and changing his clothes three times. Therein, "junction-time" (*sandhyākāla*) refers to the period beginning from the end of the night until the sun has risen to the height of a yoke.

In this context, the first twilight is said to occur at midday when the sun is positioned in the sky at a distance of one *yuga* [four cubits]; this solar disc is called the middle twilight (*madhyasandhyā*).
Furthermore, at the time of sunset, when only one *yuga* remains, it is called the third twilight.
Thus.
One who is endowed with moral conduct and vows, a skillful and learned teacher, born of a high and noble family, and possessed of firm vigor in every respect.
Devoted to mantra and tantra, with an intellect skilled in all undertakings,
subtle and proficient in the knowledge of mantras, he is always a bearer of the dharmadhātu.
I am one of great energy and splendor, indifferent to worldly dharmas;
I have faith in the dharma of the supreme sages, while being shunned by those of the world.
Having performed the recitation, knowing discernment, and following the preliminary service,
he is a knower of the mantra of Mañjughoṣa, intent upon the perceived signs of attainment.
The eleventh chapter:
One who knows the application of worldly mantras spoken by the Buddha,
having performed protection and possessing firm strength, should always be devoted to pure conduct.
I follow in every way the path taught by the Buddha;
I am diligently engaged in the recitation of mantras, which are praised by the Jina.
He is always [certain] regarding the fruits of actions seen in this world, and likewise in the next world.
One should be fearful of all evils, even those as small as an atom.
Pure, skillful, not indolent, intelligent, and pleasing to behold—
such are the mantras proclaimed by those possessing the ten powers, as well as by the sons of the Victors.
Those worldly mantras belonging even to the two families of Vajra and Antaka—
for them he constantly exerts effort, being one who upholds the meaning of their texts and treatises.
Free from disease, not lacking in power, devoid of both old age and childhood, having mastered the mantras, well-protected, and swift in action in every respect.
Not procrastinating, likewise modest, and especially skilled in discerning gestures;
a celibate student of great wisdom, wandering alone and avoiding attachment.
In this Mañjubhāṣita, the hero who has received initiation,
who is engaged in the concluding rites of recitation, and who likewise possesses mastered knowledge;

Possessing great majesty, knowing the world, and contemplating the truth of the states of existence, he is devoted solely to the highest good; he is a giver, ever intent on the welfare of living beings.
Thus, one should always indeed request a distinguished preceptor;
the mandala of mantras written by him attains accomplishment.
When the consecration is thus bestowed by him, it yields great fruit;
one who desires spiritual accomplishment, or his disciples, should always honor him like a sage.
The disciples must diligently carry out his word, which is not to be transgressed;
they should provide him with enjoyments according to their available means.
Whether it be a very small amount or a great deal, that by which one attains satisfaction—
for the sake of body and life— one should regard the mind as the father does the body.
In the Mūlakalpa, likewise, the disciple who knows the Dharma should give wealth to the preceptor;
he shall obtain fame, accomplishment, as well as long life and health.
The disciple who honors that guru attains an abundant goal;
moreover, his mantras become effective through the teacher's demonstration of the path of ritual procedure.
Through serving them, honoring them, and even worshipping them,
all the Buddhas as well as the sons of the Victorious Ones are likewise satisfied.
All the gods are always pleased when there is proper honor shown toward the guru;
this has been told in its entirety regarding gurus who perceive the mantras.
First, at the very beginning, by the practitioner who has entered the samaya,
whether it be a person equal to him, similar to him, or even superior;
A guru must never be disregarded, whether he be alone or accompanied by many;
for even by him, instruction is always given within that very system.
This should be performed for one who has attained success in mantra, as it is shown according to the capacity of sentient beings;
one should not harbor envy toward this disciple previously prepared.
The eye follows the oil; for those embodied beings who are well-established, the teacher should make that very person his disciple, for the sake of the disciple.
Where there is a succession of affection that follows one another and is considered a continuous stream of oiliness,
one should indeed impart the mantra there, as if upon a mountain range possessing a continuous flow of moisture.
In this manner, the teacher [should behave] toward the disciple, and the disciple likewise toward the sight of the guru;
both should always be eager due to the presence of awe.
For them, the path indeed consists in the constant observation of mantra practice;
both the knower of mantras and his son follow it fruitfully, like father and son.
Both the disciple and the teacher always attained steadfastness and contentment;
likewise, a son who is devoted to dharma should always be protected with great effort.
The true nature (dharmatā) of the Buddhas is indeed uninterrupted among them;
therefore, in their absence, one should bestow the mantra as prescribed upon those who are without a protector.
And the eleventh chapter:
For poor beings, and especially for those who are weak,
the practice of mantra is superior even for all other beings.
One should perform [this] at all times— whether in inferior, superior, or middling circumstances—
and always, in all matters, one should act for the sake of benefiting others.
One should bestow [the gift] even upon those who desire it, for the destiny and birth [of beings] depend on their actions;
and by the disciple himself, having received the mantra from him according to the prescribed rule.
One who desires accomplishment should strive in that which is supreme for others, following only the path taught by him and not otherwise.
Having bowed with his head as if to a father, he should depart from there at his pleasure;
then, having gone to a solitary place, he should recite the mantra concisely.
But the mendicant, whose livelihood consists of alms and who observes silence while reciting [mantras] three times a day,
should act as previously described, proceeding according to the path.
Then, following that [practice], one who serves [the teacher] should frequent places,
shrines, the great forest, mountain peaks, and likewise pure riverbanks.
In a cow-pen, or even in a great city, in a secluded place free from people, in an empty temple, under a tree, in a solitary hut, or on a mountain peak.
On the delightful banks of a great body of water, or on a sandy shore, or at a lamp-lighted spot,
and in various other charming locations previously specified.
In these and other locations, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind,
accompanied by friends who possess the proper characteristics and are experts in the meaning of the mantra, its principles, and logic.
[He was surrounded] by those who knew the truth of gestures and facial expressions, who were like himself and his equals,
heroic, having conquered attachment, virtuous, and patient.
In this teaching proclaimed by the Victor, those who possess faith should practice the mantra-conduct together with companions who are praiseworthy, endowed with the [proper] marks, and patient.
For him, all rites are accomplished without even effort;
having risen from bed in the morning and bathed in pure water, O Caitra.

In the *Śrīmūlakalpa*, it is stated that the knower of mantras, having rubbed his body with powdered clay and cow dung, should likewise bathe in water that is free of living beings and originates from rivers or great lakes.
Then, having performed the ritual filling with mantras, the practitioner of recitation, with a disciplined mind, should bathe in clean and stainless water, and must not let the proper time pass by.
Then, having risen and stood on the bank, he washed his hands with clay twenty-one times— seven, seven, and again seven.
Having sat down there, one should then use a tooth-stick;
having discarded the tooth-cleanser, one should then pay homage to the ascetic.
Having approached the Lord of the World, one should perform a delightful worship;
having praised him again and again with various offerings of hymns,
the reciter should likewise offer fragrant flowers and wealth to the Teacher.
Having bowed his head to the Buddhas and their disciples, he then made a confession before those Lords of the World,
and having offered food there in the middle, in front of the cloth painting.
Seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, remaining there in a composed state of meditative concentration,
one should diligently perform the recitation (*japa*) with that rosary; indeed,
one should recite only the specific mantra as received at that time, and not any other mantra.
The practitioner of the vow should always avoid what is excessively low or excessively high; in moderate rites, he should always mutter the mantra with a moderate voice.
He should carefully avoid speech that is too loud, as well as any other [inappropriate] speech.
The medium [mode] is praised for medium activities and is extolled by the Victors;
one should always recite with a voice that is neither too high nor too low— the medium mode—
which was joined with excellence by all the Buddhas of the past.

One should not recite [the mantra] in the vicinity of others or on a path where others perform their work; rather, one who knows the Self should always recite the mantra of medium length in a secluded place.
Furthermore, when engaged in such recitation, someone may become well-versed in the meaning of the mantra.
One who desires middling accomplishment should recite that mantra further;
thus ends the eleventh chapter of the extensive [work], for one who has heard the true meaning of the mantra when free from [the cycle of] birth.
In solitude, free from the bustle of others, the reciter should mutter the mantra during the fourth part of the night, or for half of that time,
until the solar disc has risen to the height of a yoke, glowing with a coppery-red hue.
Thus has the first twilight been described by the best of sages; the middle [twilight] is proclaimed to be four cubits, or the distance of a *yuga*.
Therefore, one should cease the recitation of the mantra from the sky [at that point], as well as when the sun rises for Diti.
Then, having ceased the recitation of mantras and performed the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*), the observer of the vow offered the water of honor (*argha*).
Thereafter, he remained constantly engaged in this teaching of the Sage,
performing the recitation of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other scriptures.
The books known as the *Daśabhūmika* should always be honored and recited; having approached them at that time, one should indeed bow to the preeminent Jinas,
as well as to one's own mantra and the Lord of Mantras, and only thereafter should one go about one's livelihood.
Acting in accordance with the proper time, eating at the proper time, having conquered his senses,
being righteous and diligent as a practitioner within the serene teaching of the Buddha,
he should enter among the villages, observing silence and always devoted to pure conduct.
The reciter should always enter for alms among righteous beings,
in water that is free of living organisms and considered pure,
and among those who possess right view, whose wives are virtuous, and who are devoted to the Buddha’s teaching.
In such a family, one seeking alms should always receive alms;
just as a well-armored warrior may enter the perils of battle,
he constantly crushes his enemies and is not slain by his foes.
In this way, a minister who lives on alms should always enter a village;
having seen pleasing forms and indeed auspicious sounds,
he should contemplate the unattractive and the attractive for the purpose of pacifying passion.

Having seen the physical body among women, adorned with the conduct of youth, one should contemplate it as impure and foul-smelling, as loathsome as putrid urine and the like; drenched in worms, situated in a cemetery, impermanent, and suffering— such is the physical body.
There, the foolish and deluded indeed wander through the five states of existence,
bound by the threads of karma that have shone for a long time; veiled by ignorance, they are deluded, like those blind from birth, with suffering as their cause.
There, beings of perverted intellect who are attached and colored by manifold forms through various desires for action sink down;
they are seen mounted upon long swings, moving back and forth.

Indeed, those beings who are devoted to impurity, whose movements and gestures are like those of a dancer, sink for a long time upon the path; born from the waters of the ocean of existence, they take on the form of a water-wheel.
For them, there is indeed no end to birth, which is submerged in the waters of suffering; likewise,
the root of suffering is declared by the Buddhas, as well as by the Śrāvakas, Bodhisattvas, and Pratyekabuddhas, to consist solely of women.
This great ocean, difficult to dry up and unshakeable— the sea of existence where beings, their consciousness deceived by women,
sink— [leads to] hell, the animal realm, and the world of Yama along with the asuras.
Whether in the human world or the divine, they constantly wander everywhere through the celestial realms; yet, powerless and deceived by women,
they sink into the great mire of the prison of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Foolish men attached to women are like jackals drawn to a corpse;
those beings who are constantly delighted therein indeed endure intense suffering,
having destroyed their pure virtues despite having entered the Buddha's teaching.

Those who are devoted to the recitation of the mantra, possessed of great vision, wise, radiant, and who have conquered their enemies— they ward off all sufferings in the ocean of existence; for them, no suffering exists.
The eleventh chapter:
For those who are self-restrained, who know the truth of Brahman, who worship their gurus and deities,
and who are devoted to their mothers and fathers, no suffering exists among women.

To those who follow the ultimate truth, the female body is impermanent, suffering, and empty; it is a tumor and a thorn for those who recite mantras. One who is lustful, foolish, and of corrupt intellect does not flee from cyclic existence.

One who is constantly addicted to women finds no accomplishment; for such a person of immoral conduct, there is neither the highest attainment, nor the middling attainment, nor even the lowest attainment in this world as a reciter.
The Lord of Sages has not prescribed the accomplishment of mantras for one who is immoral,
nor has he shown the path that leads to the city of Nirvāṇa;
how indeed could mantras succeed for a fool in this contemptible state?
Furthermore, for that person of immoral conduct in this world, there is no happy rebirth, nor indeed the heights of heaven, nor is he destined for happiness;
how much less could he attain the accomplishment of the mantras spoken by the Victorious One?
Just as a palmyra tree that has been cut down at its head is incapable of becoming green again or producing new sprouts,
so too is the accomplishment of mantra proclaimed for the fool in this world.
One who is immoral, engaged in evil deeds, constantly attached to women,
and associated with non-virtuous friends— how could such a person succeed in the king of mantras?
Therefore, one should always be self-controlled, a practitioner of recitation, and not consider the faults of women.

One should avoid attachment to them; success is ordained through them, for success is not said to belong to others. The wise man, pure, skillful, and free from attachment, delights in those women who are undistracted and free from infatuation.
One who is of noble birth, firm and brave, friendly, pleasing to behold,

and a knower of the discernment between dharma and adharma— for such a one, success is indeed not difficult to attain; thus engaged and knowing the mantra, he should enter a village for the sake of alms.

Having gone to whichever previously designated place he prefers, he should eat there according to the *Śrīmūlakalpa*. Having gone to a suitable and pure location, one of pure mind should set down his alms-bowl.
Then, having gone outside from that dwelling and washed his feet, he should first wash only his shins in water free of living organisms.

Secondly, having embraced and rubbed the shank with the left hand, and having again performed the rite with the right hand (apasavya), one should wash the hands with seven pure and clean clods of earth previously set aside. Then, taking purified and clean cow-dung from a Kapila cow— renowned for its excellence— from a vessel that is clean, stainless, and sanctified by mantras, and mixing it with water free of living organisms, one should fashion the maṇḍala of the Teacher.
First, one should especially construct for the Best of Sages [Śākyamuni] a mandala measuring one cubit; second, for the Lord of the Excellent Mantra [Avalokiteśvara]; and third, for the Family Deity.
Whenever the mantra-reciter performs this, he should always do so again [in this manner]. Fourth, it is proclaimed as the enjoyment for all sentient beings.
Here, in the south, one should always construct that square mandala for the Lokanātha and for the Three Jewels.
The second [mandala] is for the Pratyekabuddhas, and the third is for the sons of the Ten-Powered One (Buddhas). Thus, these seven mandalas are square on all sides.

One should construct them daily, measuring one cubit or half a cubit, in a secluded place; then the reciter, by doing so every day, effects the destruction of evil. Then, having risen, the mantra-practitioner should diligently wash both hands and perform ritual sipping (upaspṛśya) in pure, clean water that is free from living organisms.
When that [water] has been carefully brought in a pure vessel that is stainless and clean— from a great lake, a mountain spring, a pond, or a flowing river;

having arrived at a pure place and been drawn up by the hands of pure beings— the mantra-practitioner, having sipped it again two or three times, should always touch his face, as well as his ears, eyes, nostrils, and arms.
The Eleventh Chapter. One should touch [the head] at the crown of the head and the region of the navel with auspicious water;

one should perform this five or seven times according to the ritual rules for all [these acts]. Having become pure and endowed with the proper conduct of purification, the practitioner of recitation (*jāpin*), taking his alms-bowl, should go to a body of water.
Wherever the water flows or originates, whether from rivers, springs, or other sources, he should always wash his alms-bowl there.

Then, having risen, he should go back to the monastery or his dwelling; he should proceed to that place where he previously stayed and which is under his control. Having gone to that location, the reciter should set down his bowl; then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya), he should quickly take up the bowl once again.

One should offer the oblation to the Teacher (Śāstṛ) in a vessel made of clay, leaf, silver, gold, copper, or even bark. Having offered it, the knower of mantras should again recite his own mantra, O King of Mantras. On the specific lunar day, one should approach those who are suffering and give according to one's ability. One should not give too much as an offering in every case; the knower of mantras should not act in a way that is detrimental to himself, but rather remain disciplined in all respects.

If one maintains [the practice] with a stomach as the only measure of size, one will always be free from the affliction of hunger and thirst, and thus capable of accomplishing the purpose of the mantra.
Neither one who eats excessively nor one who eats too little is capable of following the mantra. For this very reason, the Lord of Jinas has declared for all embodied beings:
"Food is the sustenance of sentient beings; by means of it do humans live, as do gods, asuras, gandharvas, nāgas, yakṣas, and kinnaras."

Neither *rākṣasas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *bhūtas*, *ustārakas*, nor *sagrahas* exist—there is no one at all who can look upon those who are focused in meditation. The Tathāgata has declared that there are beings known as those who consume gross material food and those who consume subtle nourishment. The divine beings of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) subsist on the food of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), while the gods of the formless realm (*ārūpya*) indeed enjoy the fruit of *samādhi*.

In the *Śrīmūlakalpa*, it is proclaimed that beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) subsist on "gone-food" (*gatvāhāra*). Likewise, in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), sentient beings consume various kinds of food.

Among the gods, asuras, and mortals, some subsist on food consisting of mental desire (*kāmika*), while others subsist on morsel-food (*kabalikāhāra*). For this very reason, the Lords of Jinas have declared through the causes of the Dharma that the sustenance of all sentient beings is proclaimed to be dependent upon food. One who is constantly disciplined in recitation (*jāpin*) should eat only in moderation.
For one who is able to practice the mantras and is established in moderation regarding food, being purified in conduct and skilled in the life of a celibate student,

and possessing knowledge of the proper measure of food— for such a person, success is not difficult to attain. Just as a cartwright applies oil to the axle of a cart for the sake of its long-term stability and to enable it to bear heavy loads, even so does the mantra-knower, the master of mantras, provide food for the sake of stability.

The reciter of mantras should always nourish even a corpse for the sake of its recovery or non-decay; for the purpose of accomplishing mantras and as a cause for the equipment of awakening, one should likewise recite the mantra among mortals for the sake of favoring the world. For this very reason, the most excellent Sage of great splendor, named Kāśyapa, spoke this mantra in the past on this earth for the sake of the welfare of all beings.

This was spoken for the sake of all suffering beings in the world—those who are wretched, distressed by poverty, exhausted by toil, and afflicted; for the welfare of living beings wandering in saṃsāra, one should recite this supreme mantra for the purpose of providing sustenance to beings. Listen, all you Śrāvakas and those who rely upon the Bodhisattvas: receive this great speech, this mantra that destroys disease.

"Those beings who are afflicted by the disease of hunger, and those who are thirsty—for the sake of pacifying all suffering, listen, O you who desire the stages [of practice]! Having spoken thus, that Kāśyapa, who was like a sage and possessed of great splendor, addressed the Lord with a joyful mind. The eleventh chapter of the extensive [tantra]: "Speak the mantra, O Knower of Dharma, King of Dharma, Great Sage!"
"The time for compassion toward sentient beings has arrived.

Having spoken thus, the sages should recite the mantra in detail: With a voice like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, sounding like a drum or a cloud, possessing the tone of Brahmā and great heroism, the Jina is indeed the foremost of the Brahmas. Let the hosts of spirits who have gathered here listen!
"Whether they be legless, many-legged, two-legged, or four-legged—in brief, for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall now proclaim the mantra that brings about the arising of merit.
Sentient beings of the past, future, and those present who have come here—in brief, I shall speak; listen, you who desire the truth! Thus: "Homage to all Buddhas whose teaching is unimpeded."
"Namely: 'O Gaganagañja, bring [it] from the sky! Quickly, very quickly! Remember the pledge! O attractor, do not delay! Accomplish for me whatever is desired! Svāhā!
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Kāśyapa became silent."

In that interval, by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the words of the spells and mantras were recited in full detail; the entire sky was seen as a cloud completely filled with great food, and the whole of this triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system was seen with the vault of the sky covered by a cloud of food.
To whatever being desired food according to their own inclination, whatever nourishment they wished for, that very thing was provided to them.

For the purpose of satisfying hunger and quelling the suffering of thirst, food according to their respective desires was provided for the act of eating; and for those who were thirsty, a stream of water endowed with the eight qualities fell right there, exactly as desired.
And at that time, at that very moment, all sentient beings had their every suffering and affliction pacified and all their thirst removed.

That entire assembly, struck with wonder and filled with joy, having rejoiced and approved of what the Blessed One had spoken, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and vanished right there.
Both the Blessed One Kāśyapa and the Tathāgata dwelt in the dwellings of a Tathāgata; and this has now been spoken and approved by me as well, the Blessed Śākyamuni.

In this supreme king of manuals, the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, for the benefit of all sentient beings and for the purpose of removing hunger and thirst—especially for those who recite mantras—first of all, the reciter must accomplish this mantra.
If one is unable to go about begging for alms, one should ascend a mountain peak and recite it six hundred thousand times, subsisting on the three white foods or consuming only milk.

Then, having installed the middle-sized painting (*paṭa*) of the noble Mañjuśrī at that very same mountain peak and having performed a great worship as before, one should present a most magnificent offering (*bali*).

Having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood fuel using this very mantra spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, one should offer eight thousand oblations of fresh *audumbara* wood fuel—measuring one span (*vitasti*) and smeared with curd, honey, and ghee—or else of *śrīphala* wood fuel.
Then, at the time of midnight, a great circle of black clouds and wind will arrive; one must not be afraid,
nor should one rise and depart.
One should perform self-protection and the binding of the mandala with the eight-syllable heart-mantra of Noble Mañjuśrī, as well as for one's companions, as previously described. Then,
that black whirlwind of wind disappears,
and all those women, adorned with every ornament, garlanded with light, and illuminating the directions, appear before the practitioner.
"Arise, O Mahāsattva!
I have attained success," [the deity] says and departs; then the practitioner should offer the required gift with scented water mixed with *jāti* flowers.

Then, she vanishes right there on that very day; and together with her own twenty-five companions, or with whoever else she desires, she provides whatever food is wished for and supplies all necessary articles according to one's desire.

Then the practitioner, having dismissed [the deity] and offered the argha, should circumambulate the cloth-painting three times, take up the painting, prostrate to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and proceed to a desired location suitable for practice as previously described—a great forest, a mountain peak, or a place devoid of humans.
There, one should dwell having constructed a shelter with companions;
while dwelling in that place, one should perform rites such as traveling through the sky.

Then, the practitioner, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass as before, having installed the middle cloth-painting (*paṭa*), and having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood as before, should offer eight thousand oblations of white flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee at the three junctions of the day for twenty-one days.
Then, at the time of midnight, at the conclusion of the fire offering, one beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face;
he grants the desired boon,
whether it be the power of traveling through the sky, invisibility, or the stages of a bodhisattva.

This eleventh chapter on the ritual procedures bestows the state of a Pratyekabuddha, the state of a Śrāvaka, or the possession of the five supernormal powers; it grants long life, great sovereignty, or great wealth; or it provides the favor of kings; or, in brief, whatever one desires when practicing the mantras together with the noble Mañjuśrī—all that it gives.
Whatever one asks for, that he bestows; or he obtains all perfected substances,
and he performs the summoning of great beings.
"In brief, whatever is spoken, he performs it all; he either purifies past karma or expiates transgressions," so said the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
Furthermore, there is another intermediate method for the ritual application.

First, in a distinguished place, a pure location, or on the sandy bank of a river, having performed everything as before, one should install the cloth painting facing west and sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing east. The details should be carried out extensively;
one should recite the mantra six hundred thousand times at the three junctions of the day.
And upon the completion of the recitation, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *karṇikāra* flowers mixed with white sandalwood or saffron.

As before, having likewise kindled the fire, at the conclusion of the *homa*: if the cloth trembles, one attains the status of a mantra-master (*mantrin*); if rays of light shine forth from the cloth or if rays emerge, one attains kingship; if the cloth is enveloped in a garland of flames on all sides, one attains the kingship of the Caturmahārājakāyika gods; if speech issues forth from the cloth, one attains the three [states] of lordship over the Tridaśa, namely the state of Śakra; if the teaching of the Dharma issues forth from the cloth, one attains the state of a Bodhisattva who is a lord of the three realms; and upon touching the cloth with the crown of the head, one attains the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), reaches the seven stages (*saptabhūmi*), and is destined for the gradual attainment of the ten powers (*daśabala*).
