Then, when the practitioner has accomplished the mantra spoken by the Blessed One Kāśyapa and has attained the means for warding off hunger and thirst, he must practice the dharma suitable for accomplishing the purpose of the mantra-conduct according to that very same procedure and with those very same implements; otherwise, there is no success.

In this way, the practice of following the gradual mantra-conduct should be performed with equanimity; it will certainly succeed, including the ritual implements, medicinal herbs, and the remaining jewels and gems as previously described.
In that place at that time, the mantra-knower, the reciter of mantras, whose mind was focused on the prescribed ritual, being pure by birth, [ate] white rice.
Having eaten with a satisfied mind and with his senses fully nourished, he should always take that remnant of the alms-bowl and go to a river of auspicious waters.
Having set it aside in a secluded spot, the observer of the vow gave it to the animals;
and having given it to the animals, he diligently washed the bowl.
Furthermore, one should carefully subject the earthenware vessel to baking; then, one should prepare the remaining vessels so that they are free from oil and free from meat.
Having completely renounced even the scent [of food], the excellent sage should use the remaining vessel;
he should not eat in that very bowl in which he wanders for alms.
One should never eat solid foods there; however, one should always avoid eating fruits from lotus leaves or those originating from water lilies.
The minister should avoid and not eat *saugandhika* flowers,
nor those leaves which grow on the *kaumuda*, the *plakṣa*, or the *udumbara* trees.
One should not use leaves from the *vaṭa* tree, nor from *karṇaśāka*, *go*, or *gulmin* trees;
one should avoid that tree with great care, nor should one dig up its wood.
One must not strip off the leaves from *nāgakesara* trees.
Nor should one ever eat at any time what has been avoided by the wise; nor should one, out of delusion, ever taste the leafy food of sages who dwell in leaf-huts.
The mantra-practitioner falls from his commitment by eating from their leaves;
the practitioner should not eat food there using other plates,
but rather those made of clay, copper, silver, or gold.
Likewise, he always took his food from vessels made of crystal and stone.
Nor did he eat from the backs of leaves, nor from the palms of his hands— those leaves produced as offerings for the Enemy of Māra, the Son of the One Possessing Ten Powers.
The practitioner of recitation should avoid those who are Pratyekabuddhas and likewise those who are Śrāvaka individuals; he should not step over their leaves nor cross over them with his feet.
The mantra-practitioner should carefully refrain from taking various kinds of cakes, as well as drinks and food, all of which have been offered.
The eleventh chapter:
A practitioner of recitation should always avoid that which has been offered to the Jinas, the followers of the Jinas, as well as the eminent Śrāvakas, or even to the Three Jewels.
Even the slightest mantra does not succeed for embodied beings who [neglect it];
how much less so the divine [mantra] which is esteemed as the source of all auspiciousness and supreme well-being?
Neither the rites for nourishment nor those for pacification—which fulfill all desires—will succeed for one who eats the sacrificial offerings after having offered them.
The mantras of one who is pure, skillful in character, compassionate, and likewise righteous— indeed, of one who delights in the practice of purity— succeed everywhere.
Having first given food to all there, the reciter should not eat;
he should not eat any other food, but should eat only that which has been offered by others.
One who knows the mantra and partakes of even a very small amount of food that has been offered by oneself— success stands within the hand of such a person who is thus engaged.
By this procedure, the practitioner who observes the vow should take his food;
for this is highly praised by the sages in the accomplishment of all mantras.
I have briefly explained the procedure prescribed by rule for all acts of eating;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the mantra for the purification of everything.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*upaspṛśya*), the reciter should always recite this mantra;
then, having recited it seven times for the purification of the body, the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) [should proceed].
O assembly of beings and deities, listen to the detailed explanation of its meaning; having reflected upon all matters to be done, the sage should utter this mantra.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
It is as follows: “Oṃ oṃ, O destroyers of all sins!
Destroy, destroy all that is employed by the wicked! Recall the pledge! Hūṃ jaḥ svāhā!”
With this mantra, whatever rice-meat or other food one consumes should be consecrated with the mantra before eating.
Having eaten and performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana), one should, as before, stroke the entire body starting from the crown of the head; then one should rest.
Having rested for a moment, a half-watch, or three-quarters of a watch, one should then pay homage to the cloth painting (paṭa) and recite the books of the True Dharma of all the Buddhas.

One should recite any one of these: the Noble Prajñāpāramitā, the Noble Candrapradīpa Samādhi, the Noble Daśabhūmika, the Noble Suvarṇaprabhāsottama, the Noble Mahāmāyūrī, the Noble Ratnaketudhāriṇī, or the Noble Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa. One should recite it until [the image] reaches the size of the sun.

Then, having dedicated [the merit] and recited [the text] according to one's ability, one should remove the book or cover it with clean cloth; having prostrated before the True Dharma, one should then descend to a riverbank or go to a great body of water to bathe. Having taken clay from a dry place and consecrated it seven times with the mantra of the tree, one should pour water upon it with this mantra.
With which one?
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
It is as follows: Oṃ sāra! Bind the wicked! Paralyze them! Hūṃ! To the bearer of the blue lotus, who assumes the form of a sporting youth! Bind, bind! Remember the pledge! Sphaṭ, sphaṭ! Svāhā!

Having performed protection with this mantra, one should perform the binding of the directions, the binding of the mandala for one’s companions, the binding of the mouth, the summoning of all the wicked and non-wicked, and the binding of the semen (*śukra*), by tying a thread over which the mantra has been recited seven times around the waist and encircling it on all sides.

At all times, during the entire period of recitation as well as at the time of bathing, one should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times for the purpose of destroying and pacifying evil obstacles.
Thereafter, one accomplishes all rites.
In all rites, one should perform the placement of the great mudrā with five crests (*pañcaśikha*).
She accomplishes everything; it does not happen otherwise.
Then the practitioner, having taken earth, cow dung powder, and so forth, should bathe as he pleases.
He should bathe with water that is free of living organisms;
indeed, in all rites and at all times, he should act only with [substances] free of living organisms.

Then, having bathed with applications of clay and cow dung, or other special implements possessing fragrant scents, one should not discharge saliva, urine, feces, or the like into the water, nor should one discharge a stream of water.

Nor should one play, even while feeling compassion for all sentient beings; rather, one should regard them as being oppressed by feelings of suffering, empty and selfless, like a mother distressed by the pain of separation from her child.

Thus, the knower of mantras, though lacking in means of accomplishment, should behold himself situated in the depths of the ocean of saṃsāra, obstructed by such afflictions as being bound, falling, being scattered, and being destroyed;
and having observed himself as one without a dwelling, without mantras, without refuge, and with a dejected mind.
One should meditate while standing in water up to the neck, or while standing in water up to the navel;
indeed, having established one-pointedness of mind right there in the midst of the water.

First of all, there is a great lotus stalk, endowed with great lotus flowers, adorned with great lotus petals, made of jewels of beautiful appearance, with a base (*gaṇḍa*) fashioned from lapis lazuli, leaves of emerald, filaments of ruby, and a thousand petals of crystal; it is fully blossomed, adorned with blossoming *jātasphaṭika* flowers. This is the eleventh section of the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*). Upon it, one should meditate on the Lord Buddha seated upon a lion-throne made of jewels, adorned with many gems, covered with a pair of fine cloths. One should meditate on him teaching the Dharma, golden-white in color, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, adorned with a halo of light, of immense proportions as if scraping the very sky, and seated in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

To the right, the noble Mañjuśrī, endowed with all excellent ornaments, stands—not seated—holding a fly-whisk (*cāmara*) for the Blessed One; his body is reddish-white or the color of powdered saffron. And to the left is the noble Avalokiteśvara, white as an autumn reed, with a fly-whisk held in his hand.

Thus, there are eight bodhisattvas: Ārya Maitreya, Samantabhadra, Kṣitigarbha, Gaganagañja, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Apāyajaha, Ārya Vajrapāṇi, and Sudhana—these ten bodhisattvas [are to be visualized] on the right. On that same spot, one should meditate upon eight pratyekabuddhas: Candana, Gandhamādana, Ketu, Suketu, Sitaketu, and Aṣṭaupāriṣṭanemi. Also in that very place are the eight great śrāvakas.
Namely: the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, Gavāmpati, Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, Pilindavatsa, the noble Rāhula, Mahākāśyapa, and the noble Ānanda.
One should meditate on an infinite community of monks in the presence of these great śrāvakas.
One should meditate on an infinite number of pratyekabuddhas in the presence of the pratyekabuddhas.
And one should meditate upon the infinite assembly of bodhisattvas in the eight stations of the great bodhisattvas.
One should meditate upon the sky thus adorned, accompanied by the great circle of the assembly.

Standing in water reaching up to one's navel, one should perform worship of the Blessed One with various kinds of flowers—both divine and human—including *māndārava*, *mahāmāndārava*, *padma*, *mahāpadma*, *dhātu-kārika*, and *indīvara* blossoms; and with various large-sized heaps of flowers of immense proportions.

One should perform a delightful worship for all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas with powders, parasols, banners, and flags—both divine and human—as well as with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lamps.
In this manner, all offerings and services, such as bali-offerings, incense, and food, whether divine or human, should be presented.
Furthermore, one should meditate on oneself being illuminated by a ray of light issuing from the *ūrṇā* (the hair-tuft between the eyebrows) of the Blessed One Śākyamuni.

For the practitioner who recites the mantra immediately upon entering this meditation, there is the attainment of the fruit of Brahma-merit, or he will certainly become destined for the three [vehicles].
Thus have these meditations been described by the foremost of the world for the sake of the welfare of all beings and for the benefit of practitioners of mantra.
Then, for the benefit of all mantra-practitioners, the Sage, the most excellent and supreme among beings, taught this foremost meditation at the beginning of the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa.
When that first mandala-shape of aversion has been well explained,
then the second mandala and, beyond that, the third according to the system of mantras [should be taught].
In the first [case], there is the highest accomplishment; likewise, in the middle, the supreme;
and in the lowest, the inferior accomplishment—thus spoke the bull among sages.
Likewise, the banner-like meditation is categorized as superior, middling, and inferior;
in brief, that meditation is the destroyer of all sins.
The wise should not proceed beyond this form of meditation;
for his mantras will indeed reach perfection when they are well-established in this meditation.

Having meditated upon the meditation as described according to the ritual according to one's desire, the practitioner of recitation should indeed dismiss the mantra there, having offered the water-offering (argha) as is convenient.
Having crossed that flood of water, one should then proceed at ease to the previously designated place, which is prescribed by rule and well-restrained.
Then the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra as previously prescribed;
having performed the rite, he should dismiss the mantra and the deities who were invoked there.
Then, having likewise performed the protection of his companions,
he— being skilled, knowing the true principles of ritual action, and devoted to the performance of rites— is considered [fit for the task].
Having praised the Supreme Person with various offerings of hymns,
as well as his own mantra, the Lord of Mantras, the Śrāvakas, and the Pratyekabuddhas who possess the rhinoceros-like horn.
Then, rising again from that seat, the mantra-reciters [beheld] the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, who are capable of bestowing grace upon the three worlds.
Having gone far from his dwelling to a place sheltered from the wind,
he should discharge phlegm, snot, urine, and excrement.
During the day one should face north, and at night one should face south;
the practitioner of mantra recitation should never contemplate worldly affairs while in those positions.
The eleventh chapter:
One should not recite there a mantra spoken by one's own kula for its specific rite;
rather, one should sit upon the ground, distinguished by the signs of a favorable rebirth and other such marks.
Having touched water that is pure and filtered through the hem of a clean garment,
one should wash both feet up to the knees with exactly seven handfuls of earth.
One should perform seven [hand-washings] after urinating; thirty when discharging feces; two at both ends of the hand;
and likewise two for spitting and two for clearing nasal mucus.
Then, having sipped water, they proceeded toward their dwellings on the ground from afar; having reached the mere sound [of them], they traveled by a path the distance of an arrow-shot.
Beyond that, as far as one desires, in the direction ending with the south, outside [the village],
[one should avoid] places with clouds, fields, saline soil, and likewise those strewn with sand.
But avoiding rivers, he should avoid the far bank of a river, a shrine, a refuse heap, or anything impure;
he should go to a secluded spot in private, confident, at the edge of a forest, devoid of people.
At that time, however, the practitioner of the mantra should discharge the impurity;
one who recites mantras and knows the proper time should not suppress the natural urges.
Then, having gone to a pure region as desired at the end [of the rainy season],
one should construct a hut or a shelter near a spring in that place according to the rules and as is comfortable.
At dawn, or in a secluded, covered, and hidden place, or even at night,
one should always practice the recitation of the mantra in silence, free from all attachments.
Once the urine and feces have been removed, the observer of the vow should always perform purification using clay that is soft, pleasant to the touch, well-ground, and free from living organisms.
Having taken three [clods] as well as one, one should always place them at the anus, at both ends of the hands, and likewise on the ground;
this was previously prescribed for the practitioner by the Tree.
Having diligently washed his feet, first the right and then the other,
the practitioner of *japa* should always keep his feet joined together with one another.
The detailed purification for those who recite mantras was explained previously;
however, the purification consisting of being free from odor and stains was taught by the pure ones of old.
In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, this purity for those who follow the mantra has been stated in brief:
through being free from the stain of odors, one shall always be pure indeed.
"This is seen in all tantras," said the Lord of Sages;
then the ascetic practitioner, having performed ritual ablution, devoted himself to recitation and to the performance of successful rites.
Purification of the mind through the previously mentioned rite is declared to be the fivefold purity for practitioners in all tantras.
Purity of body, as well as purity of speech and meditation, is proclaimed;
the fourth is the purity of truth, while water is said to be the fifth.
Those who possess the true Dharma, have conquered anger, know the tantras, and perceive the scriptures;
those skilled in the meaning of subtle reality, who know the mantras and are diligent in ritual action.
For those who are skilled in the causes and in the inner self, accomplishment is not difficult to attain;
one should not speak of false worship that is devoid of truth and Dharma.
Cruel and even more cruel, O Caitra, devoid of all truth,
causing hatred, full of wrath, harsh, and striking me down.
But one who is devoid of truth and dharma, who oppresses other beings, who is deceitful, afflicted in mind, and abandoned by all wholesome qualities— [one should avoid her].

One who constantly practices violence, one of immoral conduct, one who follows false dharma, one who is always intent on muttering mantras for selfish ends, and likewise one who indulges in vulgar sexual practices— these should always be avoided.
False speech and anger are indeed censured by all the Buddhas and by the wise Bodhisattvas, who are exceedingly afraid of the next world.
Furthermore, in this world, those who desire to attain accomplishments on earth must always avoid false speech, both as solitary rhinoceros-like practitioners and as disciples.
Those who speak false accusations go to the most terrible hells;
furthermore, they always dwell among animals, as well as in the world of Yama.
Those who live by falsehood dwell eternally in those very hells:
Tapana, Durmati, Paure, Kālasūtra, and Pratāpana.
The eleventh chapter: A living being who speaks falsehood shall dwell for many eons in Sañjīva, in Asipatravana, and likewise in the thicket of Śālmalī trees.
How indeed can the mantras be accomplished for one who speaks falsely?
Deluded by false speech, he causes living beings to tremble;
therefore, that person of deluded action does not perceive the accomplishment of the mantra.
The speech of one who reviles the mantra-practitioners brings no success;
for he by whom the teaching of the Buddhas has been rejected upon this earth,
he therefore falls into a terrible state of great fear due to ignorance.
In the Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, and Pratāpana hells,
he shall dwell for a great eon (mahākalpa) due to my destruction of the True Dharma (saddharma).
Foolish people, having despised the true Dharma and being shrouded in blinding darkness, are cooked in a most terrible hell.
Out of ignorance or childishness, deluded and possessed of false pride,
those who indeed despise the King of Vidyās fall into a terrible hell.
Therefore, one should not commit evil, nor engage in contemptible and false actions;
for despising the true Dharma and holding false views are indeed censurable.
Therefore, always being faithful, one should constantly practice the ritual procedures of the mantra;
speaking the truth, knowing the mantra, and always intent on the welfare of sentient beings,
the knower of the mantra should devote himself to the mantra— for him, success is indeed certain.
One performs various actions— superior, inferior, and middling—
for it is activity that accomplishes action, not inactivity that is ever beneficial.
For one who is fully engaged in ritual action and its performance, success shall always be attained;
because all purposes are contained within the purpose of ritual action, the action is the constant purpose of the rite.
That which is devoid of action and that which has action as its purpose, as well as the object of action, are joined with action;
perform always that action which is fruitful and which is indeed action itself.
Thus, duty, action, and its fruit—duty, action, and fruit—are always present;
the fruitless reaches fruition, and that very fruit is ever-fruitful.

Both fruitless and fruitful, all indeed arise from fruit; through conjunction the mantra is accomplished, for conjunction is the means of accomplishing the mantra. Through non-conjunction and disjunction, disjunction becomes the means of accomplishing conjunction.
But the relationship of the probandum and the probans is not established among them;
for substances that are already established are everywhere contradictory causes of establishment.
For those whose mantras are not yet established, the mantras are the means for accomplishment.
That which the agent most desires to reach is the object (*karman*); it arises from an action performed by one desiring to attain that object.
One should not perform non-action among all actions, for there are causes for action;
one who is endowed with the meaning of mantra and tantra should undertake every rite.
One should undertake the rite that has been begun, and one who is inactive should not undertake it at all.
"Mantras do not succeed for any embodied beings if the ritual action is not undertaken;
this was sung of old by the supreme sages who proclaim all the true Dharma, as the commitment of the sons of the Conquerors regarding the recitation of mantras."
The practitioner, knowing all mantras, [should follow] the other path taught here in this King of Rituals (kalparāja) in the form of mantra, which is the cause of awakening;
for in this, all my mantras will always be effective through proper application.

In a very short time, he shall attain his desired perfection for the sake of Śiva and all beings— perfection attained by the perfectly awakened ones through the form that leads to the city of Nirvāṇa.
Likewise, the path to enlightenment is eternal and fulfills all actions and purposes;
Buddhahood is the primary state, the ultimate goal, and its final resort.
Thus, one shall attain accomplishment here without effort, along with its fruits.
Those who know the phenomena of diverse karmas shall accomplish the mantras;
this attainment of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and liberation has been briefly described by the foremost of Jinas as the accomplishment that fulfills all aims.
The eleventh chapter:
A seeker shall obtain abundant wealth and the basis for the highest rebirth; likewise, one shall always become a lord of yakṣas, or at the very least, a king.
He shall attain sovereignty over all practitioners among the worlds of men, gods, and asuras;
likewise, he makes their activities fruitful,
provided he is always endowed with purity and right conduct, and devoted to ethical discipline and meditation.

Then the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra spoken for all mantras; thus the practitioner performs various rites— superior, middling, and even inferior— as the mantra-master desires prosperity.
In the lowest [level], there is an increase in enjoyments; in the middle, for those with bodies above [the earth];
and by the highest [level] alone, the practitioner of recitation attains the most excellent state.
At the end of the recitation, the mantra-master should rest for as long as he deems necessary.
One should perform the sādhana there when the time has arrived;

thus, for the reciter, all rites are accomplished. Nevertheless, the mantra-practitioner who always performs the ritual according to the rules there effects the destruction of men's sins throughout the succession of their karmas.
Success remains for that person until he attains the state of being the foremost among men;
furthermore, the reciter of the mantra should repeat the mantra for the sake of destroying evil, whereby his actions are destroyed and the mantras—
whether they be the highest, the middling, or those honored by the world as inferior— become effective.
By means of recitation (*japa*), they exhaust entirely whatever evil has been committed throughout a succession of births;

thus, for all embodied beings, their sins perish. She makes [the practitioner] beautiful, adorned with various limbs and ornaments, delightful, and endowed with all excellent qualities, and he eternally attains the sovereignty of a king among the *yakṣas*.
"By reciting the mantra of the Tathāgatas, they attain the accomplishment of all aims.

Thus concludes the fourth chapter, the detailed section on the ritual procedures for all activities—including the rules for recitation, fire offerings (*homa*), meditation, and the conduct of purity, as well as the methods for accomplishing the rites useful for practice—taken from a single day’s portion of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again surveyed the entire abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Listen, Mañjuśrī!

For those beings who follow your vidyā-mantras and are engaged in the welfare of all sentient beings, listen to that method of the rosary for reciting mantras—by which mantras are recited and by which they are not—which is common to all mantras and serves as a means for the practice in all tantras. Listen well and take it to heart."
When this had been said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Excellent, Blessed One!"
"Therefore, out of compassion for us, please speak for the benefit of those beings who have entered the observances of all mantra practices, and for the sake of all sentient beings.
When Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to him: "Listen, Mañjuśrī!"
I shall explain it in detail and with its divisions, by which beings engaged in the practice of all mantras accomplish all their aims.
And what is that?

First of all, there is the mantra: [Mantra follows] ...which is the first. Thus, having been empowered by the Buddhas of the three times, this mantra accomplishes all purposes for those who apply themselves to the practice of mantras. It is the supreme among all mantras, the king of all mantras, the sovereign of all mantras, the great sovereign of all mantras, the chief of all mantras, the supreme of all mantras, the most excellent of all mantras, the best of all mantras, the foremost of all mantras, the highest of all mantras, the unsurpassed of all mantras, the peerless of all mantras, the incomparable of all mantras, the matchless of all mantras, the unequaled of all mantras, the unequalled of all mantras, the unassailable of all mantras, the invincible of all mantras, the unconquerable of all mantras, the indestructible of all mantras, the indeclinable of all mantras, the unshakeable of all mantras, the unalterable of all mantras, the unchangeable of all mantras, the unbreakable of all mantras, the uncrushable of all mantras, the unassailable of all mantras, the unassailable by all mantras, the unassailable by all gods, the unassailable by all Māras, the unassailable by all Brahmās, the unassailable by all Śakras, the unassailable by all world-protectors, the unassailable by all Yakṣas, the unassailable by all Rākṣasas, the unassailable by all Pretas, the unassailable by all Piśācas, the unassailable by all Kumbhāṇḍas, the unassailable by all Pūtanas, the unassailable by all Kaṭapūtanas, the unassailable by all Skandas, the unassailable by all Unmādakas, the unassailable by all Apasmārakas, the unassailable by all Ojohāras, the unassailable by all Jambhakas, the unassailable by all Vetālas, the unassailable by all Kūṣmāṇḍas, the unassailable by all Mahākālas, the unassailable by all Kāpālikas, the unassailable by all Kāpālinīs, the unassailable by all malevolent beings, the unassailable by all malevolent spirits, the unassailable by all malevolent deities, the unassailable by all malevolent powers, the unassailable by all malevolent influences, the unassailable by all malevolent omens, the unassailable by all malevolent portents, the unassailable by all unassailable by all malevolent times, the unassailable by all malevolent places, the unassailable by all malevolent directions, the unassailable by all malevolent intermediate directions, the Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous!
It is as follows: Oṃ, act, act for the sake of all goals! Accomplish, accomplish! O deluder of all the wicked!
O you who rest upon the sky!
"Viśodhaya svāhā.

With this mantra, one should perform all rites regarding rosaries (*akṣasūtra*), such as the rites of purification, piercing, grasping, and purging. First, one should consecrate the tree from which the rosary beads are to be taken.
Then, having performed the protection ritual thirty-seven times and observing the vow,
he should sleep there for one night; and in his dream, he sees a non-human being, either beautiful in form or deformed, who has been there for a long time.
The son of Sumitrā should take his garment as required;
then that practitioner, having risen in the morning, should go to that tree and observe a dream— whether it be deformed or exceedingly fierce.
The mantra-practitioner should avoid that tree; O Lord, one should go elsewhere.
First, however, is the Rudra-rosary, and after that, the Indra-rosary.
This is the twelfth chapter from the extensive [tantra].
One who desires to obtain the fruit of the *putrañjīvaka* or any other such tree should climb it together with companions well-equipped for ascending trees; or,
in the absence of companions, one may climb it alone while reciting mantras.
Stationed upon the fruit of the upward-reaching branches, having emerged from those upward-reaching branches,
one who grasps the fruit of the upward-reaching branches should employ the upward-directed action;
for this supreme accomplishment has been proclaimed by the foremost of beings.
In the middling [case], the middling accomplishment is attained; in the inferior, indeed, the fruit is even lower.
Having taken up these among them, and always maintaining freedom from malice toward living beings, those who seek material wealth attain success through the trees in the western direction.
In the north, one should bring forth the deities beginning with those born of the Yakṣa womb; this rite of summoning is renowned for the sake of pacifying the interests of all beings—
whether they be gods, asuras, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, or rākṣasas.
O Ordainer, he performs his actions well for the nourishment of the welfare of all beings;
he brings to fruition every action performed upon the earth. Those branches situated in the eastern direction are the source of fruit.

One should always apply effort toward them for the sake of attaining long life; for therein one achieves various forms of accomplishment through their fruits. That branch which extends toward the south and is rich with leaves and shoots—[in that one should act].

The reciter should avoid that [tree], because its branches growing toward the south take away the lives of sentient beings; however, those fruits which have grown upon the branches facing east should be used as beads for recitation,
for they equally destroy the sins of enemies.
The reciter of mantras should avoid those [fruits] with great effort, for they are causes for much demerit;
those fruits which are described as hanging from downward-pointing branches cause one to go to the netherworld (rasātala) and to the women of the dānavas.
A rosary made from those fruits is highly praised;
according to the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, by means of that [rosary], one may go to whichever lower abodes or netherworlds (*pātāla*) one desires.
Having entered there, the practitioner of recitation (*jāpin*) attains divine bliss.

If one remains attached to the female spirits of the asuras, one would stay for an eon and dwell in the household; therefore, having performed the protection and being accompanied by companions, the reciter should descend from all those [states] after obtaining the fruit of the practice, and then proceed as he pleases.
Having gone to a distant place, the practitioner of mantra should always remain in a pure location; there,
having taken beads produced from seeds, he should thoroughly purify them in every respect.
Having thoroughly purified the eyes in every way, one who is endowed with mantras should pierce them;
whether three, seven, eight, or once, the knower of the essence of mantras should always purify those twenty-one times with the preceding mantra.
Purification is desired after seven or eight recitations;
the practitioner should prepare a cord made of five triple-strands of thread spun by a maiden, using lotus stalks.
One who knows the reality of mantras should take that [wood], which is fine, subtle, well-rounded,
always free of holes from insects, unblemished, or at least not contemptible;
it should be beautiful, of lovely color, without cracks, and likewise not split.

The practitioner of mantras, ever diligent, should with great care always prepare a rosary from *rudrākṣa* seeds, or *sutajīva*, or indeed *indrākṣa* fruit— be it an *ariṣṭa* that is beautiful, constant, unblemished, and esteemed for its fruit.
Then, a rosary (akṣamālikā) may be made from gold, silver, ruby, crystal, or equally from śārī, excellent sāra-wood, or even pearl; one should fashion various garlands using these materials.
One should also fashion auspicious garlands from other divine gems;
with a concentrated mind, one should string them upon a thread using round, earthen beads,
or other small beads made of fruits or derived from minerals.
In the twelfth chapter, one who recites the mantra with diligence should carefully fashion a string of knots from the tips of *kuśa* grass—
either one hundred and eight, twenty-five, or fifty for the middling [rite].
A mantra-practitioner, being composed in mind, should string this rosary of beads;
he should make the "eldest" (jyeṣṭhikā) rosary consist of one thousand and eight beads.
This fourfold rosary is to be strung daily by constant practitioners of mantra.
Then, one should indeed string a garland of three strands or even two,
using rings made of flower-metal, gold, silver, or likewise copper; in brief, one should string the garland in this manner.
Then, having formed a loop at the end, one should place it in due succession;
one should wrap it around until the three joints remain clearly bound,
and then, having made it appear in the shape of a mandala.
Having bathed in auspicious water or in a pure river, one should wrap [the image] in all kinds of ornaments, adorned with the appearance of pearl necklaces and fashioned in the form of a necklace.
Having bathed as before, he should emerge from the water; then,
having sipped water according to the rule, he should wash his hands, which are bound by the sacrificial cord,
with the five products of the cow and likewise with powdered clay.
Having washed [the image] in auspicious water and having anointed it with fragrant unguents and excellent pigments, such as white sandalwood and saffron,
one should then carefully wash it and proceed from there to the temple.
Having gone to their respective places where that middle-sized painting is located—
wherein is the foremost of Jinas, the chief of Munis, the Lion of the Śākyas, the best of men—
the image of the Teacher, as well as the supreme relics of the Jina upon the earth, one should always [worship] there.
Having placed it nearby on that cloth, while it is present before him,
one should recite [the mantra] one thousand eight hundred times, and one hundred and eight times in a single session.

Having fasted for a day and night and having performed the recitation (*jāpa*) previously according to the prescribed measure, one should give the rosary to the most excellent of sages; then, having likewise recited over it the same number of times, one should place the rosary right there during the night.
There, the knower of mantras should sleep upon the ground strewn with kusha grass; if he sees an auspicious dream-vision therein,
his success is ordained as fruitful according to what was indicated by that dream.
If this is seen by the disciples of the Buddha and the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas] in a dream,
and if, having seen it in a dream, one likewise offers a garland,
then for them the mantras that accomplish all aims will be unfailingly successful.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the detailed section on the ritual for rosaries, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra which is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.

Then indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having looked again and again toward the abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, there exists your own chapter of mantras (*mantrapaṭala*) which, through its entirely arranged specific ritual procedures, is employed in the rite of fire-oblation (*homakarman*). For a practitioner of the vidyā who is engaged therein, there is a specific rule for the service of the fire; established therein, all beings engaged in the practice of the vidyās apply themselves."
And what are those secret mantra words of the vidyā?
They are as follows: Oṃ uttiṣṭha haripiṅgala!
O red-eyed one! Give! Cause to be given!
HŪṂ PHAṬ PHAṬ! Destroy all obstacles, SVĀHĀ!
This, O Mañjuśrī, is the supreme heart-mantra of fire, which accomplishes all rites and grants all desires.
First of all, the practitioner, having recited this Heart of Fire once, should offer three oblations of clarified butter into the fire;
thus the fire becomes summoned.
For one who applies it in this manner, there are three kinds of fuel-wood for the rites of pacification, enrichment, and subjugation.
For the purpose of pacification, aśoka wood is especially recommended;
it should be one vitasti, one hasta, or even three aṅgulas in length,
smooth in appearance and excellent— this is the prescribed rule.

One should avoid a site that is hollow or porous, or one resembling a parrot’s wing; likewise, one should avoid what is green, white, or black in color, and that which has been eaten by worms. One should select a site that is not hollow. One should join together [the materials] in such a way that it is without cavities.
Those of excellent color and superior quality,
free from impurity, neither too dry nor too moist, and not burnt— these one should employ; however, one should avoid those that are incomplete, crooked, or excessively tall.
Having likewise prepared the fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) as a square on all sides,
one should carefully dig it downwards with a measurement of four cubits,
or three cubits, two cubits, or even one cubit.
It should always be free from living beings and established in the form of a lion; it should be shaped like a lotus, and then the altar (vedi) should be made circular all around,
or else one should carefully construct it as a square or in the shape of a bow.
One should fashion a three-pronged [implement] with two tips resembling the form of a vajra; it should be two cubits wide in this fire-pit,
located in a pure, well-swept place, or likewise on an excellent riverbank.

And in a solitary place, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, or likewise on a mountain peak, as well as always in an empty temple and in a great forest, one should perform the fire sacrifice with great intensity.
Those places for the performance of the rite which have been described by the foremost of persons—
these locations are declared to be suitable for the ritual of *homa* in every respect.
Having sat upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass at a distance of one cubit from there, the knower of mantras should especially perform the *homa* ritual in that place.

Success will be swiftly attained in these very places; of this there is no doubt. Facing either the east or the north, one should perform rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*);

however, the mantra-practitioner should avoid those fierce (*raudra*) rites toward the south. Success in pacification occurs when facing east, and in nourishment when facing north; the practitioner should always begin the recitation of mantras with these orientations. One should perform the rite of nourishment using *bilva*, *āmra*, *plakṣa*, or *nyagrodha* trees.

One should avoid all wood used for malevolent rites (*ābhicāruka*), as well as dry, bitter, sour, or pungent wood; these are always forbidden by the sages for rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*). For such rites, fresh wood is recommended. Similarly, wood from trees used in fierce rites (*raudra*) is always avoided by the sages.

In the absence of these specific types of fuel-wood (*samidh*), one should prepare wood suitable for them. It should be spread all around with *kuśa* grass, and both ends [of the wood] should be prepared accordingly.

With *kuśa* grass that is green, glossy in appearance, and resembling the neck of a peacock—one should always perform rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) with such [grass]. Likewise, one should always perform fire-rituals (*pāvakakarmāṇi*) with dry blades of grass that resemble emeralds or the sky; however, these are prohibited here by the supreme Jinas. The Thirteenth Chapter.

In water that is stainless, pure, and always free from insects, one should sprinkle it all around and perform a circumambulation. Then, with a composed mind, having sipped water according to the rule, one should fashion a torch of a proper size from clean grass-blades—measuring about a cubit—and then carefully ignite the fire. One must never do so by means of the breath from the mouth or with the hem of a garment.

Deprived of both lower and upper garments, one should not [use] anything else for clothing. Nor should one fan the fire with the wind of the hands, nor with a fan, nor likewise with a cloth, nor even with leaves, while desiring to delight [the deity]. When the fire has been kindled and the wind has been stirred by these means, the one who knows the mantras and seeks to perform the *homa* should, being well-composed, cause it to blaze. Then, having performed the ritual circumambulation three times, keeping the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).

Then one should indeed offer three oblations of cow-derived clarified butter (*ājya*). Thereafter, one should perform prostrations to all the Buddhas and Protectors, and then worship one’s own *mūlamantra* and its Lord according to one's desire. Then, while the *Agnihṛdaya* mantra is being recited, the practitioner—whose self is united with the fire—should always summon [the deity] with fragrant flowers. One who knows the mantras and is discerning should constantly summon [the deity] and provide a place for him.

Having provided a seat and a place with that mantra and no other, one should offer three pieces of fuel-stick (samidh) soaked in curd, mixed with clarified butter, and anointed with honey, for the purpose of worshipping the fire through the ritual of mantra in every respect. Then, one should prepare the sacrificial material placed between both [fires], combined with clarified butter and honey, and likewise mixed with curd. One should perform [this] a thousand times, or a mere hundred thousand, or even one hundred and eight times.

The secret mantra-practitioner, having likewise recited the mantra once, should cast [the oblation] into the fire. One should offer oblations into a fire with garlands of flames or likewise into one with a single flame for rites of pacification (*śāntika*); and for rites of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), into a smokeless fire. For fierce rites (*raudrakarman*), one should offer into a smoky fire; these are censured though described by the Best of Jinas. Now, regarding the color of the fire when engaged in the ritual of homa: if it is white in color, it is always praised by the Best of Jinas for pacification.

Indeed, mantras are accomplished for one who offers oblations there in a white fire; likewise, success in nourishing rites (*pauṣṭika*) is always desired in a red-colored fire. In a black or smoke-colored fire, as well as in a tawny one, there is accomplishment related to injury (*pāyika*). Thus, this threefold accomplishment is set forth according to the three types of color;
whether it be of another color, the color of clouds, or described as having various forms and colors—there is no accomplishment of mantras in those cases here upon the earth.

Having seen such a peacock, blazing and endowed with various forms and colors, one should again begin the ritual action, provided that the mantra has been recited once more and the accomplishment of the mantra is attained. One should then proceed with the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the rite prescribed by the rules; having performed the dismissal and the invocation, one should utter the fire-mantra within this very mandala as previously prepared, in accordance with the ritual procedure.
With that very [fire], one should perform the rites of dismissal (*visarjana*) and invocation (*āhvāna*). One should perform all rituals with that very [fire] during that specific rite;

likewise, one should undertake the conduct regarding the fire (*agnicaryā*) and the observances (*vrata*) for the cloth-painting (*paṭa*). There, the mantras indeed become effective, as was previously stated by the Tathāgatas. One should perform the rituals described by the Jinas everywhere, and never any other rituals, especially not those that are sinful.

One should not accept that which is rejected by the best of Jinas, being contrary [to the teachings] and despised by the world. Arise! You shall become either a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), a bodhisattva, or a sovereign of the earth;

furthermore, upon attaining the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), you will likewise achieve the state of a god or spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*). This is the thirteenth chapter from the extensive [tantra], concerning one who is constantly engaged in knowledge and is skilled in the rites of fire-offerings (*homakarman*) upon this painting.

Whether it be sovereignty over Pātāla, or [mastery] over those who move through the atmosphere; the state of being a terrestrial deity or a Yakṣa; or for the purpose of attracting a Yakṣī, or always [for the sake of] kingship, overlordship, or even a kingdom, a district, or a village; the state of being a Vidyādhara or an Asura; or for the purpose of bringing under control all sentient beings, and for the attraction of spirits (bhūtas), great beings (mahāsattvas), and high-souled ones—namely, the Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas who abide on the ten stages (daśabhūmi).

If one can summon even a god by means of the fire-oblation (homa), how much more so a human being on earth? One should likewise employ the oblation for the sake of attaining the rank of commander-in-chief, as well as sovereignty specifically in the world, and even the status of a king who has brought all beings under his control. For the purpose of subjugating all beings or even a king upon this earth, one should always perform every rite entirely through the oblation; thus, with a self fully disciplined in every way, one should resort to every ritual action.

His supreme rite for the sake of the highest good will certainly succeed; even middling or inferior rites will likewise be accomplished. All substances therein are said to achieve success in three ways; when the fire-offering (*homakarma*) is performed, successful accomplishment is seen. Having bound the five-crested mudrā and recited the Keśinī mantra, one who is intent on self-protection should perform all ritual acts.
When engaged in the rite of fire offering (*homakarman*), one should then recite this mantra seven or eight times, thinking: "In this rite, may this always be [accomplished].
*Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānāmapratihataśāsanānām | Tadyathā—oṃ jvala tiṣṭha hūṃ ru ru viśvasambhava sambhave svāhā.*

By means of this application of the mantra, the knower of mantras should repeatedly recite it over a piece of wood—either twice or seven times—and offer it into the fire. Or, one should sprinkle flowers, incense, perfumes, and indeed everything on all sides with water consecrated by the recitation of this very mantra. Thereafter, one should undertake all ritual activities according to the prescribed rules.
It should be performed with the very same preliminary practice in all ritual acts.
Having bound the glorious Mahāmudrā with its topknots facing east and west,
and having performed the protection ritual, one should then always recite the mantra of Keśinī.
Those who are confident should undertake all actions for the sake of success,
provided that auspicious omens are seen and sounds are always favorable.
His mantras are indeed successful in granting boons according to his desire;
employed in the initial rites, they proceed by means of the mantra.
Complete success, including every fruit thereof, is ordained for them;
as well as the sound of the word "Victory," the beating of drums, and the resonance of kettledrums.
Success is indeed declared everywhere for one who relies upon the rite of fire-offerings (homa),
as well as for other excellent omens or the auspicious cries of birds.
Various kinds of resonant sounds and meanings have been praised by the Victors;
they are excellent, divine, auspicious, celestial, delightful, and manifold in their tones.
Parasols, banners, and flags, as well as adorned women,
a full water-pot, and the sight of the half-moon are causes for success.
Or those who possess many excellent forms and colors, who are praiseworthy and honored by the world—
for them, the mantras of various domains are accomplished upon being seen.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter-section from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvataṃsaka*.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Then the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Mañjuśrī, there exists [this]..."

He is the one who grants permission for all mantras useful for the practice of the secrets of your vidyās; he is the Lord and the eldest of all mantras—both mundane and supramundane—which have entered the cloud of Dharma spread from the Tathāgata’s treasury of Dharma and possess the nature of space. Just as a prince is the eldest among all beings, so too is the Tathāgata here declared the eldest, the most excellent, the bull among men, the Buddha, the Blessed One. Thus indeed, O Prince!

Among all mantras, this King of Vidyās is declared to be the foremost, the most excellent, as previously designated by the Tathāgatas—the Blessed Buddhas whose merit is equal to the sands of inexpressible Ganges rivers. It is the supreme heart-essence (*paramahṛdaya*) and the supreme secret of the Tathāgata Ratnakeśin; it is esteemed as all-auspicious, praised and extolled by all Buddhas, the consoler of all Buddha-beings, the destroyer of all sins, the granter of all desires, and the fulfiller of all hopes.
And what is that?
In that interval, from the circle of hair between the eyebrows of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, there issued forth a ray of light named "Exhorter of All Buddhas.

Having illuminated all the Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, above and below, and having gladdened the minds of all sentient beings, it vanished into the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Blessed One Śākyamuni.

And from the uṣṇīṣa of the Blessed One, there issued forth the King of Vidyās named Ekākṣara, whose form was adorned with flames on all sides, who was unobservable by any beings, invincible, arisen from a great ocean of majestic power, his body adorned with a halo of light, possessing various forms and the appearance of a great universal monarch.

Having emerged, he illuminated the entire expanse of the sky; surrounded by all the kings of vidyās, preceded by many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of vidyās, being honored by all the supramundane kings of the vidyā-cakravartins, praised by all mantras, and empowered by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—those great beings who have attained the stage of the tenth ground—he filled the whole vault of the sky. His body was adorned with great maṇi-jewels beautified by divine gems; possessing a lovely form, exceedingly radiant, and emitting hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of emanations in various forms, he uttered the sound of the single syllable, released a great net of light rays, and stood in the atmosphere above the Blessed One Śākyamuni, gazing directly at him while illuminating the entire realm of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and the great circle of the assembly.

In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, the Blessed One Śākyamuni then [taught] the single-syllable sovereign of vidyās, the heart of all Tathāgatas, named Ratnaketu—the supreme heart and most profound secret of the Tathāgata Ratnaketu—which was established by all the Blessed Tathāgatas; which was spoken and rejoiced in by Sālendrarāja, Amitābha, Duḥprasaha, Sunetra, Suketu, Puṣpendra, Supinānta, Lokamuni, Kanaka, and other Tathāgatas; and which was uttered and approved by all the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the past. And what is that?
It is as follows: "Bhram.

This, Mañjuśrī, is the supreme heart-mantra of all Tathāgatas, the single-syllable great purifier known as the Vidyā-Cakravartin, which possesses all virtues. When this is practiced, all mantras are accomplished.

O Youth! Those who [practice] this supreme king of manuals belonging to you—which is compatible with all mantras, the highest secret, the foremost authorized [teaching], and the purifier of all karmic obscurations—must certainly accomplish it. O Youth!
Within this king of your manuals, all worldly and transcendent mantra-tantras among all mantras are to be accomplished.
Having performed protection by means of this, one becomes unassailable by all spirits;
thus, one is not overcome by any obstacles, whether mundane or supramundane.
And when this was spoken by the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lord of Universal Jewels, the entire great trichiliocosm shook like a leaf,
all the Buddha-fields were illuminated, and all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, became assembled together.

In that assembly circle, all those seated in the Śuddhāvāsakāyika heaven, as well as all the bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages and are irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, along with all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and beings of great psychic power, shall come under his control, impelled by the rays of light of the King of Vidyās.

Furthermore, many other beings dwelling in infinite and boundless world-systems, who were situated in the miserable destinies of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, were touched and illuminated by that great radiance of light; with their sensations of suffering awakened and brought to an end, their minds became filled with joy, and they would certainly become established in the three vehicles.
Then the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, having gazed upon that great assembly circle, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Listen, Mañjuśrī! This is the fourteenth chapter."

This King of Vidyās is of great supernatural power, the sole hero, effective for all rites, the universal monarch of all vidyā-kings, the fulfiller of the hopes of all sentient beings, and has entered into the extensive ritual manuals of your own mantra-tantras. He is the common ground for the accomplishment of all mantras, a being of great authority and great energy, the means by which practitioners purify the path to awakening through their specific wisdom and skillful means, and the accumulation of merit for the sequence of establishing [beings] in nirvāṇa and ascending to sit upon the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa). In brief, this is the extensive ritual manual, the procedure for the cloth-painting (paṭavidhāna), and the maṇḍala, along with the methods for accomplishment and the prior conduct of mantra-practice, wherein established beings shall accomplish this Great Universal Monarch, the King of Vidyās, the great hero, the supreme lord of all mantras, the light-maker, the fulfiller of all hopes, the Guide, who is for the welfare of the entire world, appearing like a Buddha in person—the Self-Existent One (svayambhū)—who performs all rites whether superior, excellent, middling, or inferior.
He who leads to security, who is auspicious, peaceful, and the destroyer of all sins;
the God even of the gods, the preeminent sage among sages.
The Buddha is boundless like the sun, pure, and renowned throughout the world;
he knows the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and is the unclouded limit of reality.
I shall declare the excellent ritual manual for those desiring prosperity; listen!
First, one should prepare a divine cloth that is free of hair and devoid of adhesions.
One should likewise draw this upon a new, white, and especially well-woven cloth,
measuring two cubits in length and one cubit in width.
On such an auspicious, pure, and beautiful day,
when the moon is bright, white, and full, and when one is under a good vow and free from the wearing of bark garments;
On a white cloth that removes impurities, on fine silk (dukūlaka),
on woolen cloth (ātasya), on bark-fiber cloth (vālkalai), or on any pure material free from woven threads;
It should not be produced by worms or wind, nor should it cause harm to living beings;
likewise, it should not be made of silk, but rather whatever else is praised as excellent.
On such an excellent cloth, one should have a temple painted;
having depicted the image of the Teacher, adorned with a garland of light-halos.
Then, having painted him in golden color, garlanded with flames, solitary, hidden in secret, situated on a mountain, and of great majesty— this is the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa.
One should indeed fashion a canopy of fine cloth adorned with strings of jewels; above it, one should depict both deities being held aloft.
One should indeed construct a jeweled garland atop the mountain, and it should be adorned all around with pearl necklaces and half-necklaces beneath a canopy.
Having carefully drawn everything above the king of mountains,
one should likewise draw below the mountain the great ocean, completely submerged.
And on the edge of the cloth, one should likewise draw flowers all around:
*nāgakesara*, *punnāga*, *vakula*, and *yūthikā*.
The *mālatī* flower, as well as the *priyaṅgu*, *kuravaka*, blue lotus (*indīvara*),
*saugandhī*, and thereafter the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*).
Various kinds of flowers as well as other fragrant substances—
these very flowers and [other items], for the sake of worship, they offered to the Teacher in a manner pleasing to the mind,
according to the previously prescribed rite, upon the superior cloth-painting as well as upon the [other] cloth-painting.
The sūtra, the weaver, and likewise the painter are considered [to be included];
one should paint on the most pure day during the fortnight of miracles (prātihārakapakṣa).
When the time has thus arrived and the recitation is being performed,
everything that was previously mentioned for him should be carried out in its entirety.
One should paint the entire universe of the Teacher, radiant with color, richly adorned, endowed with many forms, and possessing a luster like that of the *kaṇikāra* flower;
one should paint it as having the appearance of a *campaka* blossom, depicted in the color of gold.
Having thus painted the Sage, born of jewels, endowed with these characteristics:
One should depict that jewel of a Buddha, the illustrious Ratnaiketu, the most excellent among the foremost of sages, who has attained mastery over all dharmas.
The fourteenth chapter: [He is] seated upon a mountain of jewels, adorned with jewel-caves,
sitting cross-legged, and bestowing the teaching of the Dharma.
Having drawn the hero with a slightly smiling face outside the cave, with his mind fixed in meditation, one should likewise draw him below and on all sides.
The practitioner is seated at the corner of the edge of the cloth, with his knees covered in camphor,
his hands occupied with incense, and his body slightly bent forward.
One should arrange the upper robe according to the specific attire and insignia;
then one is consecrated by the mantra in this ritual manual spoken by Mañjughoṣa.
One who is perfected in the conduct of the mandala and is constantly consecrated— such a person,
being himself consecrated, is skilled and confident within this mandala of all mantras.
In that regard, those who possess sound reasoning are always considered beneficial for one's own protection;
likewise, the highly resplendent king, having thoroughly examined them, should protect his allies as well.
The teacher was highly enthusiastic toward those who had undertaken the observance of the vow;
he was possessed of great wisdom, ever affectionate, illustrious, and compassionate.
One should likewise indicate the characteristics of all the assistants:
one, two, three, or even eight, as well as others.
One should make the disciples well-prepared, yet one should also avoid making them too numerous;
one should always follow the previously seen procedure for this mandala.
Those maṇḍalas of Mañjughoṣa which were first taught by the One Possessing Ten Powers should not be drawn by anyone else, nor for any other ritual purpose.
In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, I shall now declare the dimensions of the mandala of great splendor:
it should be four cubits, two cubits, or likewise eight cubits and beyond.
In a pure place, on a riverbank, and especially on a mountain peak,
one should perform the ritual as previously observed using powder of five colors.
It was square, with four gates, adorned with four archways,
having four corners, level, divine, and possessing a splendor equal to divine conduct.
One who has good companions should undertake [the practice] that is brilliant with colors, variegated, beautiful in hue, very lovely, fragrant, and well-formed.
Observing the vow of silence, practicing the eightfold observances, with an unafflicted mind, knowing the proper measure, righteous, and always engaged in silent recitation;
Having undertaken deeds free from evil, remaining neutral toward rites of pacification and enrichment, one should then enter and draw the Teacher with colored powders.
First, all of that should be drawn: the Tathāgata Ratnaketu, of great splendor, seated in a cave and adorned with various jewels.
One should depict him on the cloth seated in the paryanka posture, turning the wheel of Dharma, and worshipped by the śāstṛs, exactly as described.
One should decorate it with three rows of lines and also with mudrās,
covering every row on all sides.
Among them, one should appoint a great lord as a universal monarch (cakravartin), who is neither isolated nor combined with others, and whose conduct is free from confusion.
Exerting diligent effort, one should draw him who resembles the rising sun, possessing the form of a youth and radiant with light, following after the great wheel.
Having the appearance of a great king, adorned with a crown and ornaments,
wearing a tiara, the Great Being is decorated with every kind of finery.
He is clothed in a beautiful lower garment and wears a variegated silk upper robe; he possesses a gentle complexion adorned with garlands, and is embellished with flowers and fine raiment.
In the fourteenth chapter,
[he sees] the god of great heroism and power, his face slightly smiling, smelling a *vakula* garland with his very right hand.
He is indeed of beautiful and lovely form, devoid of both children and the elderly;
his left hand always holds a wheel, and he wears a blazing garland while touching [the wheel].

Then one should paint that form, seated in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka), with one arm resting [upon the knee], possessing a divine luster of color, beautiful in appearance, and established in its true form.
Seated upon this fragment of jewels, the Great Radiance, the Benefactor of all beings,
has always proceeded as the granter of boons for all mantras.
Blazing with the form of fire, adorned with a beautiful mandala,
and encircled by a garland of flames on all sides, it blazes forth when fanned by the wind.
Thus, by means of the applications of mantras, such a person of great heroism, who accomplishes all mantras, is ignited upon the earth among human beings.
For whoever beholds [it], that righteous-souled one is liberated from all sins—
even one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution, is of immoral conduct, or is dull-witted.
Indeed, all sins are pacified; one is liberated merely by seeing the Lord, for the mandala of the Discus-wielder, the God of gods, is seen as soon as it is beheld.
At that very moment, one is liberated from the sins mentioned previously; then, O Lord, having purified the eastern gate with the mantra alone of the All-pervading One.
Encircled by archways and adorned on all sides with plantain trees,
one should fashion a completely manifest mandala of beautiful form in its entirety.
One should always respectfully offer the bali, incense, lamp, and pure perfumes and garlands according to the very same ritual procedure as before.
One should place a full water-pot in the center directly in front of the practitioner of the wheel;
that pot is called Vijayā, and the knower of mantras must not move it.
Likewise, the fire-pit should first be prepared according to the ritual prescribed by rule;
the commencement of the fire-oblation rite must be performed with the *vibhu-mantra* and no other.
In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, one should perform eight thousand fire oblations (homa) using a fire fueled by *khadira* wood,
as well as with *pālāśa*, *śrīkaṇṭha*, *bilva*, *udumbara*, and *akṣa* wood.
One should diligently offer apāmārga in all rites,
or sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter and saturated with the scent of burnt offerings.

In all rites, one should always offer oblations one thousand and eight times at the three junctions of the day; the previously prescribed bathing and wearing of the garment [should also be performed].
The wise have declared the Triśūla to be an auspicious asterism for the previously mentioned rites,
as well as for recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), and other such acts.
One should perform [the rites] with a mantra-conjoined family of universal monarchs,
or indeed with the single-syllable [mantra] alone, for all ritual actions.
Endowed with great power and purpose, this solitary hero should always practice the ritual manual of all mantras, constantly reciting them among them.
All ritual procedures— those of the mundane world approved by the world,
as well as those transcending the world— are accomplished, along with the kings of vidyā who possess great heroism and perform great austerities.
All mantras indeed attain accomplishment through this ritual manual; for it was taught by the sages as well as by the sons of those who possess the ten powers.
By Śakra and the other world-protectors, by Viṣṇu, Īśāna, and Brahmā, as well as by the Moon and the Sun, or by others such as the lords of the Yakṣas and the Rākṣasas.
By the mahoragas and kinnaras, as well as by the best of sages on earth, by the garuḍas, the mātṛs, the worlds, and likewise by others designated as sentient beings.
Those mantras which have indeed been spoken attain accomplishment here; they are the attractors of all mantras and the leaders of all rites.
He possesses mastery over all mantras, is the leader of all rites,
and holds dominion over all spirits through the extensive tantras and mantras.
This single-syllable mantra makes the recitation of all practitioners fruitful;
merely by being recited, it attracts all the deities.
The fourteenth chapter: Mastery over all ritual manuals; this single-syllable Great One performs various forms, manifold and well-described by the virtuous.
One who has applied oneself correctly shall accomplish worldly mantras;
having made the cloth-painting perfectly clear and beautiful to behold in its entirety.
One should place it in a pure location, on a riverbank or a mountain peak;
following the application of the preliminary rite, one should always face westward.
The practitioner, facing the east and seated upon a bundle of darbha grass, should perform the recitation undisturbed according to the ritual procedure.
Neither too loud nor too soft, and not with a mind intent on anything else—
by thus avoiding the disparagement of all beings, one shall attain swift success in this world.
With a mind of loving-kindness, he always [regards] those in the world who are suffering,
wretched, without a protector, dejected in spirit, afflicted by calamity, and extremely weak.
Having fallen into this terrible saṃsāra, one who is filled with compassion then attains success;
therefore, one should always perform the great worship before the cloth-painting with diligence.
One should contemplate or indeed perform the mental, human, and divine [rites] arising from the heart for the sake of the Universal Cloth of the Lord of Jinas.
In that very place, the practitioner, knowing the ritual procedure for the principles (tattva), should construct a fire-pit;
there, indeed, he should offer oblations into the well-prosperous fire.
Having worshipped with white sandalwood, camphor, and saffron mixed together,
the knower of mantras should offer sixteen oblations into the blazing fire.
One should constantly kindle a powerful fire using wood originating from the Khadira, Lakṣya, Nyagrodha, or Pālāśa trees.
In the absence of these woods, one should collect another wood;
likewise, [one may use] picumarda, kadamba, and that which originates from madana.
All those with thorns are declared to be avoided in sinful rites;
one should perform rites for pacification and nourishment using the single-syllable mantra alone.
In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, success shall be swift for him who performs even sinful deeds;
for here, all mantra-holders together with their rites are detailed in this extensive ritual manual.
When applied by one free from conceptual construction, they always attain success;
then the mantras are drawn forth and indeed become bestowers of boons.
Of fuel-sticks of *palāśa* or *udumbara*, or indeed of *plakṣa* or *nyagrodha*,
smeared with clarified butter, mixed with curd, and combined with honey, he should offer them with a concentrated mind.
On this earth, a mantra-practitioner desiring sovereignty should offer oblations on all sides;
for one desiring a kingdom, he should offer saffron and sandalwood to the Goddess who has attained the kingdom.
Desiring sovereignty over the Vidyādharas and the gods,
one should offer thirty-six hundred thousand oblations of lotuses together with their filaments.
At the conclusion of the fire offering, one should indeed present the respectful offering (arghya) there to the Teacher;
then the supreme cloth, marked with the Jina, blazes forth on all sides.
And as soon as it is touched, one shall fly up to the abode of Brahmā—reaching as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven and as far as the depths of the netherworlds.
In this interval, he always becomes the king of all the siddhas;
possessed of great heroism and firm in his vows, he causes all malevolent beings to flee.
He shall always be the king of the Vidyādharas in the accomplishment of his rites;
furthermore, he shall live for the duration of a kalpa, traversing the long path of existence.
Passing away at that great time, he is destined for enlightenment;
this other [topic], the constant nature of karma, has thus been explained both in brief and in detail.
Having gathered white lotuses combined with white sandalwood, one should perform a hundred lakhs of oblations; he shall behold Ratnaketu.
Having seen that supreme Jina, one shall then possess the five superknowledges;
one shall live for a long time, a great eon, and become an attendant of the Buddha.
And then he beholds the Buddhas residing throughout the infinite directions; he should constantly worship them and dwell together with them. This is the fourteenth chapter of the extensive [tantra].
There is a single realm named Ratnāvatī where that Blessed One dwells—
the most excellent, supreme, foremost Tathāgata Ratnaketu.
There he dwells eternally, purified by mantra; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, another desired rite has been taught by the foremost of persons.
The practitioner of mantra, having combined equal parts of nāgakeśara, camphor, sandalwood, and saffron, should then perform seventy-eight hundred thousand oblations.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, the God, accompanied by his discus, always arrives here pleased and ready to grant boons, and touches the practitioner upon the head.
As soon as he is touched by that, the practitioner becomes the lord of the seven stages;
he is called a Bodhisattva, the legitimate son of the Jinas.
He will certainly be destined for the culmination of enlightenment and will receive his prophecy;
from that point onward, whatever knowledge and object of knowledge belongs to the Son of the Victor [is attained].
He knows the course, majesty, and power of all mantras;
he shall possess the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) upon merely seeing that King of Mantras.
Whenever he constantly manifests his own body in various forms, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, he is always devoted to the practice of worship.

At that very moment, he becomes intent upon the work of awakening; in a single instant, he then travels to the worlds and Buddha-fields. He wanders everywhere through thousands of world-systems and universes, and at that time beholds the conduct of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Diligently engaged in their service, he hears the Dharma from them.
Furthermore, there is another rite here for the arising of a Cakravartin or a Jina:
one should offer a lamp characterized by a pure wick and ghee,
placed in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay.
When those lamps have been ignited by men numbering one hundred thousand, arranged in groups by hundreds of thousands of navigators,

and when women and men with lamps in their hands surround the cloth painting (*paṭa*) known as the "Form of the Teacher" (*śāstṛbimba*) from all sides, one should offer worship during the ritual action according to the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*.

When all have proceeded together and are consecrated with a single mantra, one should offer [the oblation] with the mantras of the Teacher; at that very moment, one should declare the attainment of success.
There is a roar of thunder on all sides and the sound of kettledrums.
Indeed, many hosts of gods let out cries of "Excellent!
Then the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, stationed in the sky, exclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent, O wise one! You have performed a well-done deed."
You no longer behold the suffering submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, for you have taken refuge in Buddhahood— secure, auspicious, and fearless—
and in the pure, stainless Eightfold Path practiced by the virtuous.
O you who are protected by the single-syllable wheel, you have taken refuge in me in the form of a mantra. There remains no other task for you, as you are established in the supreme goal—
this which is known for its great power and proclaimed by all the Buddhas.
Taking wood made of *nimba*, one should fashion a three-pronged vajra with tips on both sides; in the middle and on the flanks, one should fashion the origin of the thunderbolt (*kuliśa*).
Having then purified it with mantras, one should place it before the cloth painting in the lower part.
Then, having touched it, the mantra-practitioner, being composed in meditation, should recite the mantras sixteen hundred thousand times; when this is completed, success is desired.
Then that vajra, emitting a single flame, blazes forth on all sides.
Then he rises up, ascending to the inconceivable;
from there he goes to the world of Brahmā or to another realm equal to the gods. Then, traveling through the sky, he becomes the foremost among all the perfected ones (siddhas).
He indeed exercises sovereignty over the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others;
thereafter, he becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) in the presence of the gods,
performing various kinds of physical manifestations.
The fourteenth chapter:
For ten intermediate kalpas he shall remain for a long time without being moved;
partaking of happiness, always worthy of worship, handsome and possessed of beauty at all times.
One who possesses the thought of awakening and conducts themselves accordingly becomes free from the suffering of birth;
such a person becomes a god or a siddha, entirely devoid of all evil.
Upon passing away from that state, they will become a human being devoted to manifold happiness.
Abiding while traversing all states of existence, one becomes destined for enlightenment.
Infinite and diverse activities, honored for the sake of the many worlds,
are recited in this King of Mantras according to the detailed extent of the Kalpas and the non-Kalpas.
It brings about sovereignty over the earth, the state of Śakra, or the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin);
likewise, it performs superior feats among the Vidyādharas and the gods.
Or, it assumes many forms and appearances, as is described here.
When properly employed by the mantra-practitioner, one attains all accomplishments.

At night, having ascended a couch and reciting the *acintya* [mantra] while observing the vow, the practitioner attains accomplishment at dawn; the reciter shall become possessed of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).

Having stepped upon a corpse in a cremation ground, the practitioner, remaining motionless, should recite the single-syllable mantra of great significance; success is desired at dawn. If one staying in the cremation ground recites this King of Vidyās of great majesty, [success is attained].

Within six months, one attains accomplishment and achieves whatever fruit is desired. Whether in this place or that, wherever it may be, the mantra of great power brings about accomplishment for one who remains there and is properly employed by practitioners.
A white parasol, as well as a sword, a jewel, sandals, earrings, a necklace,
armlets, a cloth, and a finger-ring; likewise a waist-band, a garment, a staff, and a water-pot.
The sacred thread, the turban, armor, and even the leathern shield;
the deerskin, the lotus, the rosary, and the sandals—
all these are the most excellent ornaments, and both are equal in this world.
By gods, humans, and others alike, all ornaments indeed attain perfection for the reciter before the cloth-painting;
likewise, every substance, mineral, ornament, and even jewels [attain perfection].

All the various weapons should be arranged before the cloth-painting; once recited over them, they become purified. When empowered by eight hundred thousand recitations, all of them together will blaze forth. By merely touching them while reciting, the practitioner shall rise up.
Furthermore, the natures of sentient beings, appearing in various forms and shapes,
may be ornaments or weapons, either made of clay or existing by their own nature; they may also have the nature of beautiful forms and movements, or even resemble various flocks of birds.
