All beings that are proclaimed, whether artificial or indeed natural— whether they possess the notion of a sentient being or are devoid of such a notion— are accomplished when worshipped with mantras,
arranged with various substances, and fashioned from various elements.
Or else, having placed [the image] before the cloth painting according to the previously seen ritual procedure— [an image] highly honored among the destinies and wombs—
the mantra-practitioner should touch it and recite six hundred thousand and seven [hundred thousand mantras].
At the conclusion of the recitation, when those [seeds] blaze forth, one attains abundant accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Upon merely being touched by them, one may fly up in the four directions;
one shall live long and attain the long-lasting happiness of the gods here on earth.
In whatever manner this King of Vidyās of great supernatural power is applied,
in that very manner he shall be pleased and shall always become a granter of boons;
whereas those engaged in other rites through rituals involving extensive kalpas [attain results only gradually].
By these very means, the great-souled King of Vidyās is swiftly accomplished.
One who is pure, possesses a pure mind, and is constantly devoted to pure deeds—
the knower of mantras— attains pure accomplishment in a pure place.
One should know that action and its fruit correspond; from superior [action] comes superior [fruit], from middling [action] comes middling, and what follows is considered inferior.
This is the fourteenth chapter.

The *karma* mantra, having bestowed abundant wealth, performs the activities of a spirit; yet, if unaccomplished, the success of the rite yields only a meager result. However, through constant recitation alone, one becomes possessed of great enjoyment and great power.

It always brings about favor from kings and the status of a minister for the reciter. His evil is destroyed; whether the king of mantras is recited once, twice, or seven times, it becomes a great protection for oneself.
[The text provided consists solely of a double slash (//) and contains no content to translate.]
Recited eight times, it provides protection for companions from all sides;
furthermore, the mantra-practitioner should then consecrate both garments with the mantra.
Both garments, when consecrated with mantras, liberate one from all diseases;
by touching them while those mantras are recited, the fever of embodied beings is destroyed.
Or, if one carefully consecrates water with mantras and sprinkles it upon the eyes of an angry person,
that angry individual will be destroyed as soon as he is seen by the practitioners of mantra.
And as for those hosts of spirits who are wicked, harmful, and performers of evil deeds—
one should gaze upon their faces with the king of mantras recited thirty times.
One should also consecrate one's own hand again and again;
by warding off their blows, one is liberated from all embodied beings.
One should constantly perform the bathing, drinking, and feeding of children while reciting the excellent,
supreme mantra worshipped by the gods sixty times.
All the wicked ones— the flesh-eaters, the mothers,
and the seizing spirits— being terrified by the mantra, perish and always abandon the foolish.
In this manner, he performed many such deeds upon the surface of the earth;
likewise, he always acted swiftly toward human beings.
Whatever beings there are that have crept forth, whether various stationary or moving,
whether poisonous or non-poisonous— they all perish when struck by the mantra.
Whatever various sufferings there may be, and whatever sensations experienced by sentient beings, when cast away by the King of Mantras, they swiftly bestow peace.
The various sufferings of exhaustion and great pestilences that have arisen will be swiftly destroyed by reciting this mantra as requested in the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa.
One should perform the fire-offering rites with fragrant blue lotuses mixed with honey, sugar, and clarified butter; eight thousand such flowers, duly worshipped, should be offered.
Through the *śānti* rite with sesame seeds, living beings and the people attained well-being;
such were the many rites that had arisen over many eons.
When well-employed by the ministers, it indeed swiftly accomplishes everything;
by mere recitation, one should effect the destruction of the enemies' wrath.
For those who possess many extensive ritual manuals (*kalpa*) endowed with the meaning of numerous mantras,
their accomplishment (*siddhi*) is said here to occur through the methods prescribed therein.
One certainly performs minor rites through the recitation of mantras;
indeed, by means of such recitation, one always swiftly accomplishes all purposes.
For the purpose of subjugating all beings, it is prescribed that one should recite [the mantra] at the three junctions of the day and always perform the rite of fire-offering with *mālatī* flowers.
When prepared with white sandalwood, camphor, and saffron,
the mantra always brings success to the excellent reciter.
One who recites the mantra while performing daily oblations shall accomplish their desired aims;
indeed, the daily oblation is prescribed as being performed with camphor and other such substances.
One should accomplish various rites as they are conceived according to one's desire;
from even a very small rite, an abundant manifestation of prosperity arises.
Success in all intermediate rites is said to be constant;
therefore, one should especially perform the fire-oblation (homa) in all ritual actions.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the detailed exposition on the ritual procedures for the maṇḍala and the means of accomplishment for the universal monarch (*cakravartin*), from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi was present there in the midst of the assembly.
Having sat down, he rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
Excellent, excellent, Blessed One!

Well-taught, well-proclaimed, and most excellently spoken is this great Dharma-cloud issued forth from the application of vidyā-mantras; it is the heart of all Tathāgatas, the sovereign wheel-turning king of great vidyās, the fulfiller in every way of the extensive great kalpa, fruitful, and the unsurpassed path to enlightenment for those who follow the practice of vidyā—including the various rites, twilight recitations, fire offerings, and conduct. It is the cause and sign produced by the conditions of karma with visible results, the source of great wonders, skilled in ascending the stage of the Ten Powers, and the certain destination for ascending the seat of enlightenment.

"Therefore, it would be well if the Blessed One, the Teacher, would explain the signs of the time for the manifestation of dreams that are conducive to the accomplishment of mantras, so that beings who follow the practitioners of *vidyā* may undertake the rites for the sake of the signs of success, and so that all *vidyās* may become fruitful through the signs of those rites."
When this had been said, the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi:
"Excellent, excellent, O Lord of Yakṣas!

You have set out for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great mass of beings, and for the sake of all practitioners of vidyās."
Listen to that; attend to it well and thoroughly, and I shall speak it to you.

First, having gone to a place free from attachment for all activities—the commencement of the preliminary rite—one should go to a mountain peak, a riverbank, a cave, or a hut, and having constructed a dwelling in a pure location, one should install [the deity] upon a cloth-painting (paṭa) and perform a great worship. According to that very same procedure as before for all rites, during the bright fortnight or the fortnight of miracles, necessarily on an auspicious day, at night during the first watch, having combined white sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, and having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations in front of the cloth-painting, measuring four cubits, while the smoke has ceased and the flames have subsided into embers. At the conclusion of that homa, one should offer eight thousand lotus flowers.
[The image] should be anointed with white sandalwood paste.
At the conclusion of the fire offering (homa), having formed the mudrā, one should offer a seat upon an auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha) using the mantra of one's own deity and that very mantra.
One should perform the fire offering with this mantra.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
It is as follows: Oṃ, you who possess the form of a youth, show, show yourself! Manifest your own majesty! Report my dream to me exactly as it was! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, having performed protection with this mantra, one should perform all other ritual acts during the fire-oblation (*homakarma*).

Then, having spread out the finest *kuśa* grass, one should sleep in front of the painting—neither too far nor too near—with a bundle of *kuśa* grass as a pillow for the head, while devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first watch of the night. Having bowed to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, confessed one's misdeeds, and surrendered oneself to all the Buddhas, one may then yield to sleep at one’s ease.
Dreams that occur during the first watch of the night are known to arise from phlegm;
those in the second watch, arising from bile, are censured by the world.

One should recognize a dream in the third watch as being caused by wind (vātika), and in the fourth as arising from truth; however, in one dominated by phlegm (śleṣmika), such dreams are always seen at the beginning of sleep.
O Rāma, he then beholds himself as a vast heap of jewels, pearl necklaces, and abundant masses of water, extending for three yojanas.
Surrounded on all sides by flowing rivers and submerged in the great ocean—
standing there, one indeed beholds that very place situated within one's own body.
There, that region was filled on all sides with lotus ponds,
as well as pleasure-boats, gardens, taverns, and dwellings.
And he would see the Himālaya mountain or some other great mountain situated within a vast river, being carried away on all sides by the waters.
He sees a mountain, a rock, and a king, all piled together with crystals; he sees it covered with nets of pearls and a heap of pearls.
That bearer of the *kahā* sees a great rain and a flood of water,
as well as a white, bright umbrella, or even a pale ornament.
An elephant of white form is said to be the dream for one with a phlegmatic constitution (kaphin);
or else, the sight of a white yak-tail fan, a man, or even a garment [is indicative].
One should touch from all sides rock salt and other salts,
as well as cotton, linen, silk, iron, silver, and aloe-wood.
In dreams characterized by phlegm, one may experience touching or swallowing;
likewise, there are dreams of beans, bloated corpses, sesame paste, and rice with molasses.
The fifteenth chapter and section:
Regarding those with an excess of phlegm (*kaphin*), various kinds of bean-based foods are desired in dreams;
others include *svastika* cakes, *apūpikā* cakes, *kṛsara*, and *pāyasa*.
For one with a phlegmatic constitution (śleṣmika), the consumption of these in a dream is prescribed;
likewise, *śaṅkulī*, *parpaṭa*, various edibles, and diverse kinds of soups.
From touching and even from eating them in a dream, there is an increase of phlegm and impurities;
these various kinds of foods and edibles are thus considered [impure].
From eating or touching those [substances], one experiences the activities of dreams characteristic of the phlegmatic humor;
likewise, food, bedding, vehicles, and mounts originate from the same source as the living beings [associated with that humor].
If dreams involving touching, ascending, or seeing [the deity] are seen during the first watch of the night, all of this is said to apply to one of phlegmatic temperament (kaphin).
Such are the dreams involving water-born creatures,
or various sights of foods to be chewed and swallowed, and of things that cause phlegm.
Having seen their activities in dreams, those belonging to the phlegmatic humor (śleṣmika) are indeed described by the Leaders of the World as being inconceivable and distinct from one another.
For those with a predominance of bile (pittika), however, their own [dreams] occur during the second watch of the night;
they see forms like blazing fire or things produced from various jewels.
A person whose mind is overwhelmed by bile sees in a dream a fire or a great meteor blazing in every direction.
One should recognize the sight of rubies, other gems, or anything originating from precious stones in a dream as belonging to a person of bilious (paittika) temperament.
From attending to fire, from touching it, and even from consuming it,
various yellow-colored substances are seen by those fainting from bile in their dreams.
One who, afflicted by a bodily excess of bile, sees in a dream the sun always blazing and its heat perpetually harsh, [is near death].
If one sees that sky as gold-colored and the surface of the earth as yellow in a dream, it arises from a depletion of bile (pitta).
In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, one who is overcome by bile sees, at the time of dreaming, the vault of the sky blazing all around, increasing, and shining brightly.
At that time, the earth, the mountain, or the mass of rock will be gold-colored;
likewise, the great elephant and the vehicle will always consist entirely of gold.
One who is situated in the state of their own nature (*svabhāva*) and is overcome by the activity of *pitta* perceives everything as consisting of gold—
the vessels, the vehicles, the ornaments, and the mounts.
Furthermore, sitting or lying upon a seat or bed made of gold,
as well as touching or mounting such objects, results in dreams characterized by the pitta humor.
Clad in yellow garlands and garments, adorned with yellow cloth,
rich with yellow-splendid perfumes, and wearing a yellow sacred thread.
And he who perceives himself as having a yellow appearance in a dream,
due to the arising of a bile-induced fainting spell, sees it during the second watch of the night.
Various dreams of such diverse kinds as those you have described to me, which appear yellowish and arise from bile, are produced by the humor of bile.
In the middle course, they are not specified for embodied beings who favor bile;
however, appearing in many forms, they arise with a yellow luster.
Dreams arising from bile have been described by the foremost of the world;
now those dreams arising from wind are indeed told during the third watch:
all the directions are seen as radiant with light on every side.
And there is also travel through the sky, as well as a sacred ford in the vault of heaven.
For it wanders constantly everywhere, in the atmosphere and across the vault of the sky; such is described as a wind-born dream.
Jumping, leaping, and climbing trees;
the recitation of all the scriptures, and especially of the mantras.
Excessive talking and chatter,
as well as climbing thorny trees and eating extremely bitter food, [are causes] in the case of vātika [diseases].
The fifteenth chapter.
For one with a vāta disorder, there should be the consumption of pungent and sour foods among all edibles,
as well as fruits that primarily cause the obstruction of vāta and provoke vāta.
In dreams, the consumption of those specific foods and substances that increase wind (vāta) is indicated as being caused by wind; likewise,
a person becomes deranged in mind through contact with or even the consumption of such things.
One who sees himself as a servant of all beings, or even as their master,
in a dream, is known to have a wind disorder (vātika);
such a person exhibits various forms of movements and speaks with various signs and expressions.
Various terrifying utterances occur in dreams characterized by wind;
such dreams as these have been described by the foremost of men,
applied in three ways to those possessed of passion, hatred, and delusion.

One should recognize that for those possessed by passion (*rāga*), [the dream] arises from phlegm (*śleṣman*); that which arises from hatred (*dveṣa*) is born of bile (*pitta*); and that which arises from delusion (*moha*) is born of wind (*vāta*). Furthermore, when these are mixed, it is a combination of them.
A dream-affliction called "passion" consists of the observation of sexual intercourse.
In that context, when a dream arises from phlegm (śleṣman), there is a count of women; when it arises from bile (pitta), it is characterized by quarrels with enemies;
and when it arises from delusion (moha), it appears as a state of stupor accompanied by the loss of memory.
Indeed, dreams are always seen as being joined with that which is intermingled;
therefore, by every means, those who perceive reality have declared that what is called a dream is devoid of substantiality and is equal to the time of action.
Those of a phlegmatic nature are said to be handsome,
pleasant-spoken, long-lived, yet dull-witted; they possess a glossy complexion, are self-confident, fair-skinned, tall and well-proportioned, and are always devoted to the company of women.
Those who are most righteous, eternally brave, always devoted to great honor,
and designated by birth under a [favorable] lunar mansion— such kings, as well as others established for the purpose of generalship, should be free from envy and unblemished.
Those who live by their actions are born in Bhogavatī;
the fruit of one's own karma is what is ordained, for the leaders of the world have taught that there is no mantra devoid of action, nor is there any action superior to mantra.
Therefore, success is said on this earth for a being of phlegmatic temperament;
he shall attain mastery over the earth and great enjoyment. However, the reciter should not excessively consume any phlegmatic foods.

These dreams, when indulged in excessively, result in the occurrence of pure [auspicious] matters; therefore, the wise practitioner, being endowed with skillful means, should not indulge in them at that time, nor should he sleep then, as it has been described for one whose purpose is to break [the cycle].
The conduct of a person of bilious temperament (paittika) is always described as follows: he is prone to anger with an expression of hatred, is dark-complexioned and weak,
and is always cruel, performing cruel deeds.

He is always heroic and daring, possessing strength and intelligence without needing counsel; he speaks much, has many friends, and has attained mastery over many scriptures; he is righteous, firm in his undertakings, and is described as one whose resolve is free from hatred.
One born under Śakra is wise and highly intelligent, yet characterized by malice;

he is brave, hateful, and desirous of much wealth. He is knowledgeable of the world and pleasant to behold, yet he is also liberated from worldly ties, free from longing, steadfast, and always difficult to endure.
He will be proud, envious, and angry, yet always beloved by women;
he will be possessed of great energy, firm in counsel, and born into great luxury.
Having stepped upon sentient beings according to their acquisition of karma,
his mantras that obstruct life-breath always achieve success.
For a seeker who desires to accomplish a fierce and powerful rite quickly,
those actions which involve the destruction of living beings will succeed for that embodied practitioner.
Whatever various ritual applications (prayoga) are performed by all mantra-practitioners, they are accomplished with diligence; [this does not apply] to the rituals of other sentient beings.
The Fifteenth Chapter on Rituals:

Those mantras which are indeed characterized by hatred and cause affliction to other beings, as well as the mantras of others—these are severed; for one who possesses a mind of wrath, success is achieved [in their destruction].
Krodha-mantras are effective for the purpose of seizing the property of others and for obstructing the lives of others; however, one should not employ them in other types of mantras.
Furthermore, this being born of hatred exercises sovereignty;
he is either black in color, or dark, or fair, or a mixture of these.
A man who utters "moṃ" is born wrathful and deprived of a golden complexion;
he is born with a coarse, smoky, or tawny hue.
One born in the zodiac sign of Scorpio is brave, cruel, and likewise greedy;
situated in the domain of the planet Mars, he is subject to phlegm, O Bṛhaspati.
For one who consumes pungent and sour flavors becomes a moderate eater;
his life-span is long, and he possesses memory and wisdom.
I shall now describe the conduct and behavior of one afflicted by wind (vātika):
he is discolored, has a dry complexion, and his stature is neither too large nor too weak.
The wise man’s intellect is perpetually lost; his heart is unstable and lacks firmness;
there is trembling of the limbs, vertigo, vomiting, and excessive discharge.
He will indeed be a glutton, a constant eater, and a man of many words;
he will be an adversary to all people, yet he will have many friends.
Though he may be born on the surface of the earth with poor conduct and even in misery,
the secret mantras for invisibility are indeed said to grant him success.
Those foods which provoke the wind (vāta) follow after him;
therefore, the practitioner of recitation (jāpī), desiring the accomplishment of his rites, should never consume them.
But for these beings who are overcome by delusion and whose wind-humors are provoked, these [rites] born of delusion are prescribed;
they are accomplished through deluded mantras.
The accomplishment of delusions for the deluded is always desired in those [constellations],
when the moon is in a water-born sign and is aspected by a planet that signifies truth.
One should not perform auspicious rites when a person afflicted by wind (vātika) is overwhelmed by passion, nor should one perform rites for subjugation,
attraction, enchantment, or the paralysis of spirits.
Even among beings dominated by wind, these characteristics of dreams— which reveal the truth— are declared through delusions that give rise to evil.
Indeed, these were described by the sages of old as accomplishing all goals:
Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and Leo.
Libra, Virgo, and likewise Scorpio, Sagittarius and Capricorn,
Aquarius and Pisces, the elephant, the celestial being, the monkey, and the asura.
The Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and others who are proclaimed among men—
these have been described as the zodiacal signs (rāśis) of many beings by the foremost of teachers.
There are many kinds of diverse meanings described through various types of karma;
in all those actions, the full extent of qualities bears fruit.
Indeed, it is taught that embodied beings are never liberated from karma and its qualities;
moreover, when joined with the qualities of karma, one brings about rebirth.
In the mantras that possess accomplishment, a quality conjoined with dharma and artha arises;
the reciter, knowing the reality of qualities, [discerns] the merit and demerit of the bonds of karma.
One does not perform beneficial action if there is no proper application even toward the qualities;
for it is the application that accomplishes the action, not an application devoid of qualities.
Endowed with the qualities of ritual action, he will accomplish it;
for ritual action preceded by the prescribed method was taught of old by those possessed of the ten powers.
Action consists of the qualities of karma; it is observed as the activity of the sentient being.
Arising from karma, various forms like those in a dream are perceived.
Therefore, by means of the dream-sign, extensive ritual activities should be performed—those which are manifold in form, diverse, delightful, and pleasing to behold.
Those who possess great enthusiasm and great heroism, and who long for accomplishment, see both obstacles in form and formless ones as the causes of their dreams.
The fifteenth is the non-ordinary cloth;
success is ordained among the superior, inferior, and middling [beings].
Those who are fierce and performers of cruel deeds always have dreams that are immediately effective.
The highest worldly activities, which are capable of producing virtues in the foremost of people, lead to success over a long period of time through constant practice.
Various dreams are seen by those who recite mantras for the sake of attaining mantra-siddhi; however, for the sake of the non-attainment of mantras, sleep and lethargy are produced.
At that time, the mantra for destroying obstacles is prescribed; one should employ those mantras, which take the form of skillful means, by the practitioners of recitation.
Then the great wrathful one Padabhujas, as well as Ṣaṇmukha, were manifested;
the four-syllabled great mantra issued from the form of Kumāra.
Of terrible form and most formidable, born in the likeness of a boar,
that very Kālarātri is the sovereign for the purpose of destroying all obstacles.
Clad in a tiger skin, with a serpent’s hood hanging down, sword in hand, that being of great courage and immense luster had the appearance of Death himself.
Cruel toward all obstacles and intent on slaying the Vināyakas, let all beings indeed hear this most formidable mantra of the Tantra.
The destroyer of wicked beings, the remover of all obstacles,
and the accomplisher of all mantras— O hosts of gods, listen to me!
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! O you who practice that [teaching]— He He, Great Wrathful One,
Six-faced One!
Six-legged one!
Destroyer of all obstacles!
Hūṃ hūṃ!
Why do you delay, O Vināyaka!
O bringer of the end of life!
Destroy my bad dream!
laṅga laḍṅgha, remember the samaya! phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!

As soon as this Great King of Wrath was spoken, all the obstructors and Vināyakas— afflicted, terrified, with broken hearts and trembling minds— paid homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, and they stood firm in the sacred pledge (*samaya*).
In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed that entire abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and that great circle of the assembly, spoke thus: "O hosts of gods!
This King of Wrath shall subdue and wither, together with their entire kin, any wicked being who might obstruct a practitioner while the worldly and transcendent mantras are being accomplished."

And it shall not cause the obstruction of life; having heated and dried [the practitioner], it will establish them in the state of stability, remaining for the sake of the reciter’s protection, preservation, and guarding.
For whoever should thus transgress the pledge and would harm the practitioner protected by the King of Wrath, [the mantra] will cause him to swell with suffering.
"His head shall split into seven pieces like the cluster of an arjaka flower"—
having spoken thus, the best of sages then addressed Mañjughoṣa.
O Kumāra!
[I shall explain] the extensive exposition of all purposes regarding your mantras,
specifically for practitioners who have been liberated through the meaning of the mantra-tantras.
This, which destroys all obstacles, was taught in the tantra by Krodharāja;
indeed, it was likewise employed in this manner by the Lords of the World in the past.
For the destruction of wicked obstacles and the subduing of the wrath of enemies,
one who recites this mantra should always read it constantly during the nights.
This [teaching], which serves for the protection of sentient beings and the destruction of bad dreams,
has been taught by the leaders of the world for the accomplishment of the purpose of all mantras.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the auspicious characteristics of men,
among whom the mantras— whether superior, inferior, or middling— attain accomplishment.
He was radiant, wise, golden-hued, and large-bellied;
he had wide eyes, was very gentle, free from excessive passion, and devoid of anger.
One with blood-red corners of the eyes and who speaks kindly attains the highest success;
he has thin skin, a darkish complexion, slender limbs, and is not overly tall.
Possessing great energy and great luster, contented and auspicious in every way,
he is preeminent by birth, pure, of few desires, and humble.
His success is seen to be preeminent in all undertakings;
he is complete in his limbs, dark-complexioned from the front, and possessed of great majesty.
The fifteenth chapter: One who is unafflicted in mind, wise, a celibate practitioner, always pure,
constantly delighting in dwelling [in seclusion], knowing the world, and virtuous in conduct.
He is always well-friended, ever-generous, and always acts with moderation;
he is pure, skillful in character, and always devoted to cleanliness and right conduct.
For one who speaks the truth and is compassionate, the supreme [attainment] succeeds;
he is always of noble birth, righteous, and possessed of the full expansion of all excellent qualities.
Devoted to his mother and father, honoring Brahmins and guests,
and being exceedingly compassionate and steadfast— for him too, there is supreme accomplishment.
Dark-complexioned yet radiant, affectionate, speaking little, always pure,
desiring wholesome food, and approaching a pure wife.
For one who knows the world, is highly esteemed by beings, and possesses supreme accomplishment—
neither too short nor too tall, with hair like crushed collyrium— [success is attained].
With eyes of affectionate hue, pure, and always devoted to bathing,
he was full of faith in the Three Jewels; for him too, the supreme accomplishment was attained,
as he was engaged in the most excellent deeds and understood the dispositions of sentient beings.
Patient, speaking kindly, and gracious toward the Son of the Conqueror.
Then his supramundane accomplishment remains fruitful;
he is a great being, of great heroism, of great majesty, and a keeper of great vows.
Possessing great wealth, a knower of mantras, and one who understands the reality of all tantras—
he is foremost among the Kṣatriyas by caste, or else a wise Brāhmaṇa.
He was always devoted to women and full of passion; moreover, he appeared golden-hued in complexion, tall and fair, with a prominent nose and mighty arms.
He has long arms and is heroic, desiring great sovereignty;
he is well-disposed toward the sons of the Jina and worships the goddesses known as women.

Devoted to the three jewels and adorned with the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), he was exceedingly compassionate and steadfast; at times he was prone to anger, and at other times he possessed great brilliance.
In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, one who possesses great wealth, great generosity, and great splendor, who is difficult to overcome,
beloved by women, and heroic— his success is said to be supreme.
One who delights in arrogance, is brave, and is always attached to women;
one who has a golden complexion, eats little, is broad-chested, firm, and pure.
Compassionate, merciful, skillful, and knowledgeable of the world, he was highly esteemed for his virtues;
a constant reciter of mantras and a devotee of the Jinas, he was Prabhankara.
Among them, the sons of the Śrāvakas and the Khaḍgins are always present;
furthermore, the foremost person in the world is preeminent in complexion in the second auspicious [kalpa].
He was free from physical defects, complete in all his limbs, yet always fierce and impetuous;
he was generous by nature, had conquered his enemies, and was a judge of both righteousness and unrighteousness.
A person who is neither too stout nor too emaciated, neither too tall nor too short, is considered a middling human being; for such a one, even the highest accomplishment is possible.
With copper-colored nails that are very glossy, with palms of the hands that are red and pure,
and with the soles of the feet being red and lustrous up to their edges, he is adorned with the marks of the wheel and the svastika.
A person endowed with the hundred thousand auspicious marks sees on his hands and feet banners, arches, fish, flags, lotuses, and water-lilies.
Such a person is considered the most excellent, destined for supreme accomplishment;
his teeth are white, without gaps, prominent, and even like mountain peaks.
He has a prominent nose and wide eyes; his eyebrows and chin are well-knit and auspicious; he possesses the marks of eyelashes like those of a cowherd, and his black pupils are adorned with stars.
He whose forehead is broad, whose head is auspicious and shaped like a parasol,
and whose ears are beautiful and well-formed, possesses a head shaped like a turban.

His jaw is always shaped like a lion's, his lower lips possess a luster equal to that of a ripe bimba fruit, his tongue is seen to have the reddish hue of a lotus petal, and his palate is likewise intensely red.
The neck is like a conch shell, the shoulders are full and well-developed;
the armpits and chest are auspicious, and the breast is likewise broad and excellent.
The fifteenth chapter:
The region of the navel is slightly deep, broad, firm, and auspicious;
the navel is deep and spirals to the right, without a network of veins.
His arms were long and his biceps great; his hips were marked with the sign of a lion;
his thighs were rounded, and his elbows were free from scars.
His shanks are said to be like those of the eneya antelope, well-proportioned, and round;
his feet are fleshy and elevated with well-formed toes.
The two [feet] are reddish, with red nails, glossy, elevated, and adorned with flesh;
then the two heads are beautiful, pleasing to behold, and possess the color of the surface of the earth.
They are unjoined, pure in color, praiseworthy, and marked by worldly signs;
moreover, above them, the network of veins is not protruding.
The two groins for the passage of excrement should be deep and situated on the right;
they are praised when they are very small and the two testicles are always round and auspicious.
It is celebrated in many ways as being both limited and unlimited;
when it is based on the pure [state] within the group of limbs (aṅgajāta) and at the end of the passion (rāga).
If, during the improper time for eating, one's own urine is seen to be blue or red in color due to the consumption of various kinds of food and drink;
When the [substance] known as *sattva* is abundant in its flow, unctuous, and marked by auspicious characteristics, the highest accomplishment (*uttamā siddhi*) is desired for such a subject.
One who voids excrement three times and urinates six times, who is devoted to pure conduct and is clean,
and who indeed lies down at the end of the watch and rises in the morning— such a person, O living beings, [is purified].
Its purification is always seen as most excellent, effective for all rites,
and yielding various kinds of fruits or abundant prosperity.
One characterized by middling marks shall become an enjoyer [of pleasures],
as will one born under the asterisms of Puṣya, Revatī, or Phalgunī.
During the asterisms of Maghā, Anurādhā, Citrā, Rohiṇī, and Kṛttikā,
the progenitor (Janaka) is visible when situated therein, being capable and marked by planetary signs.
Success is seen in those [rites] performed at dawn;
likewise, at midday, in the morning, and also at the end of the day, the planets are pure.
The Moon is white, Mercury is yellow, and Jupiter is yellow;
they are observed for the sake of accomplishing the tasks of all living beings according to their respective capacities.
And in this interval, those humans who have been born as performers of auspicious deeds—
for them, mantras succeed without effort in accomplishing all aims.
Always at midday, in the afternoon, and at sunset—
at these intervals, cruel planets always gaze upon embodied beings.
The Sun, Mars, the malefic planets, Ketu, Rāhu,
and Saturn, as well as those chief among the planets who cause the destruction of actions through meteors;
At that time, Tārā becomes most terrible, as does Kṛṣṇāṣṭimā;
the fierce Kālamārakuru is seen there by virtue of that time.
At the time of sunrise, Mercury beholds the earth;
at a height of one *yuga* (four cubits), Jupiter beholds it from his chariot.
Venus, the lord of wealth, is seen by him in the solar conjunction;
from midday onwards the moon waxes, which is the manifestation for those embodied as the moon.
During the period of Mercury, there will be sovereignty; during that of Jupiter, it brings wealth and enjoyment;
during that of Venus, there is the attainment of riches, great kingship, and an abundance of enjoyments.
O long-lived one, likewise, sovereignty under the Moon is fruitful;
and similarly, when the Sun is at midday, it is said to be equal to a neutral aspect.
When midday has passed, the sun always gazes toward the direction [of the zenith] at a distance of one *yuga*;
the comet is described as being neither high nor low [at that point].
Rāhu, Śanaiścara, Tama, Kāla, and Yugāntaka;
beyond them, in the eastern direction, are Niṣṭa, Ariṣṭa, Ulka, and Kampa.
When the sun has turned copper-red at sunset, resembling a mass of vermilion—
[there appears] that chief of planets who possesses the form of a young boy.
This concludes the fifteenth chapter from the extensive collection [of the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*].
With a spear in hand and exceedingly cruel, he appeared like a glowing coal; then, as the sun was cast at the end of the eon, the sources of the auspicious planets [were eclipsed].
One born when Mars is in conjunction with the Sun becomes cruel and impulsive;
one born when Mars is in conjunction with Saturn is wrathful, greedy, and arrogant.
When the Ketu planets are excessively smoky, they give rise to the outbreak of diseases;
people will always be impoverished, afflicted by illness, greedy, and dull-witted.
The time for earthquakes and portents, for meteors and the malevolent planets,
for tremors, thunderclaps, and the stars, as well as for the fierce lightning-bolt, the vajra-ariṣṭa, and other such omens of the Ṛbhus and others, is revealed; indeed,
the terrible appearance of Rāhu is seen by all living beings.
Through the killing of a goat, mortals are always born as poor, helpless, and immoral people, as well as sinful thieves; they become afflicted with suffering,
lepers, those with many diseases, and those who are one-eyed, lame, or afflicted with skin diseases.
Eunuchs and impotent men, childless and unfortunate, women who are despised among women, as well as other men and women who are loathed for their adherence to false views—[all these are excluded].
Worlds are born in many ways from the very birth-charts (jātakas);
among those, white and yellow planets are excellent, as they bring about auspicious births.
In terms of color, those with white and yellow lusters are praised as described by the Jinas;
these four are the foremost among the planets: Venus, the Moon, Jupiter, and Mercury.
For the sake of accomplishing the vision of those [deities] in all ritual actions,
and for the sake of foolish beings, birth here is always auspicious for the reciter.
All forms of prosperity are said by the foremost beings in the world to be perpetually sweet,
even for a mere moment, or the blink of an eye, or even the snap of a finger.
The birth of these [planets] has been briefly described by the leaders of the world;
this alone is the authoritative measure for the planets who contemplate the world.
In this manner, they arise constantly at this very time according to reality;
these evildoers revolve perpetually on the wheel of fortune.

In the *Śrīmūlakalpa*, those who always perform auspicious or inauspicious deeds [through] the mantra as one [single entity] are indeed established in the world of the gods. However, if among them some should develop even a slight evil intention,
they are born again in many ways due to their attachment to the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious [karma].
They say that this is the "vision" of these planets who consume the fruits of karma; moving with great speed, they approach living beings as they move about.
The visible and the invisible, my swift movement in an instant;
from that, time is calculated—this measure of time has been shown by those of foremost intelligence.
Hereafter, I shall explain that which is always determined in the *jātaka*.

Next, the twelve muhūrtas, which are the causes for attaining specific times at various intervals, shall be described; furthermore, those who are unfit vessels will be mentioned, as well as whether or not they are causes for spiritual success.
One should observe the omens of the world again and again through sightings and non-sightings,
as well as the ruin of the kingdom, famine, and the prosperity or misfortune of the king.
Then, O King, at all times, there was a perception of both the opportune and the inopportune moment;
moreover, there were tremors of comets, thunderclaps, and meteors accompanied by smoke.
The movement of the constellations, days of the week, and stars, both auspicious and inauspicious; the conduct of all beings, and their deeds that are either propitious or calamitous.
I shall now describe the conduct of the flesh-eating mothers and those of fierce nature who cause harm, as well as those wicked beings who subsist on raw meat.
There, the deities are pleased with those whose intellects are fixed upon the supreme jewel of the Dharma—
those who are ever-engaged in virtuous deeds and possess minds of loving-kindness and compassion.

I shall describe in detail the conduct of those whose actions, objects, and intellects are directed toward the virtuous, who rely on the fulfillment of others, and who are drawn by the utterance of mantras for the purpose of consuming medicinal herbs; therein I shall explain the characteristics upon which they depend—
those who, having entered the human path, remain by taking recourse in the bodies of others.
The fifteenth chapter.
Furthermore, the gods spoke thus to him because of their pride:
"Those attendants present there are of two kinds—both gods and asuras."
They too proceed there in two ways—again, as cruel and as common;
they too proceed there in two ways, toward the fivefold destinies of the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Residing there, they proceed through three types [of rebirths]: twenty, thirty, and an incalculable number;
from the Akaniṣṭha heaven down to the lords of the Yāma gods, who are beyond counting.
As far as the realms and worlds are infinite, so too are their virtues and non-virtues;
as many as there are worldly beings, and as many as there are noble disciples.
Of the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as their own legitimate sons, the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas established on the ten stages.
All sentient beings are likewise eternally dependent upon the womb of existence;
all foolish creatures are dependent upon the various realms of rebirth.
The characteristics and conduct of all Buddhas— who are forever liberated from the serpent of saṃsāra— are eternally and universally present at all times.
I shall explain in detail the truth regarding their speech and gestures:
how all beings are summoned by means of mantras, tantras, and logical applications.
One who knows the mantras for entering and extracting [a spirit] should [perform the rite] upon one who has taken refuge in another's body,
with skillful practitioners who understand virtuous actions, who are vigilant, and who are devoted to recitation.
By all those who practice without delusion and are capable of both restraint and favor,
the worlds on the surface of the earth have been drawn forth into the human realm by means of mantra-recitation.
I shall now explain in truth all the signs of accomplishment for them,
as well as for the sake of conforming to the bodies of those humans who are constantly afflicted by disease.
It is always intended for the sake of dharma and ultimate liberation;
therein lies the suppression of the wicked and the honoring of the pure.
The subjugation and the favoring [of beings] are fashioned through mantra and tantra;
here, for wind, phlegm, and bile, there are three types and threefold applications.
For them, one should provide pacification; indeed, a threefold sequence is prescribed.
Among these, one should always perform the medical treatment for humans by means of mantras.

The conceptualization of the great elements (mahābhūta-vikalpa), however, is traditionally held to be "the element" (bhūta) and "that which exceeds the elements" (bhūtādhika). Likewise, that which is overcome by the elements is called "the over-element" (adhibhūta).
When a living being produces ill-health through an external element (*adhibhūta*),
then that element is classified as being of two types.
Thus, that which is sentient is eternally conceived as non-sentient;
bile, phlegm, and vitality, as well as the other four great elements, with space as the fifth— water conjoined with fire,
and earth conjoined with wind.
The wise always say that he is not reckoned among sentient beings;
indeed, the one of great splendor declared him to be the foremost lord of the world's summit.
For that which is not reckoned as a sentient being is non-human, while that which is human is a sentient being; thus spoke the one of supreme intelligence, the best among speakers.
Whether it be a non-human or a human multitude of beings, including the gods,
for the sake of the welfare of all beings, he spoke again with words of omniscience.
Thus has karma, which gives rise to the fruits of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, been taught by the Buddhas of the past, the future, and likewise those of the present.
The mere word of the Buddhas necessarily brings about the result;
because of that cause and the commonality of the spiritual lineage (gotra), accomplishment itself is clearly perceived.
They call it omniscient knowledge—secure, peaceful, and eternally pure;
established in pure selflessness, this ultimate reality is held to be liberation.
This very path among sentient beings has been proclaimed as this sūtra;
therein, he spoke the entire teaching on mantras, medicinal herbs, and spells.
The reality that has been and will be, supremely honored by all scriptures,
the world-transcending selflessness of phenomena, the state that is eternally peaceful and auspicious.
The fifteenth chapter:
This is the word of the Omniscient One; it is the ultimate state of that [Omniscient One].
It is solely through conceptualization that the arising of the knowledge of the Omniscient One is described.
The power of all the Buddhas and the wise Bodhisattvas,
as well as the accomplishment of mantras in all rites, is shown everywhere.
For this very reason, the Lord of Sages has proclaimed this King of Ritual Manuals;
by proceeding along this path in the form of mantras, it leads embodied beings [to liberation].
One attains the city of Nirvana, which possesses the tranquil wealth of freedom from decay;
it is free from sorrow, stainless, secure, culminates in enlightenment, and is eternally auspicious.
This tantra, which is the teaching of all Buddhas for those who recite mantras,
has been declared upon the earth as the supreme method for mantra-reciters.
All knowledge and the objects of knowledge are bound by the causes of karma;
all this, however, is the meaning of mantra, which flows toward the threefold awakening.
The complete knowledge of the Buddhas has been revealed here in this eon,
and for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, it has been set in motion throughout all worlds.
Whatever is found in this *Kalparāja* is not seen in other *kalpas*;
and whatever has been taught in other *kalpas* by the sons of the Munis, those best of sages.
Indeed, this is the detailed ritual procedure for all mantras;
for this very reason, it was taught by the Lord of Jinas for the sake of all embodied beings.
And upon the surface of the earth, throughout these three worlds, there is no one who has not been brought under control or subdued by this sovereign king of rituals.
When the Moon of Sages has set and the circle of the earth is empty,
he will carry out the purpose of the teaching while this world remains in this eon.
The youth Mañjughoṣa, ever auspicious among all beings,
shall likewise perform the work of a Buddha in this world and in this teaching.
Having heard the non-substantiality of this King of Kalpas, those who have long desired it will gain faith through hearing it even once; for them, accomplishment shall always be attained.
In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, this speech is always auspicious and never in vain for all beings,
regarding those practitioners who are constantly devoted to recitation and fire-offerings among all spirits.
Whatever knowledge functions among the three types of knowledge,
that very same [knowledge] functions here in this most excellent king of ritual manuals.
The establishment of mantras is here declared to be the teaching of the Buddhas;
yet that mantra is free from conceptual construction, though it is spoken here within the realm of conceptual construction.
He brings about the welfare and misfortune, the auspicious and inauspicious,
the destinies, the intellects, as well as the very nature of all beings, and the prosperity and adversity of the worlds.

This very [reality] is elaborated upon in the Kalpa; yet the Tathāgatas are themselves free from elaboration. Though they have transcended the world and are self-awakened, they are spoken of here for the sake of the world.
Transcending all worldly conditions,
he performs various and manifold deeds that are honored by the world.
Engaged in ritual activities through the king of mantras and likewise beneficial to the multitude of sentient beings,
that youth Mañjughoṣa performs the work of a Buddha.
Its purpose is the accomplishment of qualities and the foundation of the world, both auspicious and inauspicious;
I am indeed the requester and the speaker, for one who does not request is not said to speak the Dharma.
Exclusively for the benefit of all sentient beings, that which was spoken by the Buddhas of the past shall now be proclaimed as spoken by the Buddha.
One who has faith will see that the lineage of the Buddhas shall remain uninterrupted;
for them, the wisdom of the omniscient one will arise in all activities of the practitioners of mantra.
But only that action which proceeds from the knowledge of the Omniscient One is praised;
one's own previous karma in this world is now being experienced.
Therefore, one should perform actions that are difficult to accomplish here in these births;
thus, the mantras become effective without effort, and the bondage of karma is severed even in this world.
Success may be attained even in this life through action;
therefore, all the Buddhas have praised action alone.
That rite performed according to the prescribed method brings success quickly even in this world;
yet foolish beings, deluded, wander about deprived of the proper method.
Therefore, in every respect, action alone is praised;
one who is disciplined shall accomplish the goal through the method joined with action.

Likewise, an action performed contrary to the prescribed rules does not reach fulfillment even after a very long time. Indeed, there is no liberation without meditations, nor is there liberation devoid of meditation.
Therefore, when meditative concentration and liberation are joined together, they are called enlightenment.

Thus ends the section on the performance of all ritual actions from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Now begins the sixteenth chapter. Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes (*Śuddhāvāsabhavana*), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
Listen, Mañjuśrī!

I shall explain in detail, as previously indicated within the midst of the assembly circle (*parṣanmaṇḍala*), the extensive section on the ritual activities for accomplishing all aims belonging to you;
this was requested by the illustrious Vajrahasta, the King of Yakṣas.

Thus, in this context, all this has been told concerning the auspicious and inauspicious dreams associated with the meaning of all mantras for those who recite them; [this was spoken] by the King of Yakṣas,
with a joyful mind, having placed his joined palms upon his head.
Having bowed his head to the Teacher, he joyfully addressed him with these words:
"For the sake of favoring the worlds, this has been spoken by the one of supreme intelligence;
likewise, out of compassion for me and for the welfare and happiness of all beings."

The auspicious and inauspicious dreams of those who recite all mantras, their conduct and the expansion of their qualities, the empowerment of sentient beings, the lowest states and the supreme destinies and wombs, and the activity of the knowledge of causes.
Knowledge of the past and future, knowledge of the present, the auspicious and the inauspicious— all this is all-pervading knowledge, the activity of the omniscient one's wisdom;
it is without appearance, without an object of support, free from conceptual proliferation, yet manifested through proliferation.
Endowed with the most excellent forms of mantras, auspiciousness and peace have been proclaimed;
indeed, the power of all Buddhas has been described by the one of supreme intelligence,
especially for those who recite mantras and are engaged in the meaning of all mantras.
Karma, the fruit of karma, and likewise the time of action;
the recipient, the place, and the attire— these were prompted in the context of dreams by the Yakṣarāja,
the most excellent and supreme sage, the Tathāgata of the seven mantras.
Among the Buddhas of the Fortunate Aeon (Bhadrakalpa), this seventh one is the Bull of the Śākyas,
the Lion of the Śākyas, the Conqueror of Enemies; he is designated as the seventh, the Lord of the World who brings forth light, having attained perfect enlightenment in this debased age.
The Sage of great heroism, of great wisdom, and exalted by great splendor— Vajrapāṇi, that Yakṣa Bodhisattva, paid homage to him. This is the sixteenth detailed chapter.
Then the wise Mañjuśrī, possessed of great insight, remained silent upon his own seat; having been questioned by the sage at that time,
he then exhorted the Buddha, the youngest of the sages and the best of men.

Excellent is the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, who [relates] the birth story (*jātaka*) in detail concerning the knowledge of karma— [a tale] that is ever auspicious and concerns the conduct of many beings together with the causes of their karmic knowledge.
For those who are established in their desired activities and intent upon the means for attaining the highest good,
for those reciting mantras, the signs of accomplishment regarding what is to be achieved or not achieved appear;
likewise for those in the world desiring prosperity and longing for the enjoyment of sovereign power.
"May all-pervading knowledge be revealed in brief for those who desire the attainment and preservation of the most excellent [powers] for the sake of sovereignty"—
thus spoke the supreme Sage when he was entreated by the Son of the Jina.
The wise one, possessing the voice of a kalaviṅka bird and sounding like a divine drum,
with a Brahma-like voice and the thunderous resonance of a great cloud,
inspired by the speech of the Buddha, uttered this pure verse in seven syllables.
O Prince!
May this [teaching] of those who have attained the goal of others' welfare and who act for the benefit of the world—
those who lead all beings toward the highest good— be purified and endure for the sake of liberation.

For those who possess true and inexhaustible vigor, whose minds are intent on that [truth], who delight in prideless loving-kindness, and who always take pleasure in the attainment of accomplishment among such people— for them, no other will ever attain accomplishment in this supreme mantra.

Those who always find joy in the teaching of the Holder of the Wheel (Cakradhara), or likewise of Mañjudhara, who subdue Māra and set the wheel in motion— he too, being disciplined here, becomes a Holder of the Wheel.
Proclaim that the Buddhas possess speech that is divine and enchanting, eternally free from the defects of foolish beings,
divine and delightful, pleasing to the ear, lovely, sweet, agreeable,
and a giver of the happiness that gladdens the mind— speech that is truly beautiful.

Even those sons of the Tathāgata who have entered the stages, as well as those who are the most excellent among the ten classes of gods and are distinguished in the world of the lords of gods— even they are unable to know the absence of his [nature], nor can they know his divine power through their specific Tathāgata-knowledges.

In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, those who have attained the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of yoga—whether they be of the form realm, the formless realm, the intermediate states, or born among gods, humans, or men—none exist in this world who are more distinguished than he. Among all beings, there is no one who can rival his glory;
indeed, the Buddhas declare that he is equal to Śrī and is named Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī is equal to a mere mental construction; this name was likewise given to you by previous Victors.
This designation was established for you in the Saṃjñita eon by divine Buddhas of the past and the future.
Upon hearing your name, one becomes pure; one's mind will not become distracted, but will become single-pointed.
Through this, may there be auspicious peace for him; may he attain supreme and most excellent enlightenment;

may all mantras be accomplished without exception; may he obtain birth in a noble lineage and reach the highest state; may he always rely upon the supreme Dharma and achieve accomplishment free from all obstacles.

Having accomplished all desired mantras, he will swiftly go to enlightenment; having attained enlightenment, that preeminent Sage will quickly obtain Mañjuśrī. Having gone there, he sits for the sake of the welfare of beings and turns the wheel of awakening. This merit has been proclaimed by the foremost of Jinas.
O Mañju, by recollecting your name, which brings glory, inconceivable qualities have been proclaimed by the foremost of Jinas.
May your eternal power be revealed—power that cannot be described even in countless eons by all the former foremost Jinas. O pure youth, hundreds of mantras of yours are [beyond measure].
O Mañjuśrī, this mantra-practice has been taught by all the Buddhas without exception; O Youth, this indeed pervades everywhere. This is your supreme teaching, O heroes;
those people dwelling in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens indeed seek out all sentient beings without exception.
"Never, under any circumstances, [should one say] 'this is my mantra' or 'this is your mantra.
Thus ends the detailed exposition of the chapter on verses from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni entered the samādhi called "The Miraculous Manifestation of All Tathāgatas.
Immediately upon the Blessed One Śākyamuni’s entry into that samādhi, rays of light issued forth from the circle of hair between his eyebrows.
Having the colors of blue, yellow, white, madder-red, and crystal,
it illuminated this entire Buddha-field and lit up all the intermediate spaces between world-systems; having eclipsed all the planets and constellations in a mere moment and drawn them forth,

and having caused them to return to their respective places once they were drawn in, it drew that circle of the assembly through the Buddha’s empowerment and vanished back into the tuft of hair between the eyebrows of the Blessed One, Śākyamuni.
And all the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, being obstructed by the great luminaries, distressed and terrified, approached the Blessed One, the Śākyasun;
they stood with palms joined in reverence, trembling and repeatedly falling to the surface of the earth.

Then the Blessed One, the Śākyamuni, for the sake of favoring all the planets, lunar mansions, stars, and luminaries, as well as embodied beings whose intellects were born of ignorance, uttered these words:
Listen, worthy sirs, you hosts of gods together with humans:
it is karma alone that differentiates the diversity of the world for sentient beings.

Both the accomplishment of the adamantine body (*vajrakāya*) of the Blessed Buddhas and the accomplishment of the diverse bodies of the world—including gods and asuras—caught in the wandering wilderness of *saṃsāra*, all this arises from karma; it is bound by what is auspicious and inauspicious.

In this regard, there is no agent, no doer, no Lord (*īśvara*), no Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*), nor does a Person (*puruṣa*) set anything in motion, except for that which is born of karma. All [results] are produced by the conditions of all actions and depend upon causes;
and that [result], in turn, depends upon causes and conditions.

In this way, the limit of conditions in dependent origination adheres to one another, and from the cohesion of these [conditions], it generates the great elements that bring about the manifestation of beings; and those great elements proceed toward another aggregate of existence from a beginningless course of transmigration.
And those who have set out for another destination of rebirth undergo it in its full extent and detail;
yet, fanned by the fire of knowledge— which is contrary to the obstructions of time— they utterly consume even the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) fashioned by karma,
and through the equanimity of the three vehicles, they bring about the state beyond conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*).

The karma accumulated over a long period of time by those of the Mahāyāna results in their own self-arisen gnosis (*svayaṃbhū-jñāna*). For the Pratyekabuddhas of the intermediate period, it proceeds from their own realization. For the Śrāvakas who follow the voice of another, there is sovereignty for a short time; because of that, their cognition does not proceed excessively, but rather only internal cognition proceeds for the deluded among the foolish.

In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, [there are] those of the Form Realm and the Formless Realm, as well as those of the Non-existent [Unreal], those born of desire, the divine, and those born of humans or men.
Now, among the yogins who have attained accomplishment in this world, as well as among the most distinguished men,
there is no being whatsoever who can equal his glory;
indeed, the Buddhas declare that he is equal to Śrīparikalpita and recognize him as Mañjuśrī.

Mañjuśrī, this name of yours, which is like a conceptual construction, was likewise established for you by former Victors; it was given to you in the designated aeon by divine Buddhas of the past and those yet to come.
If one hears his name and becomes pure, his mind will not be distracted;
for him, there shall be this auspicious peace, and supreme, most excellent enlightenment shall come to pass.
May all mantras be accomplished without exception; may one obtain birth in an excellent womb and take refuge in the supreme Dharma; and may there be accomplishment forever free from obstacles.

Having accomplished all desired mantras, he will swiftly proceed to enlightenment; having attained enlightenment, that foremost of sages will quickly obtain Mañjuśrī and, for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, go and sit [there].
He has awakened to the turning of the wheel of enlightenment; this is the virtue described by the foremost of Jinas.
O Mañjuśrī, when one recollects your name, inconceivable virtues are said by the foremost of Jinas.
O Pure Youth! May your eternal power be revealed—that which cannot be told even in hundreds of mantras throughout countless eons by all the former, all-pervading, foremost Jinas.
There, Mañjuśrī, the practice of mantra was spoken by all the Buddhas without exception;
O Youth, this is indeed your teaching that pervades everywhere, the supreme jewel of the heroes.

"Indeed, the beings dwelling in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens do not at any time, nor in any way, ever transgress my own mantra— those who [abide by] your mantra. Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the detailed exposition of the section on verses, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni entered the meditative absorption called "The Miraculous Manifestation of All Tathāgatas.
As soon as the Blessed One Śākyamuni had entered that absorption, rays of light issued forth from the circle of hair between his eyebrows.

Having illuminated this entire Buddha-field with colors of blue, yellow, white, madder-red, and crystal, and having lit up all the intermediate spaces between world-systems, he eclipsed all the planets and constellations in a mere moment and drew them forth;

and having drawn them forth, he established each in its own respective place, and having drawn that assembly-circle toward him through the Buddha’s empowerment, it vanished back into the circle of hair between the eyebrows of the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
And all the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, being obstructed by the great luminaries, approached the Blessed One, the Śākyasun, in distress and fear;
they stood with palms joined in reverence, trembling repeatedly and falling prostrate upon the surface of the earth.

Then the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, for the sake of favoring all the planets, lunar mansions, stars, and luminaries, as well as embodied beings whose intellects are produced by ignorance, uttered these words: "Listen, O worthy ones! O hosts of gods and humans! Karma alone divides the manifold variety of the world for sentient beings."

The perfection of the adamantine body of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the manifestation of the diverse bodies of the world—including its gods and asuras—caught in the wandering wilderness of saṃsāra, all this arises from karma; it is bound by the auspicious and inauspicious.

In this regard, there is no agent, no doer, no Lord (Īśvara), no Primal Matter (Pradhāna), nor does the Puruṣa act, unless he is impelled by something else. With the sole exception of that which is born of karma, every action is produced by causes; it depends upon a cause, and that cause in turn depends upon conditions (pratyaya).
Thus, the limit of conditions in dependent origination connects with another; and from the accumulation of phlegm, it produces the great elements that bring about the manifestation of beings.

Those great elements proceed toward another aggregate of existence from beginningless wandering, and having entered, they are reborn in various detailed divisions within different realms of existence.
The fire of the realization of non-conformity with the obstruction of other times incinerates all latencies (*vāsanā*) constructed by karma;

through the equality of the three vehicles and the state of being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*), it completely carries away the karma accumulated over the long duration of the Mahāyāna. Then, the self-arisen gnosis (*svayaṃbhū-jñāna*) of the Pratyekabuddhas who are like rhinoceroses of the middle period proceeds.

For the Śrāvakas who follow the sound of another's voice, their sovereignty over the mind is for a short time and not long-lasting; therefore, in those fools who are utterly deluded, a cognition that functions at the very limit of the vital points (marmāntara) proceeds.

In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, it is further stated: Moreover, this world-arrangement, produced by diverse karma and characterized by various regions and customs, seeks auspiciousness, the perfection of freedom from decay, and the stainless accomplishment of worldly success through karma free from sorrow and defilement.

It performs only that action which is pure, liberated from the path [of worldly existence], endowed with the eight limbs, and most cooling; it does not perform any other action, nor does it depend upon anything other than karma.
Freed from both action and non-action, he remains free from conceptual proliferation;
having set out upon the three vehicles, no other peace arises for him.
Mantra is indeed threefold; action is proclaimed to be threefold;
the accomplishment of the fruit is threefold, and the investigation is likewise threefold.
The contrary action is likewise seen to be threefold; that which is wholesome is also declared to be threefold, and it is seen again to be so therein.
Furthermore, such a lineage is the peaceful abode of mantras;
indeed, it is the peaceful lineage of nirvana belonging to the Buddhas of pure mind.
That very same action is proclaimed as the individual portion within the limbs of mantra;
likewise, the limb of astrology is devised in the world for the sake of attaining success.
That very portion of karma indeed proceeds into the portion of conditions, just as rice is recognized by its sprout among the grains of paddy.
For it is thus that accomplished substances are discerned by their characteristics,
just as the color white is conceptually constructed through conventional usage.
For in this way, for the sake of worldly practice, the principles of astrology are devised; thus, among all principles, action alone is praised.
Nowhere does a body exist without those deeds, nor without conscious activities, nor without the accounts of past lives brought forth by one's lineage.
That action is constantly perceived through various omens; nowhere is action seen as a physical form, for it remains hidden and is observed only by its effects.
Just as a fevered person is perceived by all through their various symptoms,
so too is the karma of embodied beings seen once it has taken hold within the body.
The Jātaka signs indicating auspicious and inauspicious results have been proclaimed; there are various omens and various beings arising from diverse karma.
The seventeenth chapter:
The time for military force, as well as various expeditions, and the cries of living beings which always bear auspicious or inauspicious fruits.
One observes the sign for the sake of conviction regarding success or failure;
the sign, the conduct, and the mind are thus conceptually designated as "conviction."
Therefore, with every effort, one who is engaged in recitation should depend upon the conditions; for the sake of attaining success in the mantra, he should rely upon those very conditions.
One should observe that these various actions are one's own karma,
yet they remain unmanifested by all extremely terrible obstructing forces.
"Therefore, all these are limbs," such were the words of the Sage;
the omniscient King of the Sāla Trees entered the seat of enlightenment.
He uttered a mantra that destroys all obstacles,
and which annihilates bad dreams, evil omens, and whatever is unbearable.
When that Great-Souled One, the Omniscient One, had set his mind upon enlightenment, Māra, with a malicious intent, created a most terrifying obstacle.
At the foot of that tree, he indeed beheld a great terror that was signless;
from that signless state, there arose for him many forms of terrifying phenomena.
Then, through the power of his accumulated merit, he who had long desired it shattered the pride of that Narmuci with the syllables of the mantra.
Possessing supernatural powers and great heroism, he is self-restrained and of great splendor;
through the power of his mantra, may I attain supreme enlightenment.
That very mantra shall be taught as the destroyer of ill omens,
the dispeller of bad dreams, the remover of what is difficult to endure, and the warder-off of malevolent beings.
"Let the hosts of gods indeed listen!
This king of mantras was previously spoken by the Jina Śālendrarāja for the purpose of subduing the wicked planets, constellations, and stars."
And it is true for all, being gentle-minded and awakening.
"Listen, all you hosts of spirits, whoever you may be that roam the earth—
whether footless, many-footed, two-footed, or four-footed!"
Homage to all the Buddhas, whose teachings are unimpeded, and to all beings whatsoever, whether moving or stationary, in brief, throughout the three realms.
Oṃ khakha khāhi khāhi | huṃ huṃ | jvala jvala |
Blaze, blaze! Stay, stay! Ṣṇīḥ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
This mantra, derived from the Buddha, is proclaimed as the "Blazing Heat" (Jvāloṣṇīṣa);
it accomplishes eighty-nine thousand five hundred rites.
He performs various rites esteemed as all-auspicious;
he destroys bad dreams and ill omens with a single recitation of the mantra.
He performs other rites as the master over all mantras;
he has mastery over all sentient beings; he is the Buddha, the source, the Guru.
By the mere recollection of this mantra, all obstacles are destroyed;
having spoken thus, "O Buddha, the God beyond gods," the best of sages [concluded].
They stood silent for a moment, waiting for the proper time; and then the hosts of gods remained stationed above the Śuddhāvāsa realm.
Terrified, they all—along with the foremost of gods, the lunar mansions, planets, and stars—entered into a covenant, having been addressed by Uṣṇīṣa with these mantras.
Equal in power, of great heroism, known as Uṣṇīṣa, and possessing great radiance; [the mantras] consist of one hundred, five, four, seven, eight, or ninety syllables.
Sixty-two and another seventy-five are proclaimed as the lords of the Uṣṇīṣas; this number consists of countless auspicious kings of the Mūrdhajas.

"This mantra is equal to those born from the crest of the Victor. Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the detailed section on the conditions for one's own karma, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsabhavana*) and that assembly-circle, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Mañjuśrī, there exists for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva—who is devoted to your mantra practice and intends to fulfill the conduct of a Bodhisattva—a detailed exposition of chapters concerning the sequence of activities, the timing of rituals, the application of appropriate yogic practices, and the observance of astrological cycles conducive to the practice of yoga; it is suitable for accomplishing the purpose of all mantra practices.
I shall speak it; listen to it, and attend to it well and properly."
When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Blessed One:
"It is marvelous, Blessed One!

To what extent the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have been favored with the supreme favor, they who follow all the conduct of Bodhisattvas and fulfill the purpose of all mantra-practices for the sake of sentient beings."
May the Blessed One speak for the sake of compassion toward us.
Thus addressed, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the Blessed One, remained thus in silence.
Then indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, desiring to show favor,
spoke these supreme words of Vajrendra for the benefit of all embodied beings.
O sirs!
O you who dwell in auspicious happiness!

This is the most excellent constellation; it is beneficial or harmful in every practice for the purpose of mantras, whether they be appropriate or inappropriate, and for those who are composed in meditation.
It is said that the goal is accomplished, fulfilled, and likewise favorable;
therefore, for the sake of attaining success, the practitioner of mantra should examine the mantra according to the tantra.
On an auspicious day, in a pure place, always devoted to the practice of purity,
under a praiseworthy lunar day and constellation, and always pure during the bright fortnight.
Having bathed, meditating, observing vows, and reciting mantras— one who is skilled in the meaning of the mantras and tantras—
should perform the fire sacrifice (homa), the recitation (japa), and likewise the accomplishment (siddhi) of the ritual in its full detail.
Revatī, Phalgunī, Citrā, Maghā, and Puṣya are conducive to the accomplishment of one's aims; likewise, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūlā are also described [as such].

Both Āṣāḍhas and both Bhādrapadas are always for the sake of accomplishment; likewise, Śravaṇā is for the cause of success through mantras, as are Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, the two Aśvinyas, Punarvasū, Svāti, and Revatī.
For these are praised and reckoned as those intent upon the practice of the sciences; for them, Monday has been thus declared by the rule.

During the cool season, one should perform pacifying rites (*śāntika*); thereafter, during the remaining times, for the sake of knowledge and nourishment (*vidyā-puṣṭi*). At midday, when the sun is high, [these] rites are performed; however, they are also forbidden during the time of the moon.

When the moon is situated at midnight, one should perform rites of sorcery (*abhicāruka*); for the sake of nourishment, one should accomplish the mantra for the purpose of enjoyment among men; and in all rites, one should understand the rising sun through proper application.

Likewise, in the absence of red [substances], one should perform the rite of abhicāruka (malevolent magic) during the time of the sun; thereafter, one should know it to be in the forenoon within the solar disc.
Likewise, one should always perform rites of pacification when [the sun] has risen to the height of a yoke; thereafter, the measure for Gabhastin should be known as two cubits.
One should perform rites of pacification when engaged in pacifying activities,
using the most excellent mantras and mudrās originating from the foremost family of the Victors.
When the sun has reached midday, one should perform rites of sorcery; after that time, one should employ [the rite] for the purpose of attraction and subjugation.
When the sun has reached the afternoon and is lowered to the distance of a yoke’s length, one should perform all rites; likewise, those employed for minor purposes [should be done] then.
Thereafter, O Sūryadhāna, at that time, the wise one should perform all the rites of subjugation and attraction.
When the sun has set, possessing a radiance equal to the color of blood,
one should perform those rites that have arisen with a blood-red appearance.
Those who desire their beloveds should always perform actions with passion;
however, it is taught that an action resulting in the destruction of even three lineages is censurable.

The eighteenth chapter: One who desires a maiden should swiftly perform the rite as prescribed for the appropriate time; during the first watch of the night, one should accomplish the ritual, being fully intent upon the welfare of sentient beings.
From this point onward, one should cause all rites to be performed everywhere;
at that time, at midnight, the moon-graha shall behold the earth.
At that time,

when the sun has risen, one who seeks success and employs mantras should enter the western region; thereafter, the planet [Jupiter] should be seen by the sun over the southern region, including the king.
Even in the case of a mother, one quickly obtains abundant success in one's undertaking;
both the non-reciter and the reciter obtain the fruit,
and the wise reciter accomplishes whatever siddhi he desires.

In the third watch, one should always proceed with effort toward the southwestern direction; there, the arising of results occurs. Likewise, when the sun rises, one should go toward the northern direction.
