Then, at the end of that time, when the sun has risen to the height of a *yuga*,
the knower of the Tantras, desiring the fruit of success, should go toward the intermediate direction between west and north; that region is proclaimed as the place [of practice].
The Tathāgatas have taught and explained the method for both the non-reciter and the reciter; when the mantra has been mastered and the task is to be accomplished,
one should then go toward the east at midday, or indeed in all directions.
Thereafter, one should cause the rites to be performed by others;
then at midnight, the moon, as a planet, shall behold the earth at the end of time and the end of the intermediate directions, according to the awakening of the Sage.
For those desiring accomplishment, [the time] between the east and the north is similar;
thereafter, the directions beyond that are declared, as is always stated the distinction of time for the east and south, and likewise for the intermediate directions.
In the afternoon, at that time, he entered the abode of the Daityas;
and in all the subterranean passages, among all beings dwelling in pits, and in every way among those glorious-faced ones dwelling everywhere in Pātāla— thus it is stated in the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa.
Then, at the end of the subsequent watch, when the planetary mandala has a reddish hue,
one should enter the abodes of the yakṣa classes, which are indeed very terrifying;
one should go to those surrounding dwellings, even when they are occupied during the swift moments.
As he was rising, he should accomplish the mantra born of the foundation of grace;
for one desiring to ascend to the very summit, there is either failure or indeed success.
Then the daughter of Mānava ascended her own dwelling, the pinnacle of the palace.
In the Siddhānta, it is taught that for one who is well-yoked to those very times and has reflected upon them,
the accomplishment of mantra is always attained by those skilled in mantra and tantra;
indeed, success is declared to be achieved simply by traveling in the [proper] direction.
A person who addresses [the deity] quickly obtains the arising of fruits;
a seeker should accomplish his desired aims, including those pertaining to village-dwellers and human beings.
The times have been declared according to the scriptures, as well as the directions in every respect.
The mantra-practitioner may produce [the result] everywhere, at all times and in all places;
for these [rites] are joined with all the lunar mansions, namely Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, and Mṛgaśiras.
The rite of pacification (śāntika) has been taught as arising from the convergence of cause and fruit;
one who desires wealth and seeks prosperity should always perform it under Rohiṇī while reciting mantras.
Under Ārdrā, one should perform the rite for the purpose of subjugation and attraction.
Under the asterisms of Punarvasu and Puṣya, one should accomplish the attainment of wealth and abundance—
namely, various ornaments and garments, collyrium, realgar, gorocana, red ochre, and clarified butter, all having been well-consecrated.
One should employ rites for subjugation, attraction, and intelligence under the asterism Puṣya;

likewise, under Āśleṣā, one should perform acts such as summoning and striking with weapons; and under Maghā, one should perform acts of attraction, as well as those for sovereignty and the increase of wealth.
The eighteenth chapter:
Both Phalgunīs are most excellent; he mounted his own vehicle, for various rites are performed by the hand itself.
Under Svāti and Viśākhā, one should undertake the acquisition of wealth and the performance of ritual acts;
likewise, under Anurādhā and Jyeṣṭhā— these two lunar mansions joined together—
one who desires success and one who desires sovereignty should always perform them.
One should accomplish the attainment of various earthly riches and the highest success born of yoga when these are applied to the constellations;
for both Aṣāḍhās are likewise declared to be employed in rites concerning living beings.
Success is seen everywhere among humans even with mineral substances;
one who knows the mantras and tantras should accomplish various medicinal herbs for root-rites when conjoined with the Root lunar mansion (Mūla).
In all cases during the Śravaṇa asterism, one should perform the rite described for Śrāvaṇī;
one should also apply oneself to the Dharma that leads to Nirvāṇa and to the life of renunciation.
During the Dhaniṣṭhā asterism, one should always perform the sādhana of incense and lotuses.

One who knows the proper procedure should perform acts such as planting trees, providing vehicles, and giving clothing during Śatabhiṣaj; however, one should avoid that contemptible act of merciless violence toward living beings and the obstruction of their lives.
Both Bhadrapadās are excellent for warding off calamities on earth;
indeed, when employed in undertakings, they quickly bring about prosperity, especially in the accomplishment of objectives through the command of an army.

In a kingdom, one who knows the mantras and tantras may accomplish, according to his desire, the production of wealth, ornaments such as jewelry, and various collections of minerals, provided both [the king and the practitioner] are joined under an auspicious constellation.
Under the asterism Revatī, one who knows mantras should always accomplish the acquisition of wealth arising from various minerals,
as well as the performance of mantra-rites arising from various jewels;
he should always accomplish all kinds of waters.
The Aśvinīs, the Bharaṇīs, and a portion of the Kṛttikās—
this is declared to be the domain of Mars in the vault of the sky;
on its day, one should likewise celebrate his fame and then conquer the earth with gentleness.
One should know that Kṛttikā consists of three parts; Rohiṇī and Mṛgaśiras are the two following it.
One should know this as the field of Bhārgava (Venus) in the vault of the sky;
likewise, Mṛgaśiras and Ārdrā are well-combined [with it].
Furthermore, one should know that Punarvasu, for the sake of pacification, is the field of origin;
likewise, Puṣya, Aṅgāraka, Āśleṣā, and Maghā are understood [to be fields].
This is always the field of the Sun (Bhānu); one should perform malevolent rites (*ābhicāruka*) therein.
On the day of Phalgunī, both [the moon and the sun] are marked by the signs of the planets;
one should likewise know that the field belongs to the Moon on a Monday.
Furthermore, when Hasta and Citrā are joined with their respective portions, one should perform highly esteemed rites.
It is taught that in the position of Mercury, he is the accomplisher of all rites;
when conjoined with Svātī or Viśākhā, or even possessing a portion thereof,
it is proclaimed as the second field of the Sun, without a doubt.
Anurādhā and Jyeṣṭhā are assigned to those two sons of the Earth (Mars);
the second domain of Aṅgāraka (Mars) arises from Scorpio,
and one endowed with all dharma and artha shall accomplish their goals through action.
A wise person should avoid violence and the desire to harm living beings;
rather, one should accomplish various goals and abundant ritual actions.
Both Mūla and Āṣāḍha are likewise declared to arise from the three parts of the Saṃśa.

This field of Bṛhaspati is seen situated in the sky; on earth, one whose mind is disciplined should accomplish their work according to the prescribed rules. It brings about the attainment of great enjoyments and wealth, as well as the fruitful arising of results.

One indicated by the asterism Dhanvin (Sarpa) shall bring about all prosperity; those indicated by Śravaṇā and Dhaniṣṭhā are declared to be equal to Śatabhiṣā. This is the eighteenth chapter from the extensive [work].
This second field of Śaniścara has been described in the past as the sign of Capricorn (makara), which wards off all misfortunes;
if a wise person should undertake any actions while situated therein, [they will succeed].
At that time, the mantras employed by one who knows them are accomplished without effort;
the lunar mansions designated as Aquarius were proclaimed by the sages of old as auspicious,
namely the two well-known Bhadrapadas and the illustrious Revatī.
Likewise, the first [sign] is deficient in limbs; those marked by auspicious planets and Indra are all praised and beautiful. That entire field should be given to the Guru.
This has been described in summary according to the sign of Pisces, as marked by the world.

The planet is primary everywhere; among all ritual acts, these seven are indeed declared to be the foremost for the arrival of hosts of superhuman beings. The chief planets are infinite, and the contemptible planets are likewise infinite.
For these have been declared to be neutral with respect to humans, whether they be beneficial or harmful;
thus they are specified for practitioners of mantra-recitation in their applications of the [three] natures.
Likewise, the existence and non-existence of beings, as well as time and destiny, have been proclaimed;
there is no grasping at that which is conjoined with the Dharma, nor is karma marked by the planets.
The conjunction of planets and lunar mansions is declared to be the accomplishment of mantra.
Success is not to be known as time, nor is failure said to be time;
both success and failure proceed in sequence from the time of attachment.
Those who practice the Dharma do not regard phenomena as being contrary to the Dharma.
One who is joined through the union of Dharma and action will achieve success;
it does not come from fate alone. For one who is devoid of action, there is no accomplishment; accomplishment does not arise from fate.
Therefore, both action and accomplishment depend upon fate itself.
One is not liberated from karma by fate alone; rather, fate is measured by karma, and it is taught that karma is determined by the causes ordained by destiny.
The planets are indeed liberated from karma when the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) are well-honored.
Therefore, their karma is equalized, and the accomplishment of the purpose of karma is desired.
This enumeration has been declared: action alone is ever accompanied by the gods; neither the planets, nor the zodiacal signs, nor the birth-constellations, even when well-honored, [determine fate].
One should always understand that this action is the sovereign rule, arising as it does independent of ritual injunctions.
It is taught that the arising of results always depends upon the application of method within mantras;

therefore, ritual action arises from method, and not from the planets, nor from the zodiac signs, nor from the birth-stars, lunar days, or the movements and origins of the constellations— in short, none of these.
Furthermore, there is no fixed rule for the duration of time regarding the two types of karma;
therefore, the knower of Tantra, like a seer, should always apply himself solely to dharma.
In this world, there are various other collections of infinite planetary influences.
The lunar days have been calculated in the collection by those who apply them, as well as the fields;
therefore, I shall speak in brief—listen to what is being told by me:
Aries, Taurus, Gemini, and Cancer are well-yoked.
Leo, Virgo, and Libra;
Scorpio and Sagittarius; Capricorn and Aquarius—these should be known [as the animal signs]; Pisces and Capricorn are the others.
Human, divine, and Garuḍa are the other [categories].
The hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas, animals, hungry ghosts,
and others, as well as those in the hells— all these infinite destinies born of various wombs are designated as aggregates; all these aggregates arise from a variety of elements.
Innumerable other aggregates have been proclaimed by the sages in various ways;
I shall describe their signs of movement and their basis in the wombs of sentient beings, as well as the infinite lunar mansions and planets.
And the fields have been described in many ways as being inhabited by various grahas;
thus ends the nineteenth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī,

there is a third chapter concerning the rules for the knowledge of astrology, which was spoken and approved by the former Perfectly Awakened Ones, and which is fashioned according to the purpose of your mantras and tantras."
"Listen well and attend thoroughly; take this to heart.

When the Blessed One Śākyamuni had spoken thus, Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed him as follows:
"It would be well, Blessed One, if the Blessed One would speak the *Jyotiṣajñānapaṭalatri-sara* (The Threefold Essence of the Chapter on the Knowledge of Astrology)."

That shall be for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of beings— of gods and humans— and for those beings who have entered into all mantra practices, as well as for those who have set out toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. They will easily accomplish the practice of mantras through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*),

in accordance with all beings, in conformity with the ritual procedures of yoga, and by performing their own actions as they issue from the determination of time, the conjunctions of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), days of the week (*vāra*), planets (*graha*), birth-classes (*yoni*), fields (*kṣetra*), and zodiac signs (*rāśi*).

That shall be a means for accomplishing happiness; that following of mantras shall have a happy fruition; that shall be the manifestation of the miraculous power and the empowerment of those Bodhisattvas. When Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had spoken thus, the Blessed One then said this to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!"
Since you ask the Tathāgata about this matter, listen then; pay close and careful attention,
and I shall speak for the benefit of all sentient beings.
When this had been said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to listen to the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having pervaded the entire Śuddhāvāsa abode with his radiance, entered the samādhi called "The Illumination that Surveys All Buddhas.
Immediately upon his entering it, rays of light—blue, yellow, white, madder-red, crystal-colored, and so forth—issued forth from the body of the Blessed One.

Having emerged and illuminated the buddha-fields of sentient beings, Mañjuśrī—according to the *Mūlakalpa*—illuminated all the abodes of the planets, lunar mansions, birth-sources, constellations, and stars; having illuminated the dwellings of those in the realms of hell, animals, and gods, as well as the abodes of humans and all other sentient beings situated in the expanse of the sky, and having alleviated all their sufferings, he once again dissolved back into the body of the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
Then the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, arising from that samādhi, addressed all those hosts of deities of the lunar mansions, planets, and zodiac signs:
"Listen, O you hosts of deities of all the lunar mansions!

Whoever has entered into the practice of mantras within this Dharma-vinaya and in this ritual manual (*kalpavisara*), they shall accomplish [their goal] regarding all mantras and the performance of rites involving all substances. None of you, having assembled here, should create obstacles therein; rather, you must proclaim your presence for the sake of providing protection."

For whoever should transgress this pledge, Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, instantly brings all the nakṣatras and grahas—dwelling in infinite world-systems, together with their sons, kinsmen, and retinues; he subdues them, instructs them, and leads them into the presence of the Blessed One. Standing upon the heads of them all and treading on them with his foot, he displays various miraculous feats of fierce deeds. By the empowerment of the Buddha, he deprives them of life and establishes them in the pledge. He manifests himself in a transformed form, and at the end, all the hosts of bhūtas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, nakṣatras, grahas, rāśis, niḥsattvas, garuḍas, maruts, and mahoragas—all terrified, trembling, and crying out with great lamentation—fall at the feet of the Blessed One while shaking, and speak thus:

"Save us, O Blessed One! Save us, O Sugata! We are without a protector; we are without a refuge. Terrified by the fear of the Great Wrathful King, O Blessed One, grant us our lives! Having spoken thus, they became silent, their limbs trembling. Then the Blessed One, Śākyamuni—

He addressed that assembly of constellations and planets, as well as the hosts of yakṣas, rākṣasas, pūtanas, piśācas, and mātṛs: “Do not fear, noble ones! Do not fear, noble ones! For those who have approached the presence of the Tathāgatas, there is no fear or death; indeed, noble ones, all suffering is warded off. One should go for refuge to the Buddha, the supreme among those who have overcome calamity; one should go for refuge to the Dharma, the supreme among those free from passion; one should go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the supreme among assemblies. For such a person, there shall be no horripilation [of terror].”
Those who desire the truth, the speech, and the repeated recitation [of the mantra] should be regarded as truly liberated from the fear of death and from all fears and sufferings;
no worldly fear whatsoever shall ever exist for them. This is the nineteenth chapter-section.
"May they attain that state which is the pacification of suffering, peace, freedom from fever, well-restrained, and directed toward awakening.

Then, at that very moment, by the Blessed One’s miraculous power, all their sufferings were dispelled. And Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down near Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta to listen to the Dharma;
and all those hosts of planets and constellations had all their sufferings completely stilled.

And all the banners were stilled; they sat down to listen to the Dharma, became composed, and with one-pointed minds, gazing at the Blessed One, their eyes wide with wonder, they became single-minded.

Then, out of compassion for the world, the Blessed One gave a teaching of the Dharma in such a manner that it was associated with the four noble truths; as a result, some of those beings perceived the truths, some attained the state of a *śrāvaka*, some attained the awakening of a *pratyekabuddha*, and some generated the aspirations suitable for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. All were rendered destined for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, all the gates leading to the lower realms, evil destinies, and perdition were closed, and the doors to rebirth among gods and humans were opened; the bolt on the gate of heaven was cast aside.
And they all established their commitment;

then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having understood their underlying tendencies and knowing that the time for their discipline had arrived, immediately spoke the Dharma to those beings who were ready to be trained— a Dharma concerning the enemy-like suffering that assails one, which arises from faults and has no stable foundation.
All the hosts of gods, including Abhāva, are honored here in this teaching;
therefore, exert supreme vigor for the sake of the steps leading to enlightenment,
so that you may attain the peaceful, feverless abode of the Sangha.

You shall attain the supreme, irreproachable, divine, and unobstructed state— Nirvana, which is free from sorrow, stainless, secure, ultimate, immaculate, known as equal to the sky, and characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature.

Those who meditate throughout the day on the meaning of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness as it has been fully explained will attain the ultimate state; and by means of the teachings of Mantra and Tantra, their conduct shall indeed result in the arising of bliss.
The supreme accomplishment of mantra has been proclaimed by the best of Jinas; it was taught by the wise ones as the foremost means for sentient beings through their diligent application,
and this accomplishment of mantra occurs at the time of the fruit when there is a perfect convergence.
The birth of actions is manifold, as if joined by something diverse;
from action comes manifold accomplishment, and that which is born from the womb of action is manifold.
This manifold [power] has been applied through these mantras of variegated form.
The expansions of karma have manifold meanings; karma is said to be manifold. Karma is both conceivable and inconceivable, yet it is also considered.
Therefore, the practitioner of mantras should undertake [the practice] with abundance among the various wonders of mantra.
The zodiac signs have been described; men born under them are always [of various kinds], as are the leaders of gods and asuras, and the diverse living beings and birds.
One should apply their respective characteristics to the [astrological] attainments.
Likewise, a human or a celestial being born in the zodiac sign of Aries becomes one with many offspring, much speech, and great beauty;
such a person is described as a man who possesses the character of a merchant, is brave, and is highly esteemed among women.
The Moon situated there is said to be crooked, greedy-minded, and a servant of householders; one should employ it in all undertakings.
If the Sun should be seen situated in the sign of Aries, [it is likewise].
One who serves the village and is always presiding over it should understand the limbs of the Lord;
the Moon was born situated therein, and he is that righteous Lord of the Gods. Indeed, his mind is always intent upon the kingdom.
His mantras should always be given; these are the caityas spoken by the Jina.
This is the nineteenth detailed chapter.

By that [mantra] joined with the meaning of the moon, the basis of the person is understood through its meaning; it possesses the logic of the rite of going and coming, as well as the rite of shaving the beard.
One should perform the rites of the planets but not engage in malevolent magic; one should undertake all ritual activities that bring about the blissful arising of mantra-siddhi,
and one should draw mandalas and the like, and have images of the Buddhas made.

The most excellent divine liquors, which are accomplished substances, are being prepared by the denizens of heaven; when joined with mantras, they are perfected under the lunar mansions and among the sages.
When a human is born under the constellation Mithuna, he then becomes a denizen of heaven.
And understand the signs of their destinies at the time of accomplishment:
one becomes wealthy, diligent in mind, yet deceitful and dull-witted;
if he is renowned while staying there, the stars become the ornament of the night.
Then, one becomes beloved by women, always dear to kinsmen,
wealthy, resourceful, and known as a great lord,
even if accompanied by various cruel and contemptible remaining planets.
One who is overcome by the passion of rogues and afflicted by diseases—

neither the supreme mantras for pacification (*śāntika*) nor those for prosperity (*pauṣṭika*) will succeed for him, nor those directed toward the vile, the dejected, the flesh-eaters, or the eaters of raw meat.
There will always be sightings by the foremost cruel planets;
for the sake of achieving mantras in cruel rites, one should employ these [planets],
avoiding travel there except for the first five [days].

In those [two], there is no success in coming and going, nor in any rites; likewise, for them, minor rites should be given. Everywhere, one should know that the two chief planets called Śitaka (Venus) and Pātaka (Saturn) are the two others.
The fourth [chapter] concerns the observation of the principal planets, which gives rise to prosperity:
when both are red or both are black, it is the observation of those who perform cruel deeds;
when they are white—namely the Moon and Venus—or yellow, as are Mercury and Jupiter.
The Sun and Mars are red, for they are born from the earth;
Saturn and Rāhu are black; and the remaining planets are variegated.
Their dwellings are said to be diverse, wonderfully adorned with various minerals.
Some of diverse forms, with various weapons raised, presiding over many groups of minerals, all these planets are attended by ancient sages, Apsarases, and Kinnaras.

Abiding in the sky, they have attained their forms through their color; known by their modes of movement and birth, all those who travel through the atmosphere move in conjunction with the constellations, having arrived at their stations in the firmament with various motions and activities.

They are said by all the best of sages to possess great power through their majesty, their gait, and their physical appearance and attire; they are joined with the true meaning of the principles of karma and,
on the fourth day, are associated with the four beings.
Four excellent planets have been declared: the white and the yellow ones accomplish one's goals; the remaining ones are for cruel rites, as are the red and the black ones when employed.
One should not perform any rites, especially those for pacification (śāntika), on these two planets when they are black or red, nor on the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī).
One should not perform all types of activities; one should accomplish minor tasks. A seeker of wealth should accomplish auspicious undertakings during the period of Mānuṣa Gaṇanā.
With those very [materials], the wise one should always quickly have a seat, a bed, and a temple constructed; he should cause all [necessary] fortifications to be built.
A person born while situated in the zodiac sign of Cancer appears auspicious; he shall quickly become a ruler and even a universal monarch (cakravartin).
O venerable ones, for living beings, consciousness arises from the emergence of past karma, and likewise, the vision of the Moon, Indra, the planets, and other such deities occurs.
On an auspicious day and in an auspicious place, the Bodhisattva was born; those honored by the gods are born under the conjunction of the Puṣya constellation.
The nineteenth detailed chapter:
The Buddhas, the teachers of the three worlds, as well as others possessed of great supernatural powers; kings who rule and those who destroy, and lords of many living beings.

In this world, various beings are born—those who are empty, those like the sun, those like charcoal, and those like fire; some mortals are abundant in people, while others are devoted to their actions.
Those born under Puṣya are always born with various modes of conduct; therefore, know that the fruit of karma is the destiny resulting from one's own actions.
However, those who follow right conduct and are engaged in the rites of the planets, disregarding worldly conventions in this world, teach in that same manner as the Victors.
Karma is the diversity of the world, born from the meditative concentration of the world-system; it is the vessel for all worlds, arising from the manifestation of their support.
O gods! Listen to this wonderful and most excellent account told in the world; indeed, the affectionate one related how it had arisen from karma in the past.
Then the wise Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa, possessed of great power and common to all sentient beings, made his choice out of a desire for the welfare of beings.
All that is born of karma has been explained in detail, along with the mantras and tantras; O all you gods, this is the dharma which is always attained by a single person.
To one born under the zodiac sign of Cancer, one should give a mantra for nourishment; thereafter, the sign of Leo appears before that person.
A mortal born under Siṃha would be a hunter of sheep; he would be deceitful toward women, a consumer of meat, and a dweller in mountain caves.
Likewise, the king, as the great overseer, should always have the earth governed by a commander-in-chief who is pure yet ever engaged in stern deeds.
One who is ungrateful, one who betrays secret counsel, one who is constantly devoted to sinful deeds, a betrayer of friends, always greedy, and deceitful—such a person is born thus.
Furthermore, when seen by wise men with rays that are white or yellow, one is born there as righteous; however, when seen with black rays, such a person is remembered as deceitful.

In that *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, the rite for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) is taught for those desiring success; it also brings about the arising of one who moves through the sky, transcending even the highest mind.
One should not undertake another similar action, nor should one avoid it; beyond that, the sign of Leo is traditionally known as the constellation Kanyā (Virgo).
One born therein becomes a rogue, a thief, miserly, and deceitful; though always beloved by women, he is ever greedy, cruel, and impulsive.
He is foolish, an adulterer, stubborn, and always puffed up with pride; yet, he was born under an auspicious lunar mansion and weekday, with favorable aspects from and the rising of benefic planets.
Those whose hair is seen to be yellowish-white at the tips become very wealthy; one who possesses a pure mantra is always wise when relying on a conduct of purity.
One should accomplish on the surface of the earth those mantra-tantras that have arisen, which quickly bring about one's goals and those which are proclaimed for the sake of nourishment.

The knower of mantras shall accomplish all [rites] belonging to the families of the limbs of the Victors, as well as those mantras headed by the Lord of Victors that have been proclaimed in many ways.
The knower of mantras shall accomplish all things within the signs and their respective classes; beyond that, there is the sign celebrated by the name of Libra.

One should not frequent that [place] which is well-known, abounds in ritual actions, and is dependent upon them; for the wise man, when engaged in the attainments of mantra, is born equal [to the goal].
One should not perform any ritual practice that arises from or is bound to the earth; for the sake of accomplishing all mantras, one should practice within the various states of existence and wombs.
One born under the sign situated in Libra is always seen to be crafty, wretched, greedy, and indeed envious, and is constantly addicted to [weighing] scales.
The practitioner of mantra, established in that zodiac sign, should always perform it—that which the world does not declare to be the ground for the attainment of wealth and prosperity.
When one is born under a principal planet that is entirely yellow or white, one shall not attain success in mantra, nor achieve the wealth and prosperity sought through diligent effort.
The nineteenth chapter:
All these are accomplished in a mere moment by those who are employed; when he is seen from all sides by auspicious beings who are yellow or white.
A great-souled, heroic, and righteous lord of men is born when [the Moon] is aspected by the most cruel planets born from the signs of Saturn, the Sun, and Mars.
If the meaning of the natal ascendant falls in Libra, the man becomes envious, afflicted by many diseases, and poor; he experiences the arising of suffering from illness and disease.
One who is fierce in all actions, cruel, and always impulsive should not perform rites for pacification as taught by the Lord in the essence of the Jina’s teachings.
The practitioner performs fierce rites for the wielder of the thunderbolt, including those arising from the gathering [of forces], as well as malevolent rites and various acts of warfare.
In that heap, always within that family born there, even an action censured by the supreme Jinas attains accomplishment therein.
One should avoid the expansion of primary qualities and also their power; furthermore, one should not undertake a journey to a foreign land in the direction of Māśuja.

One should not perform any rituals involving Mount Mandara as a vehicle, nor any actions concerning the conditioned or unconditioned realm of sentient beings, while the Sun is in that [Mandara] constellation.
When birth arises from a scorpion, one takes recourse in the womb of a living being; listen now as the variety of its characteristics is described.
Such a person is born on the surface of the earth as fierce, reckless, cruel, unassailable, and arrogant with pride; he is crooked, greedy, and likewise dull-witted.
A mortal born under Māgha shall be wise, righteous, learned, eloquent, and difficult to overcome; he shall be beloved by women, grateful, and firm in his prowess.

Constantly engaged in the practice of tantras and mantras, devoted to service, and a worshiper of the guru; [the planets] Venus, the Moon, Mercury, and Jupiter are the primary lords of the lunar mansions.

It is praiseworthy, conducive to the highest good, the goal to be attained, and a promoter of longevity and health; it serves for the accomplishment of seeing them [the deities] through the supreme practice of the mantra-adepts.
When Saturn, the Sun, Mars, or Rāhu behold that man in the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, he is born cruel, reckless, perverse, and a performer of fierce deeds.
And for those practitioners of cruel rites, the mantras of Vajrin become effective; Maya shall not come from any direction on days that are utterly contemptible.
Beyond that, the Tathāgatas have described the zodiac sign called Dhanus;
mortals are born there in many ways depending on their destination and location,
all of whom are auspicious in their later years but partakers of suffering in childhood.
The divisions of lifespan have been proclaimed according to their classification;
likewise, I shall describe the attainment of wealth and the perfection of purpose.
[One] should constantly destroy one's own source and cause the source of another to increase.
A mortal who takes refuge in the sign of Sagittarius (Dhanu) may have many wives, be talkative, and be fond of passion and pleasure; yet, being unrestrained,
he may also become a lord, prosperous, always capable, or even righteous.
If the aspect of the principal planets is white or yellow,
one should employ mantras arising from various weapons,
or those bearing the fruits of various arms, as well as garments, ornaments, and vehicles.
His mantras— born from the limbs favored by the Munis, accomplished through various elements and arising from the fruits of various elements— will indeed succeed;
thereafter, one should perform rituals with all kinds of substances.
The mantra-practitioner shall produce everywhere a state of existence free from the dangers of rebirth,
as well as his own dwelling, a vehicle, his own son, a residence,
all desired medicine, great wealth, and an upward path.
For his success, the liberated soul quickly comes to reside in his hand;
thereafter, when the sun is in Capricorn in the sign of Aquarius, he is seen among them as one born as a mortal. One should indeed recognize him by these signs.
Devoted to his mother and devoted to his father, renowned, highly esteemed,
and powerful; this nineteenth chapter-collection is difficult to endure for all who suffer, yet it is also known as the "Accumulator of Wealth."

One born thus becomes miserly, greedy-minded, and deceitful; however, for those planets aspected by Venus and Jupiter, all prosperity arises. But those which are black or red planets result in cruel actions, as previously described.
The knower of mantras should not go there from any of the intermediate directions;
he should accomplish wicked rites and avoid those that are undesirable, and for the purpose of inducing vomiting or traveling, he should take recourse to the northern direction.
One who has set out for the sake of the great ocean should embark upon a vessel; there he may obtain wealth produced from low-lying regions under the supervision of local authorities.
Beyond that, when the sign of Capricorn has arisen, it is known as "the Jar."
Beings born under the sign of Aquarius are always said by the best of men to have various characteristics and many marks;
they are diverse and of manifold forms, depending on their complexion and caste.
Men born in the sign of Aquarius (Kumbha) are dark-complexioned and large-eyed; they are highly esteemed, yet they are incapable of sexual union and are intent upon worldly affairs and material gain.
They are said to be grateful and righteous. Those born under the mantra-deities [of this sign] are of such nature.
In this world, planets that are white or yellow are seen and highly honored; however,
those planets that are black or red result in birth with visible defects,
poverty, stupidity, fickleness, and bring about thievery.
Such men are always born with many diseases and are impoverished;
one should not have them perform any supreme rite honored by the sages, lest they cause obstacles in all undertakings.
One should not go even after reaching the edge of the shore; therefore, it has not been described at all.
One who desires success through mantras should perform the rites of the Vajra family—whether fierce or ending in a fierce act—adorned with the syllable *sphuṭ*.
One should accomplish the mantra here, joined with the King of Wrath;
in the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, those of evil deeds and fierce deeds are accomplished when joined [with it].
Beyond that, the Tathāgatas have declared Pisces (Mīna) to be the zodiac sign.
All the men residing there are seen to possess many auspicious marks;
these forms arise from those born under the sign of Pisces (Mīna-rāśi).
Such a person is a lord, possessed of honor and intellect, illustrious, and endowed with hundreds of enjoyments and riches.
He is born on the surface of the earth as the source of all worlds;
then that wise king, who swiftly accomplishes his aims,
is born from the sight of the moon-like semen of Śukra, becoming the best of men in the world.
From the aspect of Jupiter and Mercury, he became wealthy and possessed of a tall stature and large eyes; he was always beloved by women,
a leader of men with many friends, yet he also became crooked.
Then Śukra (Venus) is born with many friends and is affectionate toward his friends;
thereafter, the Sun, the foremost of planets, is indeed cruel.
If he (the Sun) aspects that mortal, as do Saturn, Rāhu, and Mars—

Then [the planet] Dhvaja arises as cruel and difficult, just as previously described; these planets have been declared for the ends of the dark and light fortnights. One should perform all rites when they are situated in the sign of Pisces (Mīna).
Staying there, one should behold the Moon and accomplish all [aims]; beyond this, among the zodiac signs, are the elephants, humans, non-humans,
Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, Garuḍas, and those who dwell in the lotus.
Their mental emergence is characterized by their essential nature, genus, destiny, and location; one should discern it by these very signs,
just as their disposition (*sattva-prakṛti*) is explained through those signs.
Their own mantras have been spoken by these [sages], and one should employ them accordingly.

The zodiacal signs (rāśis) are said in the world to be twelve in number, arising from the [stellar] groups; they are calculated by the foremost of the planets and assigned to the lunar mansions (nakṣatras).
This nineteenth chapter, in brief, has been told; for if it were told in full detail, it would be too extensive.
At that time, it was established for human beings by means of the lunar mansions and the circles of planets.
But beyond this, the great and powerful knowledge of the gods and the sages proceeds; therein lies this human activity,
yet the vision of knowledge regarding the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha is supreme among men.

The knower of all mantras should accomplish [the rites]; those born under the zodiac signs, the lunar mansions, and the lunar days should always be practiced during the bright fortnight, for success in these is always proclaimed; however, for those who perform dark deeds, it is in the dark [fortnight].
One should perform [the rites] with white and yellow planets and during the days;
one should employ [them] on the full moon when the moon has reached its fullness in the bright fortnight,
and one should find favor on the first and third days of the bright fortnight.
On the fifth, the seventh, the tenth, the eleventh,

and likewise on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, one should perform all activities for the sake of nourishment, the yoga of pacification, and auspicious or inauspicious journeys and arrivals.

A wise and learned person, as well as those mortals endowed with prosperity, should always employ painting, the application of mantras and tantras, dancing, singing, pleasure, ornaments, vehicles, dwellings, and shaving.

The attainment of wealth, constant success, and union with beloved beings have been taught by the foremost of Sages; therefore, those who possess prosperity and seek riches should swiftly perform the accomplishment of the mantra's purpose through these various other rites.
One should meditate [on the deity] on the days of the Moon, Venus, Jupiter, and Mercury— the most excellent and divine planets— when they are well-honored, pure, auspicious,
and joined with favorable lunar dates (tithis), as briefly indicated.

One should always perform fierce rites with terrible and fearsome planetary deities (*graha*), mantras, and lunar days, according to the *Śrīmūlakalpa*, for those who perform dark deeds during the dark fortnight;
this includes the summary of destinies and locations, as well as the application of mantras and the accomplishment of their purposes.

The planets, zodiac signs, meanings of constellations, lunar days, and the rising of the moon are all declared here, along with the power of the accomplishment of actions and the rules for all ritual activities.

Thus concludes the third chapter, the Exposition on the Knowledge of Astrology, from the seventeenth major section of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the twentieth major section.
Then, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

Mañjuśrī, in this extensive ritual manual (*kalpavisara*) of yours, there are described marvelous signs and omens that dispel all causes of fear; these indicate auspicious and inauspicious events, such as the occurrence of famine or abundance, and the arrival of foreign kings. They also foretell drought or excessive rain for sentient beings and signal obstacles during great ritual accomplishments (*mahāsādhana*) and the like. Therefore, the practitioner must reflect upon what is achievable and what is unachievable in that region, and discern what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Therefore, if the signs are not auspicious, one should depart from that place and go elsewhere to accomplish them; however,
if the signs are auspicious, they should be accomplished in that very place.

And having understood this, the practitioner engaged in the practice of mantra must remain in that very state; knowing what is to be done and what is not to be done within the practice of mantra, one should understand the signs and discern what is auspicious and what is inauspicious.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, prostrating at the feet of the Blessed One, spoke again as follows:
Therefore, may the Blessed One please teach the chapter on the knowledge of omens;

it will be for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, and for all Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas engaged in the practice of mantras. It concerns the signs and marks that arise as the results of auspicious and inauspicious fruits, by which all sentient beings who have entered the practice of mantras—having known whether a task is achievable or unachievable and the timing of the omens—may determine whether they should remain or depart.
When this had been said, the Blessed One Śākyamuni addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Therefore, Mañjuśrī, listen and attend well and thoroughly; I shall speak to you.
First of all, there will be the arising of the signs of portents."
The conduct of non-human beings is indeed a source of great and beginningless fear;
for all the planets and lunar mansions, the kuśmāṇḍas, the graha-rākṣasas,
the mothers, the deities, and all the highly powerful pretas [act thus].
Then, when great portents arise, they display a sign that has a beginning, a middle, and is indeed inauspicious. 196
In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, they declare that the stability of the earth and its destruction arise from various causes;
understand this regarding all human beings upon this terrestrial plane,
as well as the various headless trunks (*kabandha*) and the swarming of birds.
These are seen everywhere in the world; therefore, one should depart from that place.
Having seen Indra’s weapon at night, and especially the bow, as well as arrows, iron shafts, nooses, and various other weapons produced for striking, [one should flee].

If at night one sees from that place various forms appearing in the sky— such as distorted figures, headless trunks, and puppets dancing in the expanse of the heavens— one should depart from that location. When such things are seen in the sky within the lunar orb, one must leave.
They say that what is hollow is a hole; it is seen within the lunar disc.
If men, both high and low, should be seen fighting within the lunar disc, one should depart from that region as if it were the world of humans.
Various life-taking beings and diverse hosts of spirits may likewise dance and fight; one should therefore depart from that place.
When standing in a visible location, [one sees] a lunar disc appearing in the shape of a mandala.
Having observed such a phenomenon, one should depart from that region;
for when all the constellations are seen fighting within the lunar disc,
whichever one falls there first, that person who is situated in the corresponding direction will quickly perish.
They call that the "direction of the gods," yet the king will certainly die.
Having seen such a being called *sattva*, which arises in various forms,
one should quickly depart from that place out of fear.
Seeing the moon there, Śara, Nārāca, and Śakti quickly perceived the harassment caused by thieves and the fear born from the falling of weapons;
they beheld it in its transformed form, serving as a refuge for various living beings.
At night, when the moon is upon the earth, one should depart from that place;
for there are birds of black color, as well as white and yellowish-white ones.
This is the twentieth chapter.
When those who are red and likewise smoke-colored, with naturally deformed appearances and discolored complexions, are seen upon the earth—
having observed such a sign, one should depart from that region.
The bright fortnight may become dark, and likewise the dark fortnight may become bright;
moreover, birds on the surface of the earth are seen with distorted forms.
Having observed such a sign, one should depart from that region.
May herds of deer and jackals all enter the village dwellings;
may beasts of prey, serpents, rogues, barbarians,
and plundering thieves cause them fear, or even famine is described for them.
Various hosts of spirits are also seen upon the surface of the earth— yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kinnaras, both of deformed and natural forms—
who dance constantly on the ground day and night.
Upon seeing such a sign, one should depart from that place; for there, men, women, and children will constantly wail bitterly upon the ground,
both by night and by day, and disease shall always prevail there.
Serpents, deformed and loathsome, are seen upon the surface of the earth—
in houses, on the roads, in temples, and near trees;
they remain pervading everywhere, and there shall be great fear.
There will be the outbreak of a great pestilence, as well as poison, boils, and fainting;
there will be famine and the ruin of the kingdom when people gather there.
Birds, dogs, and jackals will appear in deformed, unnatural, and loathsome ways.
When those with upturned beaks and distorted faces shriek in the sky at midnight or at midday, both mortals become loathed and great danger swiftly arises from the arrival of a foreign army.
In brief, there will be famine and excessive views there;
for one month or seven days, they will be tormented by great suffering. On the surface of the earth, humans will live in mutual hostility, like thieves and fire. (Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa 197–198)

There, one should depart from that region due to the fear of great weapons; for clouds appearing everywhere in the sky are seen to be crookedly formed, clearly defined in shape, fierce, and resounding with intense thundering.
Seven distinct ones are seen residing in the serpent realm, and two or four are seen in the sky, both being most terrible and possessing fearsome faces.
Upon seeing such a sign, there will soon arise great terror there, along with the affliction of a great pestilence, fever, disease, and indeed most fearsome ailments.
Then the stationary and moving poisons, which swiftly snatch away life, cause the clouds to release rain and a terrible downpour.
Beings there perish, being mutually indifferent to one another;
having observed such a characteristic, one should depart from that place.
I shall describe to you the great famine of the Great Precipice, the falling of meteors on all sides, comets, thunderbolts, and the conflagration of the quarters.
Listen: if a fall of meteors occurs on all sides, both by night and by day, a catastrophe situated within the visible sphere arises from those very meteors.
Having recognized great fear and ill-health, the mantra-practitioner should depart from there;
he should always go toward the direction in which a great meteor is blazing.
Such is the defeat of kings: wherever the face [of the omen] turns, there is fear; meteors fall from all directions throughout the night at all times.
In that region there shall be a great plague, famine, and the slaughter of kings;
and when meteors fall on all sides, both by day and by night.
Such may be the death that awaits kings and ministers;
having perceived this, one should practice the recitation of mantras, and knowing it, one should depart from that land.
If a comet falls from battle, there is danger from whichever direction its tail points; otherwise, a defeat of kings is seen in the perils of war.
Then a great upheaval occurred; meteors fell swiftly in all directions amidst the signs of the planets. Therefore, one should depart from that place immediately.
If a meteor, having entered a particular region, always falls from its station toward that direction, then there arises widespread suffering, famine, and the ruin of the kingdom; furthermore,
death occurs during travel and arrival due to the influence of those stars.
For one who is situated in this birth asterism, there shall be fear of death.
After two nights, a living being perishes, and the constellation falls to the earth;
this same rule shall apply to all sovereigns of men as well.
This deity who beholds this world as it is, when desired, must necessarily be seen at night in a dream, and during the day in an image.
One should know that his fear of death will occur within six months;
then the image either falls down or shatters by itself.
The destruction of that [kingdom] will swiftly occur, O lord of men, as the houses and various types of structures take on threefold forms of omens.
If an image is seen located in a temple or a sanctuary,
having seen such a thing, one should depart from that place.
Everywhere and on all sides, the mantra-practitioner should always behold the image as having a deformed and loathsome appearance, assuming various kinds of distortions.
Whether the practitioner sees it himself or it is seen by others on the earth,
having observed such an omen, he should depart from that place.
Likewise, if at midnight or during the third watch the stars are seen [obscured], there will be a great rain; therefore, one should depart from that region.
Likewise, during the fourth part of the night, the swiftly moving stars travel like fireflies; one should not frequent that region from any side.
In that region, they travel along the surface of the earth;
then one should go to that place where the vision becomes uncertain, where the stars move.
One should not quickly enter that region where there is great fear from rain;
that region will swiftly perish through the arrival of a foreign army.
One should know that country to be agitated by famine, the falling of weapons,
thieves, serpents, and beasts of prey, as well as the gathering of barbarians and rogues.
The lords of men shall tremble constantly from every direction at that region, their kingdoms plundered and themselves forced to seek refuge with the armies of their enemies.
They shall dwell in that region for nine years;
then they will regain their kingdom and return once more to their country.
Having understood all modifications produced by external efforts as being joined with action,
the practitioner of recitation should always begin at the proper time for action in brief.
If great meteors are seen falling constantly and from all directions, mixed together, one should depart from that region.
Meteors of many forms are seen, resting upon various bases;
there are also yakṣiṇīs of diverse appearances, possessing wondrous forms and great supernatural power.

One should examine the meteor that has appeared with these aforementioned signs, such as its blazing from two curved points, its devouring of raw flesh, and its appearance as a female demon (piśācikā).
They are proclaimed to be very long, short, or of medium length;
they may measure four cubits, two cubits, or even just one cubit.
She is seen on the surface of the earth by mortals; she is the refuge of those of great fortune, possessing great vital power and her own essential nature; she is this deity of immense majesty.
And those summoned beings of the celestial dwellers,
possessing forms of various shapes, were present when this great and terrifying battle between the gods and asuras was taking place.
"I command Śakra to go quickly here to the surface of the earth to the mortals dwelling in Jambūdvīpa— the overseers of men and the lords of men."
In this twentieth chapter,
they behold all the worlds, those who investigate dharma and adharma, who are mindful of their mothers, devoted to their fathers, and respectful toward their elders in the family.
If all the men dwelling in Jambudvīpa become holders of the great mantras and practitioners of recitation, then the gods will experience great festivals and the Daityas will suffer defeat.
At that time, the mortals dwelling on the earth in Jambudvīpa were most righteous; then Vāsava, the lord of the thirty-three gods, [bestowed] great energy upon them.
Then the Asuras, their enthusiasm shattered and their minds broken, took pride in reaching Pātāla by that very path.
As they entered their own city there with shattered pride and deep anguish,
the gods, the lords of the thirty-three, then attained great joy.
Then, throughout Jambūdvīpa, there was abundance and health; people everywhere became healthy, and men and women were freed from all suffering.
Therefore, O people, you should in every way cultivate devotion toward the Buddha,
toward the Dharma, and toward the Sangha— the supreme assembly that has transcended dualities and is free from all affliction.
Desiring to obtain all perfections from mortals, he performed worship;
then he engaged in the practice of mantra, whereby auspicious speech arose.
Establish the tenfold action according to the world, leading to the state beyond rebirth; perform it amidst the gathering of people with minds purified in three ways.

One should always abstain from killing living beings, nor should one take what is not given; one should not consort with another's wife, avoiding those who are forbidden; and one should recite [the mantra].
Be content with your own duty; take refuge in it, O best of men! One should not speak falsehood, for its ripening is nothing but suffering.
One should not utter harsh speech that brings suffering for the sake of all sentient beings, nor any speech associated with the afflictions that is devoid of meaning.
One should always practice that which is empty, endowed with the meaning of the Dharma, and indivisible;
one should constantly avoid slander and speech that causes division among others.
In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, it is stated that for one with a defiled mind, [such conduct] is everywhere forbidden by the preeminent Sages.

One should not practice the action of covetousness toward those who benefit other beings; one should avoid the action of malice arising from hatred, which never follows after what is good for others and provides no basis for compassion toward sentient beings.

People should not cause harm to other beings in any way, nor should they entertain wrong views, which destroy all wholesome qualities— such as the view that "there is no gift, no oblation, and no success through the practice of mantras."
In that way, the mantras conceived according to the meaning of all tantras do not succeed;
the arising of bliss for the Buddhas does not occur, nor is peaceful nirvāṇa desired,
nor is there such conduct or awakening resulting from the occurrence of individual objects.
Arhatship does not exist on this earth in this world, nor is it produced among phenomena;
such is the diverse nature in the world, according to the reality of things as they are—
such and other various [states] marked by manifold forms and characteristics.
The practitioner of mantra should never associate with that which arises from evil views.
Just as the ten actions have been described, it is taught that through abstention from them one goes to heaven;
their cultivation indeed results in the attainment of the goal of nirvāṇa.
When there was an undesirable defeat of the gods in the world,
the pride of the Daityas increased; then, in the abode of men, all the inhabitants of Jambūdvīpa were overcome by the arising of excessive arrogance.
They will quickly be afflicted by diseases and fall into a state of mutual delusion;
at that time, all those overseers of people, guilty of offenses against one another,
will swiftly perish, having utterly abandoned their dharma, merit, and wealth.
In battle, those kings whose minds were filled with rage met death by the falling of weapons; they did not seek refuge in the foremost of gods when threatened,
nor did those inauspicious rulers honor the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

No; those kings stood there constantly reciting mantras, yet they were quickly destroyed, and the people then perished, overwhelmed by various misfortunes. This is the twentieth chapter from the extensive [tantra].
Then those foremost Daityas, highly agitated,
quickly ascended the summit of Mount Sumeru; those best of men entered the auspicious palaces that were divided upon the terraces of Meru.
Mounted upon various excellent chariots and adorned with diverse ornaments, they cause the forest to be utterly destroyed on all sides for the sake of the dwellers of heaven;
bearing various weapons, they shall grant victory and defeat the foremost enemies.
Then they chose Khara; the Apsarases chose Bhaja; all the lords and powerful ones chose the Asuras, who were dear to Bala;
and indeed, the celestial maidens chose Sudhā and food.
Then those most excellent of the foremost gods entered that best of cities;
having gone from there to the summit of Meru, they all indeed followed Śakti into the city known as Darśanāśraya at the gate of that supreme town.
But the city of Māyā did not give rise to fear in those who took refuge in joy;

having turned back from there, all those gods indeed went to their own abodes. For even a mortal who has mastered a single mantra, if he dwells in that abode while his mantra is being recited, [attains success].
In that land, where the mantra has been recited and remains present upon the earth, there shall be no afflictions, no famine, no enemies, no diseases, nor even fear; indeed,
none of the bandits there will be able to cause harm.
There, neither affliction nor death occurs, nor do transgressions of boundaries;
neither pain, disease, fainting, fever, nor illness prevail there, for those who take refuge in him have their mantras recited and are protected upon that earthly realm.
Those excellent mantras here that originate from the family of the Lord of Jinas,
as well as the mantras belonging to the Lotus-marked [family] which are worshipped by practitioners—
therein the practitioner should recite those excellent mantras of great majesty.
Then those most excellent and noble gods shall have victory over the asuras.
Thus are the virtues described here; they are seen upon the surface of the earth. When will the logicians of various forms speak thus here on the surface of the earth?
By the Vedic revelation "This is a planet," the extensive purpose of the incarnation was sung; it was indicated by the sages as the knowledge of those marked by planets,
and therein the instruction regarding the suppression [of obstacles] shall be proclaimed.
When meteors fall, when there is a thunderous crash upon the earth's surface,
and when loud peals of thunder are heard from the sky, and the ground trembles violently— then that region is afflicted by these lunar days joined with these [planetary] positions.
An incomparable sound,
a roar as fierce as the thunder of a great cloud, is heard; it resounds swiftly,
and on the sixth, eighth, fourteenth, and thirteenth days, it is likewise heard.
Likewise, on the twelfth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight,
when these are conjoined with these lunar mansions and the best of the days of the week—
listen now to what occurred under Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, and Bharaṇī.
When [the moon] is conjoined with Pūrvabhādrapadā, Ārdrā, Maghā, or Āśleṣā, and is well-honored by the planets Śani, Śukra, Karka, and Aṅgāraka— the cruel ones— then it falls upon the earth.
When there is no rain and the water-rites fail, and a harsh sound is heard known as *nighāta*,
one should know that great danger will arise in that region, including famine, the destruction of the kingdom, fear of foreign armies, and the great terror of various diseases.
When a thunderclap falls during these aforementioned asterisms,
on inauspicious days, or when the planets are black or red,
the king in that region is always severely struck down by weapons.
At that time, in that fierce place, one should then recite [the mantra]; at that time,
various diseases appear there, and the destruction of wealth is seen— this is the twentieth chapter from the extensive collection.
In that case, death shall occur along with disease and censurable famines;
one should predict a drought during the rainy season lasting for twelve years,
as a meteor falls from the sky toward the western direction.
A tumultuous scene, crowded with death, is seen by the thieves of death;
at that time, whether at midday or when the sun has set,
even a youth sees the rising sun as red, accompanied by such auspicious sounds from the disciples.

At the three junctions of the day (trisaṃdhyā), an unpleasant sound portends ill fortune, whereas at other times it brings satisfaction; however, when such a sound occurs at midnight, there is great danger from a thunderbolt (nirghāta).
Therefore, let the best of kings have their excellent cities well-fortified.
Various groups of barbarians, rogues, and those presided over by thieves, even while acting here on this earth for the sake of seizing the property of others,
will produce a sound like a thunderclap during the remaining time.
The chief minister there shall become afflicted by many diseases;
the king will inflict the state of being plagued by many ailments upon him,
or his wife will be killed, or that chief minister himself will be slain.

All the customs officers there, relying on various castes, were slain by Death, as were those who served the physicians. The eminent merchants, the chief officials, and the kings appointed everywhere,
spoke of the measurement of midday when the Sun had become a sage.
When people heard that incomparable sound of thunder,
they realized that all over this earth they were being afflicted by diseases;
otherwise, if men had heard such a tumultuous sound, [they would have known it was for another reason].

If a thunderclap occurs suddenly and constantly from all directions, the king will not live there; likewise, if an auspicious thunderclap falls while resting upon the southern direction, and a vision of the moon is seen above, one should predict that he will soon perish.
If, in the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, one hears the sound of a thunderclap (*nirghāta*) occurring while relying on the eastern direction, then the governor of the east will perish,
as will the people dwelling there who reside within the valleys of the Himālaya mountains.
In that region, marked by a most terrifying eclipse, the lord of the people heard a sound: "The Mlecchas and thieves are being destroyed;
so too the chief calves in Vatsa and the ruler of Nepal at that time."
Those dwelling in various islands will be swiftly slain by enemies; when a terrifying sound arises in the intermediate directions, it shall be from the north above,
and the Lord of Kāmarūpa will always slay the ruler of Gauḍa.
To the east of the Lauhitya river, those known as Jarādhyakṣas, Jīvinas, Kalaśāhvās, Carmaraṅgas, Samotadyas, and Vaṅgakas—
various kings such as these he shall slay during the Bhairava planet-seizure occurring with noise.
If a sound occurs in the southeastern quarter, there will be great danger from the Kaliṅgas,
the Kosalas, and the maritime Mleccha inhabitants;
they, along with their governors, kings, and spies, shall be slain by cruel weapons.
When a great sound occurs in the eastern or western quarters—
fierce like the thundering of clouds during a massive storm by day or night—
let the assemblies of gods understand that this is a *nirghāta* (a crashing thunderbolt).

O best of men, at that time, when an auspicious lunar mansion, an excellent and most favorable ascendant, and a preeminent white lunar day had occurred, he caused both the auspicious and the inauspicious to be proclaimed among human beings, and he heard the sound [of the proclamation] throughout the earth.
At that time, there will be auspiciousness, abundance of food, health, prosperity, and the means for play; the mantra will be perfected and always grant boons to those who recite it,
and success will arise in all ritual applications.
One should also determine the results from both malefic and benefic planets;
therein, when applied to all undertakings, the accomplishment of the task occurs.
Understand now that portents (nirghāta) are described in many ways upon this earth.
The twentieth chapter:
Some [mantras] instantly take away life; some result in the manifestation of truth; some accomplish all aims; and some sounds resound with a deep resonance.
And let the hosts of gods quickly take heed of that sound;
it is firm and endowed with depth,
like the thundering roar of a long-drum, and its sound is directed right toward us.
That sound is terrifying and cruel, acting exactly as described;
at the same time as the falling of meteors, it arises from an earthquake,
and one should also apply the description of that sound as a harsh resonance.
Then one should know that there will be great fear; this [period] is characterized by the destruction of all instructions.
Consequently, one should expect violence against sentient beings, the occurrence of famine and disease, and non-human disturbances such as magical illusions.
Then, within thirty or twenty days, death shall come to the kings;
all sounds produced by fierce noises will manifest as they have been described. Now listen as I explain the occurrence of earthquakes.

Regarding the tremors occurring specifically among the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*), they should be applied everywhere in conjunction with the lunar days (*tithis*); likewise, a lunar mansion should also be joined [with others] as in the case of a thunderclap (*nirghāta*). One should apply this to all ritual actions:
if the earth shakes while in Aśvinī, one should predict famine.
In Bharaṇī and Kṛttikā, both tremors and the rising of garlands occur;
in Rohiṇī, a tremor arises that brings about the attainment of wealth;
Ārdrā and Punarvasu are likewise marked by these [omens].
If the earth should tremble in these [asterisms], there will be great fear in that region;
the Middle Country will perish, as will those regions and their kings,
if the earth together with its inhabitants should tremble during Puṣya.
In that region, one should predict auspiciousness, peace, abundance, and health;
however, when Āśleṣā moves, the entire earth quickly trembles due to barbarians, thieves, and fierce beings. —From the *Śrīmūlakalpa*.* *Note: The asterisk indicates a reference to the source text.*
When the earth trembles under the Maghā asterisms, it does so for all people, yet not everywhere;
in the land of Aṅga, the king of Magadha perishes,
and all the Magadhan districts are afflicted by disease and thieves.
If an earthquake occurs during both Phalgunī constellations,
then those residing in the valleys of the Himālaya mountains on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā will quickly be struck down by diseases, as will the inhabitants of Vṛji and Mithilā.

Then all the rulers of Vaiśālī will be slain by various afflictions; likewise, the chief Mlecchas dwelling on the ridges and in the midst of the valleys and slopes of the Himalayas, as well as the Droṇas, will be destroyed.
When the earth trembles during the two twilights, the foremost and chief superintendents of the Mlecchas are always slain by weapons; when the hands appear variegated,
the Mlecchas, thieves, and human rulers are always slain by those bearing arms.
When conjoined with the constellations Svāti, Viśākhā, and Yuktī, the entire earth trembles; and other merchants,
the best among merchant chiefs, the most excellent, the foremost, and those who are pure, are seen [to perish].
Aquatic creatures perish through diseases and the falling of weapons;
when the constellation Jyeṣṭhā is renowned,
the entire earth always wanders and also trembles violently.
When the excellent mountains, both high and low,
and the rivers cause the surface of the earth to tremble violently, then there will be a meeting of the two [armies],
and fear, as well as a censured famine, will quickly arise there.
Then, within six days, the death of the great king shall occur;
those people in the central regions will quickly perish, and the excellent cities will be destroyed.
When the earth trembles under the asterism Anurādhā, it portends the arising of auspiciousness.
If the production of crops is mediocre everywhere,
it should be known as occurring under the asterism Mūla; this is the twentieth chapter, and it trembles even among the asterisms of Āṣāḍhā.

If an earthquake should occur during the day under the asterisms of Pūrvāṣāḍhā or Uttarāṣāḍhā, it should be known that the earth will be afflicted on all sides by the arising of threefold suffering— namely, disease, famine, and robbers— and so forth.

If an earthquake occurs under the asterism Śravaṇā, the earth trembles; but if it occurs under Dhaniṣṭhā, there is abundance everywhere, along with long life and health, and the earth is free from famine and rich in crops.
This is the case if the quake occurs during the day.
If the earth should tremble during Śatabhiṣaj or Bhadrapada,
famine and the ruin of the kingdom will indeed be seen in that region; mortals there will be slain by thieves, and a loathsome famine shall prevail.
Mortals on the surface of the earth experience trembling at midnight during all the *uttarā* nakṣatras and those proclaimed as *revatī*.
Both constellations—Revatī as well as Bhadrapadā—are everywhere; indeed, it was when an earthquake occurred in all these very places that [this happened].

When the aforementioned earthquake is observed specifically among the lunar mansions, it brings happiness; these earthquakes have been fully described, as well as the thunderclaps marked by excellent signs.
At a time equal to the falling of meteors, when the afflictions of living beings caused by the three humors have emerged, that which was previously indicated in detail shall come to pass.
The caves should be constructed right there, facing all directions; they are described as being full of water, causing tremors, and endowed with light and happiness.
At the time of accomplishment, all these are seen by the mantra-reciting practitioners and likewise by the yogins when success indeed arises.
Likewise, for Bodhisattvas who have been born thus for the sake of attaining the enlightenment of a Buddha,
there are the powers of the foremost sages whose minds are devoid of [worldly] attachment through their supernatural faculties (ṛddhi).
Then, at that time, the best of gods proclaimed his arrival, and the entire earth, along with its worlds and oceans, resounded with a roar like the thundering of clouds.
A trembling arises quickly due to these very causes;
and when the earth trembles, it is silent and devoid of light.
One should describe the suffering of those hell-beings who are agitated; their bodies, exhausted by manifold miseries, are terrifying to behold.
And as they behold the suffering born of karma, O best of sages, a return is seen for those people who have uttered the proclamation of their deeds.
Understand all of this completely and retain it with a desire for happiness;
indeed, one should proclaim everything seen by Ketu situated in the sky.
By night and by day they are spoken of, and they are seen high in the sky; at midday, the Pole Star (Dhruva) is visible everywhere in its full extent.
Smoke-colored and possessing great rays, it emits smoke as a source of great terror; having reached whatever region, it causes the vault of heaven to smoke.
Indeed, in that very region, the foremost king is struck down by diseases upon the earth,
when a radiant planet, having occupied a particular weekday and lunar mansion, [exerts its influence].
When a streak of smoke is seen in the sky, one should clearly observe that very same constellation, lunar mansion, or planet which is blazing there.
At that time, the living being is indeed struck down by weapons and diseases,
because a smoke-colored line, portending great fear, is seen.
A cruel planet will undoubtedly destroy that region quickly;
moreover, a glossy, smoke-colored streak resembling the color of sapphire has appeared.
One should know that to be auspicious and pacifying, increasing longevity and health;
however, one that is rough-textured, discolored, or smoke-colored is censured.
Praiseworthy, white in appearance, and arising from four rays,
she is always declared to be gentle, bestowing the fruits of auspicious colors.
One should avoid that mountain celebrated as Puṣpalakṣmika; do not go there, for it is white like a mass of snow and resembles smooth crystal.
The twentieth chapter: One should recognize [omens] as gentle like the moon when they possess a luster of uniform, unblemished color;
they indicate auspiciousness, the accomplishment of goals, and the vision of the cessation of suffering.
Furthermore, in whatever region, or under whatever constellation, or when the circle of stars is first joined at the zenith;

When that renowned one has departed into the sky, all those stars situated throughout the heavens that were seen upon the surface of the earth have become [omens of] long life and health for everyone on every side.
A mortal who practices dharma becomes powerful, happy, and a lord; he is born as the most excellent of men—one should take refuge in that lunar mansion for him.
Or, when a planet is in a state of purity, it is said that a line which wards off all suffering is seen; wherever such a line is observed, one should know that person to be endowed with happiness.
Endowed with a joyful appearance and adorned with a gentle form,
a line of smoke-like vapor has risen into the sky, portending great terror.
If another planet is joined with a benefic or even merely situated in the sky [the tenth house],
the wise know that country to possess welfare, abundance, and health.
In that situation, for the most part, righteous omens arise from the comet; white radiance, resembling crystal, gathers from all sides.
One by one, they were known as glorious Tārakas in this celestial vault;
thereafter, they became like crystal, born from a ray of light.
The illustrious Prabhava is renowned; one should take refuge in its lunar mansion (nakṣatra), for many types of comets have been described—two thousand, three thousand, or even more.
Thirty-one [beings] arise in many ways through the emergence of various fruits of karma;
some are superior, some are middling, and some are turned away from the Dharma.
Then some [omens] arising are to be known as extremely terrible and causing great fear, yet appearing with a smooth aspect and possessing a luster like that of crystal.
It should be known as smooth and beautiful, with a luster equal to the appearance of crystal;
it should be known as smooth and beautiful, possessing a charming complexion and form.
In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, some among the animals, whether in the north, the south, or elsewhere,
arise with a radiance like that of the moon for the welfare of living beings.
These planets, possessing great strength yet being deformed and exceedingly long, are destroyers of kings when they rise in the middle [of the sky], with their rays extending toward the east.
If she moves from east to west, she will kill the ruler of the eastern region; if she moves from west to east, she will kill the king of the western region.
If rays arise on all sides, one should predict famine everywhere; for these rays that have risen in the intermediate directions presage the increase of barbarian tribes dwelling on the frontiers.
One should command that they be slain everywhere and stationed at that place—
those who are smoke-colored, discolored, coarse in appearance, and portending great terror.
The source, having gone everywhere, should indicate [the omen] among all living beings; if it is seen constantly at midday, it is auspicious in every respect during the day.
Great suffering and a great calamity will then befall kings wherever a line drawn horizontally appears upon that [figure].
Situated there, it kills the king in whichever country it has arrived; when indicated during the day in the intermediate directions, it portends the onset of a great disease.
One should predict theft, calamities, and death at that place if one sees a blue-colored comet in the sky during the day.
O rulers of the earth, these various calamities, accompanied by manifold sufferings and miseries, are said to be terrifying with their great sorrows on all sides.
When one sees the comet Ketu, red in color, situated near the moon, it portends fierce events by day and some auspicious outcomes by night.
Then, with the earth quickly drenched in blood from those struck down by weapons, the ground swiftly turned into a night-like expanse of blood.
In whatever place one may predict [an event], there the inhabited lands will arise as a source of great suffering for many beings and as a refuge for much misery.
The twentieth chapter:
She is seen in the sky in embodied form, yellow and shining with a yellow luster, resembling the color of turmeric and possessing a radiance like that of yellow orpiment.
When comets of golden hue indeed arise in the sky, one should know that there is great suffering for all living beings; such is the sign.
