The presiding deity of Mahāmārī, having awakened among the people, likewise brings destruction for twelve years through calamities such as drought and other afflictions.

They say that one which is excessively black is "fierce" (raudra), while those that are excessively smoky are to be rejected; however, one resembling the color of an atasi flower is free from the defects of fire-remnants.
Some have the appearance of great clouds, colored like blue collyrium; others have the form of boars, while some possess a radiance equal to that of cuckoos.
Terrible portents are seen in the sky; therefore, one should depart from that place. Likewise, those of cruel deeds, who are exceedingly fierce and violent, are seen there.
They say that in that region there will be great suffering, great terror, or even the onset of pestilence, as well as a terrible and great famine.
When one sees the sky filled with comets that have the appearance of *oḍpuṣpa* flowers, resembling blood-red suns, and possessing the color of blood;
When there is a widespread panic caused by disease that obstructs many living beings, one should predict the death of kings at that very moment.
If a man or a woman sees [these] suddenly, his death is ordained within seven days.
Within two nights or even three days, he is slain by weapons; then, whether by day or by night, he may suddenly see [visions] as if in a dream.
His death is ordained upon the earth at that very moment; the creature shall be slain either by poison or by weapons, without a doubt.
White and of glossy color, she brings forth happiness like the winter night; otherwise, the sight of those possessing various forms and appearances is not desired.
In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, it is taught that if [these signs] appear resting upon one's own body or the body of another, whether by night or by day, they are known to be instantly life-taking.
When one sees [the deity] of white color, with a luster equal to the moon or cow’s milk, having a form like snow or a jasmine flower, and possessing a radiance like various jewels;
For one who recites the mantra, his kingdom is said to be attained, or else spiritual accomplishment (siddhi); these portents are desired whether they appear in the body or in the temple.
Whether in one's own army or in the enemy's army, it yields fruit wherever it is situated; they call that the most excellent *kīrtitā*, which possesses a luster equal to various wonders.
They are seen everywhere by mortals as bringing many benefits; they are described by mortals as being present everywhere, whether in battle or even within a house.
The *ketus* (comets) of those belonging to the *siddha*-bodies are considered desirable and fruitful in every respect; otherwise, they are all contemptible, bestowing much suffering and fear.
All these comets marked by planetary signs have indeed been described; everything arising from the lunar days, asterisms, and zodiacal signs has been explained as before.
Through various planetary conjunctions and by means of the planets as well, those possessed of great supernatural power—just as before—all of this has been described for them everywhere in the world.
Then all of them became conscious; some possessed beautiful and uniform radiance, while others were variegated, and some were bright, glossy, and auspicious in color.
Sunetra, Netranāman, Śaśikundasamaprabha, Sudhū, Sunayana, Rugmavarṇa, and Sahaemaja.
All of them were white and variegated, arisen with various names; understand that these comets belong to the six castes as well.
One should employ the designations for those of various colors and forms; likewise for those who possess various deformities, and even those who are fierce and most terrible.
Those names which were previously mentioned by me in their entirety, as well as these others beginning with Ādya, have been declared to be the many-formed comets (ketavaḥ).
In that time, for human beings, the arising of the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds was manifested; and the conflicts of the foremost planets were seen everywhere.
In the war between the gods and the asuras, those of great power, known as Maheśas, divine and born of divine origins, indeed revealed their own selves.

All were white and auspicious in their arising, seated within the assembly of the gods; though they possessed both transformed and untransformed forms, they were contemptible with distorted complexions.
Indeed, all those who followed the side of the Asuras were practitioners of cruel deeds when the great and terrifying war between the Devas and Asuras was taking place.
The Asuras, defeated by the gods, manifest their banners; O mortal on the surface of the earth, they shall show you the sky in every direction.
White in color, always yielding auspicious fruits, desirable and beloved by the gods, they reveal themselves as those who have taken refuge in the side of the deities.
At that time, one should predict that for mortals there will soon be abundance of food and freedom from disease, when the gods are indeed defeated by the asuras at that time.
Then, indeed, comets of distorted color, impelled by cruel deeds, arise on the side of the Asuras.
Then, cruel winds blow from all sides against living beings, and great clouds, droughts, serpents, and crocodiles likewise appear.
He released water filled with poison and many diseases; at that time, he caused humans to suffer from poison, boils, and fainting.
Various rākṣasas, as well as those inhabited by daityas and yakṣas, indeed inflict violence upon human beings, desiring most terrible obstacles.
Causing suffering that obstructs the life-breaths here on the surface of the earth, a rain of stones will then fall from the sky onto the ground.
At that time, terrifying great winds blow; fierce winds blow, causing harm to many living beings.
In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, various beings belonging to the animal realm brought about the destruction of crops; many hosts of cruel spirits likewise acted thus here upon the surface of the earth.
At that time, they created obstacles for humans that threatened their very lives; indeed, there were many such occurrences, serving as the basis for numerous impediments.

Furthermore, there are various fierce beasts of prey and serpents belonging to the animal realm, as well as diverse beings dwelling in the womb of the *nāgas*, all of whom cause harm to sentient beings.
Various barbarians and thieves cause obstruction to honor; they are of the color of tawny monkeys, fierce, and born of the wind and fire.
When the gods are defeated in the world, various calamities blow forth; at that time, the mortals dwelling in Jambudvīpa always become most unrighteous.
Then those on the side of the gods are diminished by those born of the Daitya lineage, when beings endowed with dharma have assembled here upon this earth.
Delighting in the supreme Buddha-dharma, always excellent within the Saṅgha, devoted to their mother and father, possessing true integrity, they are intent upon recitation.
Then all the gods completely conquered those born from the womb of the Daityas; at that time, the earth was rich with grain and fruit and was filled with many things.
Mortals shall have long lifespans and great numbers; all kings will be righteous, bestowing happiness and devoted to the welfare of others.
Then, in those [regions], all things shall be pleasant, cool, delightful, and destroyers of disease; they shall be the cause of happiness and cooling for the world.

The seasons shall always be pleasant, cool in their course and never hot. Flocks of various birds shall always warble sweetly, and the trees on every side shall be auspicious, rich with many flowers and fruits. All living beings dwelling upon the earth shall be entirely free from disease.
And at that time, the righteous king felt no agitation;
indeed, there was abundance of grain and happiness, with various pleasure gardens and palaces.
This is the twentieth chapter.

He beholds all the various birthplaces of the men dwelling in Jambūdvīpa: trees that are always abundant in fruit, cows that yield much milk, and everywhere shrines of Dharma, wells, and ponds. All the people dwelling in Jambūdvīpa perform these acts; established in many ways and of many kinds, they remain devoted to the Dharma of living beings. Their earth is filled on every side and in every direction.

In that lowest of ages (*yugādhama*), their conduct has transgressed the bounds of propriety; one should predict results otherwise than what was intended. In such a time, actions may be fruitless or indeed fruitful, and even distorted actions born of causes may bring about auspicious results.
Thus it is said.
Thus concludes the fourth chapter, the Great Chapter on the Arising of Knowledge of Signs, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the twenty-first detailed chapter.
Then, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes (*Śuddhāvāsabhavana*), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

Mañjuśrī, in this extensive ritual manual (*kalpavisara*) of yours, which serves as a means for all accomplishments, there is a section concerning the practice of mantras for one engaged in the time of accomplishment. Regarding all mantras in all the extensive rituals, listen well and attend thoroughly to what I shall say: the designation "graha" (seizer) of Rāhu—the lord of the gods and leader of all planets—is seen in the moon, the sun, and so forth, through their conjunction with the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).

When the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, the Perfectly Awakened One, had spoken thus, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and placed his right knee upon the ground. With palms joined toward the Blessed One, he prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet; then rising once more, he gazed at the Blessed One with unblinking eyes, his eyes wide with joy, and being thrilled and delighted, he addressed the Blessed One in this way: “It would be well, O Blessed One, if you would explain the arrival of Rāhu.”

May the Blessed One explain that which indicates the time for the accomplishment of those beings devoted to the practice of mantras, as well as the arising of happiness for all beings, or the signs of the auspicious and inauspicious—
whenever you deem it to be the right time.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni gave his approval to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, saying:
"Excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you question the Tathāgata on this matter, being so intent upon the welfare of all sentient beings."

"Therefore, Mañjuśrī, listen; I shall speak and explain it for the sake of all sentient beings. First, regarding the time declared in the scriptures when the moon's orb is seized by the cruel planets, understand it exactly as it is."

When a great battle between the gods and asuras occurs and there is immense fear, then that king of the Daityas, the lord of the Dānavas, possessed of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), becomes truly terrifying. Of vast proportions, he rises up on all sides; his great stature would even exceed Mount Sumeru.
This cruel one, exceedingly arrogant and haughty, a powerful and preeminent planet, then enters the abode of the gods.
The twenty-first chapter:

Then, having touched Sumeru, the abode of the gods, with his hand, the Daitya gazes upon the Apsarases when the time comes for the sky. At that moment, the lord of the Daityas holds the full moon in his hand; various jewels have become bracelets upon his arm.
Then, in this world on earth, I am called a "graha" (seizing spirit);
when my radiance becomes red like a ruby,
then the human logicians say that it is the fiery mandala of the Lord.
But when the light in blue and red turns toward blueness,
then it should be known as "blue," whether in the moon or even in the sun; on this earth, those human logicians call it the "Māhendra" [circle],
while those same logicians then say it is the "Vāyavya-maṇḍala."
Diverse are the garlands of jewels; diverse are the origins of jewels; diverse are the treatises of the logicians; diverse are those born from the various realms of existence;
diverse indeed are their activities, and diverse is the abundance of their fruits.
"This action belongs to the foolish who are devoid of right knowledge;
therefore, one should properly apply oneself to the knowledge of the Tathāgata.
Then the Asura's vision was fixed solely upon the ignorance of the gods. He brought the chariot of the high-souled Śaśin to a complete halt.

When, at the proper time on earth, there is an eclipse of the mortals by Rāhu, and when that planet remains having overtaken the lunar disc, then one should know there is great fear; listen now regarding the constellations. When the solar disc is joined with the Moon in Aśvinī itself—
When both of these [the sun and moon] are said to be swallowed together by day and night,
the wise know that as the constant arrival of Aśvinī, which brings famine.
When the moon or the sun enters the orb of Bharaṇī, [the same result follows].

One should predict various harvests and even a period of plenty when the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu in the *kṛttikā* constellation, whether at night or at dawn; however, if it occurs at the end of a watch (*yāma*), it is harmful and censured. [From] the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*.

At that time, one should know there will be great suffering or indeed the onset of disease; this shall occur in the Middle Countries and nowhere else, as declared by kings through the arising of various portents such as the asterisms.
When the Moon or the Sun is in the sky during the asterism of Mṛgaśiras, [the following occurs].
When those two of great power have set after being eclipsed by Rāhu,
men in the eastern region will then be struck down by diseases;
one should predict that the kings and officials in that land have reached the end of their lives.
When the Moon and the Sun are in conjunction with Ārdrā and Punarvasu,
one should proclaim that the entire earth, drenched in blood, will be ravaged by barbarian lands;
they shall be struck down and shattered by one another, their lives destroyed and their lifespans ended.

At that time, when Puṣya and Āśleṣā are situated in the sky with either the Moon or the Sun, those of evil deeds in this region— formerly inferior and having become Mlecchas and thieves— are then designated as such in both the north and the south.
If, under the asterism Maghā, the orbs of the moon and the sun are eclipsed by Rāhu, and those two supreme planets set together with him,
then one should know that a great calamity will befall Jambūdvīpa in its entirety.
One should predict famine, the destruction of the kingdom,
and a great pestilence when Rāhu is in conjunction with both Phalgunīs;
he arrives at midday or at night and is released again in an instant.
From that, one should know that there will be abundance of food; it is seen throughout Jambudvīpa.
When Rāhu swallows both the moon and the sun during the Hasta constellation, they are released together at sunset; yet having set, they bring suffering.
The twenty-first chapter: A detailed exposition on the great terror of pestilence, wherein thieves are everywhere,
and kings, noble princes, and the most excellent men are then slain by diseases.
One should predict famine everywhere in all directions when Viśākhā and Svāti,
those most honored of constellations, are conjoined.
One should know that the arrival of Rāhu brings about suffering for cattle;
at that time, various leaders of families are slain by weapons.
When the two constellations Jyeṣṭhā and Anurādhā are conjoined, they are highly praised;
one should predict the arrival of Rāhu there, which portends a time of plenty.
If Rāhu eclipses the Moon situated on the earth at the Mūla asterism,
then it is eclipsed while rising, or it is eclipsed once it has risen in every respect.
If that very Rāhu, having always eclipsed the moon,
should set in the east, the eastern governors and the dwellings of the people of the eastern regions would perish.
One should predict a great falling of weapons as well as famine;
the people of Gauḍa will be divided and terrified by fear of a foreign army.
The king indeed perishes there, swooning along with his disease;
at that improper time, both Aṣāḍhas and Rāhu afflict the earth.
There, upon the surface of the earth, suffering was seen as a great disease;
then all those chief kings became evil-minded toward one another.
During the asterisms of Dhaniṣṭhā and Śravaṇā, that which is censured by the world was ordained;
indeed, the various leaders of the Gaṇas became estranged from one another at that time.
If the arrival of Rāhu is seen during the lunar mansions of Pūrvabhādrapadā as well as Śatabhiṣaj, one should predict an abundance of food.
When Rāhu's arrival occurs while the moon is conjoined with the Uttarā Bhādrapadā constellation, it is most excellent; however, its occurrence during the day is censured.
When the moon, marked by the letter *repha*, is eclipsed on all sides by Rāhu at its rising, or likewise when the sun or the lunar disc [is eclipsed] at night;
When Rāhu, together with the foremost and most excellent among the Brahmins, has set, the central regions will be afflicted and the king of Magadha will meet his death.
This is the calculation and knowledge for human beings on the surface of the earth;
this is also proclaimed as the measure of the lunar mansions.
The measure arising from the origin of the planets cannot be grasped by other humans;
indeed, the variegated garland of constellations revolves in the vault of the sky.
This is the enumeration for human beings; beyond that is the enumeration for those born of divine origins.
Whichever planet is the primary one for a person, or whichever is situated in their natal sign or zodiacal house, [that determines their nature].
The asterism was previously declared [as auspicious], yet he acts otherwise toward it;
there is no fault in a slight deviation from the measure, but there is censure for excessive talk.
At the time of measurement, this chief of planets is indeed remembered as the achiever of results;
the time that has been described should be understood, and the rule itself is now proclaimed.
If an earthquake, a thunderclap, or a meteor occurs in conjunction with a lunar mansion and a zodiacal sign,
and the sun and moon are seen situated therein along with the planets;
At that time, his [the disciple's] birth-star should be adorned with the lunar mansion; otherwise, one should know it to be fruitless, or even censurable in its radiance.
Therefore, at that time, those who have attained the perfection of mantra should perform recitation whenever the sky is seen everywhere to be of a smoky color.
Then one should know there is great fear; at that time, there is fear from an enemy army.
Furthermore, when both the moon and the sun appear smoke-colored, [great danger shall be known].
If one should search for two or three [omens] and find them there, one will encounter great danger;
such a vision occurs during the misty season, which is terrifying at all times.
One should know that the occurrence of mist in both summer and autumn is a wretched sign, indicating the onset of disease from all sides.
If a mist arises there during the day or at night, one should know that a great danger will occur for seven nights on all sides.
The twenty-first chapter: [It concerns] the constellations, planets, and lunar mansions, or the intervals between lunar days and weekdays;
everything has been explained as before, just as in the case of thunderclaps and meteors.
Within those very days, one should first apply the *dhūmikā* [practice];
then, at midnight or at midday, the *dhūmikā* always arises.
In that case, one should know there will be great agitation for kings in their preeminent cities,
whether it be in autumn, winter, summer, or even the rainy season.
The mist should be known from all sides, as well as by the stars; likewise, the auspicious or inauspicious nature [of the omen] is to be understood whether it occurs by day or by night.
One should indeed know it to be fruitless, yet it is also proclaimed as fruitful;
likewise when there is an earthquake everywhere, or when a meteor falls from one direction, or during the conjunction with Rāhu.
If smoke should arise there from all sides in the expanse of the sky,
that kingdom will soon be constantly struck down by those bearing weapons.
Prabhava is proclaimed as the source of all things, and likewise, Mṛtyu is celebrated;
from the seventh day onward, the winds on earth are preeminent in victory and are born of the quality of goodness (sattva).
Subject to the power of death, they are constantly being slain on all sides by those bearing weapons; devoid of compassion in their hearts, they seize the kingdom from one another.
When the sky appears white in the summer, those born into royal lineages will quickly be divided by weapons and merchants.
In that case, there is fear of a great disease; however, when the sun is seen rising with a blue hue, it portends the emergence of auspiciousness, appearing with a yellow radiance.
Death is declared in the summer, and it is censured in the autumn;
during the winter and the spring, a copper-colored [complexion] is observed.

Otherwise, one who appears yellowish is censured and shunned by the world; however, one who is known to be of golden complexion should be understood as praiseworthy, like the autumn following the summer.
Likewise, during the bright season of the rains, one should wear yellow or [other colors], yet not [anything else];
[the deity] appears with great majesty, possessing a luster equal to that of a great sapphire.

In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, it is said: "The sky is always to be known as the bestower of all fruits of happiness; one should know that the opposite of this indicates a place where the dwelling will suffer."
The destruction of crops, pestilence, and even famine are released;
likewise, the most grievous fear arising from liquor or the corruption of flavors shall cease.
A great and terrible roar arose in the sky at Śukra’s [abode],
instantly obstructing the vital breaths of all the kings.
Then one should arrange another matter joined with auspiciousness for the sake of prosperity,
when the sun and moon are eclipsed by Rāhu during a time of great fear.
There, various regions perished, born from the womb of diverse karmas; thereafter, another sound arose, auspicious and honored by the world.
O best of gods, O most excellent planets, you are appointed for the sake of the highest good; various mantras are perfected by you, and you provide various roots and fruits.
Whether they were all diverse or not, all those beings born of vital breath possessed various forms; their essential natures were then both manifold and deformed.
They possess various weapons and arise from various arms;
indeed, they are the foremost of all mental states, beautifully adorned by the root mantra.
All those [planets], even when accompanied by the planets, do not attain success while that which is being accomplished;
for when the moon or the sun is seized by Rāhu, even the purpose [of the planets] is seized along with them.
At that time, the reciter should constantly revolve the mantra;
all those [deities] will indeed become granters of boons and [will] come to his aid.
For this is the fruit of benefiting sentient beings; its foundation is seen therein.
The king of mantras is swiftly accomplished when recited during the planet Rāhuka.

When the moon and sun are eclipsed by the planets, the accomplishment of mantras is declared to be attained after seven years, six months, and even half-months, provided they have been properly worshipped.
The Tathāgatas have declared that success is achieved at the end of the watch or at midnight;
indeed, mantras joined with the proper ritual procedure will certainly not fail.
The twenty-first chapter:
[This applies] even to the high-souled Brahmā, let alone to humans on earth;
it applies even to the god Śakra and to Rudra, the wielder of the trident.
Even for Viṣṇu with the discus and mace in hand, or for the high-souled Tārkṣya,
success will not be attained through these rites performed devoid of the prescribed rules.
When a mantra is well-recited and joined with the causes prescribed in the Tantra,
it is accomplished even for another [practitioner] through the ritual procedure; [thus] the Vidyās, when released by humans and well-adorned with their own essential nature,
are accomplished— along with the planetary deities— when cast [into the fire], recited, and applied at the proper times.
Knowledge applied everywhere bestows its fruit;
knowledge, which consists of cause, action, and fruit, is to be sought through the investigation of causes.
One should know that action is accompanied by its cause through the arising of cause and fruit;
one should likewise apply knowledge to the fruit of action and join it with another cause.
Likewise, the Vidyā, when applied to rituals in its fourfold manner as the fourth, bestows the fruit of the action quickly; that Vidyā is joined with the causal factors.
That knowledge should be known by its fruit as highly honored even by the wise;
it is endowed with all purposes, preeminent, and effective for all rites.
When applied to ritual actions, that Vidyā bestows success through those rites;
it shall also unite one with the highest good, for this lies beyond the scope of ordinary mantras.
Understand the power [of mantras], the accomplishment of mantras, and the true nature of the world;
as well as how action may be fruitless, or how both fruit and action exist therein.
Whether it be the cause or the fruit, the mantra is seen as being applied to the principles of the world and is described by the wise.
Fruit does not destroy action or its sequence, nor does fruitless action constitute a higher ritual act.
Success in mantras arises from the undertaking of action for the sake of its fruit.
The quality [is established] through the non-connection with the sequence of substances; the sequence [of the rite] through the sequence of substance and action.
Therein, the fruit is accomplished from the king of mantras when applied to the ritual acts.
One who is endowed with the prescribed materials, established in right conduct, and engaged in ritual action—
his status as a practitioner is not to be known by his birth, for he is always joined to the fruit through his actions.
Those who possess the syllables of perfected mantras never fail to attain the state of great ritual power.
Then the minister should recite the mantra, relying upon the source of the ritual procedure.

Through the sequence of time, the qualities, the ritual procedure, the womb, and the destiny of the Sugata, all these kings of mantras are accomplished; they are the means for achieving the purpose of the ritual and the timing.
A quality (guṇa) is not to be known as a substance (dravya), nor is a quality said to be non-substantial.
Through the union of quality and substance, and through their conjunction, one should worship the mantra.
One should employ all the deities who have been worshipped by means of the face itself;
one should quickly accomplish the mantra through that measure, quality, and substance.
Sequence endowed with the quality of time, the quality of time and sequence, and action—
success well-applied within mantras is seen to be fourfold.
When applied solely to virtuous qualities, mantras bestow everywhere power, the expansion of virtues, and the arising of happiness through the conduct of sentient beings.
From all [these] arises activity, and the quality-substance is established;
yet these qualities do not exist apart from substance, nor are they devoid of substance and activity.
They would not grant accomplishment quickly through the mere arising of a desire in the mind;
for those mantras prescribed by the mind do not function through speech alone without the mind.
Nor is it to be known through mantras by any other means, nor is it other than the mind;
success is held to arise from the conjunction of the mind alone with action.
It is not inferior due to its view, nor is it desired as being devoid of action;
for right view, as well as action, speech, and mind, are properly applied.
The deities are swiftly accomplished through the application of right view and the engagement in right action, as proclaimed by the syllables of the mantra and tantra.
Together with the *mātṛkā*, they always succeed perfectly.
It is endowed with the excellence of speech at the conclusion of the ritual action and is properly joined with right view.
The twenty-first chapter. All mantras are accomplished when correctly applied to their respective ritual ends.
There is no mantra without the mind, nor is there mind without mindfulness; these two exist together.
Through right mindfulness, the mind is observed for the sake of attaining mantra-siddhi;
the Tathāgatas have not taught that a mantra is effective when it is devoid of mindfulness.
When properly applied through mindfulness and the state of meditative concentration,
they are seen to be empowered by the mantras and are brought to accomplishment through samādhi.
The cultivation of right concentration consists of mantras highly honored by the world;
these mantras are thoroughly permeated by that very concentration through their application.
There, the king of mantras is accomplished, as is the most abundant yoga;
the supreme mantra to be meditated upon through right samādhi, along with meditation and the other [limbs].
The mantras of the yogins are accomplished; success is not said to come from non-yoga.
That which was previously spoken by me has been correctly explained and well-applied.
The sages, who are compassionate toward sentient beings, have declared that success does not come otherwise;
for a mantra correctly applied to the meaning of reality will not bear fruit without intentional resolve (saṅkalpa).
Mantras are accomplished when they are correctly joined with ritual procedures and accompanied by right resolve;
the king of mantras is not honored at all when it is devoid of right resolve.
Mantras are accomplished in every way when employed with a correct livelihood;
it should be understood that the arising of happiness within mantras comes from right intention alone.
When correctly employed, mantras attain purity in one's livelihood;
those foremost mantras, when well-applied, are brought to accomplishment on this earth as prescribed.
For one who is disciplined, properly applying the fruit of the ājīna,

the mantra-practitioner— always pure, with a purified mind and delighting in right livelihood— should act with purity; for one who is pure, whose actions are pure, and who conducts himself in pure deeds at their conclusion.
Pure mantras are always effective whether in a state of impurity or purity; however,
the mantras of the flesh-eaters and those others which have been proclaimed succeed for practitioners only when spoken by flesh-eaters themselves.
In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, even those mantras that are difficult to master are accomplished when sung by Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, thieves, Garuḍas of great power, as well as Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.
Even when recited by various hosts of spirits and piśācas,
mantras do not succeed on their own if they are deficient in the prescribed ritual, nor among those who delight in impure conduct.
When joined with the prescribed ritual, even in impure states it bestows success;
therefore, one should not perform a mantra-deity rite devoid of the prescribed ritual.
Mantras accompanied by outflows (*sāśrava*) are accomplished when properly applied through ritual actions;
likewise, the noble mantras spoken by the Buddhas are to be accomplished.
Their accomplishment is declared to be well-established within the paths themselves—the Noble Eightfold Path, which is properly integrated with the Four Truths.
This [practice] is always to be honored in the fourth dhyāna; the four [limbs] are based on conduct. However, the preeminent mantras taught by the Buddha are distinguished as supreme.
Indeed, the nature of mantras, as taught by the ritual rules, is an inexpressible essence, possessing the same nature as the voidness of space; so too is that of the Noble Ones of great majesty.
O dwellers of heaven, listen as I shall describe the methods for the vidyās, which have been prescribed according to rule but are devoid of the path to supernatural powers (siddhi).

The divine mantras are accomplished through the path of the ten courses of action, through virtue, and through well-spoken words, by means of ritual action performed according to the prescribed rules.
Thus [ends the preceding section].
Now begins the twenty-second detailed chapter.
Then the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
O Mañjuśrī!
In the detailed exposition of your *Mūlakalpa*, there exists a chapter titled "The Instruction on the Knowledge of the Signs and Cries of All Beings. This I shall now speak.

Listen to that which, once known, will enable all beings engaged in the application of the practice of all mantras to discern the proper and improper time for all mantras. Listen well and attend to it thoroughly with your mind.
I shall speak.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and placed his right knee upon the ground. Bowing with palms joined toward the lion throne of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, he circumambulated the Blessed One three times, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and addressed the Blessed One as follows: "It would be well, Blessed One, if you would explain that instruction on the knowledge of the cries of all beings for the benefit of all sentient beings."
That shall serve as the requisite for the observances of all times for those who have entered into the practice of all mantras, for the sake of the signs of accomplishment;
now, O Blessed One, do what you deem appropriate.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni gave his approval to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you consider it necessary to question the Tathāgata on this matter."
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, listen; I shall explain.
When this had been said, Mañjuśrī prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, rose up, and sat down to listen to the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having surveyed the entire assembly, entered the samādhi called "The Incitement by the Sounds of All Beings.

Immediately upon the Blessed One’s entry into that state, whatever beings were dwelling in the infinite and boundless world-systems, they were all illuminated by the Buddha’s rays; and having bowed their heads to all those Blessed Buddhas and paid homage to them while remaining in those infinite and boundless world-systems, they approached the lion throne situated above the Śuddhāvāsa palace of the Blessed Śākyamuni.
And he established himself in that world-system Asahā.
Standing there, all the hosts of beings, through the power of the Buddha, manifested their own respective voices and approached the presence of the Blessed One’s feet to hear the Dharma.
Having bowed to and honored the Blessed One, they sat down in their respective places to hear the Dharma.

In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Son of the King of the Śākyas, instructed, inspired, and gladdened those beings with a discourse that was to be remembered. He gave such a teaching of the Dharma to all those lords of spirits and gods that some among them conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; some for the state of a pratyekabuddha; some for the state of a śrāvaka; some perceived the truths; some realized arhatship; and some, having established themselves in the ten paths of wholesome action, made their vows.

"May we serve infinite Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, throughout infinite millions of eons, providing them with attendance, medicinal requisites for the sick, robes, alms-food, bedding, seats, and personal belongings; and may we become certain in our attainment of the enlightenment of a Buddha."

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having understood the disposition of those beings, spoke the mantra called "Supernatural Knowledge of the Sounds of All Beings. By accomplishing this, all bodhisattvas and all beings shall understand the speech [of others] in a single moment, according to the respective positions in which all those beings are situated.
And what is that?
Homage to all Buddhas, whose teachings are unimpeded, who abide everywhere without limit, and who possess great compassion.
Oṃ, homage to the All-Knowing One, svāhā!
The ritual procedure for this is as follows:
first, having gone to a great forest, subsisting on a diet of milk and barley-gruel, or roots, fruits, and vegetables, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Bathing three times a day and wearing garments of bark, all other rules should be performed as previously prescribed.
Just as it is in the mantra-tantras arising from the Tathāgata family,
so too, having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) until the end of one hundred thousand recitations of the syllables, one should begin the actual practice (*sādhana*) right there,
even without a painted cloth (*paṭa*).

Having prepared a fire-pit measuring two cubits in depth and four cubits in width, square on all sides, and having offered an *arghya* oblation with all kinds of flowers and fruits, one should sit facing east upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass. Having kindled a new fire and ignited it with wood from milk-producing trees, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *bilva* fruits smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. This should be performed at the three junctions of the day for twenty-one days.

Then, having created a great radiance in the eastern direction, the Buddha, the Blessed One, approaches. He then touches the crown of the practitioner’s head. If the practitioner is not touched, at that very moment a voice issues forth from the Blessed One: "You have attained success; go as you wish. Having said this, he vanishes.
The twenty-second chapter.

From that time forward, the practitioner becomes possessed of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), endowed with a divine form of great power, following the conduct of a Bodhisattva, appearing as one sixteen years of age, moving according to his will, and knowing the cries of all beings; in a mere single instant, he understands the speech of all beings and becomes powerful, able to go wherever he desires.
He lives for five thousand years.
The Bodhisattva becomes irreversible.

Through twenty entries into the means of accomplishment, one certainly succeeds; therefore, no doubt should be entertained here. Even for one who has already achieved success, listen now to [the rules] regarding the recitation of the mantra—at the beginning, at the end, and in the middle.
The knowledge of sounds, their power, and their very nature are proclaimed among the dwellers of heaven— at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.
What was spoken is recited in the world, and it is celebrated in the Middle Country;
[the dialects of] Māgadha are in the Maṅga countries, and those of the best of men are in the city of Kāśi.
Just as among the people in the midst of Vṛji, Kośala,
and Malla, so did all those kings of gods choose the mantras according to their own nature.
O Vatsa, behold how Tridaśa is in Madhyadeśa and Daśārṇava in the Anta;
as it is with speech, so it is with regions.
Likewise, such speech was uttered everywhere among all the thirty gods;
and the Yāmas, the chief deities, were fashioned along with their created forms.
Then the speech uttered by the speakers, which moves through the meaning of the Middle Country,
was likewise for all those in Akaniṣṭha who possess great supernatural power.
All those excellent gods, endowed with the form realm, subsisting on the food of meditative concentration and serene, spoke these words at one time.
She possesses the intellect of Brahmā and Īśvara; her voice is like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, a resonance of sweet syllables, and a sound like that of the intoxicated cuckoo.
Whatever meaning may be conveyed by speech endowed with courage and profundity,
it is likewise honored in every way through a sidelong glance.
Those gods always reside in the Middle Country;
they are eloquent, endowed with sweet syllables, and possess smooth, deep voices.
In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, this thundering of clouds is their speech; one should observe it thus:
just as mortals in the Middle Country are honored, so too are those in Avanti.
One should likewise know the Mistress of the Gods as being perfect in speech;
for by means of speech, she is made manifest even among those who are formless and born of the sphere of the infinite consciousness.
Due to the absence of their basis, the gods did not attain [the status of] speakers of speech;
all the most excellent gods [reside] in the Middle Country,
for this speech proceeds from those who possess the consciousness of the meaning of the Middle Country.
Then there were the gods and likewise the yakṣas of great power upon the earth;
as well as many hosts of beings belonging to the divine classes,
such as the Karoṭapāṇi gods, who are ever-intoxicated, and the Vīṇakas.

The four great kings are also supported by the four modes of birth; the thirty gods, the leaders of the deities, are likewise supported together with Śakra. Furthermore, the Suyāmas are everywhere above, and they too are of beautiful form.
This speech is indeed proclaimed as the most excellent among all the hosts of gods;
just as mortals in the Middle Country are of low, superior, or middling [status],
so too is the speech of the gods of low, superior, or middling [quality].
Speech should be known as threefold: inferior, superior, and middling;
it should be known as threefold according to action: inferior, superior, and middling.
Likewise, speech in the temple should be sweet and victorious through well-spoken words.
One should apply the *ruta*, *mata*, and likewise the *jñeya* to the very acts [of recitation]. The speech of the Asuras is always that which originates from Gauḍa and Pauṇḍra;
just as the speech of the best among the Gauḍa people is adorned with sound (*śabda*).
Likewise, O best of the Daitya hosts, one should also employ the *ruta* (vocalization) for them;
and for those Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Nāgas, including the Pūtanas, who are wandering about on all sides, one should employ the *purojava* (fore-runner).
The twenty-second chapter of the extensive [tantra], concerning all those on the side of the asuras who dwell along the banks of the Vaṅga and Sāma rivers;
and [concerning] Harikele, Kalaśamukhya, and Carmaraṅga in their entirety.
One should likewise arrange them for all the regions;
one must not separate them from those three types as they have been specified. And one should always proclaim this for the gods and for those who go before them.
The presiding lords of the hosts of pretas and yakṣas, the Mothers, the Kinnaras,
and the Nāgas— listen at all times to what is spoken according to their words,
as it is in Lāḍa and Odra, in Sindh, and likewise in the north.
Indeed, one should employ that [speech] among all people everywhere;
for just as the speech of the Nāgas is called *lāḍī* by the wise,
so too is the speech of the Yakṣas for those men who dwell in the northern direction.

Just as it is proclaimed for the Garuḍas in the ocean and for the Kinnaras, so too is that speech heard everywhere in Nepal; understand it to be such. Likewise, it is the speech of the Pūtanās and of the women who dwell in the womb of the Vindhya mountains.
The speech of humans born in the Vindhya mountains and of the mlecchas is known as that of the pūtanas; this is the speech proclaimed for them.
The best of gods chose that which is the speech of the rākṣasas.
Having created the southern regions, they are celebrated among the Andhras and Lāṭas;
however, the speech of all the Draviḍas always abounds in the sound of the letter *ḍa*. Observing that [speech] through its vocal characteristics, one should assign it specifically to the Rākṣasas.
Likewise, the ancestral origins of the Rākṣasas should be known to be of three kinds;
this speech is indeed of three kinds, and one should employ it in a threefold manner. All things should be known as being of three types, and those regional dialects are likewise threefold.
One should likewise apply the threefold action and the three regions;
it should be known as threefold in every respect, for action is traditionally said to be threefold. One should employ another method there, which is equal toward all.

Various hosts of spirits have been described, dwelling upon various parts of the earth. In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, humans are said to be diverse, possessing knowledge of many languages, adorned with various treatises,
and speaking in various tongues among one another.

The doctrines of various scriptures are to be known; they possess the meanings of various mantras, they provide instruction on various rites, and various accomplishments (siddhi) are liberated [therein]. When mortals who are possessed arrive at the vessel and the place.
And for them, well-joined by means of mantras applied according to the ritual rules,
one should cause the deities who have arrived upon the earth to appear through speech alone;
one should then employ the *liṅga*, the object, the vessel, and the deity itself.
One should observe the manifestations of those possessed by deities for the sake of the highest good and for prosperity;
they are characterized by various regional customs, the emergence of various languages,
the engagement in various activities and purposes, and various physical marks.
Those whose speech outside of the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa) is unstable should clearly be known as men who are devoted to the languages of the Mlecchas;
they are cruel, terrible Rākṣasas who practice the most fierce of deeds.
Speech abounding in the sound *ḍa* and indistinct with the sound *la* is the manner of the Mārṣas;
just as the speech of those from the South is fickle and censured,
so too has this speech been described among these Rākṣasas.

Jyeṣṭhā, who cries out in many ways, possesses those intent on the three-fold recitation; she is swiftly drawn by practitioners or comes here of her own accord. Together with the grahas, these Mothers and gods seize sentient beings in many ways.
Garuḍas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, as well as piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas—
listen now as the signs of those possessed by yakṣas and pūtanas are being described.
There are flesh-eating piśācas who speak the tongues of barbarians and those who speak indistinctly.
Speech abounding in the letter *la*, while *pūtanā* ends with the letter *ḍa*;
their gaze directed upward is employed in these rites.
The twenty-second chapter.

Those who are stingy, cruel by nature, and delight in falsehood and impurity—their vision does not ascend; for their sight does not reach upward. Likewise, the speech of mothers is endowed with auspicious meaning.
The speech of the planets and the foremost of the Kumāras is absolute;
through speech endowed with the perfection of auspicious limbs, one is joined with the goals to be realized in childhood,
which is the highest excellence of power in every respect among all the inhabitants of heaven.
One should observe the speech of those possessed by the Garuḍas:
it should be known as equal to the sound "ga," appearing like the language of the Mlecchas;
it is indistinct yet clearly manifest, accompanied by renown, and the source of auspiciousness.
"O Suparṇin, protect me!"—this [mantra] wards off the pride of poison.
For their various origins, their various combinations with elemental beings, and their various colors are to be known; one should identify them by their various characteristics.
Shubhākara, Abhākara, and Abhāsanta, who dwell upon the serpent-king’s foot;
Vāsuki and the other Nāgas, righteous on the surface of the earth;
and the lords of the Uragas, dwelling there, endowed with swift speech.
One should identify each being according to their respective body and according to the specific mark by which they are characterized;
one should designate each being by that very mark.
For all those who have fallen into base views are said to be defiled.
One should understand that those who possess various marks are to be known as belonging to various classes of beings;
they are to be recognized as having various effects through their actions performed while situated in various bodies.
Indeed, there are many such types who speak with manifold characteristics.
The signs of mortals on earth who are possessed by various beings through actions performed with diverse intellects and who have taken refuge in various wombs are indeed always declared;
they indicate the speech and purpose of both gods and asuras.
[The text provided consists solely of two vertical bars (||), which in this context functions as a section break or a marker for the end of a chapter. [End of Section]
In that very same way, one should quickly apply it; when the earth has attained the state of humanity, one should then perceive the gods with a perfectly serene mind.
They look upward and in all directions,
undaunted in mind and free from agitation, joyful and endowed with beautiful forms.
With pure eyes and unblinking eyes, with glossy complexions and glossy faces,
all those foremost of gods appeared as if they were possessed of serene glances.
It should be known that some are seated upon a cross-legged posture on pure ground,
while others, having emerged from their garments, are seated as sky-goers.
The gods beginning with Brahmā are said to be absorbed in the joy of meditative concentration;
above that, in the realm of the most excellent, dwell those possessed of form and manifold forms.
Drawn by those mantras through the power of the mantra-born ones, their radiant splendor assumes a form; I shall transform that which is their support.
Absorbed in the joy of meditative concentration, their faces always bear gentle smiles; with pure and wide eyes, they constantly abide in sublime forms.
Then those gods, who possess supreme knowledge and are endowed with splendor, glory, and beauty, should instruct him.
Seated cross-legged and constantly meditating like a seer, they understand that possession through their intellect as the means for accomplishing their desired goal.
One should employ this for the welfare of all mantras as the most excellent means;
O lords of the gods, understand that everything has been thus explained.
For these have been described by the seer; they are restrained and established as seers.
Thus, the signs of those possessed by the seers have been recounted by me.
The gods have their gaze directed upwards; the *kaśmala* spirits stand with feet upturned; the *vikṛta* beings are of fierce form; and the *rākṣasas* have their hair standing erect.
Thus it was for the Mothers; for whom indeed was this seen?
The flesh-eaters stood naked, yet having attained immobility, they remained clothed.
Other malevolent spirits with feet turned upward, known as Vikṛtas, and those with hair standing erect,
roamed everywhere across the entire earth, including the banks of the rivers.

The twenty-second chapter: [The rites] at a solitary tree, in a cremation ground, at a single *liṅga*, on a sandbank, in temples, on roads, in the valleys of the Vindhya mountains, and on mountain peaks.
And even the mountain peak of Himādri, along with the abodes of Mlecchas and thieves, was drawn there by the power of the mantra; having assumed deformed shapes, they arrived.
They quickly seize those living beings who are averse to purity and right conduct;
out of fear, they may go throughout the entire earth, deluded by the search for food.
In the world, they seize [beings] in many ways, resorting to many diseases;
they possess various transformed forms and wear diverse guises.
They quickly seize the corpses and the urine-sleeping beings of living creatures; their characteristics have been described and their conduct has been clearly explained.
The previously described signs of those possessed among human beings on this earth have not been clearly perceived; however, such signs are indeed observed among humans.
O best of gods, understand that these stable types are found everywhere; thus have the signs of men possessed on this earth been described.
He gazes constantly with affection, his eyes never blinking; though he is among human beings on this earth, he is not afflicted by their nature, for he is the most excellent of gods.
He has reached the state of a bull among men, who possesses speech adorned with a multitude of words and meanings, and who is established in the Dharma conducive to the highest good.
The foremost among the best of gods has gone; he should be known as the achiever of all aims.
That which was contemplated by the reciter has entered the abode of the intellect.
One should quickly awaken all that which has been thought by the practitioner;
this is correctly explained as the excellent divine possession.
Even those who are without consciousness are always drawn to the earth by mantras;
yet the gods, being in haste, do not offer sacrifices nor speak sweet words.
Deprived of their excellence and rendered helpless, they remained observing silence;
there was nothing from them in speech, nor in thought, nor even in pride.
Therefore, the reciter should not draw that [person] in;
he should turn away from them, for even those mantras born of the Victor are incapable of accomplishing such a task.
There is nothing that cannot be attracted for those who are devoted to the meaning of the recited mantras;
likewise, noble beings are attracted by noble mantras when applied with proper method.
The marks belonging to the noble ones, which arise from the disciples of Khaṅgī—
those high-souled Bodhisattvas who abide on the ten stages.
Likewise, they are drawn forth by mantras and well-adorned with commitments (samayas), as well as by great ḍākinīs and uṣṇīṣas properly joined with the syllables of the Sage.
By the wise sons of the Buddha, born from the families of the Lotus and the Vajra, who are the foremost of mantra-holders and possess the great supernatural powers of the Kings of Wrath;
Neither other worldly mantra-kings of great supernatural power are capable, nor those who know the pledges (samaya), nor even the supreme Lord of Mantras.
To describe it, to calculate it, or even to go to that place where they always abide— equal [to one another]— the cause for their movement is the accumulation of karma.
Indeed, their cause is drawn forth by karma,
and their continuum is drawn forth at the proper time by the words spoken by the Buddhas.
Therefore, one should not disturb them with effort, nor should one vainly engage them for the sake of wealth;
those great-souled ones possess great supernatural power and are established upon the ten stages.
Indeed, all the mantras were then unable to go where those Tathāgatas were; thus, O you who are honored by the immortals, do you remember my command.
Then all those who know the mantra for the purpose of reciting it shall come; there will be signs of those who have been summoned, whether they be human or non-human.
Steadfast, with a lustrous complexion, and a skillful expounder of profound meaning—
one who has attained steadfastness and depth— will then have little perspiration.
The eminent knower of mantras, whose mind was unshakeable, being questioned,
bound his own seal upon the firmament in the direction of Suvidhi.
The twenty-second chapter: He who knows other beings is indeed supreme, the teacher of the true meaning of the nature of phenomena;
he is established in right conduct and filled with the joy of happiness, his mind permeated with compassion.
Possessing great enthusiasm and firm resolve, and teaching the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma,
he may enter a human body for even a moment or a brief instant.
Possessing many forms and beautiful form, he stands aloft in the vault of the sky;
his vision is directed toward the Buddha and the Dharma, and he holds reverence for the Saṅgha as well.
Then, for a mere moment, that great-souled one, true to his promise, having conquered anger and destroyed the three humors, remained assuming a human body.
First they should be known as bound, and later they are employed by humans; then, having been dragged and released again, they go wherever they please.
Stiff, with motionless eyes and likewise white in complexion, he was then possessed by the Aṅgaketu, possessing a voice that was steady, deep, and beautiful.
Extremely serene and possessing a massive body, he stands upon the surface of the earth,
seated in the paryanka posture, his mind filled with compassion.
That mudrā, joined with the lotus, was entered by the Great Being,
the Sage Avalokita, the most excellent Bodhisattva of great supernatural power.
Having come to the worlds of his own will for the sake of affection toward sentient beings, he— who is endowed with the supreme cause of fearlessness and established in the highest vision—
beholds the practitioner with a gaze and a mind permeated by compassion.

With faces graced by gentle smiles, some gods and the great being— the high-souled one who acts for the welfare of sentient beings— should be perceived as looking upon him with a serene form from every side, adorned with the creeper-like brows.
The fierce Bodhisattva Vajradhara, the foremost one of great supernatural power,
has entered all those who are cruel; he should be perceived as having eyes that are red at the corners and wide, with a form possessing the luster of a blue lotus, slightly visible upon his body.
Then, while touching the vajra, he binds the mudrā of his own self;

being pleased, the great-souled one, the granter of boons, who is dark in color, appears instantly before mortals and always causes them to obtain enjoyments. Thus it is said in the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa.
Then he spoke these words, smooth and profound:
"For what purpose do you ask? We shall grant you this supreme boon of action upon the earth.
To the wielder of the thunderbolt, the lotus-born one, and the Victor, he said: "The sight of the Victors is never in vain."

When the mantras, which are bestowers of boons and possess radiance, grant their fruit at those respective times, there shall be the arrival of the Jina there; for these colors have been declared according to the convention as manifesting upon the earth among human beings.
For from the Tathāgata as the basis, the emanation is said to arise from the cause of the fruit; it is called a reflection, yet the reflection is not the emanation brought forth,
just as no reflected image exists between the original form and the emanation.
He has the color of the filaments of a lotus, the hue of gold, and great splendor;
he shines like split yellow orpiment and rivals the brilliance of saffron, possessing a radiance equal to the rising sun or the *karṇikāra* flower.
Such a voice exists within the reflection, resting upon the reflection of a Buddha— a Brahma-like sound, free from noise, with the melodic resonance of a kalaviṅka bird;
it is employed through the application of logic for the welfare of all beings.
Having seen such characteristics, living beings call him a Buddha;
their lineage and ritual procedure are then those of the Vajra and Lotus families.
For worldly mantras, however, one should employ the Lord of Mantras.
Having then applied all that was previously stated, which was adorned with many introductory topics, the minister should thoroughly engage in the mantras;
he should learn the single abode of the ṛṣis as well as that of the Garuḍas.
One should employ that [mantra] of the ministers with its own characteristic mark (*svaliṅga*) and through speech;
then, this [mantra] which possesses many marks (*bahuliṅga*) and also its own characteristic mark (*svaliṅga*) shall accomplish [the goal].
Those which are sealed with their own mudrās are known as *vyantara*.
All the manifestations of possession have been explained; one's own face is difficult for others to behold.
This is the twenty-second detailed chapter;
one should apply this sequence of time to both yoga and possession.

The mantra-practitioner should ward off [obstacles] with seals of great power and with mantras as well; he should employ them on all sides once they have been merely recited. However, one who always practices otherwise than this by means of other mantras [will fail].
Then, having protected that vessel with mantras of great supernatural power,
and always with hosts of Dṛtis and messengers, as well as groups of male and female servants, one should summon the other worldly deities who possess great supernatural power.
O King of Yakṣas, at that very moment, the mantra-practitioner shall summon all the various yakṣiṇīs of great supernatural power by means of his mind, whatever he desires;
other mantras are not to be abandoned, nor are other hosts of deities ever to be sought.
But those who have come of their own accord at the proper time, one should employ them;
all these mantras bring about success and accomplish every purpose. Therefore, one should not perform other rites, nor should one avoid the state of possession (*āveśa*).
The gods of great supernatural power—divine and noble ones born of the earth—are summoned;
yet if they are engaged in a trivial matter, a violation of the samaya occurs.
Then Takṣaka gazes fixedly, and Vāsuki dances.
The great nāga Karkoṭaka, Mucilinda, Yaśasvin,
Śaṅkhapāla, Durlakṣa, and other lords of serpents danced;
then Śaṅkhapāla, Śaṅkha, Maṇināga, and Kṛṣṇila.
They wander swiftly across the ocean and fall down again and again;
like serpents, they hiss, their arrogance fueled by poison.
O best of Nagas, understand that these various beings among them are destined for the end.
Some are thrilled as they meditate, some remain motionless,
and some fall quickly with their limbs restored; with hair standing on end, they fall in various forms and indeed perform what they have heard.
Infinite [beings] wander swiftly like lotuses upon trembling water;

infinite are those born from the womb of the *nāgas*, whose numbers are enumerated in the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa* as previously described by word; this great teaching concerns those bitten and possessed by venom.
The wise one should release [the victim] with the mantra of the Wrathful King using the vajra-weapon;
he should bring them to an end by means of that very mantra, for the mantras specified here as "winged" are destroyers of calamities.

Those mantras should always be applied in every way to those bitten by venomous creatures and those possessed; likewise, one should employ the remaining mantras for obstacles and those joined with planetary afflictions.
By means of those very [mantras], one should perform the rite against the Grahas, Mātṛs, and Pūtanas.
These signs are innumerable among beings who have been bitten or possessed;
one should employ the various worldly mantras for those respective rites.
Thus has been described in its entirety the characteristic of being bitten or possessed.

Now I shall awaken [them] with speech common to both animals and humans; listen as I speak the language of the denizens of hell. When all the flocks of birds have assembled from every side, [I shall speak].

Then they made their dwelling in the village at midday in the abode of people; then they spoke words joined with the sound *repha*, which was terrifying. Those who speak cruelly, like crows, say "krakaḥ" for the letter *ka*.
They speak of fear there, and one should show hunger as well;
when peacocks and cuckoos cry out at dawn, they indicate a cruel voice and announce fear in that place.
Bucchakṣā spoke thus: "One should always prepare food;
when she is seen in all the villages, then they speak those terrifying and fearful words."
Within six months, the excellent domestic food of those in the region will perish;
they should be given milk that is like nectar and water that brings about happiness,
as well as chief birds such as śārikās, parrots, and pigeons.
The cakravākas and bhāsasvakīkas all come to Mālaya;
for when they, situated in the midst of the village, perform the Mālaya rite, this is the twenty-second chapter of the extensive [tantra].
Then they speak thus: "The cause of this great famine is drought, as well as disease, the onset of many illnesses,
spider-bites, boils, and the prevalence of great bandits."
"May you understand, indeed, that after six months, when all the flocks of birds have acted with extreme cruelty and great ferocity."
Then, while [the deity] was weeping, it was announced to all beings;
at that very time, one should apply oneself there to the path as it truly exists.
When those who speak the human language, abounding in the sound of the letter *da*,
come to this village dwelling and speak of him just as it is;
Having performed a rite for well-being at night,
one should depart from that place when the birds begin to cry out with sweet-sounding notes.
Therefore, one should announce that there will be abundance of food and good health, saying:
"When you go to the south, may the deer go before you."
Those [omens] indicate abundant success, as do the deer;
however, those that constantly dwell with dogs and jackals portend death.
The wise one, having been warned by the jackals, should not go there;
he should quickly enter his own abode. He then related that to you.
Those extremely fierce [beings] shall cry out;
the mantra-practitioner should then cause them to run ahead and proceed instantly, if he desires his own success.
If a jackal goes from left to right as one is traveling,
one should know that it is a successful journey, as indicated by the jackal.
The blue jays and all other birds, as well as the wild animals including jackals, deer, rabbits, and various species of the animal kingdom.
And when they performed a circumambulation, he said to them all: "Go; you shall become worthy of worship and possess abundant great siddhi."
In the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, it is said: "Indeed, all these—snakes, beasts of prey, and the like—are inauspicious;
if they are seen on the path, one should go elsewhere, wherever that may be."
They all said this: "There is no success;
turn back! Go to your own abodes; remain at ease in your own homes."
One who knows the mantras should not go there when it has been announced by the serpents;
if he should go, then there will be either terror or death.
Various living beings belonging to the animal realm— those dwelling in water, those moving on land, and both the stationary and the mobile— proclaim what is auspicious and inauspicious.
One should know that fear arises from contrary signs, while those who have attained a state of well-being perceive things as they are;
at that time, some among the animals became divine, and humans spoke the language of the gods.
One should employ that very speech which one intends to communicate;
by its own characteristic signs, it always indicates well-being, and even when harsh, it indicates great terror.
Then, for the sake of certain determination, the knower of mantras should apply his intellect to the various signs observed in many ways, as they reside in various wombs.
"Likewise, the speech of humans is joined with such words as speak of the middle meaning; for it is in the Middle Country that speech is expressed through both words and their referents."

They say that speech which is human is [the standard], while any other speech is that of the barbarians (mleccha); it should be understood that the speech taught in the Middle Country (madhyadeśa) is authoritative everywhere.
It is composed of sweet syllables, heart-pleasing, bringing delight to the ears,
free from faults, born of the mind, and speaks with undistracted meaning.
That which is known as human speech and its sounds is [proper] by its very nature;
all others are entirely harmful, and that speech is the language of barbarians.
Having described the human [sacrifice] or others, the sacrifice of animals is now being discussed here:
even a lion, having seized a region, would always go toward a preeminent city.
One should very swiftly and forcefully uproot that most dreadful tree;
indeed, the king of beasts cries out piteously and speaks in a state of wretchedness.
The twenty-second chapter:
One should then know that there will be great fear and a total inundation of all lands when the sound of a "king of beasts" is heard within the great city.
One should know that there will be great fear in the west, a desire for peace in the south, and the arrival of an enemy kingdom in the east.
If it occurs in the north, there will be a terrible deluge due to excessive rain;
and in all intermediate directions, it shall announce danger everywhere.
By two or three roars it should be known that there is great danger in the three directions; this has been declared by Siṃha himself regarding all [directions] starting from the south.
Four, five, or seven are known as the sixth; they say that beyond eight it is fruitless, so one should employ [the mantras] accordingly.
Standing to the south, superior by virtue of the excellence of the site both below and above,
[he established] a sanctuary at the crossroads for the sake of the welfare of the vicinity.
One should avoid that place where there is a constant sound and depart from it;
as one would act toward a lion, so should one apply this conduct toward all living beings.
Listen now to how all those known as śarabhas and śārdūlas,
out of fear of the śarabhas, always abandoned the human habitation due to their lack of protection.
However, that most excellent goddess is proclaimed as the gracious knowledge;
one should likewise employ her everywhere among the Kroshtukas.
When an elephant cries out loudly in the eastern or western part [of the city],
one should know that there will be great danger for living beings in those regions.
If crows from a cremation ground, with their beaks turned upward, indeed cry out there,
one should know that great terror is signaled by those crows.
If, when the king has set out for his minister who desires a particular region,
a crow cries out most dreadfully from the left side as he travels, [it portends misfortune].
A wise person should not go there when it has been indicated by a crow; if it cries to the right, it portends prosperity, but if it cries in front, it should be avoided.
One who knows the mantras should not go there; if he goes, he will fall under the power of death.
When a bird cries while eating cow dung, it portends the arising of happiness.
In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, one should indicate that when a crow, having ascended a temple and remaining there constantly,
caws at midnight or at such a time, it portends the ruin of the house; likewise, when that crow, having ascended a heap of grain, caws.
If it warbles very beautifully and speaks sweetly and quickly,
one should know that before long there will be the acquisition of abundant grain and wealth in many ways.
When one sees a crow cawing loudly at the door of a house, there will be an attack with weapons by thieves upon that person during the night.

If the best [mark] is on a milk-tree, one is fond of quarrels; if on a thorny tree, one is dear to strife; being mounted upon the shoulder of an elephant is auspicious, as is being upon the back of a horse.
Sovereignty rests upon the heads of the wealthy; prosperity dwells within lotus flowers;
and various kinds of riches possess the sweet warbling of melodious syllables.
That which was previously described as beneficial for all types of omens should be applied equally to all; one should employ the harsh cawing [of the crow] in the same manner.
Śivā is to be known as bestowing fruit from all sides, while to the south she is the giver of results;
all that is to be known from Siṃha, following Śiva at all times.
Cruel, with inauspicious sounds, wretched, and intent on death— [such omens portend] the non-attainment of happiness from all sides, as well as the failure of the fruit arising from the crops.
All these auspicious attendants of Śiva are said to be present at evening and dawn; if they are situated in the southern direction, they are known as the Ekāras.
The first is declared to be auspicious and most propitious; the second is proclaimed in the [second] watch;
likewise, in the third watch, it should be known that it brings wealth to the king.
In the fourth [year], there is great gain; in the fifth, she is said to bestow sons;
in the sixth, there is the acquisition of wealth; but in the seventh, it is not auspicious for one's existence.
One should know the eighth to be fruitless; thereafter, she is afflicted by fear.
Śivā acts thus there, and those [others] are also givers of misfortune beyond counting.
In the west, Śivā is to be known; at that time there will be fear of enemy armies. In the second [period], when there is a cruel king, there will be famine and wilderness.
The twenty-second chapter:
In the third [cry], there is the loss of wealth; in the fourth, the obstruction of life;
in the fifth cry that has been described, there are afflictions of disease for the ministers.
In the sixth [case], one should know there is the arrival of thieves; however, that [sixth] is auspicious in every respect.
In the seventh, there is a great disease, and in the eighth, it is censured.
If, after that, she speaks while terrified by fear, distressed, or hungry;
or if the northern howl of the jackal is always heard—
One should predict a most terrible disease in that place;
if there is a second harsh cry, then it will cause suffering.
In the third [year], there is loss of wealth; in the fourth, the occurrence of fire;
in the fifth, a great rain; and in the sixth, the king is seen to be deposed.
In the seventh [case], one should predict a great battle and a clash of weapons;
in the eighth, one should know it to be fruitless; and beyond that, whatever little one weeps.
When a jackal howls in the eastern direction during the final watch of the night, one should know that a king is approaching; however, at the second howl, it portends the arrival of shepherds.
In the third [month], death comes from the king, or it is heard that one has been imprisoned;
in the fourth, suffering arises from thieves; in the fifth, there is a threat to life.
In the sixth year, illness occurs; in the seventh, there is danger from fire;
in the eighth, one should know it to be fruitless; and for the remainder, it is always as previously described.
When the auspicious jackal howls in the south-eastern intermediate direction,
there will be happiness in the first watch of the night, and for all people in the second.
In the third [year] there is the production of wealth; in the fourth, an abundance of crops;
in the fifth, a proclamation of plenty; and in the sixth, one should predict security.
In the seventh [house], everything is to be known; in the eighth, it is always fruitless—provided that [the aspect] is always from the southern part, the western, or the middle.
It should be declared that [the asterism] Dhruvā is auspicious, while Śivā is remembered as most cruel;
by the first [lunar day] death occurs, and by the second, Brāhmaṇas are slain.
In the third [chapter] of the Gulakalpa, they say one may kill a Kṣatriya; in the fourth, a Vaiśya;
and in the fifth, those of Śūdra birth.
In the sixth [house], it destroys Mlecchas; in the seventh, thieves;
in the eighth, one should know it to be fruitless and bring great suffering to those who cry out cruelly.
When she cries out intensely in the northwestern direction, it is seen to portend the death of those who are beyond counting.
If a great disease is indicated very quickly, it portends illness for the king;
by the second [mark], the king's chief elephant, the best of tuskers, is slain.
By the third [sign], death is indeed ordained there;
by the fourth, death occurs for the chief lords of wealth.
In the fifth [year], there will be loss of wealth; in the sixth, the occurrence of disease;
and in the seventh, suffering and fear arising from all sides.
In the eighth [direction], one should know it to be fruitless; previously, indeed, it was so in all directions.
One should observe it in the north, between the east and the north, and likewise in the intermediate directions.
When a jackal howls very fiercely and swiftly,
one should observe it in the north, the east, the center, and likewise in the intermediate directions.
When a jackal howls very harshly and swiftly, then a living being is slain by death; even a leader of the people or a lord of wealth is destroyed.
By the second [digit] one kills a mother; by the third, one should predict a death by elephant;
by the fourth, those born of various wombs who live as barbarians or thieves.
In the fourth [period], there will be disease for all people at that time;
and in the fifth, a son or a minister of the king will be slain on earth.
In the sixth year, death is ordained for the lord of men by the Great Goddess;
in the seventh year, she shall destroy the kingdom and should also be declared as liberated.
One should know that on the eighth [tithi] it is always fruitless, as previously described; likewise, when it occurs during the night of the Śivas.
The twenty-second chapter:
One should know that to be a non-human spirit causing great calamity;
having departed from there, one should go away, or else provide protection with mantras.

One should perform the fire-offering rites (*homakarman*) with those renowned for their great power who are born from the lotus-family of the Victors (*jina*); therein one should prescribe pacification (*śānti*).
For there are indeed many such species of animals described at length.
Understand also the various flocks of birds and their cries;
some among the animals are of many kinds, born from the forms of plants or from excrement and urine,
while others have deformed shapes, being fierce beings who cause harm to living creatures.
Some roam the surface of the earth seeking to obstruct the life-breath of beings; some, delighting in drinking blood, wander across the earth;
others roam the surface of the earth by the scent of blood.
These various Mothers are indeed the chief of the Grahas, yet they are foolish.
The various supreme grahas, appearing in the forms of boys and girls,
roam everywhere across the entire earth in a mere instant.
Some roam for a thousand yojanas like the wind;
others take the form of animals; and some cause the destruction of living beings by their mere sight—thus they perform various deeds everywhere upon the surface of the earth.

Some [spirits] move among all humans in the world for the sake of offerings and garlands— among beings who are dead or deceased, those who are asleep, those who are struck down, and likewise those who are fighting; some [move] from the surface of the sky.

Those who know all forms should be understood as possessing many shapes and being subject to transformation; they should be known through their signs in every respect as being both auspicious and inauspicious.
All the fruits of the auspicious and inauspicious, as well as deformities and virtuous deeds, are to be known through various scriptures marked by the true meaning of worldly reality.
Always [attended] by sages, sons of the Victors, sword-wielding ones, supreme Jinas,
and Śrāvakas of great supernatural power— all established in various wombs—
